This can display configuration values available to Git in the current context. When you are inside a repository, values from applicable configuration levels may be available.
Important: If a local configuration defines the same setting as a global configuration, Git can use the repository-specific local value for that repository.
Where Does Local Configuration Belong?
Local Git configuration is associated with the specific repository. This is one reason local configuration requires you to be inside a Git repository when setting repository-level values.
My-Project │ ├── .git │ │ │ └── Repository-specific Git information │ ├── index.html └── style.css
You will learn more about the repository structure and the .git folder as you continue practicing Git.
Important Scenario
Suppose your global configuration is:
user.name = Nethaji Nani
Inside one repository, you configure:
git config user.name "Company Developer"
The result is:
Outside that specific repository ↓ Global value available → Nethaji Nani Inside that repository ↓ Local value takes precedence → Company Developer
The global setting has not disappeared. The local setting only changes which value Git uses for that particular repository.
Common Beginner Mistake
Suppose you want to change the username only for one repository but accidentally run:
git config --global user.name "New Name"
This changes your global default, which can affect other repositories that use that global value.
For a repository-specific change, go inside that repository and use:
git config user.name "New Name"
Remember: Use --global when you want a user-level default. Do not use --global when you specifically want to configure only the current repository.
Important Commands

CommandPurpose
git config --global user.name "Name"Set global username
git config --global user.email "email"Set global email
git config user.name "Name"Set username for the current repository
git config user.email "email"Set email for the current repository
git config --global --listView global configuration
git config --local --listView local configuration
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
GLOBAL → Whole computer user → Default configuration → Uses --global LOCAL → One repository → Repository-specific configuration → Local value can override global → Configure inside repository

One-Line Definition: Global Git configuration provides user-level default settings for repositories on your computer, while local Git configuration applies only to a specific repository and can override the global setting within that repository.
practice: For now, first check the global configuration you already created in Topics 11 and 12.
STEP 1 → Open Terminal ↓ STEP 2 → Run the command below ↓ STEP 3 → Check your global username and email
git config --global --list
You should find values similar to:
user.name=Your Name user.email=your-email@example.com

Optional local configuration practice: You need to be inside a Git repository before creating local settings. Since we have not yet learned git init, you can wait until the repository topics and then practice this again.
Later Practice Create Git Repository ↓ Configure Global user.name ↓ Configure Local user.name ↓ Compare the values ↓ Understand which value Git uses
Practice Goal: Understand that Global = default for your Git user on the computer and Local = specific to one repository and can take precedence there.

qna.q: Q1. What is Global Git Configuration?
qna.a: Global Git configuration contains user-level settings on your computer that normally act as default values for repositories.

qna.q: Q2. What is Local Git Configuration?
qna.a: Local Git configuration contains settings that apply specifically to one Git repository.

qna.q: Q3. Which configuration takes precedence when both global and local settings define the same value?
qna.a: The local repository configuration takes precedence for that specific repository.

qna.q: Q4. Which option is used to set a global configuration?
qna.a: The --global option is used, for example: git config --global user.name "Your Name".

qna.q: Q5. How do you configure a username only for the current repository?
qna.a: Go inside the Git repository and run: git config user.name "Your Name" without --global.

qna.q: Q6. If you change the local user.name in one repository, does it change the global user.name?
qna.a: No. The local setting belongs to that specific repository. The global setting remains unchanged.

qna.q: Q7. How can you view global configuration values?
qna.a: Use git config --global --list.

qna.q: Q8. How can you view local configuration values?
qna.a: Inside a Git repository, use git config --local --list.

qna.q: Q9. If a repository has no local user.name, which value can Git use as the default?
qna.a: Git can use the configured global user.name as the default.

items.title: Initialize a Git Repository (git init)
explanation: Simple Meaning
The command git init initializes a folder as a Git repository.
Before initialization, a normal project folder is simply a collection of files. After running git init, Git starts managing that folder as a repository and can track its history.
Normal Project Folder ↓ git init ↓ Git Repository ↓ Git can start tracking changes
Simple Rule: Use git init once to turn an existing or new project folder into a Git repository.
Before and After git init
Suppose you have a website project:
My-Website │ ├── index.html ├── style.css └── script.js
Initially, this is just a normal folder. Git is not yet tracking it as a repository.
Now open the terminal inside the folder and run:
git init
Git initializes the repository.
My-Website │ ├── .git ├── index.html ├── style.css └── script.js
The .git folder is created and contains Git's repository information and history data.
Basic Steps
STEP 1 → Create or choose a project folder ↓ STEP 2 → Open Terminal ↓ STEP 3 → Move into the project folder ↓ STEP 4 → Run git init ↓ STEP 5 → Git repository initialized ✅
Example Using Windows Terminal
Suppose your project folder is called My-Website.
Desktop │ └── My-Website ├── index.html └── style.css
First, move into the project folder:
cd Desktop cd My-Website
Then check your current location:
pwd
Now initialize Git:
git init
Git creates the repository metadata inside that folder.
What Happens When You Run git init?
The command does not automatically create commits or upload anything to GitHub.
It mainly prepares the current folder for Git version control.
Run: git init ↓ Git repository initialized ↓ .git folder created ↓ Git metadata can be stored ↓ Your project files are ready for Git tracking
Important: git init Does NOT Automatically Track Every File
After running git init, your files are not automatically committed.
Create Files ↓ index.html style.css script.js ↓ git init ↓ Repository initialized ↓ Files are NOT automatically committed ❌
You will later choose files or changes to stage using git add, and then save them in Git history using git commit.
git init ↓ Initialize Repository Then ↓ git add ↓ Stage Changes Then ↓ git commit ↓ Create Commit
Important: git init Does NOT Create a GitHub Repository
Git and GitHub are different. Running git init creates a local Git repository on your computer.
git init ↓ Local Repository Created ↓ Stored on Your Computer
It does not automatically create a repository on GitHub and does not require an internet connection.
git init │ ├── Creates local Git repository ✅ ├── Does not create GitHub repository ❌ └── Does not require internet ❌
Where Should You Run git init?
You should normally run git init inside the main folder of the project you want Git to manage.
For example:
My-Website ← Run git init here │ ├── index.html ├── css │ └── style.css └── js └── script.js
By initializing the main project folder, Git can manage the project structure below it.
Common Beginner Mistake: Running git init in the Wrong Folder
Suppose you accidentally run git init inside your Desktop instead of inside My-Website.
Desktop ← Git initialized here ❌ │ ├── My-Website ├── Other-Project ├── Photos └── Documents
Git may then treat the Desktop folder and its contents as part of that repository structure. Therefore, always check your current location before running git init.
Important Habit: Before running git init, confirm that your terminal is inside the correct project folder.
How Can You Check Your Current Folder?
Before initialization, you can check where your terminal is currently located.
In PowerShell, a prompt may already show your current location:
PS C:\Users\YourName\Desktop\My-Website>
This indicates that commands are currently being run inside the My-Website folder.
Terminal Location C:\Users\YourName\Desktop\My-Website ↓ Correct Project Folder? ✅ ↓ Run: git init
What Output Will You See?
After running git init, Git normally displays a message indicating that an empty Git repository has been initialized.
The exact wording and branch name mentioned in the output may vary depending on your Git version and configuration.
git init ↓ Initialized empty Git repository ↓ Repository ready ✅
git init and the .git Folder
You learned earlier that the hidden .git folder contains important Git repository information.
One of the main things git init does is create the repository's .git directory.
Before git init My-Website ├── index.html └── style.css ↓ git init After git init My-Website ├── .git ← Git repository data ├── index.html └── style.css
Remember: If the .git directory is present in the project root, that directory is what identifies the project as a Git repository.
Can You Run git init on an Existing Project?
Yes. You can use git init when you already have a project with files and want to start using Git version control.
Existing Project │ ├── index.html ├── style.css └── script.js ↓ Decide to start using Git ↓ Run: git init ↓ Existing Project becomes Git Repository
This is a very common workflow.
Can You Run git init in an Empty Folder?
Yes. You can also initialize an empty folder and then start creating project files.
Empty Folder ↓ git init ↓ Empty Git Repository ↓ Create Files ↓ git add ↓ git commit
Important Difference: git init vs git clone
These commands are used for different purposes.

git initgit clone
Starts a new Git repository in a folderCreates a local copy of an existing repository
Used for a new or existing local projectUsed to download/copy an existing repository
Creates Git repository metadata locallyCopies repository files and history locally
Does not require GitHubCommonly used with remote repositories
We will study git clone later in the GitHub section of the roadmap.
Complete Workflow So Far
You have now learned the beginning of a real Git workflow:
1. Install Git ↓ 2. Check Git Version ↓ 3. Configure user.name ↓ 4. Configure user.email ↓ 5. Understand configuration ↓ 6. Choose Project Folder ↓ 7. Run git init ↓ Local Git Repository Ready ✅
Important Commands

CommandPurpose
git initInitialize the current folder as a Git repository
git --versionCheck whether Git is installed
git config --listView available Git configuration values
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
Normal Folder ↓ git init ↓ Git Repository ↓ .git folder created ↓ Ready to use Git ↓ git add → git commit
One-Line Definition: git init initializes the current project folder as a local Git repository by creating the Git repository structure needed for Git to manage the project's history.
practice: Now perform your first real Git repository setup. Create or choose a small practice project folder and initialize it with Git.

STEP 1 → Create a folder called Git-Practice ↓ STEP 2 → Open Terminal inside Git-Practice ↓ STEP 3 → Confirm you are in the correct folder ↓ STEP 4 → Run git init ↓ STEP 5 → Git repository initialized ✅
git init
After running the command, Git should display a message indicating that the repository was initialized. Your project folder is now a local Git repository.
Git-Practice ↓ git init ↓ .git folder created ↓ Local Repository Ready ✅
Important check: Make sure you run git init inside Git-Practice, not accidentally in Desktop or another parent folder.

Practice Goal: Successfully initialize one local Git repository and understand that git init creates a local Git repository only. It does not automatically create commits or upload anything to GitHub.

qna.q: Q1. What does git init do?
qna.a: git init initializes the current folder as a local Git repository.

qna.q: Q2. What important hidden directory is created when Git initializes a normal repository?
qna.a: Git creates the .git directory, which contains important repository metadata and Git information.

qna.q: Q3. Does git init automatically commit all existing files?
qna.a: No. git init only initializes the repository. Files must later be staged and committed separately.

qna.q: Q4. Does git init automatically create a repository on GitHub?
qna.a: No. git init creates a local Git repository on your computer.

qna.q: Q5. Do you need internet access to run git init?
qna.a: No. git init works locally and does not require an internet connection.

qna.q: Q6. Where should you normally run git init?
qna.a: You should normally run it inside the main project folder that you want Git to manage.

qna.q: Q7. Can you use git init on an existing project that already contains files?
qna.a: Yes. You can initialize an existing project folder and then start tracking its files with Git.

qna.q: Q8. What is the main difference between git init and git clone?
qna.a: git init starts a Git repository in a local folder, while git clone creates a local copy of an existing repository and its history.

qna.q: Q9. What should you check before running git init?
qna.a: You should check that your terminal is inside the correct project folder.

items.title: Check Repository Status (git status)
explanation: Simple Meaning
The command git status shows the current state of your Git repository.
It helps you understand what is happening with your files before you take the next Git action.
Simple Rule: Whenever you are unsure about the current state of your repository, run git status.
Why is git status Important?
While working on a project, files can be in different states. You may have:

• New files Git has not tracked yet
  • Modified files
  • Files ready to commit
  • No changes at all
Instead of guessing, git status tells you the current situation.
You are working on a project ↓ Not sure what changed? ↓ Run: git status ↓ Git shows the current state ↓ You know what to do next ✅
Basic Command
Open your terminal inside a Git repository and run:
git status
Git will examine the repository and display information about the current working state.
Important: Run It Inside a Git Repository
Normally, you should run git status inside a folder that is part of a Git repository.
Git-Practice │ ├── .git ├── index.html └── style.css ↓ Run: git status ↓ Git can check repository status ✅
If you run it in a folder that is not inside a Git repository, Git cannot find repository information and will display an error.
First Time After git init
Suppose you create a new folder and run:
git init
Immediately after that, run:
git status
If you have not created or changed any files, Git will show that there is nothing to commit.
git init ↓ Repository initialized ↓ git status ↓ No files to commit yet ↓ Nothing to commit
The exact output can vary depending on your Git version and repository state.
Example: Create a New File
Suppose your repository is empty:
Git-Practice └── .git
Now create:
Git-Practice ├── .git └── index.html ← New file
Run:
git status
Git can show index.html as an untracked file.
Untracked File: A file that exists in your project but has not yet been added to Git's tracking process.
The Basic File Journey
As you learn Git, remember that files move through different states.
New File (Untracked) ↓ git add ↓ Staged (Ready for commit) ↓ git commit ↓ Committed (Saved in Git history)
git status helps you see where your files currently are in this workflow.
Example: After git add
Later, after you learn git add, the workflow will look like this:
index.html (Untracked) ↓ git status ↓ Git shows: Untracked ↓ git add index.html ↓ git status ↓ Git shows: Ready to commit
This is why git status is one of the most frequently used Git commands.
Example: After git commit
After staging and committing your changes, run:
git status
If there are no new or modified files, Git can report that the working tree is clean.
Make Changes ↓ git add ↓ git commit ↓ git status ↓ Nothing new to commit Working tree clean ✅
Modified File Example
Suppose index.html was already committed.
index.html ↓ Committed Version ↓ You edit the file ↓ Add a new heading ↓ File is Modified
Now when you run:
git status
Git can show that index.html has been modified.
This tells you that the current file is different from the last committed version.
What git status Can Help You Identify

Repository StateWhat git status Helps You See
UntrackedNew files not yet added for tracking
ModifiedTracked files changed after the last commit
StagedChanges prepared for the next commit
CleanNo changes waiting to be committed
git status Does Not Change Your Files
git status is an information command. It checks and displays repository status.
git status ↓ Checks Repository ↓ Displays Information ↓ Does NOT: ├── Delete files ├── Modify files ├── Create a commit └── Upload to GitHub
Important: You can safely run git status whenever you want to check your repository. It does not stage, commit, delete, or upload your work.
git status and GitHub
git status works with your local Git repository.
Your Computer │ └── Local Git Repository ↓ git status ↓ Check Local Repository State
You do not need GitHub or an internet connection to check the status of your local repository.
Real Workflow Example
Imagine you are working on a website.

START Run: git status ↓ Check current state Create index.html ↓ Run: git status ↓ New file detected Later: git add index.html ↓ Run: git status ↓ Check staged changes Later: git commit ↓ Run: git status ↓ Check whether repository is clean
You will use git status repeatedly throughout your entire Git workflow.
Common Beginner Mistake
Beginners sometimes run several Git commands without checking what state the repository is in.
Make changes ↓ Run commands without checking ❌ ↓ Confusion: What changed? What is staged? What is committed?
A better habit is:
Make changes ↓ Run: git status ↓ Understand current state ↓ Take the correct next action ✅
Common Outputs You May See

SituationMeaning
Nothing to commit / working tree cleanNo uncommitted changes to save
Untracked filesNew files exist but have not been added for tracking
Changes not staged for commitA tracked file has been modified but is not staged
Changes to be committedChanges are staged and ready for the next commit
You will understand each of these states in much more detail in the upcoming topics.
Complete Workflow So Far
Install Git ↓ Check Git Version ↓ Configure Username ↓ Configure Email ↓ Understand Configuration ↓ git init ↓ Local Repository Created ↓ git status ↓ Check Current Repository State ✅
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
Before doing anything ↓ Not sure about repository state? ↓ git status ↓ Git tells you: What is new? What changed? What is staged? What is ready to commit?
One-Line Definition: git status displays the current state of your Git repository, helping you identify untracked files, modified files, staged changes, and whether your working tree is clean.
practice: Now use the Git repository you created in Topic 15 and check its status.
STEP 1 → Open Terminal inside your Git-Practice folder ↓ STEP 2 → Run git status ↓ STEP 3 → Read the current repository state
git status
Next, create a simple file such as index.html inside the same Git-Practice folder.
Git-Practice │ ├── .git └── index.html ← Create this file ↓ Run git status again
git status
Observe how Git now reports the new file as untracked. Do not worry about staging it yet — git add is the next topic.
Before creating file ↓ git status → Nothing to commit Create index.html ↓ git status → Untracked file detected
Your task: Run git status at least twice — once before creating a new file and once after creating it. Compare the output.
Practice Goal: Understand that git status does not change anything. It simply shows the current state of your repository and helps you see what Git knows about your files.

qna.q: Q1. What does git status do?
qna.a: git status displays the current state of your Git repository.

qna.q: Q2. Does git status change or delete your files?
qna.a: No. git status only displays information about the repository state.

qna.q: Q3. Do you need to run git status inside a Git repository?
qna.a: Yes. Normally you run it inside a Git repository or one of its subfolders so Git can find the repository information.

qna.q: Q4. What is an untracked file?
qna.a: An untracked file exists in your project but has not yet been added to Git's tracking process.

qna.q: Q5. What does a modified file mean?
qna.a: It means a tracked file has changed compared with its last committed version.

qna.q: Q6. What can git status tell you about staged changes?
qna.a: It can show changes that are staged and ready to be included in the next commit.

qna.q: Q7. Do you need GitHub or internet access to use git status?
qna.a: No. git status works with your local Git repository.

qna.q: Q8. When is a good time to use git status?
qna.a: Use it whenever you want to know the current state of your repository, especially before or after Git actions.

qna.q: Q9. What is the basic file journey in Git?
qna.a: A new file can move from Untracked → Staged using git add → Committed using git commit.

qna.q: Q10. Why is git status considered one of the most useful Git commands?
qna.a: Because it helps you understand what changed, what is untracked, what is staged, and whether there are changes left to commit.

items.title: Stage Changes (git add)
explanation: Simple Meaning
The command git add moves selected file changes from the Working Directory to the Staging Area.
In simple words, git add tells Git:
I want these changes included in my next commit.
Simple Rule: Make changes → use git add to select changes for the next commit → use git commit to save them in Git history.
Where Does git add Fit?
You learned earlier about Git's working areas. The basic flow is:
Working Directory (You create or modify files) ↓ git add ↓ Staging Area (Selected for next commit) ↓ git commit ↓ Local Repository (Saved in Git history)
The most important thing to understand is that git add does not create a commit. It only prepares selected changes for the next commit.
Simple Example
Suppose your repository contains a new file:
Git-Practice │ ├── .git └── index.html ← New file
When you run:
git status
Git can show index.html as untracked.
index.html ↓ Untracked (Not selected for Git tracking yet)
Now run:
git add index.html
The file's current content is placed in the Staging Area, ready for the next commit.
index.html Untracked ↓ git add index.html ↓ Staged ↓ Ready for next commit ✅
Why Do We Need a Staging Area?
The Staging Area allows you to choose which changes should be included in your next commit.
Imagine you modify three files:
index.html → Login page changes style.css → Design changes script.js → Experimental code
You may want to commit only the login page and design changes, while keeping the experimental code out of the commit.

Working Directory │ ├── index.html ← Add ✅ ├── style.css ← Add ✅ └── script.js ← Do not add yet ❌ ↓ git add index.html style.css ↓ Staging Area │ ├── index.html └── style.css ↓ git commit ↓ Commit contains only selected changes
Important Concept: The Staging Area gives you control over what goes into the next commit. You do not always have to commit every changed file together.
1. Add One Specific File
To stage one file, write:
git add filename
Example:
git add index.html
Working Directory index.html ← Changed ↓ git add index.html ↓ Staging Area index.html ← Staged
2. Add Multiple Specific Files
You can stage multiple files by writing their names:
git add index.html style.css
index.html ← Modified style.css ← Modified script.js ← Modified ↓ git add index.html style.css ↓ Staged ├── index.html ✅ └── style.css ✅ Not staged └── script.js ⏳
3. Add All Changes in the Current Directory
A commonly used command is:
git add .
The dot . represents the current directory. This stages applicable changes under the current directory.
Current Project Folder │ ├── index.html ← Changed ├── style.css ← Changed └── script.js ← Changed ↓ git add . ↓ Changes staged for next commit
Beginner Habit: Before using git add ., run git status so you understand which changes you are about to stage.
git add Does Not Create a Commit
This is one of the most important beginner concepts.
git add ↓ Changes are staged ↓ NOT yet saved as a commit ❌ Then ↓ git commit ↓ Changes are saved in Git history ✅
Think of the Staging Area as a preparation area before creating a commit.
Check Staged Changes Using git status
After running git add, run:
git status
Git can show the changes under a section similar to:
Changes to be committed: new file: index.html
This means the file is staged and ready to be included in the next commit.
Important: Git Stages a Snapshot of the Changes
When you run git add, Git stages the current version of the file at that moment.
Suppose you write this:
<h1>My Website</h1>
Then you run:
git add index.html
Now you modify the file again:
<h1>My Website</h1> <p>Welcome!</p>
The new change made after staging is not automatically added to the staged snapshot.
Version A <h1>My Website</h1> ↓ git add index.html ↓ Version A staged Then edit again ↓ Version B Add: <p>Welcome!</p> ↓ New change remains outside staging until you run git add again
Important: If you modify a file after staging it and want the latest changes included in the next commit, you generally need to run git add again for the updated content.
Example Using One File
STEP 1 Create index.html ↓ STEP 2 git status → index.html is untracked ↓ STEP 3 git add index.html ↓ STEP 4 git status → index.html is staged ↓ STEP 5 Next topic: git commit
Example Using Multiple Changes
Suppose you change three files:
Working Directory │ ├── index.html ← Modified ├── style.css ← Modified └── script.js ← Modified
First check the status:
git status
Then decide what belongs in the next commit.
Option 1: Stage only one file:
git add index.html
Option 2: Stage two specific files:
git add index.html style.css
Option 3: Stage applicable changes under the current directory:
git add .
Then check the result:
git status
git add and Untracked Files
A new file is initially untracked. Running git add selects it for inclusion in the next commit.
Create new file ↓ Untracked ↓ git add filename ↓ Staged ↓ git commit ↓ Tracked in committed history
git add and Modified Files
The command is also used when you modify a file that Git already knows about.
index.html Already committed ↓ You modify it ↓ Modified ↓ git add index.html ↓ Updated version staged ↓ git commit ↓ New version saved in history
Common Beginner Mistake
Suppose you modify a file and immediately expect git commit to save every change automatically.
Modify File ↓ Run git commit directly ↓ Changes may not be staged ❌
The normal workflow you are learning is:
Modify Files ↓ git status ↓ Check changes ↓ git add ↓ Select changes for commit ↓ git status ↓ Verify staging ↓ git commit ↓ Save in Git history
Important Commands

CommandPurpose
git add index.htmlStage changes from one specific file
git add index.html style.cssStage changes from multiple specific files
git add .Stage applicable changes under the current directory
git statusCheck which files are staged or unstaged
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
Working Directory → Where you make changes ↓ git add Staging Area → Select changes for next commit ↓ git commit Local Repository → Save changes in Git history
One-Line Definition: git add stages selected file changes, preparing the current snapshot of those changes to be included in the next Git commit.
practice: Use the Git-Practice repository you created in Topic 15. If you already created index.html during Topic 16, continue using it.
STEP 1 → Open Terminal inside Git-Practice ↓ STEP 2 → Check the current status ↓ STEP 3 → Stage index.html ↓ STEP 4 → Check the status again ↓ STEP 5 → Observe how the file state changes
git status
If index.html is shown as an untracked file, stage it using:
git add index.html
Now check the repository again:
git status
Before git add index.html → Untracked ↓ git add index.html ↓ After git add index.html → Staged / Ready to commit ✅
Extra practice: Create another file called style.css. Run git status, then stage only that file.
git add style.css
Finally, run git status again and confirm that both files are ready for the next commit.
index.html → Staged style.css → Staged ↓ Both are ready for the next commit ✅
Practice Goal: Clearly understand the difference between Untracked/Modified and Staged. Remember: git add prepares changes for a commit, but does not create the commit itself.

qna.q: Q1. What does git add do?
qna.a: git add stages selected file changes, preparing them for inclusion in the next commit.

qna.q: Q2. Does git add create a commit?
qna.a: No. git add only places selected changes in the Staging Area. git commit is used to save staged changes in Git history.

qna.q: Q3. What command stages index.html?
qna.a: git add index.html

qna.q: Q4. What command can stage multiple specific files?
qna.a: For example: git add index.html style.css

qna.q: Q5. What does git add . do?
qna.a: It stages applicable changes under the current directory.

qna.q: Q6. Why should you run git status before using git add .?
qna.a: Because git status helps you understand which changes are present before staging them.

qna.q: Q7. What happens after running git add on an untracked file?
qna.a: The file's current content is staged and prepared to be included in the next commit.

qna.q: Q8. What happens if you modify a file after running git add?
qna.a: The new modification is not automatically added to the staged snapshot. If you want the latest change included in the next commit, run git add again.

qna.q: Q9. What is the normal basic Git workflow?
qna.a: Working Directory → git add → Staging Area → git commit → Local Repository.

qna.q: Q10. Which command can you use to verify what is staged?
qna.a: git status

items.title: Create a Commit (git commit)
explanation: Simple Meaning
The command git commit saves the changes currently in the Staging Area as a permanent snapshot in the Local Repository.
In simple words, git add selects the changes, and git commit records them in Git history.
Make changes ↓ git add ↓ Select changes for commit ↓ git commit ↓ Save snapshot in Git history ✅
Simple Rule: git add prepares changes. git commit saves the staged changes into the local Git history.
What Is a Commit?
A commit is a recorded snapshot of selected changes at a specific point in time. Each commit becomes part of the repository history.
Imagine your project changes over time:
Commit 1 Initial website ↓ Commit 2 Add login page ↓ Commit 3 Add dashboard ↓ Commit 4 Fix login validation
Git keeps these commits as history, allowing you to later inspect previous work and compare changes.
Where Does git commit Fit?
Git has a basic workflow:
Working Directory (You create or modify files) ↓ git add ↓ Staging Area (Selected changes) ↓ git commit ↓ Local Repository (Saved in Git history)
After a successful commit, the staged snapshot is recorded in the local repository.
Basic Command
A commonly used command is:
git commit -m "Your commit message"
The -m option lets you provide a commit message directly with the command.
Example:
git commit -m "Add login page"
Staged changes ↓ git commit -m "Add login page" ↓ Commit created ↓ Local Repository ↓ History updated ✅
Why Is a Commit Message Needed?
A commit message describes what the commit represents. When you later view Git history, commit messages help you understand why or what changes were saved.
Compare:
Bad / unclear ❌ "changes" "update" "final" Better ✅ "Add login page" "Fix password validation" "Update dashboard layout"
A good message makes repository history easier to understand.
Simple Example
Suppose you have already staged two files:
Staging Area │ ├── index.html └── style.css
Now run:
git commit -m "Create homepage layout"
Git creates one commit containing the currently staged changes.
Before Commit Staging Area ├── index.html └── style.css ↓ git commit ↓ After Commit Local Repository Commit: Create homepage layout ├── index.html changes └── style.css changes
Important: git commit Only Commits Staged Changes
This is a very important concept.
Suppose you modify three files:
index.html → Staged ✅ style.css → Staged ✅ script.js → Modified but not staged ⏳
Then you run:
git commit -m "Update homepage"
Only index.html and style.css are included in this commit. The unstaged changes in script.js remain outside the commit.
Remember: A normal git commit records what is currently staged, not automatically every change in your Working Directory.
Important: A Commit Is Local
When you create a commit, it is saved in your local repository on your computer.
Your Computer │ ├── Working Directory ├── Staging Area └── Local Repository ↑ git commit
Creating a commit does not automatically upload the commit to GitHub.
git commit ↓ Saved locally on your computer ✅ NOT automatically uploaded to GitHub ❌
Later, you will use git push to send local commits to a remote repository such as GitHub.
Commit History Example
Imagine you work on your website for several days:
Commit 1 → "Initial project setup" ↓ Commit 2 → "Add homepage" ↓ Commit 3 → "Add navigation bar" ↓ Commit 4 → "Fix mobile layout"
These commits form the history of your project. In a later topic, you will use git log to view this history.
Each Commit Has an Identity
Each commit has its own unique commit ID, commonly called a commit hash. Git uses this identifier to identify a specific commit in the repository history.
A full commit hash is a long value, but Git often displays a shortened version for convenience.
Commit Message: Add login page Commit ID / Hash abc123... ← Example only ↓ Unique identification of that commit
You do not need to memorize commit hashes manually at this stage. Just understand that Git can uniquely identify commits.
What Happens After a Commit?
After a successful commit, the staged changes are recorded in the repository history.
Before Commit Staging Area Changes waiting ↓ git commit ↓ Commit Created ↓ Local Repository History Updated ↓ Working state continues from this new committed version
You can then continue modifying files and create more commits as your project develops.
Example: Complete First Commit
Using your Git-Practice project:
Git-Practice ├── .git ├── index.html └── style.css
First check the status:
git status
Stage the files:
git add .
Check what is staged:
git status
Now create your commit:
git commit -m "Initial project setup"
Files created/modified ↓ git add . ↓ Files staged ↓ git commit -m "Initial project setup" ↓ First commit created ✅
What If There Is Nothing to Commit?
If there are no staged changes, Git cannot create a normal commit containing new changes.
Staging Area Empty ↓ git commit ↓ No changes available for a normal commit
This is why checking git status before committing is a useful habit.
Common Beginner Mistake: Forgetting git add
You modify a file:
Modify index.html ↓ File changed ↓ Run git commit directly ❌ ↓ Change was not staged
The normal workflow is:
Modify file ↓ git status ↓ git add filename ↓ git status ↓ git commit -m "Describe the change" ↓ Commit created ✅
Common Beginner Mistake: Thinking Commit Means GitHub Upload
A commit and a GitHub upload are different actions.

CommandWhat It Does
git addStages selected changes
git commitSaves staged changes locally
git pushSends local commits to a remote repository
Important: You can create commits and build a complete Git history without GitHub or an internet connection.
Basic Workflow You Should Remember
1. Create or modify files ↓ 2. git status ↓ 3. git add ↓ 4. git status ↓ 5. git commit -m "Message" ↓ 6. Changes saved in local history ✅
git commit vs git add

git addgit commit
Selects/stages changesRecords staged changes
Moves changes to the Staging AreaSaves a snapshot in the Local Repository
Does not create history entryCreates a new history entry
Prepares changesRecords changes
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
Working Directory "I made changes" ↓ git add "I selected these changes" ↓ Staging Area "Ready to save" ↓ git commit "Save this snapshot" ↓ Local Repository "Saved in Git history" ✅
One-Line Definition: git commit records the currently staged changes as a snapshot in the local Git repository, along with a commit message describing the saved change.
practice: Now create your first commit using the Git-Practice repository from the previous topics.
STEP 1 → Open Terminal inside Git-Practice ↓ STEP 2 → Check repository status ↓ STEP 3 → Stage your files ↓ STEP 4 → Create a commit ↓ STEP 5 → Check status again
First, check your current repository state:
git status
If your files are not yet staged, stage them:
git add .
Check again and confirm the changes are ready to commit:
git status
Now create your first commit:
git commit -m "Initial project setup"
After the commit completes, check the repository once more:
git status
Before Commit Changes staged ↓ git commit -m "Initial project setup" ↓ Commit saved locally ↓ git status ↓ Working tree clean ✅
Extra practice: Open index.html and make one small change, such as adding a heading. Then repeat the workflow.
Modify index.html ↓ git status ↓ git add index.html ↓ git commit -m "Add homepage heading" ↓ Second commit created ✅
Practice Goal: Create at least two commits and clearly understand that git add stages changes, while git commit saves the staged snapshot in your local Git history.

qna.q: Q1. What does git commit do?
qna.a: git commit records the currently staged changes as a snapshot in the local Git repository.

qna.q: Q2. What command is commonly used to create a commit with a message?
qna.a: git commit -m "Your commit message"

qna.q: Q3. Does git commit automatically save every modified file?
qna.a: No. A normal git commit records the changes that are currently staged.

qna.q: Q4. What is the difference between git add and git commit?
qna.a: git add stages selected changes, while git commit records the staged changes in the local Git history.

qna.q: Q5. Does git commit automatically upload code to GitHub?
qna.a: No. git commit saves changes locally. git push is later used to send local commits to a remote repository.

qna.q: Q6. Why is a commit message important?
qna.a: A commit message helps you understand what change was recorded when viewing the project history.

qna.q: Q7. Give an example of a good commit message.
qna.a: Examples include: Add login page, Fix password validation, or Update dashboard layout.

qna.q: Q8. What happens if there are no staged changes to commit?
qna.a: Git cannot create a normal commit containing new changes because there is nothing staged to record.

qna.q: Q9. Where is a commit stored?
qna.a: A commit is stored in the local Git repository on your computer.

qna.q: Q10. What is the basic workflow for saving changes in Git?
qna.a: Modify files → git status → git add → git status → git commit.

items.title: Good Commit Messages
explanation: Simple Meaning
A commit message is a short description that explains what a commit contains.
When you run:
git commit -m "Add login page"
The text Add login page is the commit message.
Simple Rule: A good commit message should clearly explain the change saved in that commit.
Why Are Good Commit Messages Important?
Over time, a project can contain hundreds or thousands of commits. Commit messages make the project history easier to understand.
Commit History Commit 1 → "Initial project setup" Commit 2 → "Add login page" Commit 3 → "Fix password validation" Commit 4 → "Update dashboard layout"
Just by reading these messages, you can understand the major changes made to the project.
Bad vs Good Commit Messages
Compare these commit messages:

Bad ❌Good ✅
changesAdd login page
updateUpdate homepage layout
fixFix login validation error
finalAdd user registration feature
new codeAdd password reset functionality
The problem with messages like changes or update is that they do not explain what actually changed.
Imagine Reading History Later
Suppose you return to your project after six months.
Your commit history looks like this:
Commit 1 → changes Commit 2 → update Commit 3 → fix Commit 4 → final Commit 5 → changes again
It becomes difficult to understand what happened.
Now compare it with:
Commit 1 → Create initial project structure Commit 2 → Add login page Commit 3 → Fix password validation Commit 4 → Add dashboard page Commit 5 → Update dashboard navigation
The second history is much easier to understand.
The Basic Structure of a Good Commit Message
For your current learning stage, follow this simple pattern:
Action + What changed
Examples:
Add + login page Fix + password validation Update + homepage layout Remove + unused CSS Create + database connection
This simple structure is enough for most beginner projects.
Use Clear Action Words
Good commit messages often begin with a clear action word.

Action WordExample
AddAdd login button
FixFix registration error
UpdateUpdate navigation menu
RemoveRemove unused CSS
CreateCreate user model
RefactorRefactor login validation
RenameRename dashboard component
One Commit Should Represent a Meaningful Change
A commit message should match the changes inside that commit.
For example:
Changes: Only login page added Good message ✅ "Add login page" Unclear message ❌ "Update project"
The goal is that someone reading the message should have a reasonable idea of what was changed.
Keep the Message Focused
Suppose you make these unrelated changes:
1. Add login page 2. Fix payment error 3. Change dashboard colors
Putting everything into one commit with this message is unclear:
git commit -m "Many changes"
A better approach is to create meaningful commits when the changes are logically separate.
Commit 1 → Add login page Commit 2 → Fix payment error Commit 3 → Update dashboard colors
Important Idea: Try to make the commit message accurately describe the purpose of the changes inside that commit.
Examples for Your Website Project
Imagine you are developing a learning website. Your history could look like:

Commit 1 → Create project structure ↓ Commit 2 → Add Python roadmap ↓ Commit 3 → Add Git roadmap ↓ Commit 4 → Update navigation design ↓ Commit 5 → Fix topic loading error ↓ Commit 6 → Add practice questions
Each message clearly gives an idea about the purpose of that commit.
Do Not Make Messages Too Vague
Avoid commit messages that provide almost no useful information.
Avoid ❌ "done" "changes" "update" "work" "test" "final final" "latest code" Better ✅ "Add user login form" "Fix CSS alignment issue" "Update Git roadmap content" "Add input validation tests"
Do Not Write an Entire Story
A commit message should be clear, but the basic message does not need to contain every technical detail.
For example, instead of:
Too long for a simple commit ❌ "I changed the login page because yesterday I found that users were unable to enter their password correctly and then I also changed some CSS"
A clearer message could be:
Better ✅ "Fix password input validation"
Keep the message focused on the main purpose of the commit.
Use the Imperative Style
A common Git convention is to write commit messages like an instruction or command.
For example:
Add login page ✅ Fix validation error ✅ Update homepage layout ✅ Remove unused code ✅
Instead of focusing on who performed the action:
Added login page I added login page I am adding login page
For your learning, prefer the simple action style:
Recommended Pattern: Start with an action word such as Add, Fix, Update, or Remove.
Capitalization and Punctuation
For consistency, you can start your commit message with a capital letter:
Add login page ✅ Fix database connection error ✅ Update navigation menu ✅
For short commit messages, you generally do not need to add a period at the end.
git commit -m "Add login page"
Good Commit Message Examples

ChangeGood Commit Message
Create projectCreate initial project structure
Add HTML pageAdd homepage
Add CSSAdd homepage styling
Fix login problemFix login validation error
Add dashboardAdd user dashboard
Delete unused codeRemove unused JavaScript code
Change menuUpdate navigation menu
How to Create a Commit with a Good Message
The workflow remains the same:
Make changes ↓ git status ↓ git add ↓ git commit -m "Clear description" ↓ Commit saved in local history
Example:
git add index.html git commit -m "Add homepage heading"
Before Creating a Commit, Ask Yourself
Before writing the commit message, ask:
What did I change? ↓ Why am I saving these changes together? ↓ Can I describe the main change clearly? ↓ Write the commit message
Example:
What changed? → Added a login page Commit message: → "Add login page" ✅
Commit Messages and git log
Later, when you use git log, Git displays your commit history along with commit messages.
git log ↓ Commit abc123 Author: Your Name Message: Add login page Commit def456 Author: Your Name Message: Fix login validation
This is another reason good messages are important: they make your Git history useful and readable.
Common Beginner Mistake
Do not use random messages simply because you want to finish the commit quickly.
Make change ↓ "final" ❌ ↓ Make another change ↓ "final2" ❌ ↓ Make another change ↓ "final final working" ❌
Instead:
Make change ↓ Understand what changed ↓ Write a clear message ↓ Create commit ↓ Useful history ✅
Simple Rules to Remember 🧠
GOOD COMMIT MESSAGE 1. Be clear 2. Describe the main change 3. Keep it focused 4. Use meaningful action words 5. Avoid vague words like "changes" or "final" 6. Make the message match the commit
One-Line Definition: A good commit message is a clear and meaningful description of the main change recorded in a Git commit.
practice: You do not need to learn a new Git command in this topic. Practice writing meaningful messages for changes you make.
STEP 1 → Think about what changed ↓ STEP 2 → Identify the main purpose ↓ STEP 3 → Write a clear action-based message ↓ STEP 4 → Use it with git commit
Practice with your Git-Practice project. Make a small change to index.html, such as adding a heading.
Change made: Add a homepage heading ↓ Good commit message: "Add homepage heading"
Stage and commit the change:
git add index.html git commit -m "Add homepage heading"
Practice Exercise: For each change below, think of a good commit message before checking the suggested pattern.

Change 1 → You added a login page Commit message → Add login page Change 2 → You fixed a password validation problem Commit message → Fix password validation error Change 3 → You changed the navigation menu design Commit message → Update navigation menu design Change 4 → You deleted unused CSS code Commit message → Remove unused CSS code
Now create at least three small commits in your practice repository. Each commit should represent a meaningful change and have a clear message.
Commit 1 → Add homepage heading ↓ Commit 2 → Add navigation section ↓ Commit 3 → Update homepage styling
Practice Goal: Before every commit, ask yourself: "If I read this message after six months, will I understand what this commit changed?"

qna.q: Q1. What is a commit message?
qna.a: A commit message is a short description that explains the main change recorded in a Git commit.

qna.q: Q2. What is the basic pattern for a good commit message?
qna.a: A simple pattern is: Action + What changed, for example: Add login page.

qna.q: Q3. Why is the commit message "changes" considered bad?
qna.a: Because it is too vague and does not explain what actually changed.

qna.q: Q4. Which is better: "fix" or "Fix login validation error"?
qna.a: Fix login validation error is better because it clearly describes what was fixed.

qna.q: Q5. Give three useful action words for commit messages.
qna.a: Examples include Add, Fix, Update, Remove, Create, Refactor, and Rename.

qna.q: Q6. Why should a commit message match the changes inside the commit?
qna.a: Because the commit message should accurately describe the purpose of the changes saved in that commit.

qna.q: Q7. Does a good commit message need to be extremely long?
qna.a: No. It should be clear and focused, describing the main purpose without unnecessary details.

qna.q: Q8. What is a better commit message than "final final"?
qna.a: Use a message describing the actual change, such as Update homepage styling or Fix login validation error.

qna.q: Q9. Why are good commit messages useful when using git log?
qna.a: Because git log shows commit history, and meaningful messages make it easier to understand what happened in previous commits.

qna.q: Q10. You added a user registration feature. What is a good commit message?
qna.a: Add user registration feature.

items.title: View Commit History (git log)
explanation: Simple Meaning
The command git log displays the commit history of your Git repository.
Every time you create a commit, Git stores it in the repository history. git log allows you to view that history.
Commit 1 → Initial project setup ↓ Commit 2 → Add homepage ↓ Commit 3 → Add login page ↓ Commit 4 → Fix login validation ↓ git log ↓ View commit history ✅
Simple Rule: Use git log when you want to see the commits that have been created in your repository.
Why Do We Need git log?
As your project grows, you will create many commits. After some time, you may want to know:

• What commits were created?
  • What was changed?
  • Who created a commit?
  • When was it created?
  • What is the commit ID?
git log helps you view this information.
Basic Command
Open your terminal inside your Git repository and run:
git log
Git displays commits from the newest commit to the oldest commit.
Newest Commit ↓ Older Commit ↓ Older Commit ↓ Oldest Commit
Important: By default, git log shows the newest commits first.
Example Commit History
Suppose you created these commits:
Commit 1 → Create initial project structure Commit 2 → Add homepage heading Commit 3 → Add navigation section
When you run:
git log
Git displays the history in reverse order:
Commit 3 → Add navigation section ← Newest Commit 2 → Add homepage heading Commit 1 → Create initial project structure ← Oldest
What Information Does git log Show?
A basic git log output can contain information similar to this:
commit a1b2c3d4e5f6... Author: Your Name <your-email@example.com> Date: Example date Add login page
The actual commit ID, author, email, and date will be different in your repository.

InformationMeaning
commitThe unique ID of the commit
AuthorThe person whose Git identity created the commit
DateWhen the commit was created
Commit messageA description of the saved change
Understanding the Commit Hash
Each commit has a unique identifier called a commit hash or commit ID.
commit a1b2c3d4e5f6... ↓ Unique identity for one specific commit
Git uses commit hashes to identify commits in the repository history.
You do not need to memorize the full hash. Later, you will learn situations where a shortened commit hash can be used to refer to a specific commit.
Understanding the Author
The Author information comes from the Git username and email configured when creating commits.
git config user.name ↓ Your Git name + git config user.email ↓ Your Git email ↓ Used as author information when creating a commit
This connects with the configuration topics you learned earlier.
Understanding the Commit Message
The commit message is the description you provided when creating the commit.
Example:
git commit -m "Add login page"
Later, git log can display:
Commit message: Add login page
This is why the previous topic, Good Commit Messages, is important. Clear messages make your project history easier to understand.
Complete Flow So Far
You have now learned the basic process for recording and viewing changes:
Create or modify files ↓ git status ↓ Check changes ↓ git add ↓ Stage selected changes ↓ git commit -m "Message" ↓ Save changes in local history ↓ git log ↓ View commit history ✅
Example Using Your Git-Practice Repository
Suppose your repository contains these commits:
Commit 1 → Initial project setup Commit 2 → Add homepage heading Commit 3 → Add navigation section
Run:
git log
You will see information about your commits, with the latest commit shown first.
Latest Commit Add navigation section ↓ Previous Commit Add homepage heading ↓ First Commit Initial project setup
What If You Have Only One Commit?
If your repository has only one commit, git log displays only that commit.
Repository History Commit 1 "Initial project setup" ↓ git log ↓ One commit displayed
As you create more commits, they will be added to the history.
What If You Have No Commits?
Running git log in a newly initialized repository before creating any commits will not give you a normal commit history because no commits exist yet.
git init ↓ Repository exists ↓ No commits created yet ↓ git log ↓ No commit history available yet
Important: git init creates a Git repository, but a commit history begins only after you create commits.
git log Works Locally
Like git status, git log can work with your local Git repository.
Your Computer │ └── Local Git Repository ↓ git log ↓ View local commit history
You do not need GitHub or an internet connection to view commits stored in your local repository.
git log Does Not Change Anything
git log is used to view information. It does not modify your files or repository history.
git log ↓ Displays commit history Does NOT: ├── Modify files ├── Create a commit ├── Delete a commit ├── Stage changes └── Upload to GitHub
You can safely use it whenever you want to inspect your commit history.
Common Beginner Confusion: git log vs git status
Both commands provide information, but they show different things.

CommandPurpose
git statusShows the current state of your Working Directory and Staging Area
git logShows commits already saved in repository history
git status ↓ What is happening NOW? -------------------- git log ↓ What commits happened BEFORE?
Common Beginner Confusion: git log vs GitHub
Running git log does not open or check your GitHub repository. It displays the commit history known by your local Git repository.
git log ↓ Check Local Git History GitHub ↓ Remote platform ↓ Different concept
Later, after connecting Git to GitHub, you will learn how local and remote histories work together.
A Useful Way to Think About git log
Think of your Git history as a timeline.
TIME Past ◄────────────────────── Present Commit 1 → Commit 2 → Commit 3 → Commit 4 Setup Homepage Login Bug Fix ↑ git log lets you inspect this history
Why Good Commit Messages Matter Here
Imagine running git log and seeing:
changes update final fix final2
This history is difficult to understand.
Now compare:
Create initial project structure Add homepage Add login page Fix password validation Update navigation menu
Clear commit messages make git log much more useful.
Important Commands

CommandPurpose
git logView detailed commit history
git statusView current repository state
git commit -m "Message"Create a commit that will later appear in history
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
git status → Present state Working Directory Staging Area -------------------- git log → Past history Commit 3 Commit 2 Commit 1
Simple Real-World Workflow

Day 1 Create project ↓ Commit → "Initial project setup" Day 2 Add homepage ↓ Commit → "Add homepage" Day 3 Add login page ↓ Commit → "Add login page" Day 4 Want to see history? ↓ git log ↓ View all previous commits ✅
One-Line Definition: git log displays the commit history of a Git repository, including commits, their IDs, authors, dates, and commit messages.
practice: Use the Git-Practice repository where you created commits in the previous topics.
STEP 1 → Open Terminal inside Git-Practice ↓ STEP 2 → Run git log ↓ STEP 3 → Observe your commits ↓ STEP 4 → Identify the newest and oldest commit
git log
Look at the output and identify these four pieces of information for each commit:
Commit ID / Hash ↓ Author ↓ Date ↓ Commit Message
Your latest commit should normally appear first. Your first commit should appear near the bottom of the displayed history.
Top of git log output ↓ Newest Commit ✅ ↓ Older Commits ↓ Bottom of history ↓ Oldest Commit / First Commit ✅
Extra Practice: Create one small change in your project, such as adding another heading to index.html.
Modify index.html ↓ git status ↓ git add index.html ↓ git commit -m "Add another homepage heading" ↓ git log ↓ Confirm the new commit appears at the top ✅
git status git add index.html git commit -m "Add another homepage heading" git log
Compare your history before and after creating the new commit.
Before Commit 2 Commit 1 ↓ Create new commit ↓ After Commit 3 ← Newest Commit 2 Commit 1
Practice Goal: Understand that every successful git commit creates a new entry in Git history, and git log allows you to view that history locally.

qna.q: Q1. What does git log do?
qna.a: git log displays the commit history of a Git repository.

qna.q: Q2. In what order does git log normally display commits?
qna.a: By default, git log displays the newest commit first and older commits below it.

qna.q: Q3. What information can git log show for a commit?
qna.a: It can show the commit ID, author, date, and commit message.

qna.q: Q4. What is a commit hash?
qna.a: A commit hash is a unique identifier used by Git to identify a specific commit.

qna.q: Q5. Does git log modify your files?
qna.a: No. git log only displays commit history and does not modify your files.

qna.q: Q6. Do you need GitHub to use git log?
qna.a: No. git log can display commits stored in your local Git repository.

qna.q: Q7. What is the difference between git status and git log?
qna.a: git status shows the current state of your Working Directory and Staging Area, while git log shows commits already saved in repository history.

qna.q: Q8. What happens if you run git log before creating any commits?
qna.a: There is no normal commit history to display because no commits have been created yet.

qna.q: Q9. Why are good commit messages useful when viewing git log?
qna.a: They make it easier to understand what changes were made in each commit when reading the project history.

qna.q: Q10. What happens to git log after you create a new commit?
qna.a: The new commit is added to the repository history and normally appears first when you run git log.

items.title: View Changes (git diff)
explanation: Simple Meaning
The command git diff shows the differences between versions of your files.
For beginners, the most important thing to understand is:
Modify a file ↓ git diff ↓ See what changed since the last saved/staged state
By default, git diff shows unstaged changes — changes in your Working Directory that have not yet been added to the Staging Area.
Simple Rule: git diff helps you see exactly what you changed before creating a commit.
Why Do We Need git diff?
Imagine you modify a file several times. After some time, you may forget exactly what you changed.
Original file ↓ Make change 1 ↓ Make change 2 ↓ Make change 3 ↓ Forget what changed 🤔 ↓ git diff ↓ See the differences ✅
This is useful before staging or committing your changes.
Basic Command
git diff
Run this command inside your Git repository.
Git compares your current unstaged file changes with the version Git is currently using as the comparison point for unstaged changes.
At this stage, remember the simple workflow:
File changed in Working Directory ↓ git diff ↓ View unstaged changes
Simple Example
Suppose your index.html file was previously saved in a commit like this:
<h1>Welcome</h1>
Now you modify it:
<h1>Welcome</h1> <p>Learn Git and GitHub</p>
Before using git add, run:
git diff
Git can show output similar to:
- <h1>Welcome</h1> + <h1>Welcome</h1> + <p>Learn Git and GitHub</p>
The important symbol here is:

SymbolMeaning
-Removed line from the compared version
+Added line in the new version
Do not worry about memorizing the complete diff output format yet. First understand that git diff shows what was added, removed, or changed.
Understanding Added and Removed Lines
Suppose the original file contains:
<h1>Welcome</h1>
You change it to:
<h1>Welcome to My Website</h1>
The diff may show something similar to:
- <h1>Welcome</h1> + <h1>Welcome to My Website</h1>
Git treats this as one line removed and one line added.
Old version - Welcome New version + Welcome to My Website
Where Does git diff Fit in the Git Workflow?
You have already learned the main Git working areas:
Working Directory ↓ git add ↓ Staging Area ↓ git commit ↓ Local Repository
git diff is mainly used to inspect differences between these states.
For now, focus on the default command:
Working Directory Modified changes ↓ git diff ↓ See unstaged changes
Important: git diff Does Not Change Anything
git diff is a viewing command. It does not modify your files.
git diff ↓ Only displays differences 👀 Does NOT: ├── Modify files ├── Stage files ├── Create commits ├── Delete commits └── Upload to GitHub
You can safely run git diff whenever you want to inspect changes.
git diff Before git add
A common workflow is to review your changes before staging them.
1. Modify file ↓ 2. git status ↓ 3. git diff ↓ 4. Review changes ↓ 5. git add ↓ 6. git commit
This helps you check whether the changes are correct before adding them to the Staging Area.
Example Workflow
Suppose you add a new heading to index.html.
index.html Original version: <h1>Welcome</h1> ↓ You modify the file: <h1>Welcome</h1> <h2>Git Learning Roadmap</h2>
Now check the repository:
git status
Then inspect the actual changes:
git diff
After confirming the change is correct:
git add index.html git commit -m "Add Git roadmap heading"
What Happens After git add?
This is an important concept.
Suppose you modify index.html and run:
git add index.html
The changes move to the Staging Area.
If you now run the normal command:
git diff
You may see no output for those staged changes because the default git diff command focuses on unstaged changes.
Modify file ↓ git diff ↓ See changes ✅ ↓ git add index.html ↓ Changes become staged ↓ git diff ↓ Staged changes are not shown by default
In the next related topic, you will learn how to view staged changes using:
git diff --staged
Very Important: git diff vs git diff --staged
These commands inspect different areas.

CommandShows
git diffUnstaged changes in the Working Directory
git diff --stagedChanges currently in the Staging Area
Working Directory Modified but not staged ↓ git diff -------------------- git add ↓ Staging Area Ready for commit ↓ git diff --staged
You will study git diff --staged in more detail in Topic 23.
What If You Modify a File and git diff Shows Nothing?
One possible reason is that you already staged the changes.
Modify file ↓ git add file ↓ Changes are staged ↓ git diff ↓ No output for those staged changes
In that situation, check:
git status
Then view the staged changes with:
git diff --staged
What If You Have Multiple Modified Files?
git diff can show unstaged differences from multiple modified files.
Working Directory │ ├── index.html → Modified ├── style.css → Modified └── script.js → Modified ↓ git diff ↓ View differences from all unstaged files
If you want to inspect one specific file, you can use:
git diff index.html
This is useful when a project contains many changes and you want to focus on one file.
Common Beginner Confusion: git diff vs git status
Both commands help you inspect your work, but they answer different questions.

CommandMain Question
git statusWhich files have changed and what state are they in?
git diffWhat exactly changed inside the files?
git status → WHICH files changed? -------------------- git diff → WHAT changed inside them?
Example: status + diff Together
Suppose you modify two files.
index.html → Add heading style.css → Change font size
Run:
git status
Git tells you that the files were modified.
Then run:
git diff
Git shows the actual lines that changed.
git status ↓ index.html → Modified style.css → Modified ↓ Need exact details? ↓ git diff ↓ See changed lines
git diff Helps Before Committing
Before committing, reviewing your changes can help you catch mistakes.
Make changes ↓ git diff ↓ Review carefully ↓ Correct mistakes if needed ↓ git add ↓ git commit
This is especially useful when you made many changes and want to verify what will eventually be included in your project history.
Example of Finding a Mistake
Suppose you intended to change:
<h1>Git Roadmap</h1>
But you accidentally wrote:
<h1>Gti Roadmap</h1>
Running git diff can help you notice the incorrect change:
- Git Roadmap + Gti Roadmap ❌ ↓ Notice mistake ↓ Fix file ↓ Run git diff again ↓ Correct change ✅
Simple Comparison of Current Topics

CommandPurpose
git statusCheck current file and staging state
git addStage changes
git commitSave staged changes in local history
git logView previous commits
git diffView exact unstaged changes
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
git status → What files changed? ↓ git diff → What changed inside the files? ↓ git add → Select changes ↓ git commit → Save changes
Complete Flow

Modify index.html ↓ git status ↓ See that index.html changed ↓ git diff ↓ See exactly what changed ↓ git add index.html ↓ Move changes to Staging Area ↓ git commit -m "Add homepage heading" ↓ Save in Local Repository ✅
One-Line Definition: git diff displays the exact differences in your files, and by default it is commonly used to view unstaged changes in the Working Directory.
practice: Use your Git-Practice repository. First make sure you have at least one committed version of index.html.
STEP 1 → Open index.html ↓ STEP 2 → Make a small change ↓ STEP 3 → Run git status ↓ STEP 4 → Run git diff ↓ STEP 5 → Observe the changed lines
For example, add a new heading to index.html and save the file.
<h2>Learning Git Diff</h2>
Now check which file changed:
git status
Then view exactly what changed inside the file:
git diff
git status ↓ index.html → Modified ↓ git diff ↓ - Old content + New content
Do not run git add immediately. First carefully observe the output from git diff and identify the line you added or changed.
Next: Stage the file and compare the behavior.
git add index.html git status git diff
Notice that the normal git diff may no longer show the staged change. This happens because the change is now in the Staging Area.
Now view the staged change:
git diff --staged
Before git add ↓ git diff Shows unstaged change ✅ After git add ↓ git diff Does not show that staged change by default ↓ git diff --staged Shows staged change ✅
Finally, commit your change with a meaningful message.
git commit -m "Add Git diff practice heading"
Practice Goal: Clearly understand the difference between git status (which files changed), git diff (what changed), and git diff --staged (what is currently staged).

qna.q: Q1. What does git diff do?
qna.a: git diff displays the differences between versions of your files and is commonly used to inspect exact changes.

qna.q: Q2. What does git diff show by default?
qna.a: By default, git diff shows unstaged changes in the Working Directory.

qna.q: Q3. What is the difference between git status and git diff?
qna.a: git status shows which files changed and their current state, while git diff shows the exact content changes inside the files.

qna.q: Q4. Does git diff modify your files?
qna.a: No. git diff only displays differences and does not modify your files.

qna.q: Q5. What does a + symbol usually represent in git diff output?
qna.a: It represents a line that was added in the new version.

qna.q: Q6. What does a - symbol usually represent in git diff output?
qna.a: It represents a line from the compared version that was removed or replaced.

qna.q: Q7. What usually happens when you run git diff after staging all your changes?
qna.a: The normal git diff command may show no output for those changes because they are now staged.

qna.q: Q8. Which command can be used to view staged changes?
qna.a: git diff --staged

qna.q: Q9. Can git diff help you find mistakes before committing?
qna.a: Yes. It allows you to review the exact changes and correct mistakes before staging or committing them.

qna.q: Q10. What is the recommended basic workflow before committing a change?
qna.a: Modify files → git status → git diff → review changes → git add → git commit.

items.title: Modified vs Staged vs Committed
explanation: Simple Meaning
When working with Git, your changes can exist in different states. The three most important states are Modified, Staged, and Committed.
Modify a file ↓ Modified ↓ git add ↓ Staged ↓ git commit ↓ Committed
Simple Rule: Modified means you changed a file. Staged means you selected the change for the next commit. Committed means the change was saved in your local Git history.
The Complete Journey of a Change
Suppose your repository already contains index.html. You edit the file and add a new heading.
Original committed version ↓ Edit index.html ↓ Modified ↓ git add index.html ↓ Staged ↓ git commit -m "Add homepage heading" ↓ Committed
These are not three different copies of your file. They describe the state of your changes during the Git workflow.
1. What Is Modified?
A file is Modified when you change it after the last committed version, but the new changes have not yet been staged.
Example: Your committed index.html contains:
<h1>Welcome</h1>
You change it to:
<h1>Welcome</h1> <h2>Learn Git</h2>
After saving the file, Git sees that the file has changed.
Local Repository Last committed version ↓ You edit index.html ↓ Working Directory index.html → Modified ✏️
You can check this using:
git status
Modified Means: Changes Exist in the Working Directory
Working Directory │ └── index.html Modified ✏️ The change is: Not staged yet ❌ Not committed yet ❌
At this stage, you have changed the file, but you have not told Git to include that change in the next commit.
2. What Is Staged?
A change becomes Staged when you use git add to select it for the next commit.
For example:
git add index.html
Now the current version of that change is placed in the Staging Area.
Working Directory Modified change ↓ git add index.html ↓ Staging Area Change selected for next commit 📦
Staged does not mean committed. The change is ready to be committed, but it has not yet been saved in Git history.
Staged Means: Ready for the Next Commit
Working Directory ↓ git add ↓ Staging Area index.html → Staged 📦 Ready for next commit Not committed yet ⏳
You can use git status to see which changes are staged.
3. What Is Committed?
A change becomes Committed when you run git commit and Git records the staged snapshot in the local repository history.
Example:
git commit -m "Add homepage heading"
Staging Area Change ready ↓ git commit ↓ Local Repository ↓ Commit created ✅ ↓ Change saved in Git history
Now the change is part of your local Git history.
Committed Does Not Mean Uploaded to GitHub
This is a very important concept.
git commit ↓ Saved in Local Repository ✅ GitHub updated automatically? ❌
A commit is created locally on your computer. Uploading commits to GitHub is a separate action that you will learn later using git push.
Simple Example Using One File
Let's follow index.html through all three states.
Step 1: The file was already committed.
Local Repository Commit 1 index.html <h1>Welcome</h1>
Step 2: You change the file.
<h1>Welcome</h1> <h2>Git Learning</h2>
State → Modified ✏️
Step 3: You stage the change.
git add index.html
State → Staged 📦
Step 4: You commit the staged change.
git commit -m "Add Git learning heading"
State → Committed ✅
Visualizing the Three Git States
The Commands That Move Changes

Current StateCommandNext State
Modifiedgit addStaged
Stagedgit commitCommitted
Modified │ │ git add ↓ Staged │ │ git commit ↓ Committed
How git status Shows These States
git status helps you understand where your changes currently are.
If you modify a file but do not stage it, Git can show it as modified.
Changes not staged for commit: modified: index.html State → Modified ✏️
After running git add index.html, Git can show the file under changes ready to be committed.
Changes to be committed: new file: index.html or modified: index.html State → Staged 📦
After committing, there are no longer uncommitted changes from that snapshot.
git status ↓ nothing to commit, working tree clean Latest changes → Committed ✅
Modified vs Staged

ModifiedStaged
You changed the fileYou selected the change for the next commit
Exists in Working DirectoryRecorded in Staging Area
Not ready as the staged snapshotReady for the next commit
View with git diffView with git diff --staged
Move using git addSave using git commit
Staged vs Committed

StagedCommitted
Selected for the next commitAlready saved in Git history
Exists in the Staging AreaExists as a commit in Local Repository
Can still be changed before committingAlready recorded as a history entry
Use git commit to save itView history with git log
Modified vs Committed

ModifiedCommitted
Current unsaved Git changeRecorded Git history snapshot
Not yet staged or committedAlready saved locally
Can be inspected with git diffCan be viewed in history with git log
Very Important Example: Stage Only One File
Suppose you modify two files:
index.html → Modified ✏️ style.css → Modified ✏️
Now you run:
git add index.html
The states become:
index.html → Staged 📦 style.css → Still Modified ✏️
Now run:
git commit -m "Update homepage"
Only the staged change is included in the commit.
index.html → Committed ✅ style.css → Still Modified ✏️
Important: Git allows different files to be in different states at the same time.
Another Important Example: Modify a File Again After Staging
This is an important Git concept.
Suppose you modify index.html:
Modify index.html ↓ Modified ✏️
You stage it:
git add index.html
index.html → Staged 📦
Then you edit index.html again without running git add again.
Staged version → Version A 📦 Working Directory → Version B ✏️
Now the Staging Area contains the earlier staged snapshot, while your newer changes remain modified in the Working Directory.
Important: If you make more changes after git add, run git add again if you want the newer changes included in the next commit.
Example of the Same File in Two States
Step 1 Modify index.html ↓ Step 2 git add index.html ↓ Staged Version A 📦 ↓ Step 3 Modify index.html again ↓ Staging Area → Version A 📦 Working Directory → New Version B ✏️
If you commit now, Git commits the staged Version A. The newer Version B changes remain modified unless you stage them too.
Complete Example Workflow
Suppose you add a navigation bar to your website.

STEP 1 Edit index.html Add navigation bar ↓ State → Modified ✏️ ↓ STEP 2 Run git status Confirm file is modified ↓ STEP 3 Run git diff Review exact changes ↓ STEP 4 Run git add index.html ↓ State → Staged 📦 ↓ STEP 5 Run git diff --staged Review staged changes ↓ STEP 6 Run git commit -m "Add navigation bar" ↓ State → Committed ✅
All Three States Together

StateMeaningLocationMain Command
ModifiedYou changed the fileWorking Directorygit diff
StagedSelected for next commitStaging Areagit add
CommittedSaved in Git historyLocal Repositorygit log
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
Modified ✏️ "I changed it" ↓ git add ↓ Staged 📦 "I selected it for the next commit" ↓ git commit ↓ Committed ✅ "Git saved it in history"
Connection With Previous Topics

Topic 16 → git status Shows current states Topic 17 → git add Moves selected changes to Staging Area Topic 18 → git commit Saves staged changes in Local Repository Topic 20 → git log Shows committed history Topic 21 → git diff Shows exact unstaged changes Topic 22 → You now understand how these states connect ✅

One-Line Definition: Modified means a file has been changed in the Working Directory, Staged means the change has been selected in the Staging Area for the next commit, and Committed means the staged change has been saved as a commit in the local Git repository.
practice: Use your Git-Practice repository and follow the complete journey of one file.
STEP 1 → Modify a file ↓ Observe → Modified ✏️ ↓ STEP 2 → Stage the file ↓ Observe → Staged 📦 ↓ STEP 3 → Commit the file ↓ Observe → Committed ✅
Step 1: Open index.html, add a small heading, and save the file.
<h2>Modified Staged Committed Practice</h2>
Now check its state:
git status
Expected state: index.html → Modified ✏️
View exactly what changed:
git diff
Step 2: Stage the file.
git add index.html
Check the state again:
git status
Expected state: index.html → Staged 📦 Ready for the next commit
View the staged version:
git diff --staged
Step 3: Commit the staged change.
git commit -m "Add Git states practice heading"
Now check the repository:
git status
Expected result: Working tree clean ↓ Latest change committed ✅
Finally, confirm that the commit exists in your history:
git log
Modify ↓ Modified ✏️ ↓ git add ↓ Staged 📦 ↓ git commit ↓ Committed ✅ ↓ git log ↓ See the commit in history
Extra Practice: Modify both index.html and style.css, but stage only index.html. Run git status and observe that Git can show one file as staged while the other remains modified.
index.html → Modify + git add ↓ Staged 📦 style.css → Modify only ↓ Modified ✏️ Both states can exist at the same time ✅
Practice Goal: You should clearly understand this journey: I change a file → Modified. I run git add → Staged. I run git commit → Committed in local history.

qna.q: Q1. What does Modified mean in Git?
qna.a: Modified means you changed a file in the Working Directory, but the change has not yet been staged for the next commit.

qna.q: Q2. What does Staged mean in Git?
qna.a: Staged means the change has been selected and placed in the Staging Area for the next commit.

qna.q: Q3. What does Committed mean in Git?
qna.a: Committed means the staged change has been recorded as a commit in the local Git repository history.

qna.q: Q4. Which command moves a modified change to the Staging Area?
qna.a: git add

qna.q: Q5. Which command saves staged changes in the Local Repository?
qna.a: git commit

qna.q: Q6. Which command can show the exact unstaged changes?
qna.a: git diff

qna.q: Q7. Which command can show the exact staged changes?
qna.a: git diff --staged

qna.q: Q8. Can two files be in different Git states at the same time?
qna.a: Yes. For example, index.html can be staged while style.css remains modified.

qna.q: Q9. After running git add on a file, is it automatically committed?
qna.a: No. git add only stages the change. You still need to run git commit to save it in Git history.

qna.q: Q10. You stage index.html and then modify it again. Will the new modification automatically be included in the next commit?
qna.a: No. The newer modification must be staged again with git add if you want that newer version included in the next commit.

items.title: View Staged Changes (git diff --staged)
explanation: Simple Meaning
The command git diff --staged shows the changes that are currently in the Staging Area and will be included in your next commit.
Modify a file ↓ git add ↓ Changes enter Staging Area 📦 ↓ git diff --staged ↓ See what will be committed
Simple Rule: git diff shows unstaged changes, while git diff --staged shows staged changes.
Why Do We Need It?
Before creating a commit, you may want to check exactly what you staged.
Make changes ↓ git add ↓ Changes are staged ↓ Did I stage the correct changes? 🤔 ↓ git diff --staged ↓ Review before committing ✅

This helps you verify the contents of your next commit before running git commit. Git documents --staged as a synonym for --cached; it compares the staged changes with the last commit by default. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}
Basic Command
