git diff --staged
You can also use:
git diff --cached
Both commands mean the same thing for viewing changes staged for the next commit. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}
Where Does It Fit in the Git Workflow?
Working Directory Modify file ✏️ ↓ git diff ↓ View unstaged changes ↓ git add ↓ Staging Area 📦 ↓ git diff --staged ↓ View staged changes ↓ git commit ↓ Local Repository ✅
The main purpose is simple: use it to inspect the changes you have already selected for the next commit.
Simple Example
Suppose your last committed index.html contains:
<h1>Welcome</h1>
Now you change it to:
<h1>Welcome</h1> <h2>Learning Git</h2>
First, the file is modified. Run:
git diff
You can see the unstaged change.
Now stage it:
git add index.html
The change is now staged. Run:
git diff --staged
You can now see the exact change currently prepared for the next commit.
Example Output
The output may look similar to this:
- <h1>Welcome</h1> + <h1>Welcome</h1> + <h2>Learning Git</h2>
The important symbols are:

SymbolMeaning
-Line removed from the previous committed version
+Line added in the staged version
git diff vs git diff --staged
This is the most important comparison for this topic.

CommandShows
git diffChanges not yet staged
git diff --stagedChanges staged for the next commit
Working Directory Modified but not staged ✏️ ↓ git diff ==================== git add ↓ Staging Area Staged for commit 📦 ↓ git diff --staged

Git's documentation specifically describes git diff as comparing unstaged working-tree changes with the staging area, while git diff --staged shows what has been staged relative to the last commit. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}
Important: What Happens After git add?
Suppose you make a change and then run:
git add index.html
The change moves into the Staging Area.
Before git add ↓ Modified ✏️ ↓ git diff Shows change ✅ After git add ↓ Staged 📦 ↓ git diff Usually no longer shows that staged change ↓ git diff --staged Shows staged change ✅
If all your changes are staged, running plain git diff can produce no output because it only shows changes that are still unstaged. :contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}
View What Will Be in the Next Commit
This is an easy way to remember the command:
git diff --staged ↓ "What have I prepared for my next commit?"
If you run:
git commit -m "My commit message"
Git records the currently staged snapshot. Therefore, checking git diff --staged before committing helps you review that snapshot. :contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4}
Example With Two Files
Suppose you modify two files:
index.html → Modified ✏️ style.css → Modified ✏️
Now stage only one file:
git add index.html
The states are now:
index.html → Staged 📦 style.css → Modified ✏️
Run:
git diff
This shows the unstaged changes in style.css.
Run:
git diff --staged
This shows the staged changes in index.html.
git diff ↓ style.css changes ✏️ -------------------- git diff --staged ↓ index.html changes 📦
Using git status Together With git diff --staged
A useful workflow is:
git status git diff --staged
git status tells you which files are staged, while git diff --staged shows the exact content changes. :contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}
git status ↓ Which files are staged? ↓ git diff --staged ↓ What exactly changed inside them?
Important Example: Modify Again After Staging
Suppose you modify index.html and stage it:
Modify Version A ↓ git add index.html ↓ Version A is Staged 📦
Then you edit the same file again:
Staging Area → Version A 📦 Working Directory → Version B ✏️
Now run:
git diff
You see the newer unstaged difference between the Working Directory and the Staging Area.
Then run:
git diff --staged
You see the previously staged Version A compared with the last commit.

Important: git add stages the content as it exists when you run the command. If you change the file again and want those newer changes in the next commit, you need to run git add again. :contentReference[oaicite:6]{index=6}
Visual Example of the Same File

Last Commit Version 0 ↓ Modify file ↓ Version A ↓ git add ↓ Staging Area → Version A 📦 ↓ Modify file again ↓ Working Directory → Version B ✏️ Now: git diff → Shows B compared with staged A git diff --staged → Shows staged A compared with committed version 0
Why Review Staged Changes Before Commit?
Sometimes you may accidentally stage the wrong file or an unfinished change.
Modify many files ↓ git add files ↓ Something unnecessary may be staged 😬 ↓ git diff --staged ↓ Review changes ↓ Correct staging if needed ↓ git commit
Reviewing staged changes before committing is a good habit, especially as projects become larger.
Compare the Main Commands You Learned

CommandMain Purpose
git statusSee the current state of files
git diffSee exact unstaged changes
git addStage selected changes
git diff --stagedSee exact staged changes
git commitSave staged changes in local history
Complete Workflow

1. Edit index.html ↓ Modified ✏️ ↓ 2. git status ↓ See modified file ↓ 3. git diff ↓ Review unstaged changes ↓ 4. git add index.html ↓ Staged 📦 ↓ 5. git diff --staged ↓ Review what will be committed ↓ 6. git commit -m "Add homepage heading" ↓ Committed in Local Repository ✅
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
git diff → "What changed but I have NOT staged?" -------------------- git diff --staged → "What DID I stage for my next commit?"
One-Line Definition: git diff --staged displays the exact changes currently staged for the next commit, typically by comparing the Staging Area with the latest commit.
practice: Use your Git-Practice repository. Make sure your previous work is committed before starting.
STEP 1 → Modify index.html ↓ STEP 2 → Run git diff ↓ STEP 3 → Run git add ↓ STEP 4 → Run git diff --staged ↓ STEP 5 → Compare both commands ↓ STEP 6 → Commit
Step 1: Open index.html, add a small heading, and save the file.
<h2>Learning Staged Changes</h2>
Step 2: Check the exact unstaged change.
git status git diff
Current state: index.html → Modified ✏️ Command: git diff ↓ Shows the new heading
Step 3: Stage the file.
git add index.html
Step 4: Check the file state again.
git status
Current state: index.html → Staged 📦 Ready for the next commit
Step 5: Now run both commands separately and observe the difference.
git diff git diff --staged
git diff ↓ No output for the fully staged change -------------------- git diff --staged ↓ Shows the staged change ✅
Step 6: Modify the same file again after staging it. For example, add another line:
<p>This change is made after staging.</p>
Now run:
git diff git diff --staged
git diff ↓ Shows the NEW unstaged change ✏️ -------------------- git diff --staged ↓ Shows the EARLIER staged change 📦
This is the most important practice in this topic. It demonstrates that the Working Directory and Staging Area can contain different versions of the same file.
Step 7: If you want the newer change included in the commit, stage the file again.
git add index.html
Review the complete staged version:
git diff --staged
Step 8: Commit the changes.
git commit -m "Practice viewing staged changes"
Modified ✏️ ↓ git diff ↓ Staged 📦 ↓ git diff --staged ↓ Modify again ✏️ ↓ Working Directory and Staging Area differ ↓ git add again ↓ Review staged changes ↓ git commit ✅
Practice Goal: Clearly understand that git diff shows unstaged changes, while git diff --staged shows the changes currently prepared for your next commit.

qna.q: Q1. What does git diff --staged do?
qna.a: It shows the exact changes currently in the Staging Area that are prepared for the next commit.

qna.q: Q2. What is the difference between git diff and git diff --staged?
qna.a: git diff shows unstaged changes, while git diff --staged shows staged changes.

qna.q: Q3. Which command should you use to review what will be included in your next commit?
qna.a: git diff --staged

qna.q: Q4. Is git diff --staged the same as git diff --cached?
qna.a: Yes. --staged and --cached are synonyms for this purpose.

qna.q: Q5. What does git diff --staged typically compare by default?
qna.a: It compares the staged changes with the latest commit, also known as HEAD.

qna.q: Q6. If you stage all changes and run plain git diff, why might you see no output?
qna.a: Because plain git diff shows unstaged changes, and the changes have already been moved to the Staging Area.

qna.q: Q7. You run git add index.html and then modify index.html again. What does git diff --staged show?
qna.a: It shows the version that was staged when git add was run, compared with the last commit. The newer modification remains unstaged.

qna.q: Q8. If you modify a file after staging it, how do you include the new modification in the next commit?
qna.a: Run git add again after making the newer modification.

qna.q: Q9. Does git diff --staged create a commit?
qna.a: No. It only displays staged changes. You must run git commit to create a commit.

qna.q: Q10. What is a good workflow before committing?
qna.a: Modify files → git diff → git add → git diff --staged → review → git commit.

items.title: View Commit History (git log)
explanation: Simple Meaning
The command git log shows the history of commits in your Git repository.
Every time you run git commit, Git creates a new entry in the repository history. git log allows you to view those entries.
Commit 1 → Create project ↓ Commit 2 → Add login page ↓ Commit 3 → Add dashboard ↓ Commit 4 → Fix login bug ↓ git log ↓ View complete commit history 📜
Simple Rule: git commit creates history. git log shows that history.
Why Do We Need Commit History?
As your project grows, you may create many commits. Later, you may want to know what happened in the project.
Questions you may have: What changes were made? 🤔 Who created a commit? 👤 When was it created? 📅 What was the commit message? 💬 What is the commit ID? 🔑 ↓ git log ↓ Get commit history ✅
Commit history is one of the main reasons Git is useful because it creates a timeline of your project's development.
Basic Command
git log
Run this command inside a Git repository.
Git displays commits from the current branch, usually showing the newest commit first.
Newest Commit ↓ Commit 3 ↓ Commit 2 ↓ Commit 1 ↓ Oldest Commit
Simple Example
Suppose you create three commits:
git commit -m "Create project" git commit -m "Add login page" git commit -m "Add dashboard"
Now run:
git log
You may see output similar to:

commit a1b2c3d4e5f6... Author: Nethaji Date: Mon Sep 1 10:30:00 2026 +0530 Add dashboard commit b2c3d4e5f6a7... Author: Nethaji Date: Mon Sep 1 10:00:00 2026 +0530 Add login page commit c3d4e5f6a7b8... Author: Nethaji Date: Mon Sep 1 09:30:00 2026 +0530 Create project
The actual commit IDs, author names, and dates on your computer will be different.
Understanding git log Output
A normal git log entry contains several important pieces of information.
commit a1b2c3d4... ↓ Commit ID Author: Nethaji ↓ Who created the commit Date: Mon Sep 1... ↓ When the commit was created Add dashboard ↓ Commit message
1. Commit ID
Every commit has a unique identifier called a commit hash or commit ID.
commit a1b2c3d4e5f6...
The real commit ID is a long hexadecimal value. Git often allows you to use a shorter unique beginning portion when referring to a commit.
For now, remember:
Every Commit ↓ Has a unique ID 🔑 ↓ Used to identify that specific commit
2. Author
The Author field shows the name and email associated with the person who created the commit.
Author: Nethaji
This connects with the Git username and email configuration you learned earlier.
git config user.name ↓ Git records author information ↓ git commit ↓ Commit history shows author
3. Date
The Date field shows when the commit was created.
Date: Mon Sep 1 10:30:00 2026 +0530
This helps you understand the order and timeline of project changes.
4. Commit Message
The commit message explains the purpose of the commit.
Add dashboard
Good commit messages make the history easier to understand.
Bad history ❌ Update Changes Fixed Test -------------------- Clear history ✅ Create project Add login page Add dashboard Fix login validation
Commit History as a Project Timeline
You can think of git log as the timeline of your project.
Day 1 Commit → Create website ↓ Day 2 Commit → Add navigation ↓ Day 3 Commit → Add login page ↓ Day 4 Commit → Fix login validation ↓ Day 5 Run git log ↓ See project history 📜
git log vs git status
These commands answer different questions.

CommandMain Question
git statusWhat is happening right now?
git logWhat happened in previous commits?
git status ↓ Current state Modified? Staged? Clean? ==================== git log ↓ Previous history What commits were created?
git log vs git diff

CommandPurpose
git diffView changes that have not yet been committed
git logView commits that already exist in history
Current uncommitted changes ↓ git diff ==================== Already committed changes ↓ git log
Important: git log Shows Commits, Not Current Uncommitted Changes
Suppose you have this situation:
Commit 1 → Create index.html Commit 2 → Add login page ↓ You now modify index.html But do NOT commit it yet
If you run:
git log
You will see Commit 1 and Commit 2, but your new uncommitted modification will not appear as a new commit in the history.
Uncommitted change ✏️ ↓ git diff / git status Committed history 📜 ↓ git log
View a Shorter History with git log --oneline
Normal git log can display many details. For a shorter view, use:
git log --oneline
Example output:
a1b2c3d Add dashboard b2c3d4e Add login page c3d4e5f Create project
This usually shows a shortened commit ID and the commit message on one line.
Normal git log ↓ Detailed information -------------------- git log --oneline ↓ Short commit history
Why git log --oneline Is Useful
When your repository has many commits, the shorter view makes it easier to quickly understand the history.
a1b2c3d Add dashboard b2c3d4e Add login page c3d4e5f Create project Quick project timeline ✅
You will often use git log --oneline when you want a quick overview.
Viewing the Latest Few Commits
You can limit the number of commits displayed using:
git log -n 3
This displays the latest three commits.
You can change the number:
git log -n 5
git log -n 3 ↓ Latest 3 commits -------------------- git log -n 5 ↓ Latest 5 commits
Useful Combination: --oneline with a Limit
You can combine options:
git log --oneline -n 5
This gives a compact view of the latest five commits.
Short Commit ID → Commit Message Short Commit ID → Commit Message Short Commit ID → Commit Message Short Commit ID → Commit Message Short Commit ID → Commit Message
Understanding HEAD in the History
When you run git log, you may see something like:
commit a1b2c3d4... (HEAD -> main)
For now, understand this simply:
HEAD ↓ Points to your current commit
If you are currently working on the main branch, HEAD -> main means your current position is at the latest commit of that branch.
You will understand branches and HEAD in greater detail later in the branching section.
Complete Example
Suppose you perform these actions:

Create project ↓ git commit -m "Create project" ↓ Add index.html ↓ git commit -m "Add homepage" ↓ Add style.css ↓ git commit -m "Add website styles" ↓ Fix a CSS issue ↓ git commit -m "Fix navigation styling"
Now run:
git log --oneline
You may see:
f4e5d6c Fix navigation styling c3d4e5f Add website styles b2c3d4e Add homepage a1b2c3d Create project
The newest commit appears first, followed by older commits.
Useful Commands for Viewing History

CommandPurpose
git logView detailed commit history
git log --onelineView compact commit history
git log -n 3View latest 3 commits
git log --oneline -n 5View compact latest 5 commits
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
git status → What is happening NOW? -------------------- git diff → What changed but is not committed? -------------------- git log → What has ALREADY been committed?
Complete Git Flow So Far

Modify file ↓ git status ↓ Check current state ↓ git diff ↓ Review unstaged changes ↓ git add ↓ Stage changes ↓ git diff --staged ↓ Review staged changes ↓ git commit ↓ Create commit ↓ git log ↓ View commit history 📜
One-Line Definition: git log displays the commit history of a Git repository, allowing you to view previous commits, their IDs, authors, dates, and commit messages.
practice: Use your Git-Practice repository. Make sure you have at least 3 commits before starting this practice.
STEP 1 → Create or confirm multiple commits ↓ STEP 2 → Run git log ↓ STEP 3 → Identify commit details ↓ STEP 4 → Run git log --oneline ↓ STEP 5 → Compare detailed and compact history
Step 1: First check your current commit history.
git log
Look at each commit and try to identify:
Commit ID 🔑 Author 👤 Date 📅 Commit Message 💬
Step 2: Now view the same history in a shorter format.
git log --oneline
Compare the output with normal git log.
git log ↓ Detailed history ==================== git log --oneline ↓ Short history Same commits Different amount of detail
Step 3: View only the latest three commits.
git log -n 3
Check whether exactly three commits are displayed.
Step 4: Try a compact view of the latest two commits.
git log --oneline -n 2
Latest commit ↓ Previous commit Only 2 commits displayed ✅
Step 5: Make one small change to index.html, but do not stage or commit it.
<p>This change is not committed yet.</p>
Now run these commands:
git status git diff git log --oneline
git status → Shows current modified file -------------------- git diff → Shows exact uncommitted change -------------------- git log --oneline → Does NOT show the change as a new commit
This is important: a change appears in commit history only after it is staged and committed.
Final Step: Stage and commit the change.
git add index.html git commit -m "Add commit history practice text"
Now run:
git log --oneline
Before commit ↓ New change not in history ❌ After git commit ↓ New commit appears in history ✅
Practice Goal: Clearly understand that git log shows committed history, git log --oneline gives a compact history, and uncommitted changes do not appear as commits until you run git commit.

qna.q: Q1. What does git log do?
qna.a: git log displays the commit history of the current Git repository.

qna.q: Q2. Which command creates a new entry in Git history?
qna.a: git commit creates a new commit in Git history.

qna.q: Q3. What information can normal git log display?
qna.a: It can display information such as the commit ID, author, date, and commit message.

qna.q: Q4. Does git log show uncommitted changes as commits?
qna.a: No. git log shows commits that already exist in the repository history. Uncommitted changes do not appear as new commits.

qna.q: Q5. In what order are commits usually shown by git log?
qna.a: The newest commits are usually shown first, followed by older commits.

qna.q: Q6. What does git log --oneline do?
qna.a: It shows a compact version of commit history, usually with a shortened commit ID and commit message on each line.

qna.q: Q7. Which command can show only the latest three commits?
qna.a: git log -n 3

qna.q: Q8. What is a commit ID?
qna.a: A commit ID, also called a commit hash, is a unique identifier used to identify a specific commit.

qna.q: Q9. What is the difference between git status and git log?
qna.a: git status shows the current state of your working files, while git log shows the history of commits that were already created.

qna.q: Q10. What is the difference between git diff and git log?
qna.a: git diff is used to inspect changes that have not yet been committed, while git log is used to view commits already saved in repository history.

items.title: What is a Branch?
explanation: Simple Meaning
A branch in Git is an independent line of development. It allows you to work on changes without directly affecting the main line of your project.
main ↓ Project working code ✅ Create a branch ↓ feature-login ↓ Work on login feature separately
Simple Definition: A branch is a separate line of development where you can make changes independently.
Why Do We Need Branches?
Imagine your website is working correctly on the main branch.
main ↓ Website working perfectly ✅
Now you want to add a new login feature. The feature may take several days and you may make mistakes while developing it.
Instead of directly changing the working code on main, you can create a separate branch.
main → Working website ✅ \ \ feature-login → Build login feature 🚧
You can work on feature-login without directly changing the code on main.
Simple Real-World Example
Suppose your project currently has these files:
main │ ├── index.html ├── style.css └── script.js Website working ✅
You now want to add a login page.
Create a branch for the feature:
main │ └── feature-login
Then make your changes in the new branch:
main Website working version ✅ feature-login ├── Add login.html ├── Add login CSS └── Add login JavaScript
The development work happens separately until you decide the feature is ready.
What Does "Separate Line of Development" Mean?
Suppose your project has three commits.
Commit A → Create project ↓ Commit B → Add homepage ↓ Commit C → Add navigation ↓ main
At this point, you create a new branch called feature-login.
Commit A → Commit B → Commit C │ main │ └── feature-login
Both branches initially point to the same project history. After you start making commits on the new branch, their histories can develop separately.
Branch Development Example
Commit D → Add login page feature-login ↗ / Commit A → Commit B → Commit C \ main ↓ Working code remains unchanged
Now:

BranchState
mainContains the original working project
feature-loginContains the new login feature work
The Main Idea 🧠
A branch lets you experiment or build a feature safely.
main ↓ Stable code ✅ Create branch ↓ feature-new ↓ Try new changes 🧪 ↓ If successful → Merge later If unsuccessful → main is still unaffected
This separation is one of the biggest advantages of branches.
Branch Names
A branch has a name so Git can identify it.
Examples:
main feature-login feature-dashboard fix-login-bug update-homepage
Branch names should clearly describe the purpose of the work.
Good names ✅ feature-login fix-payment-bug update-dashboard -------------------- Unclear names ⚠️ branch1 newbranch test123
main Branch
Most repositories have a primary branch commonly named main.
You can think of it as the main line of development.
main ↓ Main project development ↓ Often contains stable code
Other branches are usually created from an existing branch and are later merged when their work is ready.
Important: main is just a branch name. Git does not technically treat it as a magical or special type of branch; it is commonly used as the primary branch name.
Branches and Commits
Branches work together with commits.
Create branch ↓ Make changes ↓ git add ↓ git commit ↓ Branch gets new commit history
A branch itself is not the same as a commit.

ConceptMeaning
CommitA saved snapshot in Git history
BranchA named line that points through a sequence of commits
Simple Analogy 📚
Imagine you are writing a book.
Main Book Version ↓ Working manuscript 📘
You want to try a completely different ending.
Main Version 📘 │ └── Alternative Ending Draft ✏️
You can write and test the alternative ending without destroying the original manuscript.
A Git branch works in a similar way: it gives you a separate path for development.
Multiple Branches Example
A project can have multiple branches at the same time.
feature-login / main ──────────── feature-dashboard \ fix-payment-bug
Different features or fixes can be developed independently.

BranchPurpose
mainMain project code
feature-loginDevelop login feature
feature-dashboardDevelop dashboard feature
fix-payment-bugFix a payment problem
Important: Creating a Branch Does Not Automatically Change Branches
This is important for the next topics.
You can create a branch, but Git may keep you on your current branch depending on the command you use.
Currently on: main ↓ Create feature-login branch ↓ feature-login exists ✅ ↓ But you may still be working on main
You will learn the exact commands for creating and switching branches in the upcoming topics.
Branch Workflow
main Stable project ✅ ↓ Create feature branch ↓ feature-login ↓ Make changes ↓ Test changes ↓ Create commits ↓ Feature completed ↓ Merge into main ↓ main contains new feature ✅
What Happens After the Feature Is Complete?
After the work in a branch is finished and tested, you can combine it with another branch using merge.
main Commit A → Commit B \ feature-login Commit C → Commit D ↓ Merge ↓ main now includes login feature ✅
You will learn merging in detail later. For now, remember that branches allow separate development and merging combines development histories.
Branch vs Repository
These two concepts are different.

ConceptMeaning
RepositoryThe complete Git project containing files and history
BranchA separate line of development inside the repository
Repository 📁 │ ├── main branch │ ├── feature-login branch │ └── fix-bug branch
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
Repository → The complete project Commit → A saved point in history Branch → A separate development path Merge → Combine branch work
Complete Example

START ↓ main Website is working ✅ ↓ Need new login feature ↓ Create feature-login branch ↓ Work independently 🚧 ↓ Add login page ↓ Add validation ↓ Commit changes ↓ Test feature ↓ Merge into main ↓ main now contains the feature ✅
One-Line Definition: A Git branch is an independent line of development that allows you to work on features, fixes, or experiments separately without directly affecting another branch such as main.
practice: For this first branch topic, focus mainly on understanding the concept. The next topics will teach you the commands to create, switch, list, and delete branches.
SCENARIO ↓ main → Website is working ✅ ↓ You need to add a login feature ↓ Would you change main directly? 🤔 ↓ Create a separate branch ↓ feature-login 🚧 ↓ Develop safely ↓ Merge later when ready
Practice Task 1: Imagine your current website is working correctly on the main branch. Write down three features that you might develop in separate branches.
Example: feature-login feature-dashboard fix-navigation-bug
Practice Task 2: For each situation below, decide whether creating a separate branch would be useful.
1. Adding a completely new payment feature 2. Experimenting with a new homepage design 3. Fixing a serious login bug 4. Adding a dashboard Think: Could this work be developed separately from main?
Practice Task 3: Understand this history before moving to the next topic.
Commit A → Commit B → Commit C │ main │ └── feature-login
Both branches can initially start from the same commit. After new commits are created on one branch, their development can become different.
Practice Goal: Clearly understand that a branch is a separate line of development. You do not need to memorize branch commands yet because those are covered in the next topics.

qna.q: Q1. What is a branch in Git?
qna.a: A branch is an independent line of development where you can make changes separately from another branch.

qna.q: Q2. Why are branches useful?
qna.a: Branches allow you to develop features, fix bugs, or experiment with changes without directly affecting the main line of development.

qna.q: Q3. What is main?
qna.a: main is commonly used as the primary branch of a repository. It is a branch name, not a special type of Git object.

qna.q: Q4. Is a branch the same as a commit?
qna.a: No. A commit is a saved snapshot in Git history, while a branch represents a named line of development through commits.

qna.q: Q5. Can a repository have multiple branches?
qna.a: Yes. A repository can have multiple branches for different features, bug fixes, experiments, or other development work.

qna.q: Q6. Give an example of a useful branch name.
qna.a: Examples include feature-login, feature-dashboard, fix-payment-bug, and update-homepage.

qna.q: Q7. What is the main benefit of developing a feature in a separate branch?
qna.a: You can work on the feature independently without directly changing the code on the main branch.

qna.q: Q8. What can happen after work on a branch is completed?
qna.a: The completed and tested work can be merged into another branch, such as main.

qna.q: Q9. Does creating a branch automatically mean you are now working on that branch?
qna.a: Not necessarily. Creating and switching branches are separate concepts depending on the command used.

qna.q: Q10. Repository vs Branch — what is the difference?
qna.a: A repository is the complete Git project containing files and history, while a branch is a separate line of development inside that repository.

items.title: Why Branches Are Used
explanation: Simple Meaning
Branches are used to work on different features, bug fixes, or experiments separately without directly affecting the main working code.
main ↓ Working project ✅ Need a new feature ↓ Create separate branch ↓ Work independently 🚧 ↓ Test changes ↓ Merge when ready
Simple Rule: Use branches when you want to make changes separately and keep the main code safe from unfinished work.
Main Problem Without Branches
Imagine your website is working correctly and all your work is directly done on main.
main ↓ Website working perfectly ✅ ↓ Start building a new feature ↓ Modify existing files directly ↓ Feature is unfinished 🚧 ↓ Something breaks ❌ ↓ main is now affected
This can make development risky because unfinished or experimental changes are mixed with your main project code.
Solution: Use a Branch
Instead of directly working on main, create a separate branch for the work.
main Working project ✅ │ ├── feature-login 🚧 │ └── fix-navbar-bug 🛠️
Each piece of work can be developed independently. The main branch remains unchanged until you intentionally merge the completed work.
Reason 1: Develop New Features Safely ⭐
This is one of the most common reasons for using branches.
Suppose your website is live and working:
main ↓ Homepage ✅ Login ✅ Dashboard ✅
Now you want to add a payment feature that may require many changes.
main Working project ✅ │ └── feature-payment ↓ Add payment page ↓ Add validation ↓ Test feature ↓ Ready? → Merge into main
The unfinished payment work stays separate until it is ready.
Reason 2: Keep main Stable ⭐
A common workflow is to keep main as stable as possible.
main ↓ Stable code ✅ -------------------- feature-login ↓ New development 🚧 -------------------- fix-payment-bug ↓ Bug fix 🛠️
You can make many commits while developing on another branch without those commits changing the current code on main.
Important: Changes from one branch are not added to another branch automatically. You normally combine branch work intentionally using operations such as merging.
Reason 3: Work on Multiple Things at the Same Time
Projects often need multiple pieces of work at the same time.
Repository │ ├── main │ Stable project ✅ │ ├── feature-login │ New login feature 🚧 │ ├── feature-dashboard │ New dashboard 🚧 │ └── fix-navbar-bug Bug fix 🛠️
Branches help organize these different tasks so their development histories can remain separate.
Example: One Developer
Branches are useful even when you are working alone.
You are working alone 👤 ↓ main → Working website ↓ Create feature-dark-mode ↓ Experiment with dark mode ↓ Test it ↓ If good → Merge If not good → Do not merge
You do not need a team to benefit from branches.
Reason 4: Experiment Without Affecting Main
Sometimes you want to try an idea but you are not sure whether it will work.
main ↓ Current design ✅ │ └── experiment-new-design ↓ Try different layout 🧪 ↓ Try new colors ↓ Try different navigation ↓ Decide later
If the experiment is successful, you can later integrate it. If you do not want the experiment, your main branch remains unchanged by those branch commits.
Reason 5: Fix Bugs Separately
Branches are also useful for bug fixes.
main ↓ Website working ↓ Login bug discovered 🐛 ↓ Create fix-login-bug branch ↓ Investigate problem ↓ Fix code ↓ Test fix ↓ Merge fix into main
A clear branch name also makes the purpose of the work easier to understand.
fix-login-bug
Reason 6: Separate Unfinished Work
Some features take several hours, days, or even weeks to complete.
Day 1 → Start feature Day 2 → Add some code Day 3 → Find a problem Day 4 → Continue development Day 5 → Test feature Day 6 → Feature complete
Instead of mixing all this unfinished development directly into the main project line, you can keep it on a feature branch until it is ready.
main → Stable version ✅ feature-new → Day 1 🚧 Day 2 🚧 Day 3 🚧 Day 4 🚧 Day 5 🚧 Day 6 Complete ✅
Reason 7: Easier Code Review
In a team, a branch can represent one specific piece of work.
feature-login ↓ Only login-related changes ↓ Review changes ↓ Check code ↓ Test feature ↓ Merge when approved
This makes it easier to understand what a set of changes is intended to do compared with mixing many unrelated changes together.
Example: Team Workflow
main Stable project │ ├── Developer A │ └── feature-login │ ↓ │ Builds login feature │ ├── Developer B │ └── feature-dashboard │ ↓ │ Builds dashboard │ └── Developer C └── fix-payment-bug ↓ Fixes bug
Each developer can work on a separate task. When the work is ready, it can be reviewed and integrated into the main development line according to the team's workflow.
Reason 8: Organize Project Development
Branches can make the purpose of different development work clear.

BranchPurpose
mainMain project development
feature-loginDevelop login feature
feature-searchDevelop search feature
fix-payment-bugFix payment problem
experiment-uiTest a UI idea
Without Branches vs With Branches

Without BranchesWith Branches
All work happens directly on mainWork can be separated by task
Unfinished work can mix with stable codeUnfinished work can remain on a feature branch
Experiments directly affect the current branchExperiments can be developed separately
Multiple tasks become harder to organizeFeatures and fixes can have separate branches
Changes are mixed togetherWork can be grouped by purpose
Important Example
Imagine your project has two urgent tasks:
Task 1 → Add new dashboard feature 🚧 Task 2 → Fix critical login bug 🐛
Using branches, you could organize the work like this:
main │ ├── feature-dashboard │ ↓ │ Continue developing dashboard │ └── fix-login-bug ↓ Fix and test login bug
The two tasks can have separate commits and histories instead of being mixed into one line of development.
Branch Does Not Mean a Copy of the Entire Project
For beginners, it is useful to avoid thinking of every branch as manually creating a completely separate folder containing a full project copy.
Conceptually, a branch is a separate line of development through Git's commit history.
Commit A → Commit B → Commit C │ main │ └── feature-login ↓ Commit D → Commit E
Git manages this history efficiently. The important concept for now is that commits can develop differently after branches diverge.
Most Common Branch Workflow
1. main Stable code ✅ ↓ 2. Create feature branch ↓ 3. Work on feature ↓ 4. Create commits ↓ 5. Test changes ↓ 6. Review changes ↓ 7. Merge into main ↓ 8. main updated with completed feature ✅
Real Example: Adding a Search Feature

START ↓ main → Website working ✅ ↓ Need search feature ↓ Create feature-search ↓ Add search input ↓ Add search logic ↓ Fix problems ↓ Create commits ↓ Test feature ↓ Feature ready ↓ Merge into main ↓ Website now includes search ✅
When You Should Think About Creating a Branch
Ask yourself:

Am I adding a new feature? → Probably create a branch Am I fixing a bug? → A separate branch can be useful Am I testing an idea? → A separate branch is useful Am I making a large change? → A separate branch is useful Am I working on a separate task? → Consider a branch
The exact branching workflow can vary between projects and teams, but the core purpose remains separation of development work.
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
main → Main/stable development line feature branch → Build something new bug-fix branch → Fix a problem experiment branch → Try an idea Merge → Intentionally combine completed work
Complete Comparison

WITHOUT BRANCH main ↓ Add feature ↓ Make unfinished changes ↓ Possible problems affect main ❌ ==================== WITH BRANCH main → Stable code ✅ │ └── feature-new ↓ Develop separately 🚧 ↓ Test ↓ Ready? ↓ Merge into main ✅

One-Line Definition: Git branches are used to separate development work, allowing developers to build features, fix bugs, experiment, and collaborate without directly mixing unfinished changes into the main line of development.
practice: For this topic, focus on understanding why branches are used. The next topics will teach you the commands to create and switch branches.

SCENARIO ↓ main → Website working perfectly ✅ ↓ You need to build 3 different things ↓ Login feature Dashboard feature Fix navigation bug ↓ Should all work be mixed directly into main? 🤔 ↓ Use separate branches
Practice Task 1: Organize the following work into suitable branch names.
Task 1 → Add dark mode Task 2 → Fix login validation Task 3 → Build user dashboard Task 4 → Experiment with a new homepage design
Example thinking:
New feature → feature-... Bug fix → fix-... Experiment → experiment-...
Practice Task 2: Read this situation and explain why a branch is useful.
main → Website is live and working ✅ ↓ You want to completely redesign the homepage ↓ The work may take several days ↓ You are not sure the new design will be successful
Think about what could happen if you directly make all unfinished changes on main versus working on a separate branch.
Practice Task 3: Understand this team situation.
Developer A → Login feature Developer B → Dashboard feature Developer C → Payment bug fix
Create a mental branch structure for this work.
main │ ├── ? ├── ? └── ?
Practice Goal: Before learning branch commands, clearly understand the main reason for branches: separate the work, develop safely, and integrate completed changes when ready.

qna.q: Q1. What is the main reason branches are used?
qna.a: Branches are used to separate development work so features, bug fixes, and experiments can be developed without directly mixing unfinished changes into the main line of development.

qna.q: Q2. Why should you avoid doing all unfinished work directly on main?
qna.a: Because unfinished or experimental changes can mix with the main project code and make the main development line less stable.

qna.q: Q3. Are branches useful only for teams?
qna.a: No. Branches are useful for both individual developers and teams.

qna.q: Q4. Give three common reasons to create a branch.
qna.a: Common reasons include developing a new feature, fixing a bug, and experimenting with a new idea.

qna.q: Q5. What is the benefit of a feature branch?
qna.a: It allows a new feature to be developed and tested separately before it is intentionally integrated into another branch such as main.

qna.q: Q6. Can multiple tasks have separate branches?
qna.a: Yes. For example, feature-login, feature-dashboard, and fix-payment-bug can all be separate branches.

qna.q: Q7. If you create commits on a feature branch, are those changes automatically added to main?
qna.a: No. Branch changes are not automatically added to main. They must be intentionally integrated using an appropriate Git operation such as merging.

qna.q: Q8. Why are branches useful for experiments?
qna.a: They allow you to try changes on a separate line of development without directly adding the experimental commits to main.

qna.q: Q9. How can branches help a team?
qna.a: Different developers can work on separate features or bug fixes with separate branches, making the work easier to organize and review.

qna.q: Q10. What should you remember before learning branch commands?
qna.a: Branches are mainly used to separate development work, keep tasks organized, allow safer experimentation, and integrate completed work when appropriate.

items.title: Create a Branch
explanation: Simple Meaning
Creating a branch means creating a new line of development from your current commit.
You can use the new branch to work on a feature, bug fix, or experiment separately.
main ↓ Current project code ↓ Create new branch ↓ feature-login ↓ New development path created ✅
Simple Definition: Creating a branch creates a new named line of development that starts from your current commit.
Basic Command
To create a branch:
git branch branch-name
Example:
git branch feature-login
This creates a new branch named feature-login.
Important: Create Does Not Mean Switch ⭐
This is one of the most important things to understand.
Suppose you are currently on main:
Current branch ↓ main
Now run:
git branch feature-login
Git creates the branch:
Branches now exist: main feature-login ✅
But you are still working on main.
Before command: Current branch → main Run: git branch feature-login After command: Current branch → main New branch exists → feature-login
Important Rule: git branch feature-login creates the branch but does not automatically move you to it.
Simple Example
Suppose your repository currently has this history:
Commit A → Commit B → Commit C ↑ main
You are currently on main. Now run:
git branch feature-login
The new branch starts from the current commit:
Commit A → Commit B → Commit C ↑ ↑ main feature-login
At this moment, both branches point to the same commit.
What Happens After You Create the Branch?
Creating a branch does not immediately create a new commit.
Before creating branch: main → Commit C -------------------- After creating branch: main → Commit C feature-login → Commit C
The branch is simply created at your current position in the commit history.
Later, when you switch to that branch and create new commits, the histories can become different.
Example After New Commits
Suppose you create feature-login and later switch to it.
Initially: Commit A → Commit B → Commit C ↑ main + feature-login
Then you work on feature-login and create a new commit:
Commit A → Commit B → Commit C ↑ \ main Commit D ↑ feature-login
Now the branches point to different commits.
Create a Branch from Your Current Branch
A new branch is normally created from the commit where you are currently positioned.
For example:
You are currently on main ↓ main points to Commit C ↓ Run git branch feature-login ↓ feature-login also starts at Commit C
This is why you should know your current branch before creating a new branch.
Check Your Current Branch First
You can check the status of your repository using:
git status
Git may show information about the branch you are currently working on.
You can also list branches using:
git branch
The branch with an asterisk (*) is your current branch.
* main feature-login feature-dashboard
In this example, main is the current branch.
Common Branch Naming Examples
Choose a branch name that clearly explains its purpose.

Branch NamePurpose
feature-loginAdd a login feature
feature-dashboardAdd a dashboard
fix-login-bugFix a login problem
update-homepageUpdate the homepage
experiment-new-uiTest a new UI idea
Good vs Unclear Branch Names
Good names ✅ feature-login fix-payment-bug feature-dark-mode update-dashboard -------------------- Unclear names ⚠️ branch1 newbranch test123 abc
A meaningful name makes it easier to understand the purpose of the branch later, especially in team projects.
Step-by-Step Example
Suppose you are working on a website project.

STEP 1 Current branch → main Website is working ✅ ↓ STEP 2 Need a login feature ↓ STEP 3 Create a branch git branch feature-login ↓ STEP 4 Branches now exist main feature-login ↓ STEP 5 You are still on main ⚠️
Create Multiple Branches
A repository can contain multiple branches.
For example:
git branch feature-login git branch feature-dashboard git branch fix-navbar-bug
Your repository may now have:
Repository │ ├── main ├── feature-login ├── feature-dashboard └── fix-navbar-bug
Creating multiple branches is possible, but remember that each branch should normally have a clear purpose.
Branch Creation vs Branch Switching
These are two different actions.

ActionMeaning
Create branchCreate a new branch name and development line
Switch branchMove your working position to another branch
CREATE ↓ git branch feature-login ↓ New branch exists ==================== SWITCH ↓ Move from main to feature-login ↓ Start working on that branch
You will learn branch switching in the next topic.
Older vs Modern Commands
Git provides different commands for branch-related operations.
For this topic, focus on this command:
git branch feature-name
Later, you will learn modern commands such as:
git switch feature-name git switch -c feature-name
You will also see the older command:
git checkout feature-name
Do not worry about memorizing all of them yet. First clearly understand the difference between creating and switching.
Important Scenario ⭐
Imagine you run:
git branch feature-login
Then you immediately edit index.html and commit your changes without switching branches.
Where will the commit be created?
You were on main ↓ Created feature-login ↓ Still on main ↓ Edit file ↓ Commit ↓ Commit goes to main ⚠️
This is why understanding your current branch is extremely important.
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
git branch feature-login ↓ CREATE a new branch 🌱 But... You remain on your current branch 📍 -------------------- Create ≠ Switch
Complete Example

START ↓ Current branch → main ↓ Current commit → C ↓ Run: git branch feature-login ↓ New branch created ↓ main → Commit C feature-login → Commit C ↓ Current branch is still → main ↓ Need to switch before working on feature-login
Common Beginner Mistake
A common mistake is thinking this command:
git branch feature-login
means:
Create feature-login AND Automatically start working there ❌
It only means:
Create feature-login branch ✅
Switching is a separate step.
Summary

ConceptMeaning
git branch nameCreates a new branch
New branch starting pointNormally the current commit
Creates a commit?No
Automatically switches?No
Why create it?To develop work separately
One-Line Definition: git branch branch-name creates a new branch from your current commit, allowing a separate line of development, but it does not automatically switch you to the new branch.
practice: Use your existing Git-Practice repository. Make sure you are inside the repository before running the commands.
STEP 1 → Check current branch ↓ STEP 2 → Create feature-login ↓ STEP 3 → List branches ↓ STEP 4 → Confirm current branch ↓ STEP 5 → Create one more branch
Step 1: Check your repository status.
git status
Identify which branch you are currently working on.
Step 2: Create a new branch called feature-login.
git branch feature-login
If no error appears, the branch was created successfully.
Step 3: List all branches.
git branch
You should see something similar to:
* main feature-login
* main ↓ Current branch 📍 feature-login ↓ Branch exists but is not currently active
Step 4: Create another branch.
git branch feature-dashboard
Then list your branches again:
git branch
You should now see your current branch and the two newly created branches.
Step 5: Confirm the most important concept from this topic.
Run: git branch feature-login Result: feature-login is created ✅ But: You are still on your previous branch 📍
Practice Challenge: Without making any file changes, create these branches:
feature-profile fix-header-bug experiment-dark-mode
Use git branch afterward to verify that all branches exist.
Practice Goal: Be able to create branches and clearly understand that git branch branch-name creates a branch but does not automatically switch your current working branch.

qna.q: Q1. Which command is used to create a branch?
qna.a: git branch branch-name

qna.q: Q2. How do you create a branch called feature-login?
qna.a: git branch feature-login

qna.q: Q3. Does git branch feature-login automatically switch you to feature-login?
qna.a: No. It creates the branch but keeps you on your current branch.

qna.q: Q4. What is the most important concept in this topic?
qna.a: Creating a branch and switching to a branch are different actions. Create does not automatically mean switch.

qna.q: Q5. Where does a newly created branch normally start?
qna.a: It normally starts from the commit where you are currently positioned.

qna.q: Q6. Does creating a branch automatically create a new commit?
qna.a: No. Creating a branch does not automatically create a new commit.

qna.q: Q7. Which command can you use to list branches?
qna.a: git branch

qna.q: Q8. What does the * symbol indicate when using git branch?
qna.a: It indicates the branch you are currently working on.

qna.q: Q9. If you are on main, create feature-login, and then commit without switching, where will the commit go?
qna.a: The commit will be created on main because you are still working on main.

qna.q: Q10. Why should branch names be meaningful?
qna.a: Meaningful branch names make it easier to understand the purpose of the work, especially when multiple branches or developers are involved.

items.title: Switch Branches
explanation: Simple Meaning
Switching branches means changing your current working branch from one branch to another.
For example, if you are currently working on main, you can switch to feature-login and start working on that branch.
Current branch → main 📍 ↓ Switch branch ↓ Current branch → feature-login 📍
Simple Definition: Switching branches means moving your current working position from one branch to another.
Why Do We Need to Switch Branches?
In the previous topic, you learned that this command creates a branch:
git branch feature-login
But creating a branch does not automatically move you to it.
Run: git branch feature-login Result: main → Current branch 📍 feature-login → Created ✅
To start working on feature-login, you need to switch to it.
Modern Command: git switch ⭐
The modern Git command for switching to an existing branch is:
git switch branch-name
Example:
git switch feature-login
Before: Current branch → main 📍 Run: git switch feature-login After: Current branch → feature-login 📍
Now your working branch is feature-login.
Step-by-Step Example
Suppose your repository has these branches:
main feature-login feature-dashboard
You are currently on main:
* main feature-login feature-dashboard
The * shows your current branch.
Now run:
git switch feature-login
Check the branches again:
git branch
You should now see:
main * feature-login feature-dashboard
You successfully switched from main to feature-login.
What Changes When You Switch Branches?
Different branches can point to different commits. Therefore, when you switch branches, the files in your working directory can also change to match the branch you switched to.
main ↓ index.html style.css ==================== feature-login ↓ index.html style.css login.html
If login.html exists only in feature-login, switching from main to feature-login can make that branch's version of the project your current working files.
Simple Branch History Example
Suppose both branches originally started at Commit C:
Commit A → Commit B → Commit C ↑ main + feature-login
You switch to feature-login and create two new commits:
Commit A → Commit B → Commit C → Commit D → Commit E ↑ ↑ main feature-login
Now the branches point to different commits.
If you switch back to main, Git moves your current working position back to the commit currently pointed to by main.
Switch Back to main
If you are currently on feature-login and want to return to main:
git switch main
Current branch → feature-login 📍 ↓ git switch main ↓ Current branch → main 📍
Check Your Current Branch
You can use:
git branch
Example:
main * feature-login feature-dashboard
The * indicates the currently active branch.
You can also run:
git status
Git will show information about the branch you are currently working on.
Create vs Switch
These are different actions and use different commands.

ActionCommandResult
Create branchgit branch feature-loginCreates the branch
Switch branchgit switch feature-loginMoves to that branch
git branch feature-login ↓ Create branch 🌱 -------------------- git switch feature-login ↓ Move to branch 📍
Important: The Branch Must Already Exist
The basic git switch branch-name command switches to an existing branch.
For example:
git switch feature-login
This requires feature-login to already exist.
feature-login exists? ✅ ↓ git switch feature-login ↓ Successfully switch
If the branch does not exist, Git cannot switch to it using this basic form.
You will learn how to create and switch in one command using git switch -c in the next topic.
Older Command: git checkout
Before git switch was introduced, git checkout was commonly used to switch branches.
git checkout feature-login
This can also switch you to an existing branch.

CommandPurpose Here
git switch feature-loginModern command to switch branches
git checkout feature-loginOlder commonly used command to switch branches
For learning, understand both commands because you may see git checkout in older tutorials and existing projects.
Why Prefer git switch for Branch Switching?
The command git switch was introduced to make branch switching clearer.
git switch feature-login ↓ Clear intention: Switch branches 🔄 -------------------- git checkout ↓ Older command with multiple uses
For your roadmap, learn git switch as the modern branch-switching command, while also understanding git checkout for older workflows.
Switching Between Multiple Branches
Suppose your repository contains:
main feature-login feature-dashboard fix-navbar-bug
You can move between them when needed:
main ↓ git switch feature-login ↓ feature-login 📍 ↓ git switch feature-dashboard ↓ feature-dashboard 📍 ↓ git switch main ↓ main 📍
Only one branch is your current working branch at a time.
Important: One Current Branch at a Time
Repository │ ├── main ├── feature-login ├── feature-dashboard └── fix-navbar-bug ↓ You can work on one current branch at a time 📍
Switching changes which branch is currently checked out for your working directory.
What About Uncommitted Changes? ⚠️
Before switching branches, always be aware of your uncommitted changes.
For example:
Currently on feature-login ↓ Modify index.html ✏️ ↓ Do not commit changes ↓ Try to switch to main
Depending on the changes and the target branch, Git may allow the switch, carry changes that do not conflict, or stop you because switching could overwrite or conflict with your work.
Therefore, before switching branches, check:
git status
Good Habit: Before switching branches, run git status and understand whether you have uncommitted changes.
Safe Beginner Workflow
Check current state ↓ git status ↓ Any unfinished changes? 🤔 ↓ Understand/save/commit them as needed ↓ Switch branch ↓ git switch branch-name ↓ Check current branch again
Example: Complete Workflow
Suppose you previously created the branch feature-login.

STEP 1 Current branch → main 📍 ↓ STEP 2 Create branch git branch feature-login ↓ STEP 3 Branch exists But still on main ↓ STEP 4 Switch branch git switch feature-login ↓ STEP 5 Current branch → feature-login 📍 ↓ STEP 6 Now make feature changes
Common Beginner Mistake
Suppose you create a branch:
git branch feature-login
You then start editing files, believing you are working on feature-login.
But if you never switched branches:
Current branch → main 📍 ↓ Edit files ↓ git commit ↓ Changes committed to main ⚠️
The correct workflow is:
Create branch ↓ git branch feature-login ↓ Switch branch ↓ git switch feature-login ↓ Confirm current branch ↓ Make changes ↓ Commit
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
git branch → Create 🌱 -------------------- git switch → Move / Switch 🔄 -------------------- git branch + git switch → Create first, then start working there
Commands Summary

CommandPurpose
git branchList branches
git branch feature-nameCreate a branch
git switch feature-nameSwitch to an existing branch
git checkout feature-nameOlder command for switching to a branch
git statusCheck current repository state
Complete Branch Flow So Far

main Current branch 📍 ↓ Need new feature ↓ git branch feature-login ↓ Branch created 🌱 ↓ Still on main ⚠️ ↓ git switch feature-login ↓ Now on feature-login 📍 ↓ Make changes ↓ git add ↓ git commit ↓ Feature development history begins
One-Line Definition: git switch branch-name is used to move from your current branch to an existing branch, making that branch your current working branch.
practice: Use your existing Git-Practice repository. You should already have at least one branch besides main, such as feature-login.
STEP 1 → List branches ↓ STEP 2 → Check current branch ↓ STEP 3 → Switch to feature-login ↓ STEP 4 → Verify the switch ↓ STEP 5 → Switch back to main ↓ STEP 6 → Practice switching again
Step 1: List all available branches.
git branch
Identify the branch containing the *. That is your current branch.
Step 2: Switch to feature-login.
git switch feature-login
If your branch has a different name, use that branch name instead.
Step 3: Verify that you successfully switched branches.
git branch
You should see something similar to:
main * feature-login
* feature-login ↓ Current working branch 📍
Step 4: Switch back to main.
git switch main
Verify it again:
git branch
* main ↓ You successfully returned to main 📍
Step 5: Practice switching between your branches multiple times.
git switch feature-login git switch main git switch feature-dashboard git switch main
Only use branch names that already exist in your repository.
Step 6: Before switching, practice checking the repository state.
git status git switch feature-login
Make git status a habit when you have been working on files and want to move to another branch.
Practice Challenge: Complete this flow without looking at the answer.
Start on main ↓ Create branch: feature-profile ↓ Switch to feature-profile ↓ Verify current branch ↓ Switch back to main ↓ Verify current branch again
Hint: You already learned the command for creating a branch in Topic 27. This topic teaches you how to switch to it.

Practice Goal: Be able to identify your current branch, switch to an existing branch using git switch, verify the switch using git branch, and understand that only one branch is your current working branch at a time.

qna.q: Q1. What does switching branches mean?
qna.a: Switching branches means moving your current working position from one branch to another branch.

qna.q: Q2. What is the modern command for switching to an existing branch?
qna.a: git switch branch-name

qna.q: Q3. How do you switch to a branch named feature-login?
qna.a: git switch feature-login

qna.q: Q4. Does git switch feature-login create the branch if it does not already exist?
qna.a: No. The basic git switch feature-login command is used to switch to an existing branch.

qna.q: Q5. Which older command can also be used to switch branches?
qna.a: git checkout branch-name

qna.q: Q6. How can you identify your current branch using git branch?
qna.a: The branch marked with an asterisk (*) is your current branch.

qna.q: Q7. Can you work on multiple current branches at exactly the same time in one working directory?
qna.a: No. One branch is your current working branch at a time in the working directory.

qna.q: Q8. What can happen to your working files when switching branches?
qna.a: Your working files can change to match the commit and project state of the branch you switched to.

qna.q: Q9. What should you check before switching branches when you have been making changes?
qna.a: You should run git status and understand whether you have uncommitted changes.

qna.q: Q10. What is the difference between git branch feature-login and git switch feature-login?
qna.a: git branch feature-login creates the branch, while git switch feature-login moves you to the existing feature-login branch.

items.title: List Branches
explanation: Simple Meaning
Listing branches means viewing the branches that currently exist in your Git repository.
The basic command is:
git branch
This command helps you see your available branches and identify which branch you are currently working on.
Simple Definition: git branch displays the local branches available in your repository and marks your current branch with *.
Basic Command
git branch
Suppose your repository contains three branches. The output may look like this:
feature-dashboard feature-login * main
The * is very important.
feature-dashboard feature-login * main ↑ Current branch 📍
This means you are currently working on the main branch.
How to Identify Your Current Branch ⭐
When you run git branch, Git places an asterisk (*) before your current branch.
Example 1 * main feature-login Current branch → main 📍 ==================== Example 2 main * feature-login Current branch → feature-login 📍
Only one branch is marked as your current branch in the normal working directory.
Why Is Listing Branches Useful?
The command git branch is useful when you want to know which branches exist before switching, merging, or deleting a branch.
Need to switch branches? ↓ Run git branch ↓ See available branches ↓ Choose the correct branch ↓ Switch
It also helps prevent mistakes such as trying to switch to a branch name that does not exist.
Example: After Creating Branches
Suppose you previously ran these commands:
git branch feature-login git branch feature-dashboard git branch fix-navbar-bug
Now run:
git branch
You may see:
feature-dashboard feature-login fix-navbar-bug * main
This tells you:
Branches available: ↓ feature-dashboard feature-login fix-navbar-bug main Current branch: ↓ main 📍
Listing Branches After Switching
Suppose you switch to feature-login:
git switch feature-login
Now run:
git branch
The output may look like:
feature-dashboard * feature-login fix-navbar-bug main
The branches are still available, but the * has moved.
Before switching: * main 📍 feature-login ↓ git switch feature-login ↓ After switching: main * feature-login 📍
git branch Does More Than List Branches
You already learned that git branch can also be used to create branches.

CommandPurpose
git branchList local branches
git branch feature-loginCreate a branch named feature-login
The difference is simple:
No branch name ↓ git branch ↓ List branches 📋 ==================== Branch name provided ↓ git branch feature-login ↓ Create branch 🌱
Example: Branch Workflow So Far

STEP 1 Start on main * main 📍 ↓ STEP 2 Create branch git branch feature-login ↓ STEP 3 List branches git branch ↓ * main feature-login ↓ STEP 4 Switch branch git switch feature-login ↓ STEP 5 List again git branch ↓ main * feature-login 📍
Local Branches
The basic command:
git branch
shows your local branches.
At this stage of your roadmap, think of these as the branches currently available in your local Git repository.
Your Computer 💻 ↓ Local Repository ↓ main feature-login feature-dashboard
Later, when you connect your repository to GitHub, you will also learn about remote branches.
Remote Branches Preview
After working with GitHub, a repository may have branches stored remotely as well.
Git provides options for viewing different types of branches:

CommandPurpose
git branchView local branches
git branch -rView remote-tracking branches
git branch -aView local and remote-tracking branches
For now, focus mainly on git branch. The remote branch commands will become easier after you learn about remotes and GitHub.
Branch Names in the Output
Every line represents a branch.
feature-dashboard feature-login * main
feature-dashboard → Branch exists feature-login → Branch exists main → Branch exists * main → Current branch
The asterisk does not mean the branch is special or better. It simply identifies your current branch.
Common Beginner Situation
You want to switch to a branch, but you forgot its exact name.
Instead of guessing, run:
git branch
Example:
feature-dashboard * feature-login fix-navbar-bug main
Now you know the exact branch names available.
For example, to switch to the dashboard branch:
git switch feature-dashboard
Important Scenario ⭐
Suppose you created these branches:
main feature-login feature-dashboard
You then make changes to files and forget which branch you are currently on.
Run:
git branch
If Git shows:
main feature-dashboard * feature-login
You are currently making changes on feature-login.
Good Habit: If you are unsure which branch you are working on, run git branch or git status before making important commits.
git branch vs git status
Both commands can help you understand your current branch, but their purposes are different.

CommandMain Purpose
git branchView branches and identify the current branch
git statusView the repository's current state, including file changes and branch information
Want to see all branches? ↓ git branch 📋 Want to check changed/staged files and status? ↓ git status 🔍
Example Output Explanation
experiment-dark-mode feature-dashboard * feature-login fix-login-bug main
Let's understand it:
experiment-dark-mode → Branch exists feature-dashboard → Branch exists * feature-login → Branch exists → Current branch 📍 fix-login-bug → Branch exists main → Branch exists
What Listing Branches Does Not Do
Running the basic command:
git branch
only displays branch information. It does not:
Create a new commit ❌ Change files ❌ Switch branches ❌ Merge branches ❌ Delete branches ❌
It is mainly used here to view your local branches.
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
git branch ↓ Who are the branches? 📋 * branch-name ↓ Where am I currently? 📍
Common Commands So Far

CommandMeaning
git branchList local branches
git branch branch-nameCreate a branch
git switch branch-nameSwitch to an existing branch
git statusCheck repository status
Complete Example

START ↓ Current branch → main 📍 ↓ git branch feature-login ↓ New branch created ↓ git branch ↓ * main feature-login ↓ git switch feature-login ↓ Current branch changed ↓ git branch ↓ main * feature-login 📍
Summary

ConceptMeaning
git branchLists local branches
*Indicates the current branch
One current branchYou work on one current branch at a time
git branch nameCreates a new branch
git branch -rViews remote-tracking branches
git branch -aViews local and remote-tracking branches
One-Line Definition: git branch is used to list the local branches in a Git repository, and the branch marked with * is the branch you are currently working on.
practice: Use your existing Git-Practice repository. You should already have branches such as main and the branches you created in previous topics.
STEP 1 → List branches ↓ STEP 2 → Find current branch ↓ STEP 3 → Switch branch ↓ STEP 4 → List again ↓ STEP 5 → Create one branch ↓ STEP 6 → Verify it exists
Step 1: List all your local branches.
git branch
Look carefully at the output and identify every branch in your repository.
Step 2: Find your current branch.
Look for: * branch-name The branch with * ↓ Your current branch 📍
Step 3: Switch to another branch that already exists.
git switch feature-login
If you do not have feature-login, use another existing branch name from your git branch output.
Step 4: List branches again.
git branch
Check that the * moved to the branch you switched to.
Before switch * main feature-login ↓ After switch main * feature-login
Step 5: Create one new branch.
git branch practice-branch
Now verify that Git created it.
git branch
You should see practice-branch in the list.
Practice Challenge: Without looking at previous topics, complete this workflow.
1. List branches ↓ 2. Identify current branch ↓ 3. Switch to another branch ↓ 4. List branches again ↓ 5. Confirm the * moved ↓ 6. Switch back to main ↓ 7. Verify again
Important Check: If you ever forget which branch you are working on, run:
git branch
Practice Goal: Be able to use git branch to view all local branches, identify the current branch using *, and verify that switching branches changes your current branch.

qna.q: Q1. Which command is used to list local branches?
qna.a: git branch

qna.q: Q2. What does the * symbol mean in git branch output?
qna.a: It identifies the branch you are currently working on.

qna.q: Q3. If the output shows * main, which branch are you currently on?
qna.a: You are currently on the main branch.

qna.q: Q4. Does git branch without a branch name create a new branch?
qna.a: No. git branch without a branch name lists local branches.

qna.q: Q5. What does git branch feature-login do?
qna.a: It creates a new branch named feature-login.

qna.q: Q6. Does git branch automatically switch you to the new branch?
qna.a: No. It creates the branch but does not automatically switch your current branch.

qna.q: Q7. Which command is useful when you forget the exact name of a branch?
qna.a: git branch

qna.q: Q8. What is the difference between git branch and git status?
qna.a: git branch is mainly used to view branches and identify the current branch, while git status shows the current repository state including file changes and branch information.

qna.q: Q9. Which command can show remote-tracking branches?
qna.a: git branch -r

qna.q: Q10. Which command can show both local and remote-tracking branches?
qna.a: git branch -a

qna.q: Q11. Does running git branch modify your files?
qna.a: No. The basic git branch command only displays local branch information.

qna.q: Q12. If you switch from main to feature-login, what should happen to the * when you run git branch?
qna.a: The * should move from main to feature-login, showing that feature-login is now your current branch.

items.title: Delete a Branch
explanation: Simple Meaning
Deleting a branch means removing a branch that you no longer need.
For example, after completing a feature and merging it into main, the feature branch may no longer be needed.
main ↓ Feature branch created ↓ feature-login ↓ Feature completed ✅ ↓ Merged into main ↓ feature-login no longer needed ↓ Delete branch 🗑️
Simple Definition: Deleting a branch removes the branch reference when that branch is no longer needed.
Why Delete a Branch?
Branches are often created for temporary work such as developing one feature or fixing one bug.
feature-login → Build login feature → Work completed ✅ fix-navbar-bug → Fix navigation problem → Work completed ✅
Keeping every old branch forever can make a repository difficult to organize.
Deleting branches that are no longer needed helps keep the branch list clean.
Safe Delete Command ⭐
The common command for deleting a local branch is:
git branch -d branch-name
Example:
git branch -d feature-login
This requests Git to safely delete the local branch named feature-login.
Simple Example
Suppose your repository contains:
* main feature-dashboard feature-login
You no longer need feature-login. Run:
git branch -d feature-login
Now check the branches:
git branch
The result may look like:
* main feature-dashboard
The local feature-login branch has been deleted.
Important: You Cannot Normally Delete Your Current Branch ⭐
Suppose your current branch is:
main * feature-login
You are currently working on feature-login.
Trying to delete it directly is not allowed because it is your current checked-out branch.
Current branch → feature-login 📍 ↓ Try to delete feature-login ↓ Git prevents deleting the current branch ⚠️
First switch to another branch, such as main:
git switch main
Then delete the branch:
git branch -d feature-login
Correct Workflow
Currently on feature-login 📍 ↓ Need to delete feature-login ↓ Switch to main ↓ git switch main ↓ Delete branch ↓ git branch -d feature-login ↓ Verify using git branch
What Does Safe Delete Mean?
The -d option is the normal safe delete option.
Git checks whether deleting the branch could remove branch commits that have not been merged into another branch or are not otherwise reachable from the current history.

Branch has been safely integrated ↓ git branch -d feature-login ↓ Delete allowed ✅ ==================== Branch contains work Git considers unmerged ↓ git branch -d feature-login ↓ Git may refuse deletion ⚠️
This safety check helps prevent accidentally deleting a branch containing work you may still need.
Force Delete Command ⚠️
Git also provides an uppercase -D option:
git branch -D branch-name
Example:
git branch -D feature-login
This is a force-delete operation and can remove the branch even when the normal -d safety check would refuse.
Important: Understand why Git refuses a normal deletion before using -D. Do not use force deletion casually.

CommandMeaning
git branch -d branch-nameNormal/safe branch deletion
git branch -D branch-nameForce delete branch
-d ↓ Normal safe deletion 🛡️ ==================== -D ↓ Force deletion ⚠️
Recommended Beginner Rule
Always try the normal command first:
git branch -d branch-name
If Git refuses to delete the branch, do not immediately change -d to -D.
First understand why Git refused. Check whether the branch contains work you still need.
Run git branch -d ↓ Deleted successfully? ✅ ↓ Done OR Git refuses ⚠️ ↓ Check branch history/work ↓ Understand why ↓ Decide carefully whether force deletion is appropriate
Delete a Branch Step by Step
Suppose you have:
* main feature-login feature-dashboard
Step 1: Confirm that the branch you want to delete exists.
git branch
Step 2: Make sure you are not currently on that branch.
Here, main has *, so you can delete feature-login.
Step 3: Delete the branch.
git branch -d feature-login
Step 4: Verify the result.
git branch
Deleting Multiple Branches
You can delete branches individually when they are no longer needed.
git branch -d feature-login git branch -d feature-dashboard git branch -d fix-navbar-bug
Be careful and verify each branch name before deleting it.
Common Branch Lifecycle
A common branch workflow looks like this:
main ↓ Create feature branch 🌱 ↓ feature-login ↓ Make changes ↓ Commit changes ↓ Test feature ↓ Merge completed work ↓ Branch no longer needed ↓ Delete feature branch 🗑️
Example: Complete Feature Workflow

START ↓ main 📍 ↓ Create branch feature-login ↓ Switch to feature-login ↓ Build login feature 🚧 ↓ Create commits ↓ Feature complete ✅ ↓ Merge into main ↓ Switch to main ↓ Delete feature-login ↓ git branch -d feature-login ↓ Repository cleaned up ✅
You will learn the actual merging process in upcoming topics.
Local Branch Deletion
The commands in this topic delete local branches from your computer.
Your Computer 💻 ↓ Local Repository ↓ main feature-login feature-dashboard ↓ Delete feature-login ↓ Removed from local branch list
Later, after learning GitHub, you will also learn about deleting remote branches.
Deleting a Local Branch Does Not Automatically Delete a Remote Branch
Local and remote repositories are separate.
Your Computer 💻 feature-login │ │ Delete local branch ↓ Local feature-login removed 🗑️ GitHub ☁️ feature-login ↓ May still exist remotely
You will learn remote branch deletion after learning remotes and GitHub workflows.
Common Beginner Mistake 1
Trying to delete the current branch:
* feature-login main git branch -d feature-login
Correct approach:
git switch main git branch -d feature-login
Common Beginner Mistake 2
Immediately using force delete:
git branch -D feature-login
Better approach:
First try: git branch -d feature-login ↓ If refused ↓ Understand why Git refused ↓ Check whether work is still needed ↓ Only then consider -D
Common Beginner Mistake 3
Confusing branch deletion with deleting project files.
Deleting a branch removes the branch reference; Git may still have commits reachable through other branches if that work was merged.

The exact recoverability of commits from an unmerged deleted branch depends on repository history and garbage collection, so do not treat branch deletion as something to experiment with on important work.
Easy Way to Remember 🧠

git branch -d branch-name ↓ Delete branch normally 🗑️ -------------------- Before deleting: Can I delete my current branch? ❌ ↓ Switch first 🔄 -------------------- Git refuses deletion? ↓ Understand why ⚠️ Don't immediately force delete
Commands Summary

CommandPurpose
git branchList local branches
git branch -d branch-nameDelete a branch using normal safety checks
git branch -D branch-nameForce delete a branch
git switch mainSwitch to another branch before deleting the current one
Complete Example

Current branches: * main feature-login feature-dashboard ↓ Delete feature-login: git branch -d feature-login ↓ Check branches: git branch ↓ * main feature-dashboard ↓ feature-login removed from local branch list 🗑️
One-Line Definition: git branch -d branch-name is used to normally delete a local branch that is no longer needed, while git branch -D branch-name force deletes it and should be used carefully.
practice: Use a practice branch for this topic. Do not delete main or a branch containing work you still need.
STEP 1 → Create a temporary branch ↓ STEP 2 → List branches ↓ STEP 3 → Switch to main ↓ STEP 4 → Delete temporary branch ↓ STEP 5 → Verify deletion
Step 1: Create a temporary branch named practice-delete.
git branch practice-delete
Step 2: List the branches and confirm that it exists.
git branch
You should see practice-delete in the branch list.
Step 3: Make sure you are not currently on practice-delete.
git switch main
Then verify your current branch:
git branch
Step 4: Delete the temporary branch using the normal delete command.
git branch -d practice-delete
Step 5: Verify that the branch was deleted.
git branch
Before deletion: * main practice-delete ↓ Run: git branch -d practice-delete ↓ After deletion: * main practice-delete removed ✅
Practice Task 2: Create and delete another temporary branch.
git branch test-delete git branch git branch -d test-delete git branch
Practice Challenge: Understand what happens in this situation before running anything.
Current branches: main * feature-login You want to delete: feature-login Question: What must you do first? 🤔
Answer: Switch to another branch first, for example main, and then delete feature-login.
Important Safety Practice: Do not use git branch -D just to test the command on a branch containing important work. First become comfortable with the normal -d command.

Practice Goal: Be able to safely delete an unneeded local branch, verify that it was removed, understand that you must switch away from the current branch before deleting it, and know the difference between -d and -D.

qna.q: Q1. Which command is normally used to delete a local branch?
qna.a: git branch -d branch-name

qna.q: Q2. How do you normally delete a branch named feature-login?
qna.a: git branch -d feature-login

qna.q: Q3. Can you normally delete the branch you are currently working on?
qna.a: No. You should switch to another branch before deleting the current branch.

qna.q: Q4. If you are currently on feature-login and want to delete it, what should you do first?
qna.a: Switch to another branch, such as main, and then delete feature-login.

qna.q: Q5. What is the difference between -d and -D?
qna.a: -d performs normal branch deletion with safety checks, while -D force deletes the branch.

qna.q: Q6. Why should you try git branch -d before using git branch -D?
qna.a: Because -d provides safety checks. If Git refuses deletion, you should first understand whether the branch contains work you still need.

qna.q: Q7. Why are branches often deleted?
qna.a: Branches are often deleted after their feature, bug fix, or other work is completed and the branch is no longer needed.

qna.q: Q8. Does deleting a local branch automatically delete the same branch on GitHub?
qna.a: No. Local and remote branches are separate. Deleting a local branch does not automatically delete the remote branch.

qna.q: Q9. Which command can you use to verify that a branch was deleted?
qna.a: git branch

qna.q: Q10. What is a safe beginner workflow for deleting a branch?
qna.a: List branches, make sure you are not currently on the branch you want to delete, switch away if necessary, run git branch -d branch-name, and verify the result using git branch.

items.title: Understand main
explanation: Simple Meaning
main is usually the primary or default branch of a Git repository.
When you create a repository, Git uses a default branch name based on its configuration. In many modern repositories, that branch is named main.
Repository ↓ main 📍 ↓ Primary branch
