Simple Definition: main is commonly the primary branch of a Git repository and usually represents the main line of development.
Why Is It Called main?
A repository can contain many branches, but usually one branch acts as the primary branch.
Repository │ ├── main ⭐ ├── feature-login ├── feature-dashboard └── fix-navbar-bug
Here, main is the primary branch, while the other branches are created for specific work.
Simple Example
Imagine you are building a website.
main ↓ Website stable version ✅ feature-login ↓ Build login feature 🚧 feature-dashboard ↓ Build dashboard 🚧
You can create a separate branch to work on a feature without directly changing the primary branch.
Typical Branch Workflow ⭐
main 📍 ↓ Create feature branch ↓ feature-login ↓ Make changes ↓ Commit changes ↓ Test changes ↓ Merge completed work ↓ main updated ✅
This is one of the main reasons branches are useful: work can be developed separately and later integrated.
main Is Just a Branch Name
This is an important concept: main is not a special Git command.
It is simply a branch name that is commonly used as the primary branch.
main ↓ A branch name Git command? ❌ Special syntax? ❌ Common primary branch name? ✅
You can see it when you run:
git branch
Example:
feature-login * main
The * means you are currently working on main.
main vs Other Branches

BranchTypical Purpose
mainPrimary line of development
feature-loginDevelop a login feature
feature-dashboardDevelop a dashboard
fix-navbar-bugFix a specific bug
The names of feature branches can be anything valid, but main is commonly used for the repository's primary branch.
Example: Working Directly on main
Suppose you have a simple personal project:
main 📍 ↓ Edit index.html ↓ git add . ↓ git commit -m "Add homepage" ↓ main contains the new commit
For a small personal project, you may sometimes work directly on main.
Example: Using a Feature Branch
Suppose your current branch is main:
* main
You want to add a login page. Instead of immediately making the feature work directly on main, you can create a branch:
git switch -c feature-login
Now:
main * feature-login
Your feature work happens on feature-login.
main ↓ Create feature-login ↓ feature-login 📍 ↓ Develop login feature ↓ Commit changes ↓ Later integrate completed work into main
Why Protect main?
In team projects, main often contains important shared project code.
If every developer directly makes experimental changes there, mistakes can affect everyone.
Without separate branches: Developer A ─┐ Developer B ─┼──→ main Developer C ─┘ Many direct changes ↓ Higher risk of unwanted changes ⚠️
A common workflow is to let developers work in separate branches and integrate reviewed changes later.
Developer A → feature-login ───┐ Developer B → feature-dashboard ─┼──→ main Developer C → fix-bug ───────────┘ Separate work ↓ Review / test ↓ Integrate completed changes
Important: main Does Not Mean Automatically Production
Beginners sometimes think main always means the live production version of an application.
That is not automatically true.
main is a branch. Whether it represents production-ready code depends on the project's workflow and deployment setup.
main ↓ Primary branch ✅ Automatically live website? ❌ Not always Automatically production? ❌ Not always Depends on project workflow and deployment
Default Branch Concept
A repository can have one branch configured as its default branch. In many modern projects, that branch is named main.
The default branch is often the starting branch shown when people open the repository.
Repository ↓ Default branch ↓ Often named main ⭐
However, a repository can use another name as its default branch depending on its configuration.
main vs master
You may see older tutorials or existing repositories using master instead of main.
Older/common repository name: master Modern/common repository name: main
Both are branch names. The important thing is to check which branch your repository actually uses.
git branch
Example:
* main
or in another repository:
* master
Do not assume every repository uses exactly the same branch name.
How to Check Whether You Are on main
Run:
git branch
If the output is:
* main feature-login
You are currently on main.
You can also use:
git status
Git status normally displays information about your current branch along with the status of your working tree.
Switch Back to main
Suppose you are currently on feature-login:
main * feature-login
To switch back to main:
git switch main
Then:
* main feature-login
feature-login 📍 ↓ git switch main ↓ main 📍
main in Your Branch Workflow
Based on the topics you have learned so far, a simple workflow can look like this:
START ↓ main 📍 ↓ Create branch ↓ git branch feature-login ↓ Switch branch ↓ git switch feature-login ↓ Make changes and commits ↓ feature-login ↓ Later merge completed work ↓ main updated
Common Beginner Mistake 1
Assuming main is always your current branch.
Check instead:
git branch
* main ↓ You are on main ✅ -------------------- * feature-login ↓ You are on feature-login ✅
Common Beginner Mistake 2
Thinking every repository must have a branch named main.
Different repositories can use different branch names.
Repository A → main Repository B → master Repository C → development Branch names depend on repository configuration.
Common Beginner Mistake 3
Thinking main cannot be changed because it is a special Git keyword.
main is a branch name. Git workflows and repository settings determine how it is used.
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
main ↓ Usually the primary branch ⭐ Feature work? ↓ Create separate branch 🌱 Feature complete? ↓ Integrate work back into main 🔄
Important Commands

CommandPurpose
git branchView branches and current branch
git switch mainSwitch to the main branch
git switch -c feature-nameCreate and switch to a new feature branch
Complete Example

Initial state: * main 📍 ↓ Create feature branch: git switch -c feature-login ↓ main * feature-login 📍 ↓ Develop feature Create commits ↓ Feature complete ✅ ↓ Switch back: git switch main ↓ * main 📍 feature-login ↓ Later merge feature work into main
Summary

ConceptMeaning
mainCommon name for the primary branch
Current branchThe branch marked with *
Default branchThe branch configured as the repository's default, often main
Feature branchA separate branch for specific work
git switch mainSwitch to main
masterA branch name commonly found in older or existing repositories
One-Line Definition: main is commonly the primary or default branch of a Git repository, where the main line of project development is typically maintained.
practice: Use your existing Git-Practice repository and the branches you created in previous topics.
STEP 1 → Check your branches ↓ STEP 2 → Identify your current branch ↓ STEP 3 → Switch to main ↓ STEP 4 → Verify main is current ↓ STEP 5 → Create a feature branch ↓ STEP 6 → Switch back to main
Step 1: View all your local branches.
git branch
Step 2: Identify your current branch by finding the *.
Example: feature-login * main Current branch → main 📍
Step 3: Switch to main.
git switch main
If you are already on main, Git will keep you on that branch.
Step 4: Verify your current branch.
git branch
Confirm that the output marks main with *.
Expected idea: * main 📍 feature-login practice-branch
Step 5: Create a practice feature branch and automatically switch to it.
git switch -c feature-main-practice
Now check your branches:
git branch
You should see the * on feature-main-practice.
Step 6: Switch back to main.
git switch main
Verify again:
git branch
main 📍 ↓ Create feature-main-practice ↓ feature-main-practice 📍 ↓ Switch back ↓ main 📍
Practice Challenge: Complete this without looking at previous topics.

1. Check all branches ↓ 2. Find current branch ↓ 3. Switch to main ↓ 4. Verify * is on main ↓ 5. Create a new feature branch ↓ 6. Verify * moved to the feature branch ↓ 7. Switch back to main ↓ 8. Verify again
Practice Goal: Understand that main is a commonly used primary branch name, know how to check whether you are currently on it, and be able to switch between main and feature branches.

qna.q: Q1. What is main in Git?
qna.a: main is commonly the primary branch of a Git repository.

qna.q: Q2. Is main a special Git command?
qna.a: No. main is a branch name, not a Git command.

qna.q: Q3. What does * main mean in git branch output?
qna.a: It means main is your current branch.

qna.q: Q4. Which command switches you to the main branch?
qna.a: git switch main

qna.q: Q5. Why are feature branches created instead of always working directly on main?
qna.a: Feature branches allow specific work to be developed separately, helping keep changes isolated until they are ready to be integrated.

qna.q: Q6. Does every Git repository have to use main as its primary branch?
qna.a: No. A repository can use another branch name depending on its configuration.

qna.q: Q7. What is another branch name you may see in older or existing repositories?
qna.a: master

qna.q: Q8. Does main automatically mean the live production website or application?
qna.a: No. main is a branch. Whether it is automatically deployed or represents production depends on the project's workflow and deployment configuration.

qna.q: Q9. Which command helps you see whether you are currently on main?
qna.a: git branch. The branch marked with * is your current branch.

qna.q: Q10. Give a simple workflow using main and a feature branch.
qna.a: Start on main, create a feature branch, switch to it, make and commit changes, complete the feature, and later integrate the completed work into main.

items.title: What is Git Merge?
explanation: Simple Meaning
git merge is used to combine changes from one branch into another branch.
For example, you may create a feature-login branch, complete the login feature, and then merge that work into main.
main ↓ Create feature branch ↓ feature-login ↓ Develop login feature ↓ Commit changes ↓ Merge changes into main ↓ main contains the login feature ✅
Simple Definition: Git merge combines the history and changes of one branch into another branch.
Why Is Merge Needed?
Branches allow us to work separately. But after completing the work, we often want to bring that completed work back into the main branch.
main ↓ Stable project ↓ Create branch feature-login ↓ Add login page Add validation Fix login bugs ↓ Feature complete ✅ ↓ Merge main ↓ Contains completed login feature ✅
Without merging, the completed changes remain only on the feature branch.
Important Concept: Where You Run git merge ⭐
This is one of the most important concepts in Git merging:
You switch to the branch that should receive the changes first, then run git merge with the source branch name.
Destination branch ↓ The branch that receives changes 📥 ↓ Switch to this branch first ↓ Run git merge source-branch
Simple Example
You have two branches:
main ↓ Main project feature-login ↓ New login feature
You want the changes from feature-login to go into main.
Step 1: Switch to main.
git switch main
Step 2: Merge feature-login into your current branch.
git merge feature-login
Before: main 📍 ↓ Older project feature-login ↓ Login changes ↓ git switch main git merge feature-login ↓ After: main 📍 ↓ Older project + Login changes ✅
Easy Way to Read the Command 🧠
Suppose you run:
git merge feature-login
Git merges feature-login into the branch you are currently on.
Current branch 📍 ↑ Receives changes │ main ← feature-login Command while on main: git merge feature-login Meaning: Take changes from feature-login ↓ Bring them into main
Another Example
Suppose you are currently on feature-dashboard:
main * feature-dashboard feature-login
If you run:
git merge feature-login
Git attempts to merge feature-login into feature-dashboard, because feature-dashboard is your current branch.
Remember: git merge branch-name means merge branch-name into your current branch.
Basic Merge Workflow ⭐
STEP 1 Check branches ↓ git branch STEP 2 Switch to destination branch ↓ git switch main STEP 3 Merge source branch ↓ git merge feature-login STEP 4 Check the result ↓ git status ↓ Merge completed ✅
Visual Example
Before merging:
A ─── B ─── C main \ D ─── E feature-login
Here:
A → First commit B → Common commit C → Work on main D → Login work E → More login work
After merging feature-login into main, Git combines the branch histories.
A ─── B ─── C ─── M main \ / D ─── E ──── feature-login M → Merge result
The exact merge result can differ depending on the commit history. You will learn fast-forward merges and merge commits in the next topics.
Merge Does Not Mean Copy and Paste
Git merge does not simply copy files from one branch and overwrite another branch.
Git uses commit history to determine how the branches changed and attempts to combine those changes.
Git checks: ↓ Common history ↓ Changes on current branch ↓ Changes on source branch ↓ Attempts to combine changes
If the changes can be combined automatically, the merge succeeds. If Git cannot automatically decide how conflicting changes should be combined, a merge conflict can occur.
Successful Automatic Merge
Suppose main changes index.html while feature-login changes login.html.
main ↓ Change index.html feature-login ↓ Change login.html ↓ Merge ↓ Git can combine both changes automatically ✅
Because the changes do not conflict, Git can often merge them automatically.
When a Merge Conflict Can Happen
Suppose two branches change the same part of the same file differently.
main ↓ Change button text to: "Sign In" feature-login ↓ Change same button text to: "Login Now" ↓ Merge ↓ Git cannot automatically choose ⚠️ ↓ Merge conflict
You will learn how to intentionally create and resolve merge conflicts in upcoming topics.
Merge Direction Is Important ⭐
These two commands can produce different results because your current branch is different.

Current BranchCommandMeaning
maingit merge feature-loginMerge feature-login into main
feature-logingit merge mainMerge main into feature-login
Always ask: Which branch should RECEIVE the changes? 📥 ↓ Switch to that branch ↓ Run git merge source-branch
Common Real-World Workflow

main 📍 ↓ Create feature branch ↓ feature-login ↓ Make changes ↓ git add . ↓ git commit -m "Add login page" ↓ Feature complete ↓ Switch to main ↓ git switch main ↓ Merge feature ↓ git merge feature-login ↓ main updated ✅
What Happens to the Feature Branch After Merge?
Merging a branch does not automatically mean the branch itself disappears.
For example:
git switch main git merge feature-login
After a successful merge, you may still see:
* main feature-login
The branch still exists until you delete it.
Merge feature-login into main ↓ Changes integrated ✅ ↓ feature-login branch may still exist ↓ No longer needed? ↓ Delete branch separately 🗑️
Merge and Branch Deletion
A common workflow after successfully merging completed work is:
feature-login ↓ Work complete ✅ ↓ Merge into main ↓ git switch main git merge feature-login ↓ Verify result ↓ Branch no longer needed ↓ git branch -d feature-login
Delete the branch only after confirming that you no longer need it.
Common Beginner Mistake 1: Wrong Branch
You want to merge feature-login into main, but you forget to switch to main.
Wanted: feature-login → main But current branch: feature-dashboard 📍 Run: git merge feature-login Result: feature-login is merged into feature-dashboard ⚠️
Always check your current branch before an important merge.
git branch
Common Beginner Mistake 2: Thinking Merge Deletes the Branch
Merge combines changes and history, but the source branch may still remain.
Before merge: main feature-login ↓ Merge ↓ After merge: main → Updated ✅ feature-login → Still exists
Common Beginner Mistake 3: Merging Uncommitted Work
Before switching branches or merging, check your working tree:
git status
Uncommitted changes can sometimes prevent switching or complicate your workflow. A good habit is to understand your current changes before starting a merge.
Check Before You Merge ⭐

1. What branch am I currently on? ↓ git branch 2. Which branch should receive changes? ↓ Switch to it 3. Is my working tree in the state I expect? ↓ git status 4. Which branch contains the changes I want? ↓ Identify source branch 5. Merge ↓ git merge source-branch
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
Want: feature-login → main Step 1: Go to WHERE changes should go 📥 ↓ git switch main Step 2: Bring changes FROM the feature branch 📤 ↓ git merge feature-login
Important Commands

CommandPurpose
git branchCheck available and current branches
git switch mainSwitch to main
git merge feature-nameMerge feature-name into the current branch
git statusCheck repository state
Complete Example
Suppose your project has:
main ↓ Homepage exists feature-contact ↓ Contact page added
You want the contact page work in main.
git switch main git merge feature-contact
Meaning:
Current branch → main 📍 ↓ Receive changes from feature-contact ↓ Git combines the changes ↓ main now contains contact page work ✅
Summary

ConceptMeaning
MergeCombine changes and history from one branch into another
Current branchThe destination branch that receives the merge
Source branchThe branch whose changes you merge
git merge feature-loginMerge feature-login into the current branch
Automatic mergeGit successfully combines changes
Merge conflictGit needs manual help to resolve conflicting changes
After mergeThe source branch may still exist
One-Line Definition: git merge combines changes from another branch into your current branch.
practice: For this practice, use your existing Git-Practice repository. We will create a temporary branch, make a small change, commit it, and merge it into main.

STEP 1 → Check branches ↓ STEP 2 → Switch to main ↓ STEP 3 → Create feature branch ↓ STEP 4 → Make a change ↓ STEP 5 → Commit the change ↓ STEP 6 → Switch to main ↓ STEP 7 → Merge the feature branch ↓ STEP 8 → Verify the result
Step 1: Check your current branches.
git branch
Step 2: Switch to main.
git switch main
Step 3: Create and switch to a new practice branch.
git switch -c feature-merge-practice
Step 4: Open one of your practice files and make a small change. For example, add a new line to a text file or HTML file.
feature-merge-practice 📍 ↓ Make a small change ↓ Save file
Step 5: Check and commit your change.
git status git add . git commit -m "Add merge practice change"
Step 6: Switch back to the branch that should receive the changes.
git switch main
Step 7: Merge the practice branch into main.
git merge feature-merge-practice
Read the command as: while on main, bring the changes from feature-merge-practice into main.
feature-merge-practice ↓ Contains your new commit ↓ git switch main ↓ main 📍 ↓ git merge feature-merge-practice ↓ main now contains the change ✅
Step 8: Verify the result.
git status git log --oneline
Also open the file and confirm that the change made on feature-merge-practice is now available while you are on main.
Practice Challenge: Before running each merge command, answer these two questions:
Question 1: Which branch should RECEIVE the changes? 📥 Question 2: Which branch is the SOURCE of the changes? 📤 Then: Switch to destination ↓ Run git merge source-branch
Optional Cleanup: After confirming the merge worked and you no longer need the practice branch, delete it.
git branch -d feature-merge-practice

Practice Goal: Understand merge direction. You should be able to identify the destination branch, switch to it, and use git merge source-branch to bring committed changes from another branch into your current branch.

qna.q: Q1. What is Git merge?
qna.a: Git merge is used to combine changes and history from one branch into another branch.

qna.q: Q2. What does git merge feature-login do?
qna.a: It merges feature-login into your current branch.

qna.q: Q3. You want to merge feature-login into main. Which branch should you switch to first?
qna.a: You should switch to main first because main is the branch that should receive the changes.

qna.q: Q4. Complete the command sequence to merge feature-login into main.
qna.a: git switch main, followed by git merge feature-login.

qna.q: Q5. In git merge feature-login, which branch is the destination?
qna.a: The current branch is the destination branch.

qna.q: Q6. In git merge feature-login, which branch is the source?
qna.a: feature-login is the source branch whose changes Git attempts to merge into the current branch.

qna.q: Q7. Does git merge automatically delete the source branch?
qna.a: No. The source branch may still exist after the merge and can be deleted separately if it is no longer needed.

qna.q: Q8. What can cause a merge conflict?
qna.a: A merge conflict can occur when Git cannot automatically combine changes, such as when branches make incompatible changes to the same part of a file.

qna.q: Q9. Why should you check your current branch before merging?
qna.a: Because git merge merges the specified source branch into your current branch. Being on the wrong branch can merge changes somewhere you did not intend.

qna.q: Q10. If you are on feature-dashboard and run git merge feature-login, where will Git attempt to merge the changes?
qna.a: Git will attempt to merge feature-login into feature-dashboard because feature-dashboard is your current branch.

qna.q: Q11. What is a good command to run before an important merge to check your branches?
qna.a: git branch

qna.q: Q12. What is the easiest rule to remember for merging?
qna.a: First switch to the branch that should receive the changes, then run git merge followed by the branch that contains the changes you want to bring in.

items.title: Merge One Branch into Another
explanation: Simple Meaning
In the previous topic, you learned that git merge combines changes from one branch into another.
Now let's learn the exact process of merging one branch into another.
The most important rule is:
Rule: First switch to the branch that should receive the changes. Then run git merge source-branch.
The Two Branches You Need to Understand

Branch TypeMeaning
Destination branchThe branch that receives the changes
Source branchThe branch containing the changes you want to merge
Suppose:
Source branch 📤 feature-login ↓ Contains login changes Destination branch 📥 main ↓ Will receive login changes
Basic Example
You have two branches:
main ↓ Current main project feature-login ↓ Login feature changes
You want:
feature-login ↓ ↓ Merge changes ↓ main 📥
The correct process is:
git switch main git merge feature-login
After the merge, main receives the committed changes from feature-login.
Step-by-Step Merge Process ⭐

STEP 1 → Check branches ↓ STEP 2 → Identify source branch ↓ STEP 3 → Identify destination branch ↓ STEP 4 → Switch to destination branch ↓ STEP 5 → Check status ↓ STEP 6 → Run git merge source-branch ↓ STEP 7 → Verify merge result
Step 1: Check Your Branches
First, see the branches in your repository:
git branch
Example:
* feature-login main
The * means you are currently on feature-login.
Step 2: Identify the Source Branch
The source branch contains the work you want to bring somewhere else.
Example:
feature-login 📤 ↓ Add login page Add login validation Fix login button This is the SOURCE branch
Step 3: Identify the Destination Branch
The destination branch is where you want the changes to go.
Example:
main 📥 ↓ Receives the completed login feature This is the DESTINATION branch
Step 4: Switch to the Destination Branch ⭐
Since we want to merge changes into main, switch to main first:
git switch main
Now check:
git branch
Expected idea:
feature-login * main
Important: The branch marked with * is the branch that will receive the merge.
Step 5: Check Your Repository Status
Before merging, it is a good habit to check your repository:
git status
Make sure you understand whether you have any uncommitted changes before continuing.
Check current branch ↓ Check working status ↓ Understand current changes ↓ Then merge
Step 6: Merge the Source Branch
Now you are on main and want to bring in changes from feature-login.
Run:
git merge feature-login
Read this as:
Current branch → main 📥 Merge from → feature-login 📤 Command: git merge feature-login Result: feature-login changes → main
Step 7: Verify the Merge
After merging, check the repository status:
git status
You can also check the commit history:
git log --oneline
Finally, check your files and confirm that the changes from the source branch are now available in the destination branch.
Complete Workflow Example ⭐
Suppose your branches look like this:
main ↓ Homepage complete feature-contact ↓ Contact page created
You want the contact page changes in main.
feature-contact 📤 ↓ ↓ ↓ main 📥
Run:
git branch git switch main git status git merge feature-contact git status
The result is:
Before: main ↓ Homepage feature-contact ↓ Contact page ↓ Merge After: main ↓ Homepage + Contact page ✅
Merge Direction Is Important
Let's compare two different situations.

Current BranchCommandResult
maingit merge feature-loginfeature-login → main
feature-logingit merge mainmain → feature-login
The command changes meaning depending on your current branch.
Rule: CURRENT BRANCH 📍 ↑ Receives changes SOURCE BRANCH ↓ Provides changes Command: git merge source-branch
Example With Three Branches
Suppose your repository contains:
* main feature-login feature-dashboard
You run:
git merge feature-login
Result:
feature-login → main ✅ feature-dashboard is not changed by this merge.
Git merges the branch you specify into your current branch.
What Should Be Committed Before Merging?
Normally, the feature work you want to merge should be committed on the source branch.
feature-login ↓ Make changes ↓ git add . ↓ git commit -m "Add login page" ↓ Committed changes ✅ ↓ Switch to main ↓ Merge feature-login
This gives Git a clear commit history to work with.
Example From Start to Finish
Start on main:
* main
Create a feature branch:
git switch -c feature-about
Make changes, then commit them:
git add . git commit -m "Add about page"
Your branch now contains the new work:
main ↓ Original project feature-about 📍 ↓ Original project + About page
Switch back to main:
git switch main
Then merge:
git merge feature-about
Result:
main 📍 ↓ Original project + About page ✅
Does Merging Delete the Source Branch?
No. After merging, the source branch can still exist.
For example:
git branch
You may still see:
feature-login * main
Merge completed ✅ ↓ Changes are integrated ↓ Source branch still exists ↓ Delete separately only if no longer needed
Common Beginner Mistake 1: Merging on the Wrong Branch ⚠️
You want:
feature-login → main
But you accidentally remain on:
feature-dashboard 📍
Then run:
git merge feature-login
Git attempts to merge feature-login into feature-dashboard, not main.
Always check:
git branch
Common Beginner Mistake 2: Confusing Source and Destination
Suppose you want:
feature-login → main
Do not think:
Go to feature-login ↓ git merge main
That would instead attempt to bring main into feature-login.
Remember: Go to where the changes should go, then merge the branch where the changes come from.
Common Beginner Mistake 3: Not Checking the Result
After merging, do not immediately assume everything is correct.
Merge ↓ Check git status ↓ Check git log --oneline ↓ Check changed files ↓ Confirm expected result ✅
Quick Decision Method 🧠
Before merging, ask yourself:
Question 1: Where do I want the changes to go? ↓ That is the DESTINATION 📥 Question 2: Where are the changes currently? ↓ That is the SOURCE 📤 Then: Switch to DESTINATION ↓ git merge SOURCE
Simple Formula
Want: A → B Meaning: Changes from A should go into B Command: git switch B git merge A
Example:
Want: feature-login → main Command: git switch main git merge feature-login
Important Commands

CommandPurpose
git branchView branches and current branch
git switch branch-nameSwitch to the destination branch
git statusCheck repository state
git merge source-branchMerge source branch into current branch
git log --onelineCheck commit history after merging
Summary

StepAction
1Identify the source branch
2Identify the destination branch
3Switch to the destination branch
4Check the repository status
5Run git merge source-branch
6Verify the merge result
One-Line Definition: To merge one branch into another, switch to the destination branch first and run git merge followed by the source branch name.
practice: Use your existing Git-Practice repository. This practice will help you perform a complete merge from start to finish.

STEP 1 → Switch to main ↓ STEP 2 → Create feature branch ↓ STEP 3 → Make a file change ↓ STEP 4 → Commit the change ↓ STEP 5 → Switch to main ↓ STEP 6 → Merge the feature branch ↓ STEP 7 → Verify the change
Step 1: Check your branches and switch to main.
git branch git switch main
Step 2: Create a new branch named feature-about-practice.
git switch -c feature-about-practice
Step 3: Create a new file named about.txt inside your repository and add this text:
This file was created on the feature-about-practice branch.
Save the file.
Step 4: Check and commit the new file.
git status git add about.txt git commit -m "Add about practice file"
Your situation should now be:
main ↓ Does not yet contain about.txt feature-about-practice 📍 ↓ Contains about.txt + new commit
Step 5: Switch to the destination branch, main.
git switch main
Before merging, check whether about.txt is available on main. It should not yet be part of main.
Step 6: Merge feature-about-practice into your current branch.
git merge feature-about-practice
Remember the direction:
Current branch → main 📥 Source branch → feature-about-practice 📤 Result: feature-about-practice → main
Step 7: Verify that the merge worked.
git status git log --oneline
Also check your project files. about.txt should now be available while you are on main.
Before merge: main ❌ about.txt feature-about-practice ✅ about.txt ↓ Merge ↓ After merge: main ✅ about.txt
Practice Challenge 1: Without looking at the explanation, answer this:
You want: feature-login → main Which branch do you switch to first? ↓ main Which command do you run next? ↓ git merge feature-login
Practice Challenge 2: Create another branch named feature-footer-practice, make one small change, commit it, and merge it into main by yourself.
main ↓ Create feature-footer-practice ↓ Make a change ↓ Commit ↓ Switch to main ↓ Merge feature-footer-practice ↓ Verify result
Optional Cleanup: After verifying your merges, you can delete the practice branches if you no longer need them.
git branch -d feature-about-practice git branch -d feature-footer-practice

Practice Goal: You should be able to independently identify the source and destination branches, switch to the correct destination branch, merge the source branch, and verify that the changes were successfully integrated.

qna.q: Q1. You want to merge feature-login into main. Which branch is the source?
qna.a: feature-login is the source branch because it contains the changes you want to bring into main.

qna.q: Q2. You want to merge feature-login into main. Which branch is the destination?
qna.a: main is the destination branch because it will receive the changes.

qna.q: Q3. What is the correct command sequence?
qna.a: git switch main, followed by git merge feature-login.

qna.q: Q4. Why do you switch to the destination branch first?
qna.a: Because git merge merges the specified source branch into your current branch.

qna.q: Q5. If you are on main and run git merge feature-dashboard, what happens?
qna.a: Git attempts to merge feature-dashboard into main.

qna.q: Q6. If you are on feature-dashboard and run git merge main, what happens?
qna.a: Git attempts to merge main into feature-dashboard.

qna.q: Q7. What command can you use to check your current branch before merging?
qna.a: git branch. The branch marked with * is your current branch.

qna.q: Q8. What should you normally do with feature work before merging it?
qna.a: You should normally save the work in commits on the feature branch.

qna.q: Q9. Does merging automatically delete the source branch?
qna.a: No. The source branch can still exist after the merge.

qna.q: Q10. Give the simple formula for merging A into B.
qna.a: Switch to B first, then run git merge A.

qna.q: Q11. After merging, how can you verify the result?
qna.a: Check git status, git log --oneline, and confirm that the expected file changes are present.

qna.q: Q12. What is the biggest beginner mistake when merging branches?
qna.a: Merging while on the wrong current branch. Always check which branch should receive the changes before running git merge.

items.title: Fast-Forward Merge
explanation: Simple Meaning
A fast-forward merge happens when Git can merge a branch simply by moving the current branch pointer forward to the latest commit of another branch.
No separate merge commit is required because the current branch has not changed since the feature branch was created.
Simple Definition: A fast-forward merge happens when Git can move the destination branch forward to the latest commit of the source branch without creating a separate merge commit.
Simple Example
Suppose you start with this commit history:
A ─── B main 📍
You create a feature branch from commit B:
A ─── B main \ C ─── D feature-login 📍
While you are working on feature-login, imagine no new commits are made directly on main.
Now you switch to main and run:
git switch main git merge feature-login
Git can simply move main forward from B to D.
Before merge: A ─── B main 📍 \ C ─── D feature-login ↓ Fast-forward After merge: A ─── B ─── C ─── D ↑ main + feature-login
Why Is It Called Fast-Forward?
Think of main as a pointer showing the latest commit on that branch.
Before the merge:
A ─── B ↑ main
The feature branch continues ahead:
A ─── B ─── C ─── D ↑ ↑ main feature-login
Git does not need to combine two separate lines of development. It simply moves main forward:
A ─── B ─── C ─── D ↑ main moved forward
That forward movement gives the merge its name: fast-forward.
The Most Important Condition ⭐
A fast-forward merge is possible when the destination branch has no new commits that are separate from the source branch's history.
Example:
Start: A ─── B main + feature-login ↓ Only feature-login gets new commits: A ─── B ─── C ─── D ↑ ↑ main feature-login ↓ Fast-forward merge is possible ✅
When Does Fast-Forward Usually Happen?
A common situation is:
1. Start on main ↓ 2. Create a feature branch ↓ 3. Make commits only on the feature branch ↓ 4. main receives no new commits ↓ 5. Merge feature branch into main ↓ Fast-forward merge may happen ✅
Step-by-Step Example
Suppose your current history is:
Commit A ─── Commit B ↑ main 📍
Create a new branch:
git switch -c feature-contact
Make and commit changes:
git add . git commit -m "Add contact page"
Now the history conceptually looks like:
A ─── B ─── C ↑ ↑ main feature-contact 📍
Switch back to main:
git switch main
Then merge:
git merge feature-contact
If main has no new commits since the branch was created, Git can fast-forward:
A ─── B ─── C ↑ main 📍 feature-contact also points to C
What Does Git Output Look Like?
During a successful fast-forward merge, Git commonly shows output similar to:
Updating abc123..def456 Fast-forward file.txt | 1 + 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
The important part for this topic is:
Fast-forward
This tells you Git was able to move the branch forward instead of creating a separate merge commit.
Fast-Forward Merge vs Regular Merge
The main difference is whether Git has to combine two separate lines of development.

Fast-Forward MergeRegular Merge
Destination branch has no separate new commitsBoth branches have separate new commits
Branch pointer can move forwardGit must combine branch histories
Usually no merge commit is createdA merge commit may be created
History remains in one straight lineHistory can show branches joining together
Visual Comparison ⭐
Fast-forward situation:
A ─── B ─── C ─── D ↑ ↑ main feature-login main can move directly to D → Fast-forward ✅
Branches with separate changes:
A ─── B ─── C main \ D ─── E feature-login Both branches moved separately ↓ Fast-forward is not possible in this situation
Important: Fast-Forward Does Not Mean Files Move Faster
The word fast-forward can be confusing for beginners.
It does not mean Git copies files at a faster speed.
It describes the commit history and the fact that Git can move the destination branch pointer forward.
Fast-forward ❌ = Faster file copying Fast-forward ✅ = Move branch pointer forward in commit history
Important: You Still Use git merge
You do not normally use a separate command called git fast-forward.
You still run:
git merge feature-name
Git examines the history and determines whether a fast-forward merge is possible.
git merge feature-login ↓ Git checks commit history ↓ Fast-forward possible? ↓ Yes → Move branch forward ✅ No → Use another merge strategy/result
Example From Your Practice Repository
Suppose your repository starts here:
A ─── B ↑ main 📍
Create a branch:
git switch -c feature-fast-forward
Create fastforward.txt, then commit it:
git add fastforward.txt git commit -m "Add fast forward practice file"
Conceptually:
A ─── B ─── C ↑ ↑ main feature-fast-forward 📍
Now switch to main:
git switch main
Then merge:
git merge feature-fast-forward
Because main did not receive another separate commit, Git can move main forward to commit C.
After a Fast-Forward Merge
After the merge, both branch names may point to the same latest commit.
A ─── B ─── C ↑ ↑ main feature-fast-forward
The feature branch may still exist even though its changes are now included in main.
If you no longer need the feature branch, you can later delete it:
git branch -d feature-fast-forward
Why Is There Usually No Merge Commit?
A merge commit is useful when Git needs to join separate lines of development.
In a fast-forward situation, the destination branch is simply behind the source branch in the same line of history.
main: A ─── B feature: A ─── B ─── C ─── D main is already part of the path to D ↓ Git can move main directly to D ↓ No separate merge commit is usually needed
Common Beginner Mistake 1: Expecting Every Merge to Create a Merge Commit
Not every git merge creates a separate merge commit.
If a fast-forward merge is possible, Git may simply move the branch forward.
git merge feature-login ↓ Merge successful ↓ No separate merge commit? ✅ Possible ↓ Fast-forward merge
Common Beginner Mistake 2: Thinking Branches Must Always Look Separate
After a fast-forward merge, the commit history can look like one straight line.
A ─── B ─── C ─── D
Even though you used a feature branch, the final history may not show a separate merge commit.
Common Beginner Mistake 3: Confusing Fast-Forward With Rebase
Fast-forward merging and rebasing are different concepts.
A fast-forward merge happens when Git can move a branch pointer forward during a merge. Rebase is a separate operation that you will learn later in your roadmap.
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
main A ─── B 📍 feature A ─── B ─── C ─── D 📍 main has not changed ↓ Git can move main forward ↓ A ─── B ─── C ─── D 📍 main This is Fast-Forward Merge ⚡
Quick Decision Method
Before understanding the merge result, look at the history:

Did the destination branch receive new separate commits? NO ↓ Fast-forward may be possible ✅ YES ↓ Git must combine separate development histories ↓ Fast-forward is not possible in the normal situation
Important Commands

CommandPurpose
git switch mainSwitch to the destination branch
git merge feature-nameMerge the feature branch into the current branch
git log --onelineView commit history
git branch -d feature-nameDelete a merged branch when no longer needed
Complete Example

STEP 1 main: A ─── B ↓ STEP 2 Create feature branch main: A ─── B feature: A ─── B ↓ STEP 3 Make commits only on feature A ─── B ─── C ─── D ↑ ↑ main feature ↓ STEP 4 Switch to main ↓ git switch main ↓ STEP 5 Merge feature ↓ git merge feature ↓ STEP 6 Fast-forward A ─── B ─── C ─── D ↑ main
Summary

ConceptMeaning
Fast-forward mergeGit moves the destination branch forward to the source branch's latest commit
ConditionThe destination branch has no separate new commits blocking a straight forward movement
Merge commandYou still use git merge source-branch
Merge commitUsually not created during a fast-forward merge
HistoryCan remain in a straight line
Feature branchMay still exist after the merge
One-Line Definition: A fast-forward merge occurs when Git can move the destination branch forward to the latest commit of another branch without needing to create a separate merge commit.
practice: Use your existing Git-Practice repository. In this practice, you will create a situation where a fast-forward merge can happen.

STEP 1 → Switch to main ↓ STEP 2 → Create feature branch ↓ STEP 3 → Make a commit only on feature branch ↓ STEP 4 → Do NOT make a new commit on main ↓ STEP 5 → Switch back to main ↓ STEP 6 → Merge feature branch ↓ STEP 7 → Observe Fast-forward result
Step 1: Check your current branches and switch to main.
git branch git switch main
Step 2: Create and switch to a new branch.
git switch -c feature-fast-forward-practice
Step 3: Create a file named fastforward.txt and add this content:
This change was created for fast-forward merge practice.
Step 4: Save and commit the file.
git add fastforward.txt git commit -m "Add fast forward practice file"
Your history conceptually looks like this:
main A ─── B 📍 feature-fast-forward-practice A ─── B ─── C 📍
Step 5: Important — do not create any new commit on main. Switch directly back to main.
git switch main
Check that fastforward.txt is not yet present in your main branch.
Step 6: Merge the feature branch.
git merge feature-fast-forward-practice
Step 7: Carefully read the Git output. You should see a successful merge, and in a typical fast-forward situation Git will display:
Fast-forward
Before: A ─── B main 📍 \ C feature branch ↓ Fast-forward merge After: A ─── B ─── C ↑ main 📍
Step 8: Verify the result.
git status git log --oneline
Also check your project files. fastforward.txt should now be available while you are on main.
Practice Challenge: Answer this before performing another merge:
main → A ─── B feature → A ─── B ─── C ─── D Question: Has main received a separate new commit after the feature branch was created? Answer → No ↓ A fast-forward merge may be possible ✅
Optional Cleanup: After confirming the merge, delete the practice branch if you no longer need it.
git branch -d feature-fast-forward-practice

Practice Goal: Understand that a fast-forward merge happens when the destination branch can simply move forward to the source branch's latest commit because no separate commits were made on the destination branch.

qna.q: Q1. What is a fast-forward merge?
qna.a: A fast-forward merge happens when Git can move the destination branch forward to the latest commit of the source branch without needing a separate merge commit.

qna.q: Q2. What is the main condition for a fast-forward merge?
qna.a: The destination branch must not have separate new commits that require Git to combine two diverging lines of history.

qna.q: Q3. Do you use a separate command called git fast-forward?
qna.a: No. You normally use git merge, and Git determines whether a fast-forward merge is possible.

qna.q: Q4. If you are on main and run git merge feature-login, what may happen if main has not changed since feature-login was created?
qna.a: Git may perform a fast-forward merge and move main forward to the latest commit of feature-login.

qna.q: Q5. Does a fast-forward merge usually create a separate merge commit?
qna.a: No. Git can usually move the destination branch pointer forward without creating a separate merge commit.

qna.q: Q6. Does fast-forward mean Git copies files faster?
qna.a: No. It describes moving the branch pointer forward in the commit history.

qna.q: Q7. What happens to the commit history after a typical fast-forward merge?
qna.a: The history can remain in one straight line because no separate merge commit is required.

qna.q: Q8. Can the source branch still exist after a fast-forward merge?
qna.a: Yes. The source branch may still exist and can be deleted separately if it is no longer needed.

qna.q: Q9. Suppose main is at commit B and feature-login contains B → C → D. Can main potentially fast-forward to D?
qna.a: Yes. If main has no separate commits after B, Git can potentially move main forward to D.

qna.q: Q10. Suppose both main and feature-login received separate new commits after they split. Is a normal fast-forward merge possible?
qna.a: No. Git now has separate lines of history to combine, so it cannot simply move the destination branch pointer straight forward.

qna.q: Q11. What Git output may indicate that a fast-forward merge occurred?
qna.a: Git commonly displays Fast-forward during the merge output.

qna.q: Q12. What is the easiest way to remember a fast-forward merge?
qna.a: If the destination branch has not moved separately and is simply behind the source branch, Git can move it forward to catch up.

items.title: Merge Commit
explanation: Simple Meaning
A merge commit is a special commit created when Git combines two separate lines of development.
Unlike a fast-forward merge, Git cannot simply move the destination branch pointer forward because both branches have new commits after they split.
Simple Definition: A merge commit is a commit created by Git to join the histories of two branches when they have diverged.
First Understand Why It Is Needed
Suppose both branches start from the same commit:
A ─── B ↑ main + feature-login
Then both branches receive separate commits:
A ─── B ─── C main \ D ─── E feature-login
Now:

• main has commit C
  • feature-login has commits D and E
Because both branches moved separately, Git cannot simply move main forward to E.
main has its own new commit → C ↓ feature-login has separate commits → D → E ↓ Histories have diverged ↓ Fast-forward is not possible ❌ ↓ Git needs to combine both histories
What Is a Diverged History? ⭐
A diverged history means two branches started from the same point but later received different commits.
Common starting point ↓ A ─── B / \ C D ─── E ↑ ↑ main feature-login
Both branches now have unique work.

BranchUnique Changes
mainCommit C
feature-loginCommits D and E
When merging, Git needs to preserve both sets of history.
Basic Merge Commit Example
Suppose you are currently on main:
A ─── B ─── C main 📍 \ D ─── E feature-login
You run:
git merge feature-login
Git combines the histories and may create a new merge commit:
A ─── B ─── C ─────── M main 📍 \ / D ─── E ─────── feature-login
M is the merge commit.
It records the point where the histories were joined together.
Easy Way to Understand
Think of two roads starting from the same location.
Starting point ↓ B / \ C D → E \ / M ↓ Roads join again
The merge commit M represents the point where the two development paths join.
Fast-Forward Merge vs Merge Commit ⭐

Fast-Forward MergeMerge Commit
Destination branch has not moved separatelyBoth branches have separate new commits
Git can move the branch pointer forwardGit must join two histories
Usually no new merge commitA merge commit is created
History can remain straightHistory shows branches joining
Fast-forward:
A ─── B ─── C ─── D ↑ ↑ main feature main moves forward → D
Merge commit:
A ─── B ─── C ───── M \ / D ─── E ───────
Step-by-Step Example
Let's create a situation where a merge commit is needed.
Step 1: Start on main
A ─── B ↑ main
Step 2: Create a feature branch
git switch -c feature-contact
A ─── B ↑ ↑ main feature-contact
Step 3: Make and commit changes on the feature branch
A ─── B \ C ─── D ↑ feature-contact
Step 4: Switch back to main
git switch main
Step 5: Make a different commit on main
A ─── B ─── E main \ C ─── D feature-contact
Now both branches have moved separately.
Important: This is the key difference from the previous Fast-Forward Merge topic. Since main also has commit E, Git cannot simply move main forward to D.
Step 6: Merge the feature branch into main
git merge feature-contact
Git joins both histories:
A ─── B ─── E ─────── M main 📍 \ / C ─── D ───────
What Does the Merge Commit Contain?
A merge commit connects the history of both branches.
Parent 1 → Latest commit from main ↓ MERGE COMMIT ↑ Parent 2 → Latest commit from feature branch
For beginners, the most important idea is that a merge commit has connections to both lines of development.
Does Every Merge Create a Merge Commit?
No.
If Git can perform a fast-forward merge, it usually does not need to create a merge commit.
git merge feature-name ↓ Git checks history ↓ Can destination simply move forward? YES → Fast-forward merge Usually no merge commit NO → Histories need to be joined Merge commit may be created
What Happens to Files During a Merge?
Git tries to combine the changes from both branches.
For example:
main changes: Add footer feature-contact changes: Add contact page ↓ Merge main after merge: Add footer + Add contact page
If Git can automatically combine the changes, the merge completes successfully.
If Git cannot automatically determine how to combine conflicting changes, a merge conflict can occur. That is the next topic in your roadmap.
Automatic Merge Example
Suppose main changes one file:
main ↓ index.html ↓ Added footer
And the feature branch changes another file:
feature-contact ↓ contact.html ↓ Added contact form
Git can usually combine these changes automatically:
git merge feature-contact ↓ Git combines both changes ↓ index.html → Footer added contact.html → Contact form added ↓ Merge successful ✅
What If There Is a Conflict?
Sometimes both branches modify the same part of a file differently.
Example:
main: Button text → Login feature branch: Button text → Sign In ↓ Merge Git cannot automatically choose ↓ Merge conflict ⚠️
You will learn how to intentionally create and resolve merge conflicts in the next topics.
How Can You See Merge Commits?
You can view commit history using:
git log --oneline
For a clearer branch graph, you can also use:
git log --oneline --graph --all
Example conceptually:
* a1b2c3d Merge branch 'feature-contact' |\ | * d4e5f6g Add contact form * | h7i8j9k Update homepage |/ * x1y2z3a Previous commit
The graph helps you see where separate branches were joined.
Important: Merge Commit Is Part of History
A merge commit is not just a temporary operation.
It becomes part of your repository's commit history.
Old commits ↓ Separate branch development ↓ Merge commit M ↓ New commits ↓ Repository history continues
Common Beginner Mistake 1: Thinking git merge Always Creates M
This is not correct.
git merge ↓ Could result in: Fast-forward → No separate merge commit OR Diverged history → Merge commit may be created
Common Beginner Mistake 2: Confusing Merge Commit With a Normal Commit
A normal commit usually records changes made during one line of development.
A merge commit specifically records the joining of separate histories.

Normal CommitMerge Commit
Records a regular point in developmentRecords a point where histories join
Usually follows one previous commitConnects the merged histories
Common Beginner Mistake 3: Thinking a Merge Commit Means There Was a Conflict
No. A merge commit and a merge conflict are different concepts.
Merge Commit ✅ Git successfully joins histories Merge Conflict ⚠️ Git needs your help to combine conflicting changes
You can have a merge commit without experiencing any merge conflict.
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
One branch moves ahead alone ↓ Fast-forward may happen ⚡ Both branches move separately ↓ Histories diverge ↓ Git joins them ↓ Merge Commit 🔀
Quick Decision Method
Question: Did both branches receive separate commits after splitting? NO ↓ Fast-forward may be possible YES ↓ Histories diverged ↓ A merge commit may be needed
Important Commands

CommandPurpose
git switch mainSwitch to the destination branch
git merge feature-nameMerge the feature branch into the current branch
git log --onelineView commit history
git log --oneline --graph --allView commit history as a branch graph
Complete Visual Summary ⭐

START A ─── B ↑ main + feature ↓ Both branches get separate commits A ─── B ─── C main \ D ─── E feature ↓ Switch to main ↓ git merge feature ↓ Git joins histories A ─── B ─── C ─────── M main \ / D ─── E ─────── ↓ M = Merge Commit 🔀
Summary

ConceptMeaning
Merge commitA special commit that joins separate branch histories
Diverged historyBoth branches received separate commits
Fast-forward possible?Usually no when histories have diverged
Merge conflict?Not required for a merge commit to exist
Merge commandgit merge source-branch
HistoryShows the point where branches joined
One-Line Definition: A merge commit is a special Git commit created to combine two branches that have developed separately and whose histories cannot simply be fast-forwarded.
practice: Use your existing Git-Practice repository. This practice creates two branches with separate commits so you can understand why a merge commit is needed.

STEP 1 → Start on main ↓ STEP 2 → Create feature branch ↓ STEP 3 → Commit a change on feature branch ↓ STEP 4 → Switch back to main ↓ STEP 5 → Commit a different change on main ↓ STEP 6 → Merge feature into main ↓ STEP 7 → View the commit graph
Step 1: Switch to main and check your status.
git switch main git status
Step 2: Create and switch to a new branch.
git switch -c feature-merge-commit-practice
Step 3: Create a file named feature.txt and add some text such as:
This change belongs to the feature branch.
Then stage and commit it.
git add feature.txt git commit -m "Add feature branch file"
Your feature branch now has a commit that main does not have.
main A ─── B feature-merge-commit-practice A ─── B ─── C
Step 4: Switch back to main.
git switch main
Step 5: Create a different file named main.txt and add some text such as:
This change belongs directly to main.
Stage and commit this change.
git add main.txt git commit -m "Add main branch file"
Now the branches have diverged because both have their own new commits.
A ─── B ─── D main 📍 \ C feature branch
Step 6: Merge the feature branch into main.
git merge feature-merge-commit-practice
Because both branches have separate commits, Git cannot perform a normal fast-forward merge. If the changes do not conflict, Git should combine them and create a merge commit.
Before merge: A ─── B ─── D main \ C feature ↓ Merge After merge: A ─── B ─── D ───── M main \ / C ─────────────
Step 7: View the history as a graph.
git log --oneline --graph --all
Look for the point where Git joined the two branch histories.
Step 8: Check your project files.
After the successful merge, while on main, both files should be present:
main.txt ✅ feature.txt ✅
Practice Challenge: Before running a merge, answer these questions:
main has a new commit? → Yes feature branch has a new commit? → Yes Did both branches move separately? → Yes Can Git simply move main forward? → No Result → A merge commit may be created 🔀
Optional Cleanup: After verifying the merge, delete the practice branch if you no longer need it.
git branch -d feature-merge-commit-practice
Practice Goal: Understand the difference between a fast-forward merge and a merge commit by creating separate commits on both branches and then joining their histories.

qna.q: Q1. What is a merge commit?
qna.a: A merge commit is a special commit created when Git joins two separate lines of development.

qna.q: Q2. When is a merge commit typically needed?
qna.a: It is typically needed when both branches have received separate commits and Git cannot simply fast-forward the destination branch.

qna.q: Q3. What does it mean when branch histories have diverged?
qna.a: It means the branches started from a common commit but later received different commits independently.

qna.q: Q4. If only the feature branch moved forward and main did not receive a new commit, what merge may be possible?
qna.a: A fast-forward merge may be possible.

qna.q: Q5. If both main and feature-login received separate commits, can Git normally perform a simple fast-forward merge?
qna.a: No. The histories have diverged, so Git cannot simply move the destination branch pointer forward.

qna.q: Q6. What command do you use to merge a feature branch into main?
qna.a: First switch to main, then run git merge followed by the feature branch name.

qna.q: Q7. Does every git merge create a merge commit?
qna.a: No. A fast-forward merge usually does not require a separate merge commit.

qna.q: Q8. Does a merge commit mean there was definitely a merge conflict?
qna.a: No. A merge commit can be created successfully without any merge conflict.

qna.q: Q9. What does a merge commit represent in the history?
qna.a: It represents the point where two separate branch histories were joined together.

qna.q: Q10. What command can help you visually understand branch and merge history?
qna.a: git log --oneline --graph --all

qna.q: Q11. In this situation, which branch histories have diverged: main has commit D and feature has commit C after both started from B?
qna.a: Both histories have diverged because main and the feature branch each have separate commits after the common commit B.

qna.q: Q12. What is the easiest way to remember the difference between fast-forward and merge commit?
qna.a: If one branch simply moved ahead, fast-forward may be possible. If both branches moved separately, Git needs to join the histories and a merge commit may be created.

items.title: What is a Merge Conflict?
explanation: Simple Meaning
A merge conflict happens when Git cannot automatically decide how to combine changes from different branches.
This usually happens when two branches change the same part of the same file in different ways.
Simple Definition: A merge conflict occurs when Git finds conflicting changes and needs a developer to manually decide what the final code or content should be.
Simple Example
Suppose both branches contain this original line:
Welcome to my website
On main, someone changes it to:
Welcome to our website
On feature-login, someone changes the same line to:
Welcome to the login portal
Now Git sees:
main ↓ Welcome to our website feature-login ↓ Welcome to the login portal ↓ Merge Which version should Git keep? 🤔 Git cannot safely decide ↓ Merge Conflict ⚠️
Why Does Git Stop?
Git is designed to avoid guessing when changes conflict.
Suppose Git automatically chose one version:
Option 1 → Keep main change ❌ Feature change may be lost Option 2 → Keep feature change ❌ Main change may be lost
Instead of making the decision for you, Git stops the merge and asks you to resolve the conflict.
Important: Git does not know which change is correct. You must decide the final result.
When Do Merge Conflicts Happen? ⭐
The most common situation is:
Same file ↓ Same section of the file ↓ Changed differently in two branches ↓ Merge attempted ↓ Git cannot combine automatically ↓ Merge Conflict ⚠️
Example:

BranchChange
mainChanges line 10 to Login
feature-loginChanges line 10 to Sign In
When Git tries to merge these changes, it may need your help.
Merge Conflict Does Not Mean Every Same File Change Will Fail
This is very important.
Two branches can modify the same file without creating a conflict if they change different parts that Git can combine safely.
Example:
main changes: Line 5 → Add header feature branch changes: Line 50 → Add footer ↓ Merge Git can usually combine both changes automatically ✅
A conflict is more likely when the changes overlap or Git cannot determine how to combine them.
Visual Example: No Conflict
Original file: 1. Welcome 2. Login 3. Contact
main changes line 1:
1. Welcome to our website 2. Login 3. Contact
feature-login changes line 3:
1. Welcome 2. Login 3. Contact us today
Git can usually combine the changes:
1. Welcome to our website 2. Login 3. Contact us today
Different parts changed ↓ Git understands both changes ↓ Automatic merge possible ✅
Visual Example: Conflict
Original file: Welcome
main changes it to:
Welcome to our website
feature-login changes the same line to:
Welcome to the login page
Same original line ↓ Changed differently ↓ Git cannot safely combine them ↓ Merge Conflict ⚠️
What Happens When You Run git merge?
Suppose you are on main and run:
git merge feature-login
Git checks the changes from both branches:
git merge feature-login ↓ Git compares changes ↓ Can changes be combined automatically? YES → Merge completes ✅ NO → Merge conflict ⚠️
When a conflict occurs, Git stops before completing the merge. You must resolve the conflicting content before the merge can be completed.
What Does a Conflict Look Like Inside a File? ⭐
Git adds special conflict markers to show the conflicting sections.
<<<<<<< HEAD Welcome to our website ======= Welcome to the login portal >>>>>>> feature-login
Let's understand each section:

MarkerMeaning
<<<<<<< HEADThe changes from your current branch
Content above =======Your current branch's version
=======Separates the two conflicting versions
Content below =======The incoming branch's version
>>>>>>> feature-loginShows the incoming branch name
Understand HEAD ⭐
HEAD represents the commit currently checked out by Git. During a merge conflict, the content below <<<<<<< HEAD comes from the branch you are currently on.
Example:
You are currently on main 📍 ↓ git merge feature-login ↓ Conflict occurs ↓ HEAD section = main version Incoming section = feature-login version
You will learn more about HEAD later as Git concepts become more advanced. For now, remember: during this merge, HEAD means your current branch's version.
How Do You Resolve a Conflict?
You manually edit the file and decide what the final content should be.
For example, Git shows:
<<<<<<< HEAD Welcome to our website ======= Welcome to the login portal >>>>>>> feature-login
You might decide the final result should be:
Welcome to our login portal
Then you remove all conflict markers.
Conflict markers found ↓ Read both versions ↓ Decide final content ↓ Edit the file manually ↓ Remove conflict markers ↓ Save file ↓ Continue merge process
Important: You Can Choose More Than One Version
You do not always have to choose only the current branch or only the incoming branch.
You can:

• Keep the current branch version
  • Keep the incoming branch version
  • Combine both versions
  • Write completely new content
Example:

Current branch: Welcome to our website Incoming branch: Welcome to the login portal Possible final result: Welcome to our website login portal OR Welcome to the login portal OR Any correct final content you decide
Merge Conflict Resolution Workflow ⭐

1. Run git merge ↓ 2. Git reports conflict ⚠️ ↓ 3. Run git status ↓ 4. Open conflicting file ↓ 5. Read conflict markers ↓ 6. Decide final content ↓ 7. Remove conflict markers ↓ 8. Save file ↓ 9. git add file-name ↓ 10. Complete the merge
Check Conflicted Files
After a conflict occurs, run:
git status
Git will show that some files have conflicts that need to be resolved.
This helps you identify which files require your attention.
After Fixing the Conflict
After manually editing and saving the file, mark the conflict as resolved by staging the file:
git add file-name
For example:
git add index.html
Then check the status again:
git status
Once all conflicts are resolved and staged, Git can complete the merge.
Important Difference: Conflict vs Error
A merge conflict is not necessarily a mistake or Git failure.
It simply means Git needs human input.
Merge Conflict ⚠️ ↓ Git needs your decision ↓ You resolve the content ↓ Merge can continue ✅
Merge Conflict vs Merge Commit

Merge ConflictMerge Commit
Git cannot automatically combine some changesRecords the joining of branch histories
Requires manual resolutionCan be created without any conflict
Temporary state during mergingPart of commit history
Important: A merge commit does not mean there was a merge conflict, and a merge conflict does not mean the merge will fail permanently.
Merge Conflict vs Fast-Forward

Fast-ForwardMerge Conflict
Concerns commit historyConcerns conflicting file changes
Git can move branch forwardGit needs help combining content
May happen without file conflictsCan happen during a non-fast-forward merge
Common Beginner Mistake 1: Deleting the Wrong Content
When you see conflict markers, do not immediately delete one section without reading both versions.
Before deleting anything: ↓ Understand current branch change ↓ Understand incoming branch change ↓ Decide what final content should be ↓ Then edit safely
Common Beginner Mistake 2: Leaving Conflict Markers in the File ⚠️
Do not leave these markers in your final file:
<<<<<<< ======= >>>>>>>
After resolving the conflict, all conflict markers must be removed.
Common Beginner Mistake 3: Forgetting to Stage the Resolved File
Editing the file alone is not enough.
After resolving it, you normally stage the resolved file:
git add file-name
Common Beginner Mistake 4: Panicking 😄
Merge conflicts are a normal part of working with Git, especially when multiple developers work on the same project.
Merge conflict happens ↓ Do not panic 😄 ↓ Check git status ↓ Read the conflicting file ↓ Resolve carefully ↓ Continue
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
Git sees two different answers for the same piece of content ↓ Git refuses to guess ↓ Git asks you to decide ↓ That is a Merge Conflict ⚠️
Real-World Team Example
Imagine two developers working on the same button:

Developer A → main Changes button text to: "Login" Developer B → feature-login Changes same button text to: "Sign In" ↓ Merge branches ↓ Git sees conflicting changes ↓ Developer decides final text ↓ "Login" OR "Sign In" OR another value
Important Commands

CommandPurpose
git merge branch-nameStart merging a branch
git statusIdentify files with conflicts
git add file-nameMark a resolved file for the merge
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
Merge conflictGit cannot automatically combine changes
Common causeSame part of a file changed differently
Git's actionStops and asks for manual resolution
Conflict markersShow the conflicting versions
HEAD sectionVersion from the current branch
Incoming sectionVersion from the branch being merged
ResolutionManually decide and edit final content
After resolutionRemove markers and stage the resolved file

One-Line Definition: A merge conflict occurs when Git cannot automatically combine different changes, usually because branches changed the same part of a file, so a developer must manually decide the final content.
practice: For this topic, first understand the concept. In the next topic, you will intentionally create a merge conflict and resolve it yourself.
Scenario 1: Read the changes below and decide whether Git may need manual help.

Original: Button text = Login main: Button text = Sign In feature branch: Button text = Log In Now Question: Both branches changed the same content differently. What may happen during the merge? Answer: Merge Conflict ⚠️
Scenario 2: Read this example.
main changes: Line 5 → Add header feature branch changes: Line 50 → Add footer Question: Did both branches change exactly the same section? Answer: No ↓ Git may be able to merge automatically ✅
Practice Task: Look at this conflict marker example and identify the two versions.
<<<<<<< HEAD Welcome to our website ======= Welcome to the login portal >>>>>>> feature-login
Question 1: Which version belongs to the current branch? ↓ Welcome to our website Question 2: Which version comes from feature-login? ↓ Welcome to the login portal
Practice Task: Decide what final content you would keep.
Option A → Keep current branch version Option B → Keep incoming branch version Option C → Combine both versions Option D → Write your own final version
Practice Goal: Before moving to the next topic, you should understand why merge conflicts happen, recognize conflict markers, and know that the next step is to manually decide the final content.
Next Topic Preparation: The next topic is Create a Merge Conflict Intentionally. You will use your Git-Practice repository to create an actual conflict and see these markers yourself.

qna.q: Q1. What is a merge conflict?
qna.a: A merge conflict happens when Git cannot automatically decide how to combine changes from different branches.

qna.q: Q2. What is the most common cause of a merge conflict?
qna.a: Two branches changing the same part of the same file in different ways.

qna.q: Q3. Does changing the same file always cause a merge conflict?
qna.a: No. Git can often merge changes automatically when the branches changed different parts of the file.

qna.q: Q4. Why does Git stop when a conflict occurs?
qna.a: Git stops because it cannot safely decide which conflicting change should become the final version.

qna.q: Q5. What does the content under HEAD represent during a merge conflict?
qna.a: It represents the version from the branch you are currently on.

qna.q: Q6. What does the content below ======= represent?
qna.a: It represents the conflicting version coming from the branch being merged.

qna.q: Q7. What must you remove after resolving a merge conflict?
qna.a: You must remove all Git conflict markers such as <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>>.

qna.q: Q8. Can you combine both versions when resolving a conflict?
qna.a: Yes. You can keep one version, combine both versions, or write a completely new final version.

qna.q: Q9. What command can help identify conflicted files?
qna.a: git status

qna.q: Q10. After fixing a conflicted file, what command do you normally use to stage it?
qna.a: git add file-name

qna.q: Q11. Does a merge conflict mean the merge has permanently failed?
qna.a: No. It means Git needs your manual help to resolve the conflicting changes before the merge can continue.

qna.q: Q12. What is the main difference between a merge commit and a merge conflict?
qna.a: A merge commit records joined branch histories, while a merge conflict occurs when Git cannot automatically combine some file changes.

items.title: Create a Merge Conflict Intentionally
explanation: Simple Meaning
Now that you understand what a merge conflict is, it is time to create one yourself.
The easiest way is to make two branches change the same line in the same file differently, and then merge them.
Goal: Intentionally create conflicting changes so you can see how Git detects and reports a merge conflict.
What We Will Do

Start with one file ↓ Create a feature branch ↓ Change the same line differently on feature branch ↓ Switch back to main ↓ Change the same line differently on main ↓ Try to merge feature branch ↓ Git cannot decide which change to keep ↓ Merge Conflict ⚠️
Our Starting File
We will use a simple file named message.txt.
Initial content:
Welcome to my website
Both branches will start with exactly this same version.
Step 1: Start on main
First, make sure you are inside your Git practice repository and switch to main:
git switch main
Check your current branch:
git branch
You should see something similar to:
* main feature-merge-commit-practice
The * shows your current branch.
Step 2: Create the Starting File
Create message.txt with this content:
Welcome to my website
Then save, stage, and commit it:
git add message.txt git commit -m "Add message file"
Now Git has a common starting point for both branches.
A ─── B ↑ main B = message.txt Welcome to my website
Step 3: Create a Feature Branch
Create and switch to a new branch:
git switch -c feature-conflict
Now both branches contain the same version of message.txt:
A ─── B ↑ ↑ main feature-conflict message.txt: Welcome to my website
Step 4: Change the File on the Feature Branch
While you are on feature-conflict, open message.txt and change:
Welcome to my website
to:
Welcome to the feature branch
Now stage and commit the change:
git add message.txt git commit -m "Update message on feature branch"
Your branches now look like this:
A ─── B main \ C feature-conflict 📍 main: Welcome to my website feature-conflict: Welcome to the feature branch
Step 5: Switch Back to main
git switch main
Git now shows the version stored on main:
Welcome to my website
Important: The feature branch and main branch now have different versions of the same file, but there is not yet a conflict. A conflict happens when Git tries to combine the changes.
Step 6: Change the Same Line on main
While on main, change message.txt from:
Welcome to my website
to:
Welcome to the main branch
Stage and commit the change:
git add message.txt git commit -m "Update message on main branch"
Now we have the exact situation needed for a conflict:
main 📍 A ─── B ─── D \ C ↑ feature-conflict main changed the line to: Welcome to the main branch feature-conflict changed the same line to: Welcome to the feature branch
Why Will This Cause a Conflict? ⭐
Both branches started from the same original content:
Welcome to my website
Then each branch changed that exact content differently:

BranchNew Content
mainWelcome to the main branch
feature-conflictWelcome to the feature branch
Git cannot safely know which final version you want.
Step 7: Attempt the Merge ⚠️
Make sure you are still on main, then run:
git merge feature-conflict
Git attempts to combine the changes:
main version ↓ Welcome to the main branch feature version ↓ Welcome to the feature branch ↓ Merge Git cannot choose automatically 🤔 ↓ CONFLICT ⚠️
What Git May Display
You may see output similar to:
Auto-merging message.txt CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in message.txt Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
The exact wording can vary slightly depending on your Git version.
The important part is that Git tells you:
Git found a conflict ↓ Merge is paused ↓ message.txt needs attention ↓ You must decide the final content
Step 8: Check Git Status
Run:
git status
Git will indicate that the merge is in progress and that message.txt has conflicting changes.
Conceptually, you may see something like:
You have unmerged paths. Unmerged paths: both modified: message.txt
Step 9: Open the Conflicting File
Open message.txt in VS Code.
You should see conflict markers similar to:
<<<<<<< HEAD Welcome to the main branch ======= Welcome to the feature branch >>>>>>> feature-conflict
Understand What You Just Created ⭐

SectionMeaning
<<<<<<< HEADStart of the current branch version
Welcome to the main branchYour main branch change
=======Separator between both versions
Welcome to the feature branchIncoming feature branch change
>>>>>>> feature-conflictEnd of conflict and source branch name
Visual History of the Entire Practice

STEP 1: Common version message.txt Welcome to my website A ─── B ↑ main + feature ↓ STEP 2: Feature changes same line A ─── B \ C feature: Welcome to the feature branch ↓ STEP 3: main changes same line differently A ─── B ─── D \ C main: Welcome to the main branch ↓ STEP 4: Try to merge git merge feature-conflict ↓ Git cannot combine the same line automatically ↓ MERGE CONFLICT ⚠️
Important: Stop Here for This Topic
This topic is specifically about creating a merge conflict intentionally.
Once you successfully see the conflict markers, you have completed this practice.
Created different changes on same line ✅ ↓ Attempted merge ✅ ↓ Git reported conflict ✅ ↓ Saw conflict markers in file ✅ Practice complete 🎉
The next topic will explain how to resolve the merge conflict.
Common Mistake 1: Changing Different Lines
If you change completely different parts of the file, Git may merge automatically and no conflict will occur.
main: Change line 1 feature: Change line 20 ↓ Git may combine automatically No conflict ❌
For this practice, change the exact same line differently in both branches.
Common Mistake 2: Forgetting to Commit Before Switching Branches
For this controlled practice, commit each branch's change before switching branches.
Change file ↓ git add message.txt ↓ git commit -m "message" ↓ Switch branch
Common Mistake 3: Merging From the Wrong Branch
If your goal is to merge feature-conflict into main, you should first switch to main.
git switch main git merge feature-conflict
Remember: You normally switch to the branch that should receive the changes, then merge the other branch into it.
Common Mistake 4: Thinking Git Is Broken 😄
If you successfully create the conflict, Git is working exactly as expected.
Same content changed differently ↓ Git refuses to guess ↓ Git pauses the merge ↓ Conflict markers appear ↓ Success for this practice! 🎯
Commands Used in This Practice

CommandPurpose
git switch mainSwitch to main
git switch -c feature-conflictCreate and switch to the feature branch
git add message.txtStage the file
git commit -m "message"Save the change in Git history
git merge feature-conflictAttempt to merge the feature branch
git statusCheck the conflict state
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
Same original line ↓ main changes it → Version A ↓ feature changes it → Version B ↓ Merge ↓ Git cannot guess ↓ Conflict ⚠️
Summary

StepAction
1Create a common starting file
2Create a feature branch
3Change the same line on the feature branch and commit
4Change the same line differently on main and commit
5Merge the feature branch into main
6Git reports a conflict
7Use git status and inspect the conflict markers
One-Line Definition: To intentionally create a merge conflict, make two branches change the same part of the same file differently, commit both changes, and then attempt to merge the branches.
practice: In this practice, you will intentionally create a real merge conflict. Do not resolve it yet — the next topic is specifically about resolving it.
START ↓ main → Create message.txt ↓ Create feature-conflict branch ↓ Feature changes the same line ↓ main changes the same line differently ↓ Merge feature into main ↓ MERGE CONFLICT ⚠️
Step 1: Switch to main.
git switch main
Step 2: Create message.txt with this exact content:
Welcome to my website
Save and commit it.
git add message.txt git commit -m "Add message file for conflict practice"
Step 3: Create and switch to the feature branch.
git switch -c feature-conflict
Step 4: Change message.txt to:
Welcome to the feature branch
Save, stage, and commit it.
git add message.txt git commit -m "Update message on feature branch"
Step 5: Switch back to main.
git switch main
Step 6: Change the exact same line in message.txt to:
Welcome to the main branch
Save, stage, and commit it.
git add message.txt git commit -m "Update message on main branch"
Step 7: You should now have this situation:
main: Welcome to the main branch feature-conflict: Welcome to the feature branch Both changed the same original line differently ⚠️
Step 8: While still on main, attempt the merge.
git merge feature-conflict
Expected Result: Git should report a merge conflict in message.txt.
Auto-merging message.txt ↓ CONFLICT (content) ⚠️ ↓ Automatic merge failed ↓ Git waits for your decision
Step 9: Check the repository status.
git status
Step 10: Open message.txt in VS Code and confirm that you can see conflict markers similar to:
<<<<<<< HEAD Welcome to the main branch ======= Welcome to the feature branch >>>>>>> feature-conflict
Stop Here: Do not edit or resolve the conflict yet. Leave the repository in the conflict state so you can use the same conflict in Topic 38.
Practice Goal: Successfully create a real merge conflict and verify it using git status and the conflict markers inside message.txt.

qna.q: Q1. What is the easiest way to intentionally create a merge conflict?
qna.a: Make two branches change the same part of the same file differently, commit both changes, and then merge the branches.

qna.q: Q2. Why do both branches need a common starting version?
qna.a: Git needs a common history so it can compare how each branch changed the original content.

qna.q: Q3. In this practice, what file is used to create the conflict?
qna.a: message.txt

qna.q: Q4. What does the feature branch change the message to?
qna.a: Welcome to the feature branch.

qna.q: Q5. What does main change the message to?
qna.a: Welcome to the main branch.

qna.q: Q6. Why can Git not automatically merge these two changes?
qna.a: Both branches changed the same original line differently, so Git cannot safely decide which final version should be kept.
