qna.q: Q7. Which branch should you normally be on before merging feature-conflict into main?
qna.a: You should be on main because main is the branch that will receive the feature branch changes.

qna.q: Q8. What command attempts to create the merge conflict in this practice?
qna.a: git merge feature-conflict

qna.q: Q9. What command can you use after the conflict occurs to check the repository state?
qna.a: git status

qna.q: Q10. What markers should you expect to see inside a conflicted file?
qna.a: Git conflict markers such as <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>>.

qna.q: Q11. If main changes line 1 and the feature branch changes line 20, will a conflict definitely happen?
qna.a: No. Git can often combine changes automatically when they affect different parts of the file.

qna.q: Q12. What should you do after successfully creating the conflict for this topic?
qna.a: Verify the conflict using git status and inspect the conflict markers, then keep it unresolved for the next topic where you will learn how to resolve it.

items.title: Resolve a Merge Conflict
explanation: Simple Meaning
In the previous topic, you intentionally created a merge conflict. Now you will learn how to resolve it.
Resolving a merge conflict means manually deciding what the final content of the file should be, removing the conflict markers, staging the resolved file, and completing the merge.
Simple Definition: Resolving a merge conflict is the process of manually fixing conflicting changes so Git can complete the merge.
Where We Are Starting
From Topic 37, your repository should still be in a merge conflict state.
You attempted:
git switch main git merge feature-conflict
The conflict happened because both branches changed the same line differently:
main 📍 ↓ Welcome to the main branch feature-conflict ↓ Welcome to the feature branch ↓ Merge Git cannot decide automatically ⚠️
The Conflict Resolution Process ⭐

Merge conflict occurs ⚠️ ↓ Check git status ↓ Open conflicted file ↓ Understand both changes ↓ Decide final content ↓ Remove conflict markers ↓ Save the file ↓ Stage resolved file ↓ Complete the merge ✅
Step 1: Check the Conflict Status
First, run:
git status
Git will show that a merge is in progress and that a file needs to be resolved.
You may see information similar to:
On branch main You have unmerged paths. (fix conflicts and run "git commit") Unmerged paths: (use "git add <file>..." to mark resolution) both modified: message.txt
The exact output may vary, but the important information is:
Merge in progress ↓ message.txt has conflicting changes ↓ Git is waiting for you to resolve them
Step 2: Open the Conflicted File
Open message.txt in VS Code.
You should see content similar to this:
<<<<<<< HEAD Welcome to the main branch ======= Welcome to the feature branch >>>>>>> feature-conflict
Git has placed special markers inside the file.
Understand the Conflict Markers Again ⭐

SectionMeaning
<<<<<<< HEADBeginning of the current branch version
Welcome to the main branchChange from your current branch, which is main
=======Separates the two conflicting versions
Welcome to the feature branchChange coming from feature-conflict
>>>>>>> feature-conflictEnd of the conflict section
Step 3: Decide the Final Content
Git will not decide the correct version for you. You must decide what should remain in the final file.
You generally have four choices:
Option 1 → Keep current branch version Option 2 → Keep incoming branch version Option 3 → Combine both versions Option 4 → Write completely new content
Option 1: Keep the Current Branch Version
Since you are currently on main, the current branch version is:
Welcome to the main branch
Your final message.txt would contain only:
Welcome to the main branch
All conflict markers must be removed.
Option 2: Keep the Incoming Branch Version
The incoming branch version is:
Welcome to the feature branch
Your final message.txt would contain only:
Welcome to the feature branch
Again, all conflict markers must be removed.
Option 3: Combine Both Changes
You may decide that both changes are useful.
For example, your final content could be:
Welcome to the main branch Welcome to the feature branch
You can manually combine the changes in any correct way.
Option 4: Write Your Own Final Version
You are not restricted to either version.
For example:
Welcome to our website
As long as the final content is what you want and the conflict markers are removed, Git accepts your resolution.
For Our Practice
Let's combine the idea into one clean final message:
Welcome to our main feature branch
So replace the entire conflicted content:
<<<<<<< HEAD Welcome to the main branch ======= Welcome to the feature branch >>>>>>> feature-conflict
with:
Welcome to our main feature branch
Important: The final content in this practice is your decision. There is no special Git rule saying you must keep one branch's exact version.
Step 4: Remove All Conflict Markers ⚠️
Before saving, make sure these markers no longer exist:
<<<<<<< ======= >>>>>>>
Your file should contain only the final content you decided to keep.
Before resolution ⚠️ <<<<<<< HEAD Version A ======= Version B >>>>>>> branch-name ↓ After resolution ✅ Final Version
Step 5: Save the File
After editing the file and removing the markers, save message.txt.
At this point, you have fixed the content, but Git still needs to know that you have resolved the conflict.
Step 6: Stage the Resolved File
Run:
git add message.txt
This tells Git that the conflict in message.txt has been resolved.
Conflict occurs ↓ You manually fix message.txt ↓ Save file ↓ git add message.txt ↓ Git sees the resolved version as ready
Important: git add Does Not Automatically Fix the Conflict
You must first edit the file correctly.
This is the wrong order:
Conflict occurs ↓ git add immediately ❌ ↓ Conflict content is still not properly resolved
The correct order is:
Conflict occurs ↓ Read both changes ↓ Edit final content ↓ Remove markers ↓ Save ↓ git add file-name ✅
Step 7: Check the Status Again
Run:
git status
If all conflicts are resolved, Git should no longer show Unmerged paths.
Instead, Git will indicate that the merge is ready to be completed.
Step 8: Complete the Merge
Run:
git commit
Git may open an editor with a default merge commit message. Usually, you can keep the default message and save/close the editor.
Alternatively, you can provide a message directly:
git commit -m "Resolve merge conflict"
Resolved file ↓ git add message.txt ↓ git commit ↓ Merge completed 🎉
Complete Practice Workflow ⭐

1. Merge conflict occurs ⚠️ ↓ 2. git status ↓ 3. Open message.txt ↓ 4. Read both versions ↓ 5. Decide final content ↓ 6. Remove all conflict markers ↓ 7. Save file ↓ 8. git add message.txt ↓ 9. git status ↓ 10. git commit ↓ Merge successfully completed ✅
VS Code Can Help You Resolve Conflicts
When you open a conflicted file in VS Code, it may provide options such as:
Accept Current Change Accept Incoming Change Accept Both Changes Compare Changes
These options can make conflict resolution easier, but you should first understand what each version means.

VS Code OptionMeaning
Accept Current ChangeKeep the current branch's change
Accept Incoming ChangeKeep the branch being merged
Accept Both ChangesKeep both changes
Compare ChangesReview the differences before deciding
Important: Even when using VS Code buttons, always review the final file before staging it.
Common Mistake 1: Leaving Conflict Markers
Do not leave this inside your final file:
<<<<<<< HEAD ======= >>>>>>>
These are temporary Git markers and should be removed during resolution.
Common Mistake 2: Keeping Both Versions Without Checking the Result
Choosing both versions is not always correct.
For example:
const port = 3000; const port = 5000;
Keeping both lines could create invalid code.
Always review the final result and make sure it makes sense for your project.
Common Mistake 3: Forgetting git add
After manually fixing the file, Git needs the resolved file to be staged:
git add message.txt
Common Mistake 4: Thinking git commit Is Always the First Step
Do not immediately run git commit when a conflict occurs.
You must resolve and stage all conflicting files first.
Conflict ↓ Fix files first ↓ git add resolved files ↓ git commit
Common Mistake 5: Forgetting There Can Be Multiple Conflicted Files
A merge can produce conflicts in more than one file.
You must resolve every conflicted file before completing the merge.
Conflict in file1.txt ⚠️ Conflict in file2.txt ⚠️ Conflict in file3.txt ⚠️ ↓ Resolve all files ↓ Stage all resolved files ↓ Complete merge
How to Cancel the Merge if Needed
If you decide you do not want to continue the merge and want to return to the state before the merge started, you can abort the merge:
git merge --abort
This cancels the in-progress merge and attempts to restore the repository to its pre-merge state.
Use Carefully: git merge --abort is useful when you decide not to continue resolving the current merge.
Resolve vs Abort

ActionResult
Resolve the conflictFix the changes and complete the merge
git merge --abortCancel the current merge attempt
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
Git finds two conflicting versions ↓ Git asks: "What should the final version be?" ↓ You decide ↓ You edit the file ↓ You remove markers ↓ You stage the result ↓ You complete the merge
Commands Used

CommandPurpose
git statusCheck which files have conflicts
git add file-nameStage a resolved file
git commitComplete the merge after resolution
git merge --abortCancel an in-progress merge
Quick Summary

StepAction
1Check the conflict with git status
2Open the conflicted file
3Understand current and incoming changes
4Decide the correct final content
5Remove all conflict markers
6Save the file
7Stage it using git add
8Complete the merge using git commit
One-Line Definition: Resolving a merge conflict means manually deciding the final content, removing Git's conflict markers, staging the resolved file, and completing the merge.
practice: Continue from Topic 37. Your repository should currently have an unresolved merge conflict in message.txt.
Step 1: Check the current Git status.
git status
Confirm that Git shows an unmerged path or conflict involving message.txt.
Step 2: Open message.txt. You should see content similar to:
<<<<<<< HEAD Welcome to the main branch ======= Welcome to the feature branch >>>>>>> feature-conflict
Step 3: Read both versions and decide the final content. For this practice, replace the entire conflicted section with:
Welcome to our main feature branch
Step 4: Make sure all conflict markers have been removed before saving the file.
Remove: <<<<<<< HEAD ======= >>>>>>> feature-conflict Final file should contain only: Welcome to our main feature branch
Step 5: Save message.txt, then stage the resolved file.
git add message.txt
Step 6: Check the status again.
git status
Confirm that Git no longer reports message.txt as an unmerged path.
Step 7: Complete the merge.
git commit -m "Resolve merge conflict"
Step 8: Check the final status.
git status
Your working tree should be clean if everything was completed successfully.
Step 9: Check the commit history.
git log --oneline
You should see the history containing the changes from both branches and the completed merge.
Practice Goal: Successfully resolve a real merge conflict by manually editing the file, removing conflict markers, staging the resolved file, and completing the merge.

qna.q: Q1. What is the first thing you should do after noticing a merge conflict?
qna.a: Check the repository status, usually with git status, and identify the files that need to be resolved.

qna.q: Q2. What does resolving a merge conflict mean?
qna.a: It means manually deciding what the final file content should be so Git can complete the merge.

qna.q: Q3. Do you have to keep exactly one branch's version?
qna.a: No. You can keep the current version, keep the incoming version, combine both, or write your own final content.

qna.q: Q4. What must be removed from the file after resolving a conflict?
qna.a: All Git conflict markers such as <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>>.

qna.q: Q5. After fixing and saving a conflicted file, what command stages it as resolved?
qna.a: git add file-name

qna.q: Q6. What command completes the merge after all conflicts are resolved and staged?
qna.a: git commit

qna.q: Q7. What does Accept Current Change in VS Code generally mean?
qna.a: Keep the version from the branch you are currently on.

qna.q: Q8. What does Accept Incoming Change generally mean?
qna.a: Keep the version coming from the branch being merged into your current branch.

qna.q: Q9. Is using Accept Both Changes always correct?
qna.a: No. You should always review the final result because keeping both changes can sometimes create duplicate or invalid code.

qna.q: Q10. What should you do if you want to cancel an in-progress merge instead of resolving it?
qna.a: Use git merge --abort to cancel the current merge attempt.

qna.q: Q11. Can one merge create conflicts in multiple files?
qna.a: Yes. You must resolve and stage all conflicted files before completing the merge.

qna.q: Q12. Put these steps in the correct order: git commit, edit file, git add, merge conflict occurs.
qna.a: Merge conflict occurs → edit and resolve the file → git add the resolved file → git commit to complete the merge.

items.title: Discard Uncommitted Changes
explanation: Simple Meaning
Discarding uncommitted changes means removing changes you made to a file when those changes have not been committed yet.
You can use this when you make changes by mistake and want the file to return to the version stored in Git.
Simple Definition: Discarding uncommitted changes means removing unwanted local changes and restoring a file to its last committed version.
Simple Example
Suppose your last commit contains:
print("Hello")
Then you modify the file:
print("Hello") print("Testing")
You decide that print("Testing") was added by mistake.
Since the change has not been committed, you can discard it.
Last Commit print("Hello") ↓ You modify file ↓ print("Hello") print("Testing") ↓ Discard changes ↓ Back to last committed version ✅ ↓ print("Hello")
Where Is the Change?
Before learning the command, remember Git's working areas:
Working Directory ↓ git add Staging Area ↓ git commit Local Repository
This topic mainly focuses on changes that are in the Working Directory and have not yet been staged or committed.
Check the Status First ⭐
Before discarding anything, always check:
git status
Suppose Git shows:
Changes not staged for commit: modified: index.html
This means:
index.html was committed previously ↓ You changed it ↓ Changes are only in Working Directory ↓ Not staged ↓ Not committed
This is the situation where git restore can discard the unwanted working-directory changes.
The Command
git restore file-name
For example:
git restore index.html
Git restores index.html to the version from the current commit, removing the uncommitted working-directory changes.
Visual Workflow
Last Commit index.html = Version A ↓ You edit index.html ↓ Working Directory = Version B ↓ git restore index.html ↓ Working Directory = Version A again ✅
Important: The Changes Are Lost ⚠️
When you discard changes, those unwanted modifications are removed from your working file.
So before running:
git restore file-name
Make sure you really do not need those changes.
Be Careful: If you have important uncommitted work, do not discard it accidentally. Check your changes first using git diff.
Safe Workflow Before Discarding
1. Check git status ↓ 2. Check git diff ↓ 3. Confirm changes are unwanted ↓ 4. Run git restore file-name ↓ 5. Check git status again
Example Using a Real File
Suppose your index.html was last committed with:
<h1>My Website</h1>
You change it to:
<h1>My Website</h1> <p>Testing unwanted content</p>
Now run:
git diff
You confirm the added paragraph is unwanted. Then run:
git restore index.html
The file returns to:
<h1>My Website</h1>
Discard Changes from Multiple Files
You can specify multiple files:
git restore index.html style.css script.js
This discards the unstaged working-directory changes in those specified files.
Discard All Unstaged Changes
If you want to restore all tracked files with unstaged changes in the current directory, you can use:
git restore .
Warning: This can discard changes from multiple files. Use git diff first so you know exactly what you are removing.
What git restore Does in This Topic

SituationResult
File modified but not stagedRestores the file and removes those changes
File has unwanted local editsReturns it to the current committed version
Changes already committedThis is not the normal command for undoing the commit
Important: Modified vs Staged Changes ⭐
Suppose you run:
git add index.html
Now the change is in the Staging Area.
Working Directory ↓ git add Staging Area 📦 ↓ git commit Repository
This topic is specifically about discarding normal unstaged changes. If your changes are already staged, you need to understand the staging state before discarding them.
Next Topic: Topic 40 covers Unstage Files using git restore --staged.
Example: Why git restore May Not Do What You Expect
Suppose the last commit contains:
Hello
You modify it to:
Hello World
Then stage it:
git add file.txt
Now the change is staged.
If you are trying to understand staged changes, do not confuse this with simply restoring an unstaged working file. The next topic will explain how to remove changes from the Staging Area.
Untracked Files Are Different ⭐
Suppose you create a completely new file:
newfile.txt
Git may show:
Untracked files: newfile.txt
An untracked file has never been added to Git history. Therefore, Git does not have a previous committed version of that file to restore.
Tracked file Has previous Git version ↓ git restore can restore previous version Untracked file No previous Git version ↓ No committed version for Git to restore
Modified vs Untracked

StatusMeaning
ModifiedGit already knows the file and you changed it
UntrackedGit does not yet track the file
StagedThe changes are prepared for the next commit
How to Check Changes Before Discarding
Use:
git diff
This lets you review your unstaged changes before removing them.
You changed a file ↓ git diff ↓ Review what changed ↓ Still need changes? → Keep them Do not need changes? → git restore file-name
Practical Scenario
You are working on your website:

Last committed website ✅ ↓ Experiment with new CSS ↓ Website looks worse 😄 ↓ You do not want the CSS changes ↓ git diff ↓ Confirm unwanted changes ↓ git restore style.css ↓ Return to previous committed CSS ✅
Common Mistake 1: Discarding Without Checking
Do not immediately run:
git restore .
First check:
git status git diff
This is especially important when working on multiple files.
Common Mistake 2: Expecting git restore to Undo a Commit
Suppose you already committed a change:
Commit A ↓ Commit B ↓ You now regret Commit B
This is a different situation. You will learn commands such as git revert and git reset in later topics.
Common Mistake 3: Forgetting the Difference Between Staged and Unstaged
Always check git status first.
Changes not staged for commit ↓ Working Directory changes ↓ This topic: git restore file-name Changes to be committed ↓ Staged changes ↓ Next topic: git restore --staged file-name
Common Mistake 4: Trying to Restore an Untracked File
If a file has never been tracked, Git has no earlier version to restore.
For example:
Untracked files: test.txt
Think carefully before deleting files manually. This topic focuses on restoring changes to files Git already tracks.
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
Changed file ↓ Not staged ↓ Not committed ↓ Do not want changes? ↓ git restore file-name ↓ Back to committed version
Important Commands

CommandPurpose
git statusCheck the state of your files
git diffReview unstaged changes
git restore file-nameDiscard unstaged changes in one file
git restore .Discard unstaged changes in tracked files under the current directory
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
Uncommitted changesChanges not yet saved in Git history
Modified fileA tracked file changed locally
git diffReview unstaged changes
git restore file-nameDiscard unwanted unstaged changes in that file
git restore .Discard unstaged changes from multiple tracked files
Staged changesHandled separately; next topic explains unstaging
Untracked fileHas no previous committed Git version to restore
One-Line Definition: To discard unwanted unstaged changes in a tracked file, use git restore file-name to restore the file to its version from the current commit.
practice: For this practice, use a test file so you can safely make and discard changes.
Step 1: Check your current repository status.
git status
Make sure you understand the current state before starting.
Step 2: Create or use a tracked file named restore-practice.txt with this content:
Version 1
Stage and commit it so Git has a version to restore.
git add restore-practice.txt git commit -m "Add restore practice file"
Step 3: Modify the file without staging it.
Version 1 This change should be discarded
Step 4: Check the status.
git status
Confirm that restore-practice.txt appears as modified and is not staged for commit.
Step 5: Review exactly what changed.
git diff
Step 6: Confirm that the added line is unwanted, then discard the change.
git restore restore-practice.txt
Step 7: Open the file again. It should now contain:
Version 1
Step 8: Check the final status.
git status
The practice file should no longer show the discarded modification.
Optional Practice: Modify two tracked files, review them with git diff, and discard only one file using its filename. This helps you understand that you do not always need to discard every change.
Practice Goal: Make an unstaged change, review it using git diff, discard it using git restore file-name, and verify that the file returns to its last committed version.

qna.q: Q1. What does discarding uncommitted changes mean?
qna.a: It means removing unwanted local changes that have not been committed and restoring the tracked file to its committed version.

qna.q: Q2. What command can discard unstaged changes in one file?
qna.a: git restore file-name

qna.q: Q3. Before discarding changes, which command should you use to check the repository state?
qna.a: git status

qna.q: Q4. Which command can help you review unstaged changes before discarding them?
qna.a: git diff

qna.q: Q5. What happens to unwanted changes after git restore file-name?
qna.a: The unstaged working-directory changes in that file are removed and the file is restored to its version from the current commit.

qna.q: Q6. Are discarded changes something you should remove without checking?
qna.a: No. You should first review the changes because unwanted local work may be lost.

qna.q: Q7. What is the difference between a modified file and an untracked file?
qna.a: A modified file is already tracked by Git and has been changed, while an untracked file has not yet been added to Git tracking.

qna.q: Q8. Why is an untracked file different from a tracked modified file when restoring?
qna.a: An untracked file does not have a previous committed version in Git for git restore to restore.

qna.q: Q9. Does this topic primarily deal with changes that are already committed?
qna.a: No. This topic focuses on unwanted local changes that have not yet been committed.

qna.q: Q10. What command can discard unstaged changes from tracked files under the current directory?
qna.a: git restore .

qna.q: Q11. What should you check before using git restore .?
qna.a: Use git status and git diff to understand which changes may be discarded.

qna.q: Q12. What is the correct safe order for discarding an unwanted unstaged change?
qna.a: git status → git diff → confirm the change is unwanted → git restore file-name → git status

items.title: Unstage Files
explanation: Simple Meaning
Unstaging a file means removing its changes from the Staging Area while keeping those changes in your Working Directory.
In simple words, you tell Git:
"I added this change for the next commit, but I do not want to commit it yet." ↓ Remove from Staging Area ↓ Keep the file changes locally ✅
Simple Definition: Unstaging removes changes from the Staging Area but does not delete the changes from your file.
Remember Git Working Areas ⭐
Working Directory ↓ git add Staging Area ↓ git commit Local Repository
Suppose you modify a file:
Working Directory → Modified
Then you run:
git add index.html
The change moves to the Staging Area:
Working Directory ↓ git add Staging Area 📦 ↓ Ready for next commit
If you accidentally staged the file or changed your mind, you can unstage it.
The Main Command
git restore --staged file-name
For example:
git restore --staged index.html
This removes index.html from the Staging Area, but keeps your changes in the file.
Simple Example
Suppose your last committed file contains:
print("Hello")
You modify it:
print("Hello") print("Welcome")
Then you stage it:
git add app.py
Now the situation is:
Working Directory → Modified version Staging Area → Modified version 📦 Repository → Old committed version
You decide you are not ready to commit it. Run:
git restore --staged app.py
After unstaging:
Working Directory → Modified version ✅ Still exists Staging Area → Old version Repository → Old committed version
Very Important Difference ⭐
Compare these two commands:

CommandWhat It Does
git restore file-nameDiscards unstaged changes from the Working Directory
git restore --staged file-nameRemoves changes from the Staging Area but keeps them in the Working Directory
git restore file-name ↓ Remove unwanted local changes ❌ ------------------------- git restore --staged file-name ↓ Remove from staging only ↓ Local changes remain ✅
Visual Example
Imagine this flow:

Version 1 → Committed ↓ You edit file → Version 2 ↓ git add file ↓ Version 2 is Staged 📦 ↓ You change your mind ↓ git restore --staged file ↓ Version 2 remains in Working Directory ↓ But it is no longer Staged
How to Check Before Unstaging
Run:
git status
If Git shows something like:
Changes to be committed: modified: index.html
This means index.html is currently staged.
Then you can run:
git restore --staged index.html
Check After Unstaging
Run:
git status
Now Git may show:
Changes not staged for commit: modified: index.html
Notice what happened:
Before Changes to be committed ↓ File is Staged 📦 After git restore --staged ↓ Changes not staged for commit ↓ File is Modified locally ✏️
The File Changes Are Not Deleted ⭐
This is the most important concept in this topic.
Suppose your file contains:
<h1>My Website</h1> <p>New paragraph</p>
After running:
git restore --staged index.html
The file still contains:
<h1>My Website</h1> <p>New paragraph</p>
Only its staging status changed.
Unstage Multiple Files
You can unstage multiple specific files:
git restore --staged index.html style.css script.js
The changes remain in all the files, but they are removed from the Staging Area.
Unstage All Staged Files
To unstage all currently staged changes in the current directory, you can use:
git restore --staged .
Important: This removes changes from the Staging Area but does not delete the actual modifications from your working files.
Another Command You May See
You may also see this older and commonly used command:
git reset HEAD file-name
For example:
git reset HEAD index.html
It can also unstage a file while keeping the working-directory changes.
However, for learning this roadmap, focus first on the clearer modern command:
git restore --staged file-name
Why Would You Unstage a File?
Here are some common situations:

SituationWhy Unstage?
Accidentally used git add .You staged files you do not want in the commit
Commit is not readyYou want to continue working before committing
Wrong file stagedYou want to remove that file from the next commit
Changes belong to another commitYou want to organize commits properly
Real-World Example: git add . by Mistake
Suppose your project has:
index.html → Ready style.css → Ready script.js → Still testing
You accidentally run:
git add .
Now everything is staged:
index.html 📦 Staged style.css 📦 Staged script.js 📦 Staged
But you only want to commit index.html and style.css.
So unstage only script.js:
git restore --staged script.js
Now:
index.html 📦 Staged style.css 📦 Staged script.js ✏️ Modified but not staged
You can now commit only the files that are staged.
Common Mistake 1: Thinking Unstage Deletes the File Changes
This is incorrect.
git restore --staged file-name Does NOT mean: Delete my changes ❌ It means: Remove changes from Staging Area Keep changes in Working Directory ✅
Common Mistake 2: Confusing Unstage with Discard

ActionCommandResult
Unstagegit restore --staged file-nameChanges stay in file
Discardgit restore file-nameUnstaged changes are removed
Common Mistake 3: Running git commit After Unstaging Everything
If you unstage all files:
git restore --staged .
Then run:
git commit -m "My changes"
Git may report that there is nothing staged to commit.
You need to stage the files you want first:
git add file-name
Common Mistake 4: Forgetting to Check git status
Always use git status to understand where your changes currently are.
Modified? ↓ Check git status Staged? ↓ Unstage if needed Modified but not staged? ↓ Discard or edit if needed Ready? ↓ Stage and commit
Easy Way to Remember 🧠

git add ↓ Put changes INTO the Staging Area 📦 ------------------------ git restore --staged ↓ Take changes OUT OF the Staging Area 📦 ------------------------ The file changes remain on your computer ✏️
Commands Used

CommandPurpose
git statusCheck whether files are staged
git add file-nameStage a file
git restore --staged file-nameUnstage one file
git restore --staged .Unstage staged changes in the current directory
git reset HEAD file-nameAnother command commonly used to unstage
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
StagePrepare changes for the next commit
UnstageRemove changes from the Staging Area
Working Directory changesRemain after unstaging
git restore --staged file-nameUnstage one file
git restore --staged .Unstage multiple staged files
git restore file-nameDifferent command used to discard unstaged changes
One-Line Definition: To unstage a file, use git restore --staged file-name; this removes the change from the Staging Area while keeping the actual file changes in your Working Directory.
practice: For this practice, use a test file so you can clearly see the difference between staging and unstaging.
Step 1: Create a file named unstage-practice.txt with this content:
Version 1
Step 2: Stage and commit the file so Git starts tracking it.
git add unstage-practice.txt git commit -m "Add unstage practice file"
Step 3: Modify the file and add a new line:
Version 1 Version 2
Step 4: Check the status. The file should be modified but not staged.
git status
Step 5: Stage the modified file.
git add unstage-practice.txt
Step 6: Check the status again. Confirm that the file appears under Changes to be committed.
git status
Step 7: Now unstage the file.
git restore --staged unstage-practice.txt
Step 8: Check the status again.
git status
The file should now appear as modified but not staged.
Step 9: Open the file and confirm that your changes still exist:
Version 1 Version 2
Optional Practice: Modify two files, run git add ., then use git restore --staged file-name to remove only one file from the Staging Area. Check git status before and after.
Practice Goal: Stage a modified file, unstage it using git restore --staged file-name, and confirm that the changes still remain in the Working Directory.

qna.q: Q1. What does unstaging a file mean?
qna.a: It means removing the file's changes from the Staging Area while keeping the changes in the Working Directory.

qna.q: Q2. What command unstages a specific file?
qna.a: git restore --staged file-name

qna.q: Q3. Does git restore --staged file-name delete your file changes?
qna.a: No. It removes the changes from the Staging Area but keeps them in your Working Directory.

qna.q: Q4. What command should you use to check whether a file is staged?
qna.a: git status

qna.q: Q5. What does git status usually show for a staged file?
qna.a: The file appears under Changes to be committed.

qna.q: Q6. After unstaging a modified file, where do its changes remain?
qna.a: The changes remain in the Working Directory.

qna.q: Q7. What is the difference between git restore file-name and git restore --staged file-name?
qna.a: git restore file-name discards unstaged working-directory changes, while git restore --staged file-name removes changes from the Staging Area and keeps the file changes locally.

qna.q: Q8. What command can unstage staged changes in the current directory?
qna.a: git restore --staged .

qna.q: Q9. Suppose you accidentally run git add . and stage too many files. What can you do?
qna.a: Use git restore --staged file-name to unstage only the files you do not want in the next commit.

qna.q: Q10. Which command puts changes into the Staging Area?
qna.a: git add

qna.q: Q11. Which command takes changes out of the Staging Area while keeping them in the Working Directory?
qna.a: git restore --staged file-name

qna.q: Q12. Put these steps in the correct order: git restore --staged file.txt, modify file.txt, git add file.txt.
qna.a: Modify file.txt → git add file.txt → git restore --staged file.txt.

items.title: Amend the Latest Commit
explanation: Simple Meaning
Amending a commit means changing your most recent commit.
You can use it when you made a mistake in the latest commit, such as:

• Forgot to add a file
  • Used the wrong commit message
  • Need to add one more small change to the latest commit
Simple Definition: git commit --amend replaces the latest commit with a new updated commit.
Simple Example
Suppose you make a commit:
git commit -m "Add login page"
Your history is:
Commit 1 → Initial project ↓ Commit 2 → Add login page ← Latest commit
Then you realize you forgot to add style.css.
Instead of creating another separate commit only for the forgotten file, you can update the latest commit:
Before Commit 1 → Initial project Commit 2 → Add login page ↓ Amend After Commit 1 → Initial project Commit 2 → Add login page + style.css
The Main Command
git commit --amend
This updates the latest commit only.
Important: git commit --amend does not edit an old commit somewhere in the middle of history. It works on the most recent commit.
Scenario 1: Forgot to Add a File ⭐
Suppose your project contains:
index.html style.css script.js
You accidentally commit only two files:
git add index.html style.css git commit -m "Add website files"
Then you realize that script.js was forgotten.
First, stage the forgotten file:
git add script.js
Then amend the latest commit:
git commit --amend --no-edit
The option --no-edit means:
Keep the existing commit message ↓ Only update the commit contents
Now the latest commit contains:
index.html style.css script.js
Why Use --no-edit?
Suppose your existing commit message is already correct:
Add website files
You only want to add a forgotten file. You do not need to change the message.
So use:
git commit --amend --no-edit
Scenario 2: Wrong Commit Message ⭐
Suppose you accidentally run:
git commit -m "Add logn page"
You notice the spelling mistake: logn should be login.
You can amend the latest commit message:
git commit --amend -m "Add login page"
The history changes from:
Before ❌ Commit → Add logn page ↓ Amend After ✅ Commit → Add login page
Scenario 3: Add More Changes to the Latest Commit
Suppose you commit:
git commit -m "Add login page"
Then you immediately notice a small missing change in login.html.
Make the correction, then stage it:
git add login.html
Then amend:
git commit --amend --no-edit
The latest commit is replaced with an updated version containing the additional change.
Important Concept: Amend Replaces the Latest Commit ⭐
This is very important.
Imagine your history:
A → B → C ← Latest commit
When you amend C, Git does not simply add something inside the existing commit. Conceptually, the latest commit is replaced with a new updated commit:
Before A → B → C ↓ Amend After A → B → C'
The updated commit C' replaces the previous latest commit.
Key Idea: Amend rewrites the latest commit rather than creating a normal additional commit.
Amending Commit Content: Step-by-Step
Suppose you forgot script.js.
1. Make or identify the missing change ↓ 2. Check status ↓ 3. Stage the change ↓ 4. Amend the latest commit ↓ 5. Check history
Step 1: Check status
git status
Step 2: Stage the forgotten file or changes
git add script.js
Step 3: Amend without changing the message
git commit --amend --no-edit
Step 4: Check history
git log --oneline
Amending Only the Commit Message
If the commit content is correct and only the message is wrong, you do not need to stage anything.
Run:
git commit --amend -m "Correct commit message"
For example:
Before ❌ Add dashbord page ↓ git commit --amend -m "Add dashboard page" ↓ After ✅ Add dashboard page
Amend vs Create a New Commit

SituationRecommended Action
Just forgot a small file in the latest commitAmend the latest commit
Latest commit message has a mistakeAmend the latest commit message
Made a small immediate correction to the latest workAmend may be useful
Started completely new workCreate a new commit
Several commits have been made since the mistakeDo not use amend for the old commit
Example: When NOT to Use Amend
Suppose your history is:
Commit 1 → Initial project Commit 2 → Add login page ← Mistake is here Commit 3 → Add dashboard Commit 4 → Add profile ← Latest commit
You now discover a mistake in Commit 2.
Running:
git commit --amend
would affect the latest commit, which is Commit 4, not Commit 2.
Remember: Normal git commit --amend is for the latest commit only.
Important Warning: Amending Shared History ⚠️
Be careful when the latest commit has already been pushed to a shared remote repository and other people may be using it.
Because amend replaces the commit with a new commit, it rewrites commit history.

Local commit ↓ Amend before sharing ↓ Usually simple and safe for your own work ✅ ------------------------- Commit already pushed and shared ↓ Amend changes history ↓ Can cause problems for collaborators ⚠️
For now, remember this rule:
Rule: Amending a commit is easiest before it has been shared with other developers. Be very careful about rewriting public or shared history.
Common Mistake 1: Thinking Amend Creates Another Commit
Suppose your history is:
A → B → C
After a normal new commit:
A → B → C → D
But after amending the latest commit:
A → B → C'
Amend replaces the latest commit with an updated version.
Common Mistake 2: Forgetting to Stage New Changes
Suppose you modify a file after committing and want that modification included in the amended commit.
You should stage it first:
git add file-name git commit --amend --no-edit
The amend command uses the changes you have prepared for the updated commit.
Common Mistake 3: Changing the Message Accidentally
If you only want to add a forgotten file and want to keep the existing commit message, use:
git commit --amend --no-edit
This clearly tells Git to keep the existing commit message.
Common Mistake 4: Using Amend for an Older Commit
Remember:
git commit --amend ↓ Works with ↓ Latest commit only ⭐
Easy Way to Remember 🧠

Latest commit has a mistake? ↓ Forgot file/change? ↓ git add file-name ↓ git commit --amend --no-edit ------------------------- Latest commit message is wrong? ↓ git commit --amend -m "Correct message"
Important Commands

CommandPurpose
git commit --amendAmend the latest commit and edit the commit message if needed
git commit --amend --no-editUpdate the latest commit while keeping its existing message
git commit --amend -m "message"Replace the latest commit message with a new message
git add file-nameStage changes you want included in the amended commit
git log --onelineCheck commit history
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
AmendUpdate and replace the latest commit
Forgot a fileStage it, then use git commit --amend --no-edit
Wrong messageUse git commit --amend -m "new message"
Keep old messageUse --no-edit
Older commit mistakeAmend is not the normal solution
Shared/pushed commitBe careful because amend rewrites history
One-Line Definition: git commit --amend replaces your latest commit with an updated version, allowing you to change its content, its commit message, or both.
practice: For this practice, create a small test commit and then update it using amend.
Step 1: Create a file named amend-practice.txt with this content:
Version 1
Step 2: Stage and commit the file.
git add amend-practice.txt git commit -m "Add amend practice file"
Step 3: Check the latest commit.
git log --oneline
Step 4: Modify amend-practice.txt by adding:
Version 1 Version 2
Step 5: Stage the new change.
git add amend-practice.txt
Step 6: Add the change to the latest commit without changing its message.
git commit --amend --no-edit
Step 7: Check the history again.
git log --oneline
Notice that you updated the latest commit instead of creating a separate normal commit for Version 2.
Step 8: Now practice changing the latest commit message.
git commit --amend -m "Add amend practice file versions"
Step 9: Check the history one final time.
git log --oneline
Confirm that the latest commit now has the corrected message.
Optional Practice: Make another commit while intentionally forgetting one new file. Then stage the forgotten file and use git commit --amend --no-edit to include it in the latest commit.
Practice Goal: Learn both uses of amend: update the content of the latest commit using --no-edit and change the latest commit message using -m.

qna.q: Q1. What does git commit --amend do?
qna.a: It replaces the latest commit with a new updated version.

qna.q: Q2. Can git commit --amend normally edit any old commit in the history?
qna.a: No. It is used to update the most recent commit.

qna.q: Q3. You forgot to add script.js to your latest commit. What should you do?
qna.a: Run git add script.js and then git commit --amend --no-edit if you want to keep the existing commit message.

qna.q: Q4. What does --no-edit mean when used with git commit --amend?
qna.a: It keeps the existing commit message while updating the latest commit's content.

qna.q: Q5. How can you change only the latest commit message?
qna.a: Use git commit --amend -m "New commit message".

qna.q: Q6. If you modify a file and want its new changes included in an amended commit, what should you usually do first?
qna.a: Stage the changes using git add before running git commit --amend.

qna.q: Q7. Does amend create a normal additional commit after the latest commit?
qna.a: No. It replaces the latest commit with an updated commit.

qna.q: Q8. Why should you be careful when amending a commit that has already been shared with other developers?
qna.a: Because amend rewrites the latest commit history and can cause problems for collaborators who are using the original commit.

qna.q: Q9. Suppose your history is A → B → C and C is the latest commit. After amending C, what is the conceptually updated history?
qna.a: A → B → C', where C' is the updated commit replacing C.

qna.q: Q10. You made four commits and discover a mistake in the second commit. Will normal git commit --amend directly fix that second commit?
qna.a: No. Normal git commit --amend affects only the latest commit.

qna.q: Q11. Which command is useful when the latest commit content needs updating but its message is already correct?
qna.a: git commit --amend --no-edit

qna.q: Q12. Put these steps in the correct order when you forgot a change in the latest commit.
qna.a: Make or identify the missing change → git add the file → git commit --amend --no-edit → check the result with git log.

items.title: Revert a Commit
explanation: Simple Meaning
Reverting a commit means undoing the changes introduced by a previous commit by creating a new commit.
In simple words:
Commit A → Add feature ↓ Commit B → Feature causes problem ↓ git revert Commit B ↓ Commit C → Undo changes from Commit B
Simple Definition: git revert safely undoes the changes of a commit by creating a new commit that reverses those changes.
The Main Concept ⭐
Suppose your commit history is:
Commit 1 → Create project ↓ Commit 2 → Add login page ↓ Commit 3 → Add broken feature ❌
You want to undo the changes made in Commit 3.
With git revert:
Commit 1 → Create project ↓ Commit 2 → Add login page ↓ Commit 3 → Add broken feature ❌ ↓ Commit 4 → Revert broken feature ✅
Commit 3 is still present in the history. Git creates Commit 4 to reverse its changes.
Main Command
git revert commit-hash
For example:
git revert a1b2c3d
Git uses the specified commit hash to identify which commit should be reversed.
What Is a Commit Hash?
Every commit has a unique identifier called a commit hash.
You can view commits using:
git log --oneline
Example output:
a1b2c3d Add dashboard x9y8z7w Add login page m4n5o6p Initial project
The first value on each line is a shortened commit hash:
a1b2c3d → Add dashboard x9y8z7w → Add login page m4n5o6p → Initial project
Simple Example: Revert the Latest Commit
Suppose your history is:
Commit 1 → Initial project Commit 2 → Add login page Commit 3 → Add payment feature ❌
You discover that the payment feature is causing a serious problem.
First, check the commit history:
git log --oneline
Suppose Git shows:
a1b2c3d Add payment feature x9y8z7w Add login page m4n5o6p Initial project
Revert the payment feature commit:
git revert a1b2c3d
The history becomes conceptually:
Commit 1 → Initial project Commit 2 → Add login page Commit 3 → Add payment feature ❌ Commit 4 → Revert Add payment feature ✅
Important: Revert Does Not Delete History ⭐
This is the most important concept in this topic.
Before reverting:
A → B → C
If you revert C:
A → B → C → Revert C
Notice that C still exists.
The revert commit applies the opposite changes so that the final project state is similar to the state before C.
Remember: git revert adds history. It does not remove the reverted commit from history.
Revert vs Reset ⭐ Very Important

CommandMain Purpose
git revertCreates a new commit that undoes another commit
git resetMoves or changes the current branch history and can discard changes depending on the option used
Visual comparison:
Using git revert A → B → C → Revert C History is preserved ✅ ------------------------- Using certain reset options A → B C may no longer be part of the current branch history ⚠️
Because revert preserves history, it is often easier to understand in shared project workflows.
Revert vs Amend

CommandPurpose
git commit --amendReplace and update the latest commit
git revertCreate a new commit that reverses a specified commit
Amend ↓ Change the latest commit Revert ↓ Keep existing history ↓ Add a new commit that undoes changes
Example: Revert an Older Commit
Suppose your history is:
Commit 1 → Initial project Commit 2 → Add login page Commit 3 → Add dashboard Commit 4 → Add profile page
Later, you discover that the login page changes from Commit 2 need to be undone.
You can identify Commit 2:
git log --oneline
Suppose its hash is:
x9y8z7w Add login page
Then run:
git revert x9y8z7w
Conceptually:
Commit 1 → Initial project Commit 2 → Add login page Commit 3 → Add dashboard Commit 4 → Add profile page Commit 5 → Revert Add login page
The original login commit remains visible in history, but its changes are reversed by the new commit.
What Happens After git revert?
A normal revert usually follows this process:
Choose commit to undo ↓ Run git revert commit-hash ↓ Git calculates opposite changes ↓ A new revert commit is created ↓ History is preserved
You can then check the result using:
git status git log --oneline
Real-World Example
Imagine you are working on your website:
Commit 1 → Create homepage Commit 2 → Add login page Commit 3 → Add dark mode Commit 4 → Update payment page
After testing, you discover that the dark mode changes in Commit 3 break the website layout.
You do not want to remove Commit 3 from the project history. Instead, you create a new commit that undoes its changes:
Commit 1 → Create homepage Commit 2 → Add login page Commit 3 → Add dark mode ❌ Commit 4 → Update payment page Commit 5 → Revert Add dark mode ✅
This clearly shows what happened in the project history.
Why Is git revert Useful?

SituationWhy Revert Helps
Bad feature was committedUndo its changes with a new commit
Bug was introducedReverse the commit causing the bug
Commit was already pushedPreserve visible project history
Team members use the repositoryAvoid simply deleting shared history
Need an audit trailHistory shows both the original change and its reversal
Common Mistake 1: Thinking Revert Deletes the Commit
This is incorrect.
git revert C Does NOT mean: A → B → C is changed to A → B ❌ It means: A → B → C → Revert C ✅
Common Mistake 2: Using the Commit Message Instead of the Hash
The normal command needs a commit identifier:
git revert commit-hash
For example:
git revert a1b2c3d
Use git log --oneline to find the commit hash.
Common Mistake 3: Reverting the Wrong Commit
Before running revert, carefully check your history:
git log --oneline
Confirm:
Correct commit hash? ✅ Correct commit message? ✅ Correct changes to undo? ✅
Common Mistake 4: Confusing Revert with Restore

CommandUsed For
git restoreRestore or discard changes in your working state depending on how it is used
git revertUndo changes introduced by an existing commit using a new commit
Simple memory trick:
restore → Working files / staging state revert → Existing commit history
What If a Revert Causes a Conflict?
Sometimes the project has changed so much that Git cannot automatically apply the reverse changes.
Git may report a conflict.
The basic process is:
git revert commit-hash ↓ Conflict occurs ⚠️ ↓ Resolve the conflicting files ↓ Stage resolved files ↓ Continue the revert
You will practice conflicts more deeply in the merge and rebase topics. For now, understand that reverting can also require conflict resolution.
Cancel an Unfinished Revert
If a revert is in progress and you decide you do not want to continue, Git provides a way to abort it:
git revert --abort
This is useful when a revert encounters conflicts and you decide to cancel the revert operation.
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
Made a bad commit? ↓ Find its hash ↓ git log --oneline ↓ Run ↓ git revert commit-hash ↓ Git creates a NEW commit ↓ Bad changes are reversed ↓ Original history remains visible ✅
Important Commands

CommandPurpose
git log --onelineView commit history and short commit hashes
git revert commit-hashCreate a new commit that reverses a specified commit
git revert --abortCancel a revert operation that is in progress
git statusCheck the current repository state
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
RevertUndo a commit by creating a new commit
Original commitRemains in history
New revert commitApplies opposite changes
Commit hashIdentifies the commit to reverse
git log --onelineHelps find commit hashes
git revert commit-hashReverts the specified commit
Shared historyRevert is useful because it preserves history
One-Line Definition: git revert safely undoes the changes introduced by a commit by creating a new commit that reverses those changes while preserving the original commit history.
practice: For this practice, create a test commit and then undo it using git revert. Do not use your important project for this practice.
Step 1: Create a file named revert-practice.txt with this content:
Version 1
Step 2: Stage and commit the file.
git add revert-practice.txt git commit -m "Add Version 1"
Step 3: Modify the file so it contains:
Version 1 Version 2
Step 4: Commit this change.
git add revert-practice.txt git commit -m "Add Version 2"
Step 5: View your commit history.
git log --oneline
Identify the commit hash for Add Version 2.
Step 6: Revert the Add Version 2 commit.
git revert commit-hash
Replace commit-hash with the actual hash from your repository.
Step 7: Check the file again. It should return to:
Version 1
Step 8: Check the commit history.
git log --oneline
Confirm that the original Add Version 2 commit is still visible and that Git created a new revert commit.
Step 9: Compare what happened:
Before Revert Commit → Add Version 1 Commit → Add Version 2 ↓ git revert After Revert Commit → Add Version 1 Commit → Add Version 2 Commit → Revert Add Version 2
Important Practice Observation: The Version 2 commit was not deleted from history. A new commit was created to undo its changes.

Practice Goal: Use git log --oneline to find a commit hash, revert that commit using git revert, and verify that Git preserves the original history while creating a new commit that reverses the changes.

qna.q: Q1. What does git revert do?
qna.a: It creates a new commit that reverses the changes introduced by a specified commit.

qna.q: Q2. Does git revert delete the original commit from history?
qna.a: No. The original commit remains in history, and Git creates a new commit that reverses its changes.

qna.q: Q3. What is the basic syntax of git revert?
qna.a: git revert commit-hash

qna.q: Q4. How can you find a commit hash?
qna.a: Use git log --oneline to view commit history and shortened commit hashes.

qna.q: Q5. Suppose the history is A → B → C. What happens conceptually after reverting C?
qna.a: The history becomes A → B → C → Revert C.

qna.q: Q6. What is the main difference between git revert and git reset?
qna.a: git revert preserves history by creating a new commit that undoes changes, while git reset changes the current branch history or state depending on the reset option.

qna.q: Q7. What is the difference between git commit --amend and git revert?
qna.a: Amend replaces and updates the latest commit, while revert creates a new commit that reverses the changes of a specified commit.

qna.q: Q8. Can you revert an older commit instead of only the latest commit?
qna.a: Yes. You can specify the hash of the commit you want to revert.

qna.q: Q9. Why can git revert be useful in a shared project?
qna.a: Because it preserves commit history instead of simply removing the original commit.

qna.q: Q10. What command can you use if a revert operation is in progress and you want to cancel it?
qna.a: git revert --abort

qna.q: Q11. You committed a broken feature with hash a1b2c3d. What command can undo that commit using a new commit?
qna.a: git revert a1b2c3d

qna.q: Q12. Put these steps in the correct order for reverting a commit.
qna.a: Check git log --oneline → identify the correct commit hash → run git revert commit-hash → check the result and commit history.

items.title: Understand git reset
explanation: Simple Meaning
git reset is a command used to move the current branch to another commit and change the state of your Staging Area and, depending on the option used, your Working Directory.
In simple words, Git can use reset to say:
"Move me back to an earlier commit." The result depends on the reset mode used.
Important: git reset can affect commit history, the Staging Area, and sometimes your Working Directory. Always understand the reset mode before using it.
First Remember the Git Areas ⭐
Working Directory ↓ git add Staging Area ↓ git commit Local Repository
To understand git reset, remember that Git has these three important places:

AreaMeaning
Working DirectoryYour actual files and current changes
Staging AreaChanges prepared for the next commit
Local RepositoryYour saved commit history
The reset mode determines which of these areas are changed.
What Does HEAD Mean?
Before learning reset, you need to understand HEAD.
HEAD normally points to your current commit.
Suppose your history is:
A → B → C ↑ HEAD
This means you are currently at Commit C.
You can also refer to previous commits relative to HEAD:
HEAD → Current commit HEAD~1 → One commit before HEAD HEAD~2 → Two commits before HEAD
Simple Example
Suppose your commit history is:
Commit A → Initial project ↓ Commit B → Add login page ↓ Commit C → Add dashboard ← HEAD
You decide to reset back to Commit B:
git reset HEAD~1
Conceptually, the current branch moves back one commit:
Before A → B → C ← HEAD ↓ git reset HEAD~1 After A → B ← HEAD C is no longer the current commit on this branch.
However, what happens to the actual changes from C depends on the reset mode.
The Three Important Reset Modes ⭐⭐⭐
The three main modes you should understand are:
git reset --soft git reset --mixed git reset --hard

ModeCommit HistoryStaging AreaWorking Directory
--softMoves HEADKeeps changes stagedKeeps changes
--mixedMoves HEADUnstages changesKeeps changes
--hardMoves HEADResets changesDiscards tracked changes
Memory Trick: Soft keeps more, Mixed removes changes from staging, and Hard can remove your working changes.
1. git reset --soft
--soft moves the commit pointer but keeps your changes in the Staging Area.
Example:
git reset --soft HEAD~1
Suppose:
Before A → B → C ← HEAD C changes are committed
After:
A → B ← HEAD Changes from C → Still staged 📦 Changes from C → Still in Working Directory ✏️
You can think of it as:
Undo the commit ↓ But keep everything ready for another commit
When Is --soft Useful?
Suppose you accidentally created two commits but want to combine the latest commit changes into another commit.
A soft reset can move the commit pointer back while keeping the changes staged.
For now, the main concept to remember is:
--soft: The commit is removed from the current branch position, but the changes remain staged.
2. git reset --mixed ⭐ Default Mode
--mixed moves the commit pointer and resets the Staging Area, but keeps your changes in the Working Directory.
Example:
git reset --mixed HEAD~1
You can also commonly see:
git reset HEAD~1
Without specifying a mode, the default is normally --mixed.
Suppose:
Before A → B → C ← HEAD C changes → Committed
After:
A → B ← HEAD Changes from C → Not staged ✏️ Changes from C → Still in Working Directory ✅
The main idea:
Undo the commit ↓ Unstage its changes ↓ Keep the actual file changes
Why Is --mixed Important?
It is useful when you want to undo a commit but continue working with its changes.
For example, you made one commit containing too many unrelated changes:
Commit C ├── Login changes ├── Dashboard changes └── Profile changes
You may want to undo the commit while keeping all the changes locally so you can organize them into better commits.
3. git reset --hard ⚠️ Very Important
--hard is the most dangerous of these three modes for beginners because it can discard changes.
Example:
git reset --hard HEAD~1
Suppose:
Before A → B → C ← HEAD Working Directory → Contains C changes Staging Area → Contains C state Repository → Contains C
After:
A → B ← HEAD Staging Area → Matches B Working Directory → Matches B Changes from C can be discarded ⚠️
Warning: git reset --hard can permanently discard uncommitted changes to tracked files. Do not use it unless you clearly understand what will be removed.
Easy Comparison Using One Commit
Suppose Commit C is the latest commit:
A → B → C ← HEAD
You run a reset back to B.

CommandWhat Happens to C's Changes?
git reset --soft HEAD~1Remain staged
git reset --mixed HEAD~1Remain locally but become unstaged
git reset --hard HEAD~1Tracked changes are discarded to match B
Visual Comparison ⭐

Before Reset Repository: A → B → C ← HEAD Staging Area: C state Working Directory:C state ========================= --soft HEAD~1 Repository: A → B ← HEAD Staging Area: C changes remain 📦 Working Directory:C changes remain ✏️ ========================= --mixed HEAD~1 Repository: A → B ← HEAD Staging Area: Reset / C changes unstaged Working Directory:C changes remain ✏️ ========================= --hard HEAD~1 Repository: A → B ← HEAD Staging Area: Matches B Working Directory:Matches B ⚠️
Reset a Specific Commit
You are not limited to using HEAD~1. You can reset to a specific commit hash.
First view the history:
git log --oneline
Example:
c3d4e5f Add dashboard b2c3d4e Add login page a1b2c3d Initial project
You can reset to a specific commit:
git reset --mixed b2c3d4e
The branch is moved to that commit, with the exact result depending on the reset mode.
Using git reset to Unstage Files
You previously learned that files can be unstaged using:
git restore --staged file-name
You may also see:
git reset HEAD file-name
This form of git reset is commonly used to reset the staging state of a file while keeping its Working Directory changes.
Example:
git reset HEAD index.html
Conceptually:
Before index.html → Staged 📦 ↓ git reset HEAD index.html After index.html → Modified but not staged ✏️
git reset vs git revert ⭐ Very Important

Featuregit resetgit revert
Main actionMoves branch/HEAD and changes repository stateCreates a new commit that reverses another commit
Original historyCan rewrite the current branch historyPreserves the existing history
New commit created?Not by the reset itselfYes
Shared historyUse carefullyGenerally suitable when history should remain visible
git reset ↓ Move history/state backward ------------------------ git revert ↓ Keep history ↓ Create a new commit to undo changes
Example: Reset vs Revert
Suppose:
A → B → C ← HEAD
Using reset:
A → B ← HEAD
Using revert:
A → B → C → Revert C ← HEAD
This is why reset and revert are used for different situations.
Common Mistake 1: Thinking All Reset Modes Are the Same
They are not.
--soft → Keep changes staged --mixed → Keep changes unstaged --hard → Discard tracked changes to match target ⚠️
Always know which mode you are using.
Common Mistake 2: Using --hard Without Checking
Before using a hard reset, check your current state:
git status git log --oneline
Understand exactly which commit you are resetting to.
Beginner Rule: Never casually run git reset --hard just because a tutorial says it fixes something.
Common Mistake 3: Confusing reset with revert
Remember:
reset ↓ Moves branch/HEAD and can rewrite local history revert ↓ Creates a new commit ↓ History remains visible
Common Mistake 4: Resetting Shared History
If commits have already been pushed and other developers are working from the same branch, rewriting history with reset can cause problems.
For shared work, understand the team workflow before changing published history.
Important: Be especially careful when using reset on commits that have already been shared with others.
Easy Way to Remember 🧠

SOFT ↓ Move commit back Keep changes staged 📦 ------------------- MIXED ↓ Move commit back Keep changes locally ✏️ Unstage them ------------------- HARD ⚠️ ↓ Move commit back Reset staging state Discard tracked working changes
Important Commands

CommandPurpose
git reset --soft HEAD~1Move back one commit and keep changes staged
git reset HEAD~1Default mixed reset: move back and keep changes unstaged locally
git reset --mixed HEAD~1Explicit mixed reset
git reset --hard HEAD~1Move back and reset tracked working files to the target commit
git reset HEAD file-nameCommon way to unstage a file
git log --onelineView commits before choosing a reset target
git statusCheck your current working and staging state
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
git resetMove the current branch to another commit and reset Git state depending on the mode
HEADReference to the current commit
HEAD~1One commit before the current commit
--softKeep changes staged
--mixedKeep changes locally but unstage them
--hardReset tracked files to match the target commit and can discard changes
Reset vs RevertReset moves history/state; revert creates a new undo commit

One-Line Definition: git reset moves the current branch to a specified commit and, depending on the mode used, can keep changes staged, keep them unstaged in the Working Directory, or discard tracked changes to match the target commit.
practice: For this topic, practice only in a test repository. Do not experiment with git reset --hard on an important project.
Step 1: Check your current commit history.
git log --oneline
Step 2: Create a file named reset-practice.txt containing:
Version 1
Step 3: Stage and commit it.
git add reset-practice.txt git commit -m "Add Version 1"
Step 4: Modify the file:
Version 1 Version 2
Step 5: Stage and commit Version 2.
git add reset-practice.txt git commit -m "Add Version 2"
Step 6: View the history. You should now see the latest Version 2 commit.
git log --oneline
Step 7: Practice Mixed Reset ⭐ Move back one commit while keeping the Version 2 changes in your file.
git reset HEAD~1
Step 8: Check the status.
git status
Observe that the Version 2 changes remain locally but are no longer staged or committed.
Step 9: Open reset-practice.txt and confirm that it still contains:
Version 1 Version 2
Step 10: Stage and commit Version 2 again so you can continue practicing.
git add reset-practice.txt git commit -m "Add Version 2 again"
Step 11: Practice Soft Reset Move back one commit but keep the changes staged.
git reset --soft HEAD~1
Step 12: Run:
git status
Observe that the Version 2 changes are still staged and ready to commit.
Step 13: Compare the two experiments:
Mixed Reset ↓ Changes remain locally Not staged ----------------- Soft Reset ↓ Changes remain locally Still staged

Optional Observation: After understanding the concept, create a disposable test commit and experiment with git reset --hard HEAD~1. Before running it, check git status and understand that tracked changes can be discarded. Use this only in your test repository.
Practice Goal: Clearly understand the difference between --soft, --mixed, and --hard, especially what happens to the commit history, Staging Area, and Working Directory.

qna.q: Q1. What is git reset mainly used for?
qna.a: It is used to move the current branch to another commit and change Git state depending on the reset mode.

qna.q: Q2. What does HEAD normally represent?
qna.a: HEAD normally refers to the current commit.

qna.q: Q3. What does HEAD~1 mean?
qna.a: It means one commit before the current HEAD commit.

qna.q: Q4. What are the three important reset modes?
qna.a: The three important modes are --soft, --mixed, and --hard.

qna.q: Q5. What happens with git reset --soft HEAD~1?
qna.a: The branch moves back one commit, while the changes from that commit remain staged.

qna.q: Q6. What happens with git reset HEAD~1 by default?
qna.a: It normally performs a mixed reset: the branch moves back one commit, the changes are unstaged, but they remain in the Working Directory.

qna.q: Q7. What happens with git reset --hard HEAD~1?
qna.a: The branch moves back one commit, the Staging Area is reset, and tracked working changes are reset to match the target commit, so changes can be discarded.

qna.q: Q8. Which reset mode keeps changes staged?
qna.a: --soft

qna.q: Q9. Which reset mode keeps changes locally but unstages them?
qna.a: --mixed

qna.q: Q10. Which reset mode is the most dangerous because it can discard tracked changes?
qna.a: --hard

qna.q: Q11. What is the main difference between git reset and git revert?
qna.a: git reset moves the branch and changes Git state, while git revert creates a new commit that reverses another commit and preserves the existing history.

qna.q: Q12. What should you check before using git reset?
qna.a: Check git status and git log --oneline so you understand your current changes and the commit you are resetting to.

qna.q: Q13. Which command is commonly used to unstage a specific file using reset?
qna.a: git reset HEAD file-name

qna.q: Q14. Put these modes in order from keeping the most reset changes ready for commit to discarding tracked working changes.
qna.a: --soft → --mixed → --hard.

qna.q: Q15. Why should you be careful when using reset on commits already shared with other developers?
qna.a: Because reset can rewrite the current branch history and cause problems for people who are using the original shared history.

items.title: Difference Between git restore, git reset, and git revert
explanation: Simple Meaning
git restore, git reset, and git revert are all related to undoing changes, but they work at different stages of Git.
The easiest way to understand them is to ask:
Where is the change? Working Directory? ↓ restore Staging Area? ↓ restore / reset Already committed? ↓ reset / revert
Main Idea: git restore is mainly used for restoring file or staging state, git reset changes the current branch and Git state, and git revert creates a new commit that reverses an existing commit.
First Remember the Git Workflow ⭐
Working Directory ↓ git add Staging Area ↓ git commit Local Repository
These three commands affect different parts of this workflow.

CommandMain Area
git restoreWorking Directory and Staging Area
git resetStaging Area and commit/branch state
git revertCommitted history
1. git restore
git restore is mainly used to restore files to a previous state.
Suppose you modify a file:
Last Commit → index.html was working ✅ ↓ You modify index.html ↓ Current file has unwanted changes ❌
You can discard the current uncommitted changes using:
git restore index.html
Conceptually:
Before Committed version → Working Working file → Modified ❌ ↓ git restore index.html After Working file → Restored to the committed version ✅
Restore a Staged File
Suppose you accidentally staged a file:
Modify file ↓ git add index.html ↓ index.html is Staged 📦
You can remove it from the Staging Area while keeping your actual file changes:
git restore --staged index.html
Conceptually:
Before index.html → Staged 📦 ↓ git restore --staged index.html After index.html → Modified ✏️ Not staged
Remember: git restore is commonly used when you want to undo file changes or change staging state without moving your branch to another commit.
2. git reset
git reset can move the current branch to another commit and can also change the Staging Area and Working Directory depending on the reset mode.
Suppose your history is:
A → B → C ← HEAD
You can move back one commit:
git reset HEAD~1
Conceptually:
Before A → B → C ← HEAD ↓ git reset HEAD~1 After A → B ← HEAD
What happens to C's changes depends on whether you use --soft, --mixed, or --hard.
Reset Modes

ModeCommit PositionStaging AreaWorking Directory
--softMoves backKeeps changes stagedKeeps changes
--mixedMoves backUnstages changesKeeps changes
--hardMoves backResets stateDiscards tracked changes to match target ⚠️
You also learned that reset can commonly be used to unstage a file:
git reset HEAD index.html
However, for unstaging, the modern command you have already learned is:
git restore --staged index.html
3. git revert
git revert is used to undo the changes introduced by an existing commit by creating a new commit.
Suppose:
A → B → C ← HEAD
You discover that Commit C introduced a bug. You run:
git revert commit-hash
Conceptually:
Before A → B → C ↓ git revert C After A → B → C → Revert C ← HEAD
Commit C remains visible in history. Git creates a new commit containing changes that reverse C.
Remember: git revert does not simply remove the old commit. It adds a new commit that undoes its changes.
The Biggest Difference ⭐⭐⭐
Suppose you make a change. The correct command depends on where that change currently exists.

1. Change is only in your file ↓ Use restore ------------------------- 2. Change is staged ↓ Use restore --staged or reset for staging state ------------------------- 3. Change is already committed ↓ Use reset or revert depending on your goal
One Scenario Through All Three Commands
Imagine you have this project:
Commit A → Create project ↓ Commit B → Add login page ↓ Commit C → Add dashboard
Scenario 1: You Modified a File but Did Not Commit
You change index.html and the changes are wrong:
Commit B → Last saved version ↓ You modify index.html ❌ ↓ Not staged Not committed
Use:
git restore index.html
This restores the file's working state from the appropriate source, typically the current committed version when used this way.
Scenario 2: You Staged a File by Mistake
Modify index.html ↓ git add index.html ↓ Staged by mistake 📦
Use:
git restore --staged index.html
Result:
File changes → Still exist ✏️ Staging state → Removed 📦❌
Scenario 3: You Committed by Mistake but Want to Keep the Changes
Suppose the latest commit was created too early:
A → B → C ← HEAD C was committed too early
You may use a mixed reset:
git reset HEAD~1
Result:
A → B ← HEAD Changes from C → Still in Working Directory ✏️ Changes from C → Not staged
Scenario 4: A Committed Change Is Bad but History Should Remain
Suppose Commit C contains a broken feature:
A → B → C ❌
Use:
git revert C
Result:
A → B → C → Revert C ✅
The original commit remains visible, and a new commit reverses its changes.
Direct Comparison Table ⭐

Featuregit restoregit resetgit revert
Main purposeRestore file or staging stateMove branch/HEAD and reset Git stateUndo a commit using a new commit
Affects Working Directory?CanDepends on modeApplies reverse changes as a new commit
Affects Staging Area?Can with --stagedYes, depending on usage/modeNew commit is created through the revert operation
Moves HEAD?NoYes, when resetting to another commitNo backward movement of history
Creates a new commit?NoNoYes
Preserves existing history?YesCan rewrite current branch historyYes
Visual Comparison

git restore Change file state Working Directory ← Restore file Staging Area ← Can unstage with --staged ========================== git reset Move branch/state backward A → B → C ← HEAD ↓ Reset ↓ A → B ← HEAD Result depends on reset mode ========================== git revert Keep history Add opposite commit A → B → C ↓ Revert C ↓ A → B → C → Revert C
Simple Memory Trick 🧠
RESTORE ↓ "I want my file/staging state back." RESET ↓ "I want to move my current branch/state back." REVERT ↓ "I want to undo an old commit but keep history."
restore vs reset

git restoregit reset
Mainly restores file or staging stateCan move HEAD/current branch to another commit
Does not normally rewrite branch historyCan rewrite current branch history
Useful for restoring files or unstaging with --stagedUseful for changing commit and staging state
reset vs revert

git resetgit revert
Moves branch/HEAD to another commitKeeps existing history and adds a new commit
No new undo commit is automatically createdCreates a new commit
Can rewrite current branch historyOriginal history remains visible
Reset mode controls what happens to staged and working changesReverses the changes from a specified commit
restore vs revert

git restoregit revert
Mainly handles current file or staging stateHandles an existing committed change
Does not create a commitCreates a new commit
Useful before committing unwanted changesUseful for undoing changes from an existing commit while preserving history
Decision Guide ⭐

Did you make changes but NOT commit them? ↓ Yes → Want to discard file changes? ↓ git restore file-name ---------------------------- Did you stage a file by mistake? ↓ Yes → Want to keep file changes but unstage? ↓ git restore --staged file-name ---------------------------- Did you commit changes and want to move your branch back? ↓ Yes → Understand reset mode first ↓ git reset ---------------------------- Did you commit bad changes and want to preserve history? ↓ Yes ↓ git revert commit-hash
Common Mistake 1: Using revert for Uncommitted Changes
git revert works with commits.
If your change is only in the Working Directory and has not been committed, reverting is not the normal solution.
Uncommitted file changes ↓ Think restore Existing commit ↓ Think revert or reset
Common Mistake 2: Thinking reset and revert Are the Same
They can both help undo committed work, but their approach is different.
reset ↓ Moves branch/history state revert ↓ Adds a new commit ↓ Reverses previous changes
Common Mistake 3: Using reset --hard Without Understanding
Before using:
git reset --hard
Remember that it can discard tracked changes to make your Working Directory match the target commit.
Beginner Rule: Check git status and git log --oneline before using destructive reset operations.
Common Mistake 4: Thinking restore Always Means "Go Back One Commit"
git restore is about restoring file or staging state. It is not the same as moving your branch backward through commit history.
restore → Restore file/staging state reset → Move branch/state revert → Add a commit that undoes another commit
Real-World Example
Imagine you are working on your website.
Working on Login Feature 1. Change login.html 2. Stage login.html 3. Commit login feature 4. Later discover a bug
Different problems require different commands:

ProblemPossible Command
You changed login.html but want to discard current changesgit restore login.html
You staged login.html but want to unstage itgit restore --staged login.html
You committed too early and want to move back while keeping changesgit reset HEAD~1
A committed feature is bad and you want to preserve historygit revert commit-hash
Important Commands

CommandPurpose
git restore file-nameDiscard current changes in a file by restoring it from the selected source
git restore --staged file-nameRemove a file from the Staging Area while keeping Working Directory changes
git reset HEAD file-nameCommon way to reset the staging state of a file
git reset HEAD~1Default mixed reset back one commit
git reset --soft HEAD~1Move back one commit and keep changes staged
git reset --hard HEAD~1Move back and reset tracked files to match the target ⚠️
git revert commit-hashCreate a new commit reversing a specified commit
Quick Summary ⭐

If You Want To...Think About
Discard uncommitted file changesgit restore
Unstage a file but keep its changesgit restore --staged
Move your branch back to another commitgit reset
Undo a committed change with a new commitgit revert
Preserve visible history while undoing a commitgit revert

One-Line Definition: git restore restores file or staging state, git reset moves the current branch and changes Git state depending on the mode, and git revert creates a new commit that reverses the changes of an existing commit while preserving history.
practice: For this topic, practice in a test repository so you can clearly see the difference between restore, reset, and revert.
Part 1: Practice git restore
Step 1: Create or use a file named undo-practice.txt and commit this content:
Version 1
Step 2: Modify the file without committing:
Version 1 Wrong change
Step 3: Check the status.
git status
Step 4: Discard the current file change.
git restore undo-practice.txt
Step 5: Open the file and confirm it returns to:
Version 1
Part 2: Practice unstaging with restore
Step 6: Modify the file again:
Version 1 Version 2
Step 7: Stage it.
git add undo-practice.txt
Step 8: Check the status and confirm the file is staged.
git status
Step 9: Unstage it while keeping the file changes.
git restore --staged undo-practice.txt
Step 10: Check the status again. The file should still be modified but no longer staged.
git status
Part 3: Practice git reset
Step 11: Stage and commit Version 2.
git add undo-practice.txt git commit -m "Add Version 2"
Step 12: View the history.
git log --oneline
Step 13: Move back one commit using the default mixed reset.
git reset HEAD~1
Step 14: Check both the status and the file.
git status
Observe: the commit moved back, but the Version 2 changes remain in your Working Directory and are unstaged.
Part 4: Practice git revert
Step 15: Commit Version 2 again.
git add undo-practice.txt git commit -m "Add Version 2 again"
Step 16: Find the hash of the latest Version 2 commit.
git log --oneline
Step 17: Revert that commit.
git revert commit-hash
Step 18: Check the history again.
git log --oneline
Observe that the original Version 2 commit is still present and Git created a new revert commit.
Final Comparison:
restore ↓ Undo current file/staging state reset ↓ Move branch/state back revert ↓ Keep history Create a new commit to undo another commit
Practice Goal: Perform one real example of each command and identify whether the change was in the Working Directory, Staging Area, or commit history before choosing the correct command.
