qna.a: git restore is mainly used to restore file state or staging state without moving the current branch to another commit.

qna.q: Q2. Which command can discard current uncommitted changes in a file?
qna.a: git restore file-name

qna.q: Q3. Which command can unstage a file while keeping its Working Directory changes?
qna.a: git restore --staged file-name

qna.q: Q4. What is the main purpose of git reset?
qna.a: git reset moves the current branch to another commit and changes Git state depending on how it is used and which mode is selected.

qna.q: Q5. What are the three important reset modes?
qna.a: --soft, --mixed, and --hard.

qna.q: Q6. Which reset mode keeps changes staged?
qna.a: --soft.

qna.q: Q7. Which reset mode keeps changes locally but unstages them?
qna.a: --mixed.

qna.q: Q8. Which reset mode can discard tracked Working Directory changes?
qna.a: --hard.

qna.q: Q9. What is the main purpose of git revert?
qna.a: git revert creates a new commit that reverses the changes introduced by a specified existing commit.

qna.q: Q10. Does git revert delete the original commit?
qna.a: No. The original commit remains in history, and a new commit is created to reverse its changes.

qna.q: Q11. You changed index.html but have not staged or committed it. You want to discard the change. Which command should you think about?
qna.a: git restore index.html

qna.q: Q12. You staged index.html by mistake but want to keep your code changes. Which command should you think about?
qna.a: git restore --staged index.html

qna.q: Q13. You committed changes too early and want to move your branch back while keeping the changes locally. Which command should you think about?
qna.a: A mixed reset, such as git reset HEAD~1, depending on the exact situation.

qna.q: Q14. A bad commit was already made and you want to undo its changes while preserving the visible history. Which command should you think about?
qna.a: git revert commit-hash

qna.q: Q15. What is the easiest memory trick for these three commands?
qna.a: restore = restore file or staging state; reset = move branch/state; revert = create a new commit that undoes another commit.

items.title: What is Git Stash?
explanation: Simple Meaning
Git stash temporarily saves your unfinished changes so you can switch tasks without committing those changes.
Think of it like putting your current work into a temporary storage box:
Working on Feature A ✏️ ↓ Not finished yet ↓ Urgent task appears! ↓ git stash ↓ Current changes saved temporarily 📦 ↓ Working Directory becomes clean ↓ Work on the urgent task
One-Line Definition: git stash temporarily saves your uncommitted changes so you can clean your working state, do something else, and later restore those changes.
Why Do We Need Git Stash?
Imagine you are working on a new login feature.
Current Branch → main You are working on: ├── login.html modified ├── style.css modified └── script.js modified Work is not finished yet ❌
You have not completed the feature, so you do not want to commit incomplete work.
Suddenly, your manager asks you to immediately fix an important production bug.
Unfinished Login Feature ✏️ ↓ Urgent Bug Fix 🚨 ↓ Need to temporarily save current work
This is where Git stash is useful.
Without Git Stash
Without stash, you might have to do something like:
Option 1 → Commit unfinished work ❌ Option 2 → Copy changes somewhere manually ❌ Option 3 → Leave changes and risk confusion ❌
Instead, you can temporarily save your changes using:
git stash
Basic Git Stash Workflow ⭐
Suppose you currently have unfinished changes:
Working Directory login.html → Modified ✏️ style.css → Modified ✏️ script.js → Modified ✏️
You run:
git stash
Conceptually:

Before Stash Working Directory ├── login.html modified ├── style.css modified └── script.js modified ↓ git stash Stash Storage 📦 ├── login.html changes ├── style.css changes └── script.js changes Working Directory → Clean
Your unfinished changes are temporarily stored, allowing you to work on something else.
Simple Real-World Example
Imagine you are building your website.
9:00 AM ↓ Start building Dashboard Feature 10:30 AM ↓ Dashboard is only 60% complete 11:00 AM ↓ Urgent bug: Login page is broken 🚨
You do not want to commit the unfinished dashboard feature just to switch tasks.
You can do:
git stash
Then:
Dashboard changes → Temporarily saved 📦 ↓ Working Directory → Clean ↓ Fix Login Bug ↓ Commit Bug Fix ↓ Return to Dashboard Work
How Do You Get Your Changes Back?
After completing the urgent work, you can restore your saved changes.
Two important commands are:
git stash apply git stash pop
We will learn the detailed difference between apply and pop in the upcoming topics.
For now, remember:
git stash ↓ Temporarily save changes -------------------- Later ↓ Restore saved changes ↓ git stash apply or git stash pop
Where Does Git Store the Stash?
Git stores stashed changes in a special stash list inside your local repository.
You can view your saved stashes using:
git stash list
Example output may look like:
stash@{0}: WIP on main: Add dashboard stash@{1}: WIP on main: Update login page
Each stash has an identifier such as:
stash@{0} → Latest stash stash@{1} → Previous stash stash@{2} → Older stash
You Can Have Multiple Stashes
You are not limited to only one stash.
For example:
First unfinished task ↓ git stash ↓ stash@{0} Later, another unfinished task ↓ git stash ↓ stash@{0} → Newest stash stash@{1} → Previous stash
Git can keep multiple temporary sets of saved changes.
The newest stash is normally shown as stash@{0}.
What Git Stash Is Mainly Used For ⭐

SituationWhy Stash Helps
Feature is unfinishedTemporarily save work without committing
Need to switch tasksClean your current working state
Urgent bug appearsSave current work and fix the bug
Need to change branchesTemporarily move unfinished changes aside
Want to return laterRestore the saved work
Git Stash Does Not Mean Permanent Backup
A stash is mainly intended for temporary work.
If your work is important and complete enough to save permanently, a normal commit is usually more appropriate.
Temporary unfinished work ↓ Think → git stash 📦 ---------------------- Meaningful completed work ↓ Think → git commit 💾
Important: Do not treat git stash as a replacement for proper commits. A stash is mainly for temporarily setting aside work.
Git Stash vs Git Commit ⭐

Featuregit stashgit commit
PurposeTemporarily save changesPermanently record a project version
Used forUnfinished or temporary workMeaningful completed changes
Part of normal commit history?NoYes
Commit message required?No for basic stashYes
Can return to work later?Yes, by applying or popping the stashYes, through commit history
Visual Comparison

git commit Working Changes ↓ git add ↓ Staging Area ↓ git commit ↓ Commit History 💾 ======================== git stash Unfinished Changes ↓ git stash ↓ Temporary Stash Storage 📦 ↓ Working Directory becomes clean ↓ Restore changes later
Example Workflow
Suppose your current work looks like this:
main branch index.html → Modified style.css → Modified Feature is unfinished
Check your changes:
git status
Then temporarily save them:
git stash
Check the status again:
git status
Conceptually, the workflow is:
Modified Files ✏️ ↓ git stash ↓ Changes temporarily saved 📦 ↓ Working state becomes clean ↓ Do another task ↓ Return later ↓ Restore stash
Common Mistake 1: Thinking Stash Creates a Normal Commit
git stash does not add your changes as a normal commit in your branch's regular commit history.
git commit ↓ Normal project history ------------------- git stash ↓ Temporary stash storage
Common Mistake 2: Forgetting About Stashed Changes
Because stashed changes are temporarily moved away from your Working Directory, beginners can sometimes forget that they created a stash.
Check saved stashes using:
git stash list
If you think some work has disappeared after using stash, check the stash list before assuming it is lost.
Common Mistake 3: Using Stash Instead of Proper Commits
Suppose you finish an important feature today but keep it only in stash for a long time.
That is usually not the best workflow.
Finished meaningful feature ↓ Use a proper commit Temporary task interruption ↓ Use stash
Common Mistake 4: Thinking Stash Is Only for Switching Branches
Switching branches is one common reason to use stash, but stash is more generally useful whenever you need to temporarily set aside uncommitted work.
Need to switch tasks? → Stash can help Need to fix urgent bug? → Stash can help Need a clean working state? → Stash can help
Easy Memory Trick 🧠
STASH = TEMPORARY STORAGE BOX 📦 Working on something ↓ Not finished ↓ Need to do another task ↓ Put current work in the stash 📦 ↓ Do other work ↓ Come back later ↓ Take your work out
Important Commands for This Section

CommandPurpose
git stashTemporarily save current changes
git stash listView saved stashes
git stash applyRestore a stash while keeping it in the stash list
git stash popRestore a stash and normally remove it from the stash list if successful
git stash dropDelete a stash
For this topic, focus mainly on understanding git stash. The remaining stash commands will be covered in the next topics.
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
Git stashTemporarily saves uncommitted work
Main purposeSwitch tasks without committing unfinished work
After stashingYour Working Directory is typically cleaned of the stashed changes
Multiple stashesYes, Git can keep multiple stashes
View stashesgit stash list
Restore laterUse git stash apply or git stash pop
Permanent replacement for commit?No
One-Line Definition: git stash temporarily stores your unfinished uncommitted changes, allowing you to clean your current working state, work on another task, and restore those changes later.
practice: For this topic, create a small test repository. The goal is to see your unfinished changes disappear temporarily from the Working Directory and appear in the stash.
Step 1: Check your current repository status.
git status
Step 2: Create a file named stash-practice.txt with this content:
Version 1
Step 3: Stage and commit the file.
git add stash-practice.txt git commit -m "Add stash practice file"
Step 4: Modify the file with unfinished work:
Version 1 Working on Feature A Feature A is not finished yet
Step 5: Check the status. The file should appear as modified.
git status
Step 6: Temporarily save your unfinished changes.
git stash
Step 7: Check the status again.
git status
Observe that your stashed tracked changes are no longer present in the Working Directory state.
Step 8: Open stash-practice.txt. It should return to the committed Version 1 state.
Version 1
Step 9: View your saved stash.
git stash list
You should see at least one stash entry, such as stash@{0}.
Step 10: Understand what happened:

Before stash stash-practice.txt ├── Version 1 ├── Working on Feature A └── Feature A is not finished yet ↓ git stash After stash Working file → Version 1 Saved temporarily 📦 ├── Working on Feature A └── Feature A is not finished yet

Practice Goal: Understand that git stash is useful when work is unfinished and you need to temporarily set it aside without creating a normal commit. In the next topics, you will practice restoring, applying, and deleting stashes.

qna.a: git stash temporarily saves your uncommitted changes so you can clean your current working state and restore those changes later.

qna.q: Q2. When is Git stash useful?
qna.a: It is useful when you have unfinished work but need to temporarily switch tasks, fix an urgent bug, or get a clean working state.

qna.a: Not necessarily. If the work is temporarily unfinished, git stash can save the changes so you can return to them later.

qna.a: Use git stash list.

qna.a: No. A commit is part of the normal project history, while a stash is mainly temporary storage for setting aside work.

qna.a: git stash

qna.q: Q9. Which command shows all saved stashes?

items.title: Save Unfinished Work with Git Stash
explanation: Simple Meaning
When you have unfinished changes, you can use git stash to temporarily save them without creating a commit.
The basic command is:
git stash
Think of it as temporarily putting your current work aside:
Unfinished Work ✏️ ↓ git stash ↓ Changes saved temporarily 📦 ↓ Working Directory becomes clean ↓ Do another task ↓ Restore work later
When Should You Save Unfinished Work?
Suppose you are working on a dashboard feature, but it is not complete yet.
Current Work Dashboard Feature ├── dashboard.html modified ├── style.css modified └── script.js modified Status → Unfinished ⚠️
Suddenly, you need to work on something else.
For example:
You are building Dashboard ↓ Feature not finished ↓ Urgent bug appears 🚨 ↓ Need to fix another issue immediately
You do not want to lose your current changes, but you may also not want to create a commit for incomplete work.
In this situation:
git stash
Basic Workflow ⭐
First, check your current changes:
git status
Example situation:
On branch main Changes not staged for commit: modified: dashboard.html modified: style.css
Now save the unfinished work:
git stash
Conceptually:
Before git stash Working Directory ├── dashboard.html → Modified ✏️ └── style.css → Modified ✏️ ↓ git stash Stash Storage 📦 ├── dashboard.html changes └── style.css changes Working Directory → Clean
Step-by-Step Example
Imagine this file already exists:
dashboard.txt
Current committed content:
Dashboard Version 1
Now you start working on a new feature:
Dashboard Version 1 Add user profile section Add sales chart Add notifications
The work is not finished yet.
Check Git:
git status
Git shows the file as modified.
Now save the unfinished work:
git stash
After stashing, the file returns to its committed state:
Dashboard Version 1
Your new unfinished changes are not gone. They are temporarily saved in the stash.
What Happens After git stash?
After you run:
git stash
You can verify the result using:
git status
Your tracked Working Directory changes that were stashed should no longer appear as current modifications.
You can also check the saved stash:
git stash list
Example:
stash@{0}: WIP on main: Latest commit message
Important Flow
1. Start working ↓ 2. Make changes ↓ 3. Work is unfinished ↓ 4. Run git stash ↓ 5. Changes saved temporarily 📦 ↓ 6. Work on another task ↓ 7. Return later ↓ 8. Restore the stash
Real-World Scenario ⭐
Imagine you are working on a website feature.
Task A → Build Dashboard You have completed only 50% ↓ Need to stop temporarily ↓ Task B → Fix Login Bug urgently
Instead of committing unfinished dashboard code:
git stash
Then you can focus on the urgent task:
Dashboard Work → Saved in Stash 📦 ↓ Fix Login Bug ↓ Commit Login Bug Fix ↓ Return to Dashboard Work ↓ Restore Stash
Save Work with a Message
When you have multiple unfinished tasks, it is helpful to give your stash a meaningful message.
You can use:
git stash push -m "Dashboard work in progress"
Later, when you run:
git stash list
You can more easily identify what each stash contains.
stash@{0} → Dashboard work in progress stash@{1} → Login page styling stash@{2} → Navbar changes
Why a Stash Message Is Useful
Suppose you create several stashes without remembering what they contain.
stash@{0} → ??? stash@{1} → ??? stash@{2} → ???
This can become confusing.
A descriptive message makes your temporary work easier to identify:
stash@{0} → Dashboard work in progress stash@{1} → Fix responsive navbar stash@{2} → Login page experiment
Git Stash vs Commit

SituationRecommended Action
Work is complete and meaningfulCreate a commit
Work is unfinished temporarilyUse stash
Need to switch to urgent workUse stash if appropriate
Want permanent project historyUse commit
Important Difference ⭐

git commit ↓ "Save this as part of my project history." ------------------------ git stash ↓ "Temporarily put this work aside." ------------------------ Later ↓ Restore the stashed work ↓ Continue development ↓ Commit when appropriate
What About Untracked Files?
A basic git stash does not include untracked files by default.
For example:
Modified tracked file → style.css ✏️ New untracked file → test.html 📄
If you run:
git stash
The modified tracked file can be stashed, while the untracked file may remain in your Working Directory.
If you specifically want to include untracked files, use:
git stash -u
Or:
git stash --include-untracked
Important: Remember the basic rule: git stash is mainly for your current tracked changes. Use -u when you also need untracked files included.
Common Mistake 1: Thinking Stashed Work Is Lost
After running git stash, your changes disappear from your current files. This does not automatically mean the work was deleted.
First check:
git stash list
Changes disappeared from Working Directory ↓ Check git stash list ↓ Stash found 📦 ↓ Changes can be restored later
Common Mistake 2: Stashing Without Checking Status
Before saving work, it is a good habit to check what changes currently exist:
git status
This helps you understand what you are temporarily setting aside.
Common Mistake 3: Using Stash for Everything
Do not keep completed work permanently in stashes.
Temporary interruption ↓ Stash 📦 Meaningful completed feature ↓ Commit 💾
Easy Memory Trick 🧠
SAVE UNFINISHED WORK Working on Feature A ✏️ ↓ Need to stop temporarily ↓ Put it in a temporary box 📦 ↓ git stash ↓ Do other work ↓ Come back later ↓ Restore the work
Important Commands

CommandPurpose
git stashTemporarily save current changes
git stash push -m "message"Save changes with a descriptive message
git stash -uSave changes and include untracked files
git stash listView saved stashes
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
Save unfinished workTemporarily store changes using Git stash
Basic commandgit stash
Working Directory after stashStashed tracked changes are temporarily removed from the current working state
View saved workgit stash list
Add messagegit stash push -m "message"
Include untracked filesgit stash -u
One-Line Definition: To save unfinished work in Git, use git stash to temporarily set aside your uncommitted changes, allowing you to work on something else and restore those changes later.
practice: In this practice, you will create unfinished changes, save them using git stash, verify that your Working Directory is clean, and confirm that the work exists in the stash.
Step 1: Go to your existing practice repository and check its current status.
git status
Make sure you understand the current state before starting. Ideally, begin with no unfinished changes.
Step 2: Create or use a tracked file named stash-work.txt. If it is new, add and commit it first.
git add stash-work.txt git commit -m "Add stash work file"
Step 3: Add unfinished work to the file:
Project Version 1 Working on dashboard Add user statistics Add sales report Feature not finished yet
Step 4: Check the status.
git status
Confirm that stash-work.txt appears as modified.
Step 5: Save the unfinished work temporarily.
git stash
Step 6: Check your status again.
git status
Observe how the Working Directory changes after stashing.
Step 7: Open stash-work.txt.
Compare its current content with the unfinished changes you wrote before running git stash.
Step 8: Check whether Git saved your work in the stash.
git stash list
You should see a stash entry such as stash@{0}.
Step 9: Create another unfinished change in the same file.
Project Version 1 Start another experiment
Step 10: Save this work with a descriptive message.
git stash push -m "Second dashboard experiment"
Step 11: View all stashes.
git stash list
Observe that Git can store multiple temporary sets of unfinished work.
Final Observation:

Unfinished Changes ↓ git status ↓ Modified files visible ✏️ ↓ git stash ↓ Current work temporarily removed 📦 ↓ git status ↓ Check working state ↓ git stash list ↓ Saved work is visible in stash storage
Practice Goal: You should be able to identify unfinished work, save it temporarily with git stash, verify the result using git status, and confirm the saved work using git stash list.

qna.q: Q1. Which basic command is used to save unfinished work temporarily?
qna.a: git stash

qna.q: Q2. Why would you use git stash instead of committing?
qna.a: You may use git stash when work is temporarily unfinished and you need to set it aside without adding an incomplete change as a normal commit.

qna.q: Q3. What should you check before stashing your work?
qna.a: Use git status to understand what changes currently exist.

qna.q: Q4. How can you view all saved stashes?
qna.a: git stash list

qna.q: Q5. Can you add a message when saving a stash?
qna.a: Yes. You can use git stash push -m "your message".

qna.q: Q6. Why is adding a stash message useful?
qna.a: It helps you identify what unfinished work is stored when you have multiple stashes.

qna.q: Q7. What command can include untracked files when creating a stash?
qna.a: git stash -u, also known as git stash --include-untracked.

qna.q: Q8. Scenario: You are halfway through building a dashboard, but an urgent login bug must be fixed. What could you do?
qna.a: You can temporarily save the unfinished dashboard changes with git stash, work on the login bug, and restore the dashboard work later.

qna.q: Q9. If your changes disappear from the Working Directory after git stash, are they necessarily lost?
qna.a: No. Check git stash list because the changes may have been temporarily saved in the stash.

qna.q: Q10. Is git stash a replacement for normal commits?
qna.a: No. Git stash is mainly temporary storage, while commits are used to record meaningful project history.

qna.q: Q11. What is the basic workflow for temporarily saving unfinished work?
qna.a: Check the changes, run git stash, work on another task, and later restore the saved stash.

items.title: View Git Stashes
explanation: Simple Meaning
After saving unfinished work using git stash, you can view all your saved stashes using:
git stash list
This command shows the temporary changes currently stored in Git's stash storage.
Unfinished Work ✏️ ↓ git stash ↓ Saved in Stash Storage 📦 ↓ git stash list ↓ View all saved stashes
One-Line Definition: git stash list displays the list of changes that you previously saved temporarily using Git stash.
Why Do We Need git stash list?
Imagine you saved unfinished work several times:
Monday ↓ Save Dashboard Work 📦 Tuesday ↓ Save Login Styling 📦 Wednesday ↓ Save Navbar Changes 📦
After a few days, you may forget exactly what work you saved.
You can check your stash storage using:
git stash list
Example Output
Suppose you have saved three different sets of unfinished work. You might see something like:
stash@{0}: On main: Navbar changes stash@{1}: On main: Login page styling stash@{2}: On main: Dashboard work
Each line represents one saved stash.
Understanding Stash Numbers ⭐
Git identifies each stash using a name such as:
stash@{0} stash@{1} stash@{2}
The number helps identify a particular stash.
Usually:
stash@{0} → Newest stash stash@{1} → Previous stash stash@{2} → Older stash
When you create a new stash, it normally becomes stash@{0}, and the older stashes move down the list.
Example: How the List Changes
First, you save Dashboard work:
git stash
Now:
stash@{0} → Dashboard work
Later, you save Login work:
git stash
Now:
stash@{0} → Login work ← Newest stash@{1} → Dashboard work ← Older
Later, you save Navbar work:
git stash
Now:
stash@{0} → Navbar work ← Newest stash@{1} → Login work stash@{2} → Dashboard work ← Oldest
Important Concept ⭐
stash@{0} does not permanently belong to one specific piece of work.
It means the newest stash currently in the list.
Today stash@{0} → Dashboard work Create a new stash tomorrow ↓ Tomorrow stash@{0} → New work stash@{1} → Dashboard work
So, when working with multiple stashes, check the list before assuming which work belongs to a particular stash number.
Viewing a Specific Stash
git stash list gives you a summary of the saved stashes.
If you want to inspect the changes inside a specific stash, you can use:
git stash show stash@{0}
This helps you see information about the selected stash.
View the Actual Changes
To see a more detailed diff of the changes stored in a stash, use:
git stash show -p stash@{0}
The -p option shows the patch, which means the detailed line-by-line changes.
Conceptually:

git stash list ↓ Shows WHICH stashes exist ---------------------- git stash show stash@{0} ↓ Shows information about ONE stash ---------------------- git stash show -p stash@{0} ↓ Shows detailed changes inside ONE stash
Using a Stash Message
If you create a stash with a message:
git stash push -m "Dashboard work in progress"
You can later identify it more easily when viewing the stash list:
git stash list
Conceptually, you may see:
stash@{0} → Dashboard work in progress
Messages are especially useful when you have several stashes.
Without Descriptive Messages
stash@{0} → Some work stash@{1} → Some other work stash@{2} → Another change
After some time, this can become difficult to understand.
With Descriptive Messages
stash@{0} → Fix responsive navbar stash@{1} → Dashboard chart experiment stash@{2} → Login page styling
Now it is easier to identify the unfinished work you want to restore.
Complete Workflow
Make changes ✏️ ↓ Work is unfinished ↓ git stash ↓ Changes saved temporarily 📦 ↓ Continue with another task ↓ Later... ↓ git stash list ↓ Find the stash you need ↓ View or restore that stash
Common Situation: "Where Did My Changes Go?"
Suppose you run:
git stash
Then you open your file and your recent unfinished changes are gone from the Working Directory.
Do not immediately assume they were deleted.
First run:
git stash list
You may find that Git temporarily stored them in a stash.
Changes missing from current file ❓ ↓ Check git status ↓ Check git stash list ↓ Stash found 📦 ↓ Work can be inspected or restored later
Common Mistake 1: Confusing Stash List with Commit History
These commands show different things:

CommandShows
git logNormal commit history
git stash listTemporary saved stashes
git log ↓ Commit History 💾 ---------------------- git stash list ↓ Temporary Stash Storage 📦
Common Mistake 2: Thinking stash@{0} Is Always the Same Work
This is not correct because stash numbers can change when you add or remove stashes.
Before new stash stash@{0} → Dashboard After creating new stash stash@{0} → Login stash@{1} → Dashboard
Always check git stash list when you have multiple stashes.
Common Mistake 3: Forgetting Old Stashes
If you create many stashes and never check them, you may eventually forget what unfinished work they contain.
Use:
git stash list
regularly when you work with multiple temporary changes.
Easy Memory Trick 🧠
git stash ↓ PUT work INTO temporary storage 📦 ---------------------- git stash list ↓ LOOK at what is INSIDE storage 📋
Important Commands

CommandPurpose
git stash listView all saved stashes
git stash show stash@{0}View information about a specific stash
git stash show -p stash@{0}View detailed changes in a specific stash
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
View all stashesgit stash list
Newest stashNormally stash@{0}
Previous stashNormally stash@{1}
Inspect one stashgit stash show stash@{0}
Detailed changesgit stash show -p stash@{0}
Normal commit historygit log, not git stash list
One-Line Definition: git stash list is used to view all temporarily saved stashes, helping you identify and manage unfinished work that you previously set aside.
practice: In this practice, you will create multiple stashes and use git stash list to understand how Git stores and orders them.
Step 1: Go to your practice repository and check whether you already have saved stashes.
git stash list
If you have old practice stashes, carefully observe them. Do not delete important work.
Step 2: Create or use a tracked file named stash-list-practice.txt and make sure it has been committed at least once.
Step 3: Add this unfinished change:
Dashboard work Add user statistics Add sales chart
Step 4: Save it with a message.
git stash push -m "Dashboard practice"
Step 5: View the stash list.
git stash list
Find the newest stash. It should normally be shown as stash@{0}.
Step 6: Create another unfinished change:
Login work Add username validation Add password validation
Step 7: Save it with another message.
git stash push -m "Login practice"
Step 8: View the stash list again.
git stash list
Observe how the newest stash becomes stash@{0} and the previous stash moves down.
First stash stash@{0} → Dashboard practice ↓ Create another stash Second stash stash@{0} → Login practice ← Newest stash@{1} → Dashboard practice
Step 9: Inspect the newest stash.
git stash show stash@{0}
Step 10: View detailed changes inside the newest stash.
git stash show -p stash@{0}
Practice Goal: You should understand how to view all saved stashes, identify the newest and older stashes, and inspect the contents of a specific stash before restoring it.

qna.q: Q1. Which command is used to view all saved stashes?
qna.a: git stash list

qna.q: Q2. What does stash@{0} normally represent?
qna.a: It normally represents the newest stash currently in the stash list.

qna.q: Q3. What normally happens to older stash numbers when you create a new stash?
qna.a: The new stash normally becomes stash@{0}, and the existing stashes move down the list.

qna.q: Q4. Which command can show information about a specific stash?
qna.a: git stash show stash@{0}

qna.q: Q5. Which command shows detailed line-by-line changes stored in a stash?
qna.a: git stash show -p stash@{0}

qna.q: Q6. Does git stash list show normal commit history?
qna.a: No. git stash list shows temporary saved stashes. Normal commit history is viewed using git log.

qna.q: Q7. Scenario: You saved Dashboard work yesterday and Login work today. Which stash is normally stash@{0}?
qna.a: The Login work, because it is the newest stash.

qna.q: Q8. Why should you check git stash list before working with multiple stashes?
qna.a: Because stash numbers can change, so checking the list helps you identify which unfinished work is stored in each stash.

qna.q: Q9. If your changes disappear after running git stash, what should you check first?
qna.a: Run git stash list to check whether the changes were saved in the stash.

qna.q: Q10. What is the main purpose of git stash list?
qna.a: Its main purpose is to display and help identify unfinished changes that were previously saved temporarily in Git's stash storage.

items.title: Restore a Git Stash
explanation: Simple Meaning
After temporarily saving unfinished work using git stash, you can restore that work when you are ready to continue.
The basic command is:
git stash apply
Think of the complete process like this:
Unfinished Work ✏️ ↓ git stash ↓ Work saved temporarily 📦 ↓ Do another task ↓ Later... ↓ git stash apply ↓ Unfinished work returns ✏️
One-Line Definition: Restoring a stash means bringing previously stashed changes back into your Working Directory so you can continue working on them.
Why Restore a Stash?
Suppose you were working on a Dashboard feature but had to stop because an urgent Login bug appeared.
Task A → Build Dashboard ↓ Work unfinished ↓ git stash 📦 ↓ Task B → Fix Login Bug ↓ Commit Login Bug Fix ↓ Ready to continue Dashboard ↓ Restore the stash
Now you want your unfinished Dashboard changes back.
You can use:
git stash apply
Restore the Latest Stash
By default, you can restore the latest stash using:
git stash apply
The latest stash normally refers to:
stash@{0} → Latest stash
So conceptually, this restores the newest saved work.
Step-by-Step Example
Imagine your committed file contains:
Dashboard Version 1
You start adding unfinished changes:
Dashboard Version 1 Add user statistics Add sales chart Add notifications
You need to stop temporarily, so you run:
git stash
Your Working Directory returns to the previous committed state:
Dashboard Version 1
Your unfinished changes are now saved in the stash.
Later, when you are ready to continue:
git stash apply
Your unfinished changes are brought back:
Dashboard Version 1 Add user statistics Add sales chart Add notifications
Restore a Specific Stash ⭐
If you have multiple stashes, first check them:
git stash list
Example:
stash@{0}: Login practice stash@{1}: Dashboard practice stash@{2}: Navbar practice
If you specifically want to restore the Dashboard work, use its stash reference:
git stash apply stash@{1}
This tells Git which stash you want to restore.
Important Workflow with Multiple Stashes
git stash list ↓ Check available stashes 📋 ↓ Choose the required stash ↓ Example: stash@{1} ↓ git stash apply stash@{1} ↓ Changes restored to Working Directory
What Happens to the Stash After git stash apply? ⭐
This is an important concept.
When you use:
git stash apply
Git restores the changes, but the stash normally remains in the stash list.
Before apply stash@{0} → Dashboard work 📦 ↓ git stash apply Working Directory → Dashboard changes restored ✏️ Stash Storage → stash@{0} still exists 📦
You can verify this using:
git stash list
This is useful because you still have the stash available if you need it again.
Why Does git stash apply Keep the Stash?
Imagine you restore the work and then something goes wrong. Since the stash still exists, you have an extra copy of those saved changes.
Stash 📦 ↓ Apply changes ↓ Changes restored ✏️ ↓ Stash still exists 📦
This makes git stash apply useful when you want to restore the work without immediately removing the saved stash.
Restore Latest vs Specific Stash

CommandPurpose
git stash applyRestore the latest stash
git stash apply stash@{0}Explicitly restore stash@{0}
git stash apply stash@{1}Restore a specific older stash
Example with Multiple Stashes
Suppose your stash list is:
stash@{0}: Login page changes stash@{1}: Dashboard changes stash@{2}: Navbar changes
If you run:
git stash apply
Git normally applies the latest stash:
Restored → Login page changes
If you want Dashboard changes instead:
git stash apply stash@{1}
Then:
Restored → Dashboard changes
Check Before Restoring
Before applying a stash, it is a good habit to check your current repository state:
git status
Also check the available stashes when necessary:
git stash list
This helps you understand:

• What changes currently exist?
  • Whether your Working Directory is clean?
  • Which stash do you want to restore?
Recommended Safe Workflow

1. Check current changes ↓ git status ↓ 2. Check saved stashes ↓ git stash list ↓ 3. Choose the required stash ↓ 4. Restore it ↓ git stash apply OR git stash apply stash@{n} ↓ 5. Check the result ↓ git status
Possible Conflict When Applying a Stash
Sometimes your current files may have changed since you created the stash.
For example:
Earlier ↓ Create stash from dashboard.html Later ↓ Make different changes to dashboard.html Now ↓ Try to apply old stash Git may need to combine changes
If Git cannot automatically combine the changes, a conflict can occur.
Conceptually:
Current File Changes + Stashed Changes ↓ Can Git combine them automatically? Yes → Changes applied ✅ No → Conflict ⚠️
Do not worry about mastering stash conflicts now. The important point is that restoring a stash can sometimes require conflict resolution when the same code has changed.
Common Mistake 1: Applying the Wrong Stash
If you have multiple stashes, do not assume you remember which work belongs to each stash number.
First check:
git stash list
If needed, inspect a stash:
git stash show stash@{0}
Then apply the correct one.
Common Mistake 2: Thinking Apply Deletes the Stash
Remember:
git stash apply ↓ Restore changes ✏️ ↓ Stash remains 📦
Do not confuse this with git stash pop, which you will learn in the next topic.
Common Mistake 3: Applying a Stash Without Checking Current Changes
If you already have uncommitted changes, applying another stash can make the Working Directory more complicated or cause conflicts.
Before restoring, check:
git status
Easy Memory Trick 🧠
git stash ↓ PUT work into the temporary box 📦 ---------------------- git stash apply ↓ TAKE A COPY of the work back ✏️ The box still remains 📦
Important Commands

CommandPurpose
git stash listView available stashes
git stash applyRestore the latest stash
git stash apply stash@{0}Restore a specific stash
git statusCheck the repository before and after restoring
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
Restore latest stashgit stash apply
Restore specific stashgit stash apply stash@{n}
Check stashes firstgit stash list
Check current changesgit status
After applyChanges are restored and the stash normally remains
Possible issueConflicts can occur if changes cannot be combined automatically
One-Line Definition: git stash apply restores previously saved changes from a Git stash into your Working Directory, while normally keeping the original stash available for later use.
practice: In this practice, you will create unfinished work, stash it, restore it using git stash apply, and verify that the stash remains available afterward.
Step 1: Go to your practice repository and check the current state.
git status
Try to understand your current changes before starting the practice.
Step 2: Use a tracked file named restore-practice.txt. If it does not already exist, create, add, and commit it first.
git add restore-practice.txt git commit -m "Add restore practice file"
Step 3: Add unfinished content:
Dashboard Version 1 Add user statistics Add sales chart Add notifications Work is unfinished
Step 4: Check the modified file.

Step 5: Save the unfinished work in a stash.
git stash push -m "Restore practice dashboard work"
Step 6: Check your current file and status after stashing.
git status
Observe that the unfinished changes are no longer part of your current Working Directory state.
Step 7: View the saved stashes.
git stash list
Step 8: Restore the latest stash.
git stash apply
Step 9: Open restore-practice.txt and confirm that your unfinished Dashboard changes returned.
Step 10: Check the repository status.
git status
You should see the restored changes as uncommitted changes in your Working Directory.
Step 11: Check the stash list again.
git stash list
Important observation: after git stash apply, the stash should normally still exist.
Optional Challenge: If you have multiple practice stashes, use git stash list to identify one and restore it explicitly.
git stash apply stash@{1}

Create unfinished work ✏️ ↓ git stash ↓ Work saved 📦 ↓ Working Directory returns to previous state ↓ git stash list ↓ Confirm stash exists ↓ git stash apply ↓ Changes restored ✏️ ↓ git stash list ↓ Original stash still exists 📦
Practice Goal: You should be able to restore the latest or a specific stash using git stash apply and understand that applying a stash normally restores the changes without removing the saved stash.

qna.a: git stash apply

qna.q: Q2. How do you restore a specific stash?
qna.a: Use git stash apply followed by the stash reference, for example: git stash apply stash@{1}.

qna.q: Q3. Which command should you use to see available stashes before restoring one?
qna.a: git stash list

qna.a: The changes are restored to the Working Directory, and the stash normally remains in the stash list.

qna.a: git stash apply stash@{1}

qna.a: The saved stash remains available, which can be useful if you need to inspect or use those saved changes again.

qna.a: Check your current repository state using git status and check the available stashes using git stash list when needed.

qna.a: Yes. A conflict can occur if the current changes and the stashed changes cannot be combined automatically.

qna.a: No. It restores changes to your Working Directory. You can later decide whether to modify, stage, and commit those changes.

qna.a: git stash temporarily saves unfinished changes, while git stash apply restores previously saved changes.

items.title: Git Stash Apply vs Pop
explanation: Simple Meaning
Both git stash apply and git stash pop restore previously saved stash changes.
The main difference is what happens to the stash after the changes are restored.
git stash apply ↓ Restore changes ✏️ Stash remains 📦 ---------------------- git stash pop ↓ Restore changes ✏️ Stash removed 📦❌
One-Line Difference: git stash apply restores a stash and keeps it, while git stash pop restores a stash and removes it after a successful apply.
git stash apply
The command:
git stash apply
restores the latest stash to your Working Directory.
Example:

Before Stash Storage 📦 stash@{0} → Dashboard work Working Directory → Clean ↓ git stash apply After Working Directory → Dashboard work restored ✏️ Stash Storage 📦 stash@{0} → Dashboard work still exists
The important point is:
Apply = Restore + Keep Stash
git stash pop
The command:
git stash pop
also restores the latest stash to your Working Directory.
However, after successfully applying the stash, Git removes that stash from the stash list.
Before Stash Storage 📦 stash@{0} → Dashboard work Working Directory → Clean ↓ git stash pop After Working Directory → Dashboard work restored ✏️ Stash Storage → Stash removed 📦❌
The important point is:
Pop = Restore + Remove Stash
The Main Difference ⭐

CommandRestores Changes?Stash Remains?
git stash applyYesYes
git stash popYesNo, after successful apply
Simple Example
Suppose your stash list contains:
stash@{0}: Dashboard work
Option 1: Using Apply
git stash apply
Afterward:
Working Directory → Dashboard work restored ✏️ Stash List → stash@{0} still exists 📦
Option 2: Using Pop
git stash pop
After a successful pop:
Working Directory → Dashboard work restored ✏️ Stash List → Dashboard stash removed 📦❌
Why Would You Use Apply?
Use git stash apply when you want to restore the changes but keep the stash as a temporary backup.
Stash important unfinished work 📦 ↓ Restore it using apply ↓ Continue working ↓ Original stash still exists as a backup
This can be useful when you want to be extra careful before deleting the saved stash.
Why Would You Use Pop?
Use git stash pop when you want to restore the work and no longer need that stash after it has been successfully applied.
Stash work 📦 ↓ Ready to continue it ↓ git stash pop ↓ Work restored ✏️ ↓ Stash removed ↓ Continue development
Real-World Scenario
Imagine you are working on a Dashboard feature.
Monday ↓ Start Dashboard feature ↓ Work unfinished ↓ git stash 📦 Tuesday ↓ Fix urgent Login bug ↓ Commit the fix Wednesday ↓ Return to Dashboard work
Now you have two choices.
Choice 1: Safe restore
git stash apply
Dashboard work restored + Original stash remains
Choice 2: Restore and remove
git stash pop
Dashboard work restored + Stash removed after successful apply
Specific Stash with Apply
If you have multiple stashes:
stash@{0}: Login work stash@{1}: Dashboard work stash@{2}: Navbar work
You can restore a specific stash using:
git stash apply stash@{1}
The selected stash remains available afterward.
Specific Stash with Pop
You can also specify which stash you want to pop:
git stash pop stash@{1}
After the selected stash is successfully applied, Git removes that stash from the stash list.
Important: Check Your Stashes First ⭐
When you have multiple stashes, first check:
git stash list
Example:
stash@{0}: Login experiment stash@{1}: Dashboard work stash@{2}: Navbar changes
Then decide which one you need.
git stash list ↓ Identify required work ↓ Need backup? ↓ Yes → git stash apply No → git stash pop
Important Difference When Something Goes Wrong
When applying stashed changes, Git may sometimes encounter conflicts if the current files and stashed changes cannot be combined automatically.

With git stash pop, the stash is removed only after Git successfully applies it. If applying the stash fails because of conflicts, Git normally keeps the stash so you can resolve the situation without losing it.
git stash pop ↓ Try to restore stash ↓ Successful? Yes → Restore changes + Remove stash No / Conflict → Stash normally remains
Common Mistake 1: Thinking Apply and Pop Are Completely Different
Both commands have the same main purpose: restoring stashed changes.
The difference is mainly what happens to the saved stash afterward.
Both restore work ✏️ apply → Keep stash 📦 pop → Remove stash after successful apply 📦❌
Common Mistake 2: Using Pop Without Checking the Stash
If you have multiple stashes, first check:
git stash list
Otherwise, you might restore and remove the wrong stash.
Common Mistake 3: Forgetting That Apply Keeps the Stash
If you use git stash apply, your stash list can still contain the old stash even after the changes are restored.
This means:
Changes restored to Working Directory ✏️ AND Saved copy still exists in Stash Storage 📦
Later, you can manage or delete that stash when you no longer need it.
Easy Memory Trick 🧠
APPLY = Apply a COPY of the stash = Keep the stash 📦 ---------------------- POP = Take the work out = Remove it from stash storage 📦❌
Complete Decision Flow

Need to restore unfinished work? ↓ Check git stash list ↓ Choose required stash ↓ Do you want to keep the stash? Yes ↓ git stash apply ↓ Restore + Keep 📦 No ↓ git stash pop ↓ Restore + Remove after successful apply 📦❌
Important Commands

CommandPurpose
git stash listView all saved stashes
git stash applyRestore latest stash and keep it
git stash apply stash@{1}Restore a specific stash and keep it
git stash popRestore latest stash and remove it after successful apply
git stash pop stash@{1}Restore a specific stash and remove it after successful apply
Quick Summary

Conceptgit stash applygit stash pop
Restores changesYesYes
Keeps stashYesNo, after successful apply
Useful whenYou want to keep a backupYou are finished with the temporary stash
Latest stash commandgit stash applygit stash pop
Specific stashgit stash apply stash@{n}git stash pop stash@{n}
Final Definition: git stash apply restores stashed changes while keeping the stash, whereas git stash pop restores stashed changes and removes the stash after it has been successfully applied.
practice: In this practice, you will perform both git stash apply and git stash pop so you can clearly see the difference between keeping and removing a stash.
Part 1: Practice git stash apply
Step 1: Check your current repository status.
git status
Step 2: Create or use a tracked file named apply-pop-practice.txt. Make sure it has been committed at least once.
Step 3: Add unfinished content:
Dashboard Feature Add statistics Add sales chart Work is unfinished
Step 4: Save the work with a message.
git stash push -m "Apply practice"
Step 5: Check the stash list.
git stash list
Step 6: Restore the work using:
git stash apply
Step 7: Check the stash list again.
git stash list
Important observation: The changes returned to your Working Directory, but the stash should still exist.
Before apply Stash → Apply practice 📦 ↓ git stash apply After apply Working Directory → Changes restored ✏️ Stash → Still exists 📦
Part 2: Prepare another stash for Pop
Step 8: First remove or safely handle the restored changes from Part 1 so you can create a new practice stash. Use your current Git knowledge carefully and check git status.
Step 9: Add another unfinished change:
Login Feature Add username validation Add password validation Work is unfinished
Step 10: Save this new work.

Step 11: View your stashes.

Step 12: Restore the latest stash using:
git stash pop
Step 13: Check your stash list again.

Important observation: After a successful git stash pop, the popped stash should no longer appear in the list.
Before pop Stash → Pop practice 📦 ↓ git stash pop After successful pop Working Directory → Changes restored ✏️ Stash → Removed 📦❌
Final Comparison:
git stash apply ↓ Restore changes ✏️ Keep stash 📦 ---------------------- git stash pop ↓ Restore changes ✏️ Remove stash after successful apply 📦❌
Practice Goal: You should be able to use git stash apply when you want to restore and keep a stash, and git stash pop when you want to restore and remove the stash after it is successfully applied.

qna.a: git stash apply restores the changes and keeps the stash, while git stash pop restores the changes and removes the stash after a successful apply.

qna.q: Q2. Do both apply and pop restore stashed changes?
qna.a: Yes. Both commands restore previously stashed changes.

qna.q: Q3. Which command should you use if you want to keep the stash as a backup?
qna.a: git stash apply

qna.a: git stash apply

qna.q: Q6. Scenario: You are ready to continue your stashed work and no longer need the temporary stash after restoring it. Which command can you use?
qna.a: git stash pop

qna.q: Q7. How do you restore a specific stash and keep it?
qna.a: Use git stash apply followed by the stash reference, for example: git stash apply stash@{1}.

qna.q: Q8. How do you restore a specific stash and remove it after a successful apply?
qna.a: Use git stash pop followed by the stash reference, for example: git stash pop stash@{1}.

qna.q: Q9. What command should you run before choosing between apply and pop when multiple stashes exist?
qna.a: git stash list

qna.q: Q10. If git stash pop encounters a conflict and cannot successfully apply the stash, is the stash normally removed?
qna.a: No. Git normally keeps the stash when the pop cannot be successfully completed.

qna.q: Q11. Complete the sentence: Apply means restore and ______ the stash.
qna.a: Keep

qna.q: Q12. Complete the sentence: Pop means restore and ______ the stash after a successful apply.
qna.a: Remove

items.title: Delete Git Stashes
explanation: Simple Meaning
A Git stash is temporary storage for unfinished changes. When you no longer need a saved stash, you can delete it.
The two main ways are:
git stash drop
Delete one specific stash.
git stash clear
Delete all stashes.
One-Line Definition: Deleting a Git stash means permanently removing saved temporary changes that you no longer need.
First Check Your Stashes ⭐
Before deleting anything, always check which stashes currently exist:
git stash list
Example:
stash@{0}: Login feature work stash@{1}: Dashboard changes stash@{2}: Navbar experiment
Now you can decide which stash you no longer need.
Delete One Specific Stash
Use:
git stash drop stash@{1}
This deletes only the specified stash.
Example before deleting:
stash@{0} → Login feature 📦 stash@{1} → Dashboard changes 📦 stash@{2} → Navbar experiment 📦
Run:
git stash drop stash@{1}
After deleting:
stash@{0} → Login feature 📦 stash@{1} → Navbar experiment 📦
Notice that the stash positions can change after deletion.
Delete the Latest Stash
The latest stash is normally stash@{0}.
You can delete it using:
git stash drop stash@{0}
Conceptually:
Before stash@{0} → Latest work 📦 stash@{1} → Older work 📦 ↓ git stash drop stash@{0} After Latest work → Deleted ❌ Older work → Moves to stash@{0} 📦
What Happens After Deleting a Stash?
Suppose you have:
stash@{0}: Login work stash@{1}: Dashboard work stash@{2}: Navbar work
You delete:
git stash drop stash@{1}
Git removes the Dashboard stash.
The list is then reorganized:
stash@{0}: Login work stash@{1}: Navbar work
This is why you should run git stash list again after deleting stashes instead of assuming the old stash numbers remain the same.
Delete All Stashes ⚠️
If you are completely sure that you no longer need any saved stashes, use:
git stash clear
Example:
Before stash@{0} → Login work 📦 stash@{1} → Dashboard work 📦 stash@{2} → Navbar work 📦 ↓ git stash clear After No stashes remain ❌
This removes all stashes, so be very careful before using it.
drop vs clear ⭐

CommandWhat It Does
git stash drop stash@{1}Deletes one specific stash
git stash drop stash@{0}Deletes the latest stash
git stash clearDeletes all stashes
Safe Workflow Before Deleting

1. Check available stashes ↓ git stash list ↓ 2. Identify the stash you no longer need ↓ 3. Make sure the work is not important ↓ 4. Delete one stash ↓ git stash drop stash@{n} ↓ OR ↓ Delete everything only if sure ↓ git stash clear
Real-World Example
Imagine you stashed unfinished Dashboard work:

Create Dashboard changes ↓ git stash 📦 ↓ Fix urgent Login bug ↓ Return to Dashboard work ↓ git stash apply ↓ Dashboard changes restored ✏️ ↓ Finish Dashboard work ↓ Commit changes ✅ ↓ Stash no longer needed ↓ git stash drop
After your restored work is safely committed and you are sure you do not need the temporary stash anymore, deleting it helps keep your stash list clean.
Important Relationship: Apply, Pop and Drop
These three commands are closely connected:

CommandResult
git stash applyRestore changes and keep stash
git stash popRestore changes and remove stash after successful apply
git stash dropDelete stash without restoring it
Stash exists 📦 Need the changes? ↓ Yes → Apply or Pop No → Drop ---------------------- Want all stashes removed? ↓ git stash clear
Important: Drop Does Not Restore Changes
This is a very important difference.

git stash apply ↓ Restore changes ✏️ Keep stash 📦 ---------------------- git stash pop ↓ Restore changes ✏️ Remove stash after successful apply 📦❌ ---------------------- git stash drop ↓ Do NOT restore changes Remove stash 📦❌
Therefore, do not use git stash drop if you still need the changes stored inside that stash.
Common Mistake 1: Deleting Before Checking
Do not randomly run git stash drop without checking which stash contains which work.
First run:
git stash list
Then identify the correct stash.
Common Mistake 2: Assuming Stash Numbers Never Change
Suppose:
stash@{0}: Login stash@{1}: Dashboard stash@{2}: Navbar
After deleting stash@{1}, the remaining stash positions may change:
stash@{0}: Login stash@{1}: Navbar
So check the list again before performing another deletion.
Common Mistake 3: Using clear Too Quickly ⚠️
The command:
git stash clear
removes every stash. Use it only when you are certain that none of the saved work is needed.
Easy Memory Trick 🧠
APPLY → Restore + Keep 📦 POP → Restore + Remove 📦❌ DROP → Remove only 📦❌ CLEAR → Remove ALL 📦📦📦❌
Complete Stash Workflow

Unfinished work ✏️ ↓ git stash ↓ Saved temporarily 📦 ↓ Later, need the work? Yes ↓ Want to keep stash? Yes → git stash apply No → git stash pop ---------------------- No, don't need the work? ↓ git stash drop stash@{n} Don't need ANY stashes? ↓ git stash clear
Important Commands

CommandPurpose
git stash listView all available stashes
git stash drop stash@{n}Delete one specific stash
git stash drop stash@{0}Delete the latest stash
git stash clearDelete all stashes
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
git stash listSee saved stashes
git stash dropDelete one stash
git stash clearDelete every stash
After dropRemaining stash positions may change
Important warningDrop does not restore the changes
Final Definition: Use git stash drop stash@{n} to permanently delete one specific stash and git stash clear to remove all stashes when you are sure the saved changes are no longer needed.
practice: In this practice, you will create multiple stashes, delete one specific stash, observe how the stash list changes, and finally understand the difference between drop and clear.
Step 1: Check your existing stashes.
git stash list
If you have important existing stashes, do not delete them for this practice. Use a separate practice repository if necessary.
Step 2: Create some temporary changes in a tracked practice file and save the first stash.
git stash push -m "Login practice"
Step 3: Create another temporary change and save it.
git stash push -m "Dashboard practice"
Step 4: Create one more temporary change and save it.
git stash push -m "Navbar practice"
Step 5: View all your practice stashes.
git stash list
Observe the order of the stashes. The newest stash is normally at stash@{0}.
Example stash@{0} → Navbar practice 📦 stash@{1} → Dashboard practice 📦 stash@{2} → Login practice 📦
Step 6: Choose one practice stash that you no longer need and delete it. For example:
git stash drop stash@{1}
Step 7: View the stash list again.
git stash list
Important observation: Confirm that the selected stash was removed. Also notice that the remaining stash positions may have changed.
Step 8: Practice deleting one more specific stash only after checking its current position.
git stash list git stash drop stash@{n}
Step 9: Do not run git stash clear on important stashes. Only use it in your practice repository when every remaining practice stash can safely be removed.
Optional Final Step: If all remaining stashes are only practice data and you no longer need them:
git stash clear
Step 10: Verify the result.
git stash list

Create multiple stashes 📦📦📦 ↓ git stash list ↓ Identify one unnecessary stash ↓ git stash drop stash@{n} ↓ git stash list again ↓ Observe updated stash positions ↓ Only if ALL are unnecessary ↓ git stash clear ⚠️

Practice Goal: You should be able to safely inspect stashes with git stash list, delete one specific stash using git stash drop stash@{n}, understand that stash positions can change after deletion, and know that git stash clear removes all stashes.

qna.q: Q1. Which command shows all available stashes?
qna.a: git stash list

qna.q: Q2. Which command deletes one specific stash?
qna.a: git stash drop followed by the stash reference, for example: git stash drop stash@{1}.

qna.q: Q3. Which command deletes all stashes?
qna.a: git stash clear

qna.q: Q4. Does git stash drop restore the changes before deleting the stash?
qna.a: No. git stash drop removes the stash without restoring its changes.

qna.q: Q5. Scenario: You have stash@{0}, stash@{1}, and stash@{2}. You only want to delete stash@{1}. Which command should you use?
qna.a: git stash drop stash@{1}

qna.q: Q6. Why should you run git stash list before deleting a stash?
qna.a: Because you need to identify which stash contains the work you want to delete and avoid accidentally removing important changes.

qna.q: Q7. Can stash numbers change after deleting a stash?
qna.a: Yes. After a stash is deleted, the remaining stashes can be renumbered, so you should check git stash list again.

qna.q: Q8. What is the difference between git stash drop and git stash clear?
qna.a: git stash drop deletes one selected stash, while git stash clear deletes all stashes.

qna.q: Q9. Which is safer when you only want to remove one unnecessary stash: drop or clear?
qna.a: git stash drop is safer because it deletes only the stash you specify.

qna.q: Q10. Complete the sentence: git stash drop removes ______ stash, while git stash clear removes ______ stashes.
qna.a: one specific stash; all

qna.q: Q11. If you still need the changes stored in a stash, should you use git stash drop?
qna.a: No. You should first restore or otherwise safely preserve the changes before deleting the stash.

qna.q: Q12. Put these commands in a safe order: git stash drop, git stash list.
qna.a: First run git stash list to inspect the stashes, then run git stash drop with the correct stash reference.

items.title: What is Git Rebase?
explanation: Simple Meaning
git rebase is a Git command used to move or replay commits from one branch on top of another branch.
In simple words, it takes your branch's commits and places them after the latest commits from another branch.
One-Line Definition: Git rebase moves or reapplies the commits from your current branch on top of another branch, creating a new linear commit history.
Simple Example
Suppose you create a feature branch from main.
main A ─── B \ C ─── D feature
Here:
A → First commit B → Second commit on main C → Your feature commit D → Another feature commit
Later, new commits are added to main:
main A ─── B ─── E ─── F \ C ─── D feature
Your feature branch is now based on the older commit B. You want your feature work to continue from the latest main history.
While you are on the feature branch, you can run:
git rebase main
Git conceptually takes your feature commits C and D and reapplies them after F.
Before Rebase A ─── B ─── E ─── F main \ C ─── D feature ---------------------- After Rebase A ─── B ─── E ─── F ─── C' ─── D' feature
Notice the new commits C' and D'. Git replays the changes and creates new commits on top of the latest main.
Why Are the Commits Shown as C' and D'? ⭐
This is an important concept. Rebase does not simply move the original commits to a different position.
Git creates new versions of those commits with the same changes applied to a new base.
Original History B → C → D Rebase onto F F → C' → D'
Because C' and D' are newly created commits, they have different commit identities from the original C and D.
Simple Real-World Scenario
Imagine you are working on a Dashboard feature.
main ↓ Create feature branch ↓ You work on Dashboard ↓ Other developers add new commits to main ↓ main becomes newer ↓ Your feature branch is based on older history
You can update your branch history by rebasing it onto the latest main.
Before main → New updates available feature → Your work based on old main ↓ git rebase main ↓ After Latest main → Your feature commits
Basic Rebase Workflow
Suppose you want to rebase your feature-login branch onto main.
Step 1: Switch to your feature branch.
git switch feature-login
Step 2: Make sure you have the latest information from main. If you are working with a remote repository, you may first update your local information appropriately.
Step 3: Rebase the current branch onto main.
git rebase main
Conceptually:
Current branch = feature-login ↓ git rebase main ↓ Take feature-login commits ↓ Replay them after latest main commits
Important: Which Branch Should You Be On?
This is very important.
Before running:
git rebase main
You normally switch to the branch whose commits you want to replay.
Example:
main feature-login ← You want to update this branch ↓ Switch to feature-login ↓ git rebase main
So:
Memory Rule: First switch to the branch you want to update, then rebase it onto the branch whose history you want to use as the new base.
What Does Rebase Actually Do?
Think of the process like this:
Your feature commits C → D ↓ Temporarily separate C D ↓ Move to latest base main → A → B → E → F ↓ Replay commits A → B → E → F → C' → D'
The final result is a cleaner, straight-line history.
Why Use Rebase?
One major reason is to create a linear commit history.
Without rebase, branch history may look like:
A ─── B ─── E ─── F ─── Merge Commit \ / C ─── D ───────────────
After rebasing:
A ─── B ─── E ─── F ─── C' ─── D'
This can make commit history easier to read because the commits appear in one straight line.
Rebase Does Not Mean Merge
Both merge and rebase can integrate changes from one branch with another, but they do it differently.

MergeRebase
Combines branch historiesReplays commits onto a new base
Can create a merge commitCreates new versions of rebased commits
Preserves existing historyRewrites the history of the rebased commits
History can show branchesOften produces a linear history
You will learn Merge vs Rebase in the next roadmap topic, so for now focus on understanding what rebase does.
Important Concept: Rebase Rewrites History ⭐
Because Git creates new versions of the commits, rebase changes commit history.
Before C → D After rebase C' → D' Same changes may be replayed, but the commits are new.
This is why you need to be careful when rebasing commits that other people are already using.
When Should You Be Careful?
A common safety rule is:
Do not casually rebase shared or public commit history. If other developers already have the original commits, rewriting them can make collaboration more complicated.
For example:
You and Developer A both use the same branch ↓ You rebase old commits ↓ Commit history changes ↓ Developer A still has the old commits ↓ Histories no longer match easily ⚠️
You will study this topic in more detail later: When you should not rebase shared/public history.
What If There Is a Conflict During Rebase?
A conflict can happen if Git cannot automatically replay one of your commits on top of the new base.
Latest main changes + Your feature commit ↓ Git tries to replay changes ↓ Can combine automatically? Yes → Continue rebase ✅ No → Conflict ⚠️
When a conflict occurs, the general process is:
Conflict occurs ↓ Fix the conflicting file ↓ git add file-name ↓ git rebase --continue ↓ Git continues replaying commits
You can also cancel an unfinished rebase and return to the state before the rebase started:
git rebase --abort
For this topic, just understand these commands. Conflict handling during rebase will become easier after you practice basic rebase first.
Important Rebase Commands

CommandPurpose
git rebase mainRebase the current branch onto main
git rebase --continueContinue after resolving a rebase conflict
git rebase --abortCancel the rebase and return to the previous state
Easy Memory Trick 🧠
REBASE = Change the BASE Old base ↓ A → B \ C → D New base ↓ A → B → E → F → C' → D'
Remember: git rebase main means:
Take the commits from my current branch and replay them on top of main.
Complete Visual Example

STEP 1: Create feature branch A → B main \ C feature STEP 2: main gets new commits A → B → D → E main \ C feature STEP 3: Switch to feature A → B → D → E main \ C ← current branch STEP 4: git rebase main A → B → D → E → C' feature
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
RebaseReplay commits onto another branch as the new base
git rebase mainRebase the current branch onto main
ResultYour commits appear after the target branch's commits
Commit historyRebased commits are recreated as new commits
Main benefitCan produce a cleaner linear history
Important warningBe careful when rewriting shared/public history
Conflict commandgit rebase --continue
Cancel commandgit rebase --abort

Final Definition: Git rebase takes commits from your current branch and reapplies them on top of another branch, changing their base and creating new versions of those commits to produce an updated, often linear history.
practice: In this practice, you will create a feature branch, make commits on both main and the feature branch, then use git rebase main to move the feature commits on top of the latest main history.
Step 1: Go to your practice repository and check the current branch.
git branch
Step 2: Make sure your main branch has at least one committed file. For example, create a simple project file and commit it.
Step 3: Create a feature branch and switch to it.
git switch -c feature-rebase
Step 4: Make a change for your feature and commit it.
git add . git commit -m "Add feature work"
Step 5: Make one more feature change and commit it.
git add . git commit -m "Update feature work"
Your feature branch now has its own commits.
Step 6: Switch back to main.
git switch main
Step 7: Make a new change on main and commit it.
git add . git commit -m "Update main branch"
Now the branches have different histories:
main A → B → E \ C → D feature-rebase
Step 8: Switch back to your feature branch.
git switch feature-rebase
Step 9: View the history before rebasing.
git log --oneline --all --graph
Step 10: Rebase your current feature branch onto main.
git rebase main
Step 11: View the history again.
git log --oneline --all --graph
Observe how the feature commits now appear after the latest commit from main.
Before Rebase A → B → E main \ C → D feature ↓ git rebase main After Rebase A → B → E → C' → D' feature
Optional Challenge: Compare the commit IDs before and after the rebase. Notice that rebased commits can receive new commit IDs because Git recreates them on the new base.
Safety Practice: If you intentionally create a rebase conflict while experimenting, do not panic. Fix the conflict, stage the resolved file, and continue:
git add file-name git rebase --continue
If you want to completely cancel an unfinished rebase experiment:
git rebase --abort

Practice Goal: You should understand that git rebase main takes commits from your current branch and replays them on top of main, producing a history where your feature commits come after the latest main commits.

items.title: Merge vs Rebase
explanation: Simple Meaning
Both git merge and git rebase are used to bring changes from one branch into another.
The main difference is how they combine the history.
One-Line Difference: Merge combines two branch histories, while Rebase takes commits from one branch and replays them on top of another branch.
The Same Starting Situation
Suppose you created a feature branch from main.
A ─── B main \ C ─── D feature
Then new commits are added to main:
A ─── B ─── E ─── F main \ C ─── D feature
Now both branches contain different commits. You want to combine the changes. You can use either Merge or Rebase, depending on the workflow.
Option 1: Merge
Suppose you want to bring the latest main changes into your feature branch.
First switch to the branch you want to receive the changes:
git switch feature
Then merge main:
git merge main
Git combines the histories.
Before Merge A ─── B ─── E ─── F main \ C ─── D feature ↓ git merge main After Merge A ─── B ─── E ─── F \ \ C ─── D ──────── M feature
M represents a merge commit when Git needs to create one. The history shows that two lines of development were joined together.
Option 2: Rebase
Using the same starting situation, switch to the feature branch:
git switch feature
Then run:
git rebase main
Git takes the feature commits C and D and replays their changes after the latest main commit.
Before Rebase A ─── B ─── E ─── F main \ C ─── D feature ↓ git rebase main After Rebase A ─── B ─── E ─── F ─── C' ─── D' feature
The commits are shown as C' and D' because Git recreates the rebased commits on the new base.
Most Important Visual Difference ⭐
Merge preserves the branch structure:
A ─── B ─── E ─── F \ \ C ─── D ──────── M
Rebase creates a linear history:
A ─── B ─── E ─── F ─── C' ─── D'
Easy Memory Trick: Merge brings two histories together. Rebase changes the base and puts your commits after another branch's latest commits.
Merge vs Rebase Comparison ⭐

FeatureMergeRebase
Main ideaCombine historiesReplay commits on a new base
HistoryCan show branchesUsually creates a linear history
Original commitsPreservedRebased commits are recreated
Commit historyDoes not rewrite existing commitsRewrites the rebased commit history
Merge commitMay create oneNormally does not create one for the rebase itself
Shared historyGenerally saferRequires caution
Visual resultBranching history possibleStraight-line history possible
Important: Both Can Handle the Same Goal
Suppose your feature branch needs the latest changes from main.
You can use Merge:
git switch feature git merge main
Or Rebase:
git switch feature git rebase main
Both approaches can update your feature branch with changes from main. The important difference is the resulting commit history.
When to Think About Using Merge
Merge is useful when you want to combine histories without rewriting existing commits.
Two histories exist ↓ Keep both histories as they are ↓ Join them together ↓ MERGE
This is especially easy to reason about in shared branches because the existing commit history is preserved.
When to Think About Using Rebase
Rebase is useful when you want your branch commits to appear after the latest commits from another branch and you want a cleaner linear history.
Feature based on old main ↓ main gets new commits ↓ Move feature work to latest base ↓ Replay feature commits ↓ REBASE
A common use is updating your own feature branch with the latest main history before integrating the feature.
Important Safety Rule ⭐
Do not casually rebase commits that other people are already using.
Why?
Rebase creates new versions of commits.
Original commits C → D ↓ Rebase New commits C' → D' ↓ Old and new commit histories are different
If another developer already has C and D, rewriting those commits can make the shared history more complicated.
Simple rule:

Personal/local branch: Rebase can often be useful.
Shared/public branch: Be very careful with rebase; do not rewrite history casually.
Example: Working Alone
You create your own feature branch:
main → Latest project commits ↓ feature-login → Your personal work
While working, main receives new changes. Before finishing your feature, you may rebase your personal feature commits onto the latest main.
git switch feature-login git rebase main
Conceptually:
Latest main ↓ Your feature commits replayed after it ↓ Linear feature history
Example: Team Collaboration
Suppose multiple developers are already using a shared branch.
Shared branch ├── Developer A ├── Developer B └── You
If you rewrite the branch history using rebase, the other developers may still have references to the old commits.
Shared history ↓ You rewrite commits with rebase ⚠️ ↓ Other developers still have old history ↓ Synchronization becomes more complicated
This is why merge is often easier and safer for preserving shared history.
Conflict Handling: Merge vs Rebase
Both merge and rebase can produce conflicts when Git cannot automatically combine changes.
During a merge:
Conflict ↓ Fix file ↓ git add file-name ↓ Complete the merge
During a rebase:
Conflict ↓ Fix file ↓ git add file-name ↓ git rebase --continue
If you want to cancel an unfinished rebase:
git rebase --abort
Think of It as Two Different Questions
Question 1: Do I want to preserve the existing branch history?
If yes, think about Merge.
Question 2: Do I want to replay my branch commits after the latest commits from another branch?
If yes, think about Rebase.
Want to JOIN histories? ↓ MERGE ---------------------- Want to CHANGE the base of commits? ↓ REBASE
Common Beginner Mistake
Do not think that Rebase is always better because the history looks cleaner.
Do not think that Merge is always worse because it can create a branching history.
They solve similar integration problems in different ways. The correct choice depends on the project's workflow and whether the history is private or shared.
Easy Analogy 🛣️
Imagine two roads.
Merge: Keep both roads and build a junction where they meet.
Road A ──────────┐ ├── Join Road B ──────────┘
Rebase: Move your road's starting point so it continues after the latest part of another road.
Before Main road: A → B → E → F Feature road: C → D After Rebase Main + Feature: A → B → E → F → C' → D'
Command Comparison

GoalMergeRebase
Update current feature with maingit merge maingit rebase main
Current branchBranch receiving the mergeBranch whose commits are replayed
Cancel during operationDepends on merge stategit rebase --abort
Continue after resolved rebase conflictNot applicablegit rebase --continue
Complete Example
Starting situation:
main A → B → E → F \ C → D feature
Using Merge:
git switch feature git merge main
A → B → E → F \ \ C → D ───── M
Using Rebase:
git switch feature git rebase main
A → B → E → F → C' → D'
Quick Summary

ConceptMergeRebase
What happens?Histories are combinedCommits are replayed on a new base
History shapeCan branch and joinUsually linear
Rewrites commits?NoYes, rebased commits are recreated
Shared historyGenerally easier and saferUse caution
Cleaner historyNot always linearOften linear
Main commandgit merge branch-namegit rebase branch-name

Final Definition: Merge combines the histories of two branches while preserving existing commits, whereas Rebase takes commits from the current branch and recreates them on top of another branch, often producing a cleaner linear history but rewriting the rebased commits.
practice: In this practice, you will create the same branching situation and try both merge and rebase. The goal is to visually understand the difference in commit history.
Step 1: Use a separate practice repository so you can experiment safely.
Step 2: Start from main and make sure you have an initial commit.

Step 3: Create a feature branch.

Step 4: Make two commits on the feature branch.

Step 5: Switch back to main.

git add . git commit -m "Update main part 1" # Optional second change git add . git commit -m "Update main part 2"
Step 7: View the diverged history.
git log --oneline --all --graph
You should conceptually see something like: A → B → E → F main \ C → D feature-test
Merge Practice: Switch to your feature branch and merge main.
git switch feature-test git merge main
Step 8: View the history.
git log --oneline --all --graph
Observe how Git combines the histories. Depending on the exact history, Git may create a merge commit.

Important: For the Rebase practice, do not try to rebase the already-merged branch and expect the original comparison. Create a fresh practice branch from the same earlier situation, or recreate the practice repository.
Rebase Practice: Recreate the situation where main and your feature branch have separate commits. Then switch to the feature branch.
git switch feature-test
Step 9: Rebase the feature branch onto main.
git rebase main
Step 10: View the history again.
git log --oneline --all --graph
Compare the results MERGE main commits + feature commits ↓ Histories join ---------------------- REBASE main commits ↓ feature commits replayed after main ↓ More linear history
Step 11: Write down the main observation from your practice:
Expected understanding:
Merge → Combines histories while preserving the existing commits. Rebase → Replays feature commits after the latest commits from the target branch.
Optional Challenge: Record the commit IDs of your feature commits before rebasing. After the rebase, compare the history and observe that the rebased commits have been recreated.

Practice Goal: You should be able to look at a Git history graph and explain why Merge can create a branch-and-join history, while Rebase replays commits after a new base and can create a linear history.

qna.a: Merge combines two branch histories, while Rebase takes commits from the current branch and replays them on top of another branch.
