items.title: Basic Rebase
explanation: Simple Meaning
In the previous topics, you learned what Rebase is and the difference between Merge vs Rebase. Now you will learn how to perform a basic rebase step by step.
The basic idea is simple: switch to the branch whose commits you want to replay, then run git rebase branch-name.

Basic Syntax: git rebase branch-name
This takes commits from your current branch and replays them on top of branch-name.
Starting Example
Suppose you have two branches: main and feature-login.
You originally created feature-login from main.
A ─── B main \ C ─── D feature-login
Here:
A → Initial project commit B → Existing main commit C → Add login page D → Add login validation
Later, new work is added to main:
A ─── B ─── E ─── F main \ C ─── D feature-login
Now feature-login was created from the older commit B, while main has progressed to F.
Goal of the Rebase
You want the feature commits to be based on the latest version of main.
Current situation main → A → B → E → F feature-login → A → B → C → D Goal main → A → B → E → F feature-login → A → B → E → F → C' → D'
To achieve this, Git replays your feature commits after the latest commit in main.
Step 1: Check Your Current Branch ⭐
Before rebasing, always check which branch you are currently on.
git branch
Example output:
main * feature-login
The * means you are currently on feature-login.
This is important because git rebase main affects the current branch.
Memory Rule: The branch you are currently on is the branch whose commits Git will replay.
Step 2: Switch to the Branch You Want to Rebase
If you are not already on feature-login, switch to it:
git switch feature-login
Now:
Current branch ↓ feature-login
This means the commits from feature-login are the commits that may be replayed.
Step 3: Run the Rebase Command
Now run:
git rebase main
Git reads this conceptually as:
Current branch: feature-login ↓ Take commits from feature-login ↓ Use main as the new base ↓ Replay feature commits after latest main
What Happens Internally?
Before the rebase:
A ─── B ─── E ─── F main \ C ─── D feature-login
Git identifies the commits that exist on feature-login but are not part of main.
Feature-only commits C → D
Then Git uses the latest main commit as the new base:
A → B → E → F ↑ New base
Finally, Git replays the feature changes:
A → B → E → F → C' → D' feature-login
The commits are shown as C' and D' because rebasing recreates those commits on a different base.
Step 4: Check the Result
After rebasing, check the history:
git log --oneline --all --graph
Before rebase, the graph may conceptually look like:
* E main * B | * D feature-login | * C |/ * A
After rebase, the graph becomes more linear:
* D' feature-login * C' * F main * E * B * A
Important: Rebase Changes Only the Current Branch
Suppose you run this while on feature-login:
git rebase main
The feature-login branch is rebased onto main.
main A → B → E → F feature-login before A → B → C → D feature-login after A → B → E → F → C' → D'
Git does not move the main branch forward during this operation. Your current branch is the branch being changed.
General Basic Rebase Pattern ⭐
You can remember basic rebase using this pattern:
1. Check branch ↓ git branch 2. Switch to branch you want to update ↓ git switch feature-name 3. Rebase onto another branch ↓ git rebase main 4. Check history ↓ git log --oneline --all --graph
Another Example
Suppose you have a branch called feature-payment and want to rebase it onto develop.
First switch to the feature branch:
git switch feature-payment
Then run:
git rebase develop
Conceptually:
Take commits from: feature-payment ↓ Replay them on top of: develop
Important Pattern: git rebase X means take commits from my current branch and replay them on top of branch X.
What If Git Finds No New Commits to Rebase?
Sometimes your branch may already contain the latest history from the target branch.
In that situation, there may be nothing new for Git to replay.
main A → B → C \ D → E feature If feature is already based on latest main, Git may have little or nothing to change.
What If a Conflict Happens?
Git applies the feature commits one by one on top of the new base. If one of those changes conflicts with the newer changes, Git pauses the rebase.
Replay commit C ↓ Success ✅ ↓ Replay commit D ↓ Conflict ⚠️ ↓ Git pauses
The general process is:
1. Read the conflict ↓ 2. Fix the conflicting file ↓ 3. Stage the resolved file ↓ 4. Continue the rebase
git add file-name git rebase --continue
Git then continues replaying the remaining commits.
Cancel a Rebase
If you start a rebase and decide you want to return to the state before it started, you can abort the rebase:
git rebase --abort
Before rebase ↓ Start rebase ↓ Problem or unwanted result ↓ git rebase --abort ↓ Return to pre-rebase state
Basic Rebase vs Interactive Rebase
For this topic, you are learning basic rebase.

Basic RebaseInteractive Rebase
git rebase maingit rebase -i
Move commits onto a new baseEdit the commit sequence and history
Simple branch updateMore advanced history editing
Main focus of this topicNext roadmap topic
Do not confuse these two. First become comfortable with normal git rebase branch-name.
Common Beginner Mistakes ⚠️
Mistake 1: Running rebase from the wrong branch.
Wrong current branch ↓ git rebase main ↓ Wrong branch commits are rebased
Always check:
git branch
Mistake 2: Thinking main is automatically changed.
If you run git rebase main while on a feature branch, Git changes the feature branch's history. It does not automatically add feature commits to main.
Mistake 3: Forgetting that rebased commits are recreated.
Before: C → D After: C' → D'
This matters especially when working with commits that have already been shared with others.
Easy Memory Formula 🧠
CURRENT BRANCH ↓ Take its commits ↓ TARGET BRANCH ↓ Use it as the new base ↓ Replay current branch commits
For example:
git switch feature-login git rebase main
CURRENT = feature-login TARGET = main Result: main history → feature-login commits
Quick Summary

StepCommand / Concept
1Check your current branch using git branch
2Switch to the branch you want to rebase
3Run git rebase target-branch
4Git replays current branch commits on the target branch
5Check history using git log --oneline --all --graph
ConflictFix → git add → git rebase --continue
Cancelgit rebase --abort

Final Definition: A basic rebase is performed by switching to the branch you want to update and running git rebase target-branch. Git then takes commits from the current branch and replays them on top of the target branch's latest commit history.
practice: In this practice, you will perform a complete basic rebase yourself. Use a practice repository so you can experiment safely.
Step 1: Check your current repository status and branches.
git status git branch
Step 2: Make sure your main branch has an initial commit. If your repository already has one, continue.
Step 3: Create a feature branch and switch to it.
git switch -c feature-rebase-practice
Step 4: Create or modify a file for your feature work. For example, add a feature line to a text file, then commit it.
git add . git commit -m "Add feature part 1"
Step 5: Make another change and create a second feature commit.
git add . git commit -m "Add feature part 2"
Your feature branch now has two commits that do not exist on main.
Step 6: Switch back to main.
git switch main
Step 7: Make a different change on main and commit it.
git add . git commit -m "Add main update"
Step 8: Switch back to your feature branch.
git switch feature-rebase-practice
Step 9: View the history before rebasing.
git log --oneline --all --graph
Your history should conceptually look like: main A → B → E \ C → D feature-rebase-practice
Step 10: Confirm that you are currently on feature-rebase-practice.
git branch
You should see * feature-rebase-practice.
Step 11: Run the basic rebase.
git rebase main
Git will take your feature commits and replay them after the latest commit from main.
Step 12: View the history again.
git log --oneline --all --graph
Before A → B → E main \ C → D feature ↓ git rebase main After A → B → E → C' → D' feature
Step 13: Run git status and confirm that the working tree is clean after the successful rebase.
git status

Optional Challenge: Before rebasing, write down the commit IDs for your two feature commits using git log --oneline. After rebasing, compare them and observe that Git has recreated the rebased commits.
Conflict Practice: You can later intentionally modify the same line differently on main and the feature branch to create a rebase conflict. When that happens, practice this sequence:
# Fix the conflict in the file git add file-name git rebase --continue
If you want to cancel an unfinished rebase experiment:
git rebase --abort
Practice Goal: After this practice, you should confidently know the basic pattern: switch to the branch you want to update → run git rebase target-branch → check the new history.

qna.q: Q6. What command can you use to switch to a feature branch before rebasing?
qna.a: git switch feature-name

qna.q: Q7. What happens to feature commits C and D after they are rebased onto a newer main?
qna.a: Git replays their changes on the new base and recreates them as new commits, conceptually shown as C' and D'.

qna.q: Q8. What command helps you view the complete branch graph?
qna.a: git log --oneline --all --graph

qna.q: Q9. What is the general sequence when a rebase conflict occurs?
qna.a: Fix the conflict, stage the resolved file using git add, and then run git rebase --continue.

qna.q: Q10. What command cancels an unfinished rebase?
qna.a: git rebase --abort

qna.q: Q11. Complete the sentence: git rebase X means take commits from my ______ branch and replay them on top of ______.
qna.a: current; X

qna.q: Q12. Scenario: You are on main, but you want to rebase feature-payment onto develop. What should you do first?
qna.a: First switch to feature-payment using git switch feature-payment. Then run git rebase develop.

qna.q: Q13. What is the main goal of a basic rebase?
qna.a: To change the base of the current branch by replaying its commits on top of another branch's latest history.

qna.q: Q14. What is the key difference between basic rebase and interactive rebase?
qna.a: Basic rebase mainly replays commits onto a new branch base, while interactive rebase allows more advanced editing of commit history such as reordering, squashing, editing, or removing commits.

items.title: Interactive Rebase Basics
explanation: Simple Meaning
In the previous topic, you learned basic rebase:
git rebase main
Basic rebase moves your current branch commits onto a new base.
Interactive rebase gives you more control. It allows you to review and modify a series of commits before Git recreates them.
One-Line Definition: Interactive rebase is a Git feature that lets you review and rewrite a selected series of commits, such as changing their order, combining them, editing them, or removing them.
Basic Syntax ⭐
git rebase -i HEAD~number
For example:
git rebase -i HEAD~3
This opens the last 3 commits for interactive editing.
What Does HEAD Mean?
HEAD represents your current commit.
Older Newer A → B → C → D → E ↑ HEAD
In this example, E is the current commit, so HEAD points to E.
What Does HEAD~3 Mean?
The ~ symbol lets you move backward through commits.
A → B → C → D → E ↑ ↑ HEAD~3 HEAD
Therefore:

ReferenceMeaning
HEADCurrent commit
HEAD~1One commit before HEAD
HEAD~2Two commits before HEAD
HEAD~3Three commits before HEAD
So when you run:
git rebase -i HEAD~3
Git opens the last three commits for you to work with.
Example Commit History
Suppose your branch has these commits:
A → B → C → D → E ↑ ↑ Add login HEAD
Commit history:
A → Initial project B → Add HTML page C → Add login form D → Fix login validation E → Update login button
Now you run:
git rebase -i HEAD~3
Git opens commits C, D, and E in your configured text editor.
Interactive Rebase Screen
You may see something conceptually like this:
pick C Add login form pick D Fix login validation pick E Update login button
Each line represents a commit.
The word pick tells Git what action to perform on that commit.
The Most Important Interactive Rebase Commands ⭐

CommandMeaning
pickKeep the commit
rewordKeep the commit but change its message
editPause and modify the commit
squashCombine with the previous commit
fixupCombine with the previous commit and discard this commit's message
dropRemove the commit
You do not need to memorize every command immediately. Start by understanding pick, reword, squash, and drop.
1. pick — Keep the Commit
pick means keep the commit normally.
pick C Add login form pick D Fix login validation pick E Update login button
Result:
C → D → E All commits are kept.
If you make no changes and save the interactive rebase instructions, Git keeps the selected commits in their existing order.
2. reword — Change a Commit Message
Suppose you made a poor commit message:
pick C Add login form pick D fix pick E Update login button
You want to change fix to a better message.
Change:
pick C Add login form reword D fix pick E Update login button
Git pauses and allows you to edit the message for commit D.
For example, change it to:
Fix login validation
reword: The commit changes are kept, but the commit message is changed.
3. squash — Combine Commits ⭐
Suppose you created three commits while developing one small feature:
C → Add login form D → Fix login typo E → Fix button spacing
You decide that D and E are small fixes that should be combined with C.
Interactive rebase instructions:
pick C Add login form squash D Fix login typo squash E Fix button spacing
Git combines the commits with the previous commit.
Before C → D → E ↓ squash After C'
The new combined commit is shown as C' because Git recreates the history.
Git may then allow you to choose or edit the final commit message.
Important Rule: squash combines a commit with the commit directly above it.
Why Commit Order Matters for Squash
Consider this:
pick C Add login form squash D Fix login typo
This means:
D ↓ Combine with ↓ C
The first selected commit normally remains as the starting commit, and the squash commit is combined into the previous one.
4. fixup — Combine and Discard Message
fixup is similar to squash, but it normally discards the commit message of the fixup commit.
pick C Add login form fixup D Fix typo
Conceptually:
C + D ↓ One combined commit ↓ Use the previous commit's message
This can be useful when a small commit exists only to fix an earlier commit.
5. drop — Remove a Commit
Suppose you have:
pick C Add login form pick D Add temporary debug code pick E Update login button
You decide the debug commit should not exist in the history.
Change pick to drop:
pick C Add login form drop D Add temporary debug code pick E Update login button
Conceptually:
Before C → D → E ↓ drop D After C → E'
Be careful: removing a commit means its changes are removed from the rewritten history.
6. edit — Pause and Modify a Commit
edit tells Git to pause when it reaches that commit.
pick C Add login form edit D Fix login validation pick E Update login button
When Git reaches D, it pauses so you can make changes.
Apply C ↓ Reach D ↓ Git pauses ⏸ ↓ Modify what is needed ↓ Continue rebase

After making the required changes, the exact workflow depends on what you are modifying. Interactive history editing is more advanced, so for now understand the purpose of edit: pause during the rebase to modify that commit.
Reordering Commits
Interactive rebase can also reorder commits by changing the order of the lines.
Original order:
pick C Add HTML structure pick D Add CSS styling pick E Add JavaScript validation
Conceptually:
C → D → E
You could change the line order:
pick C Add HTML structure pick E Add JavaScript validation pick D Add CSS styling
However, be careful. Some commits depend on earlier commits. Reordering dependent commits may cause conflicts or break the code.
Important: Do not reorder commits randomly. First understand what each commit depends on.
Interactive Rebase Workflow ⭐

Check commit history ↓ git log --oneline ↓ Choose how many recent commits to edit ↓ git rebase -i HEAD~number ↓ Git opens commit instructions ↓ Choose actions: pick / reword / squash / fixup / drop ↓ Save and close editor ↓ Git rewrites the selected history
Step-by-Step Example: Reword
First check history:
git log --oneline
Suppose:
abc123 Update button xyz456 fix mno789 Add login form
Open the last three commits:
git rebase -i HEAD~3
Change:
pick mno789 Add login form reword xyz456 fix pick abc123 Update button
Save the file. Git then asks you to edit the selected commit message.
Change:
fix
To something meaningful:
Fix login validation
Result: same commit changes, better commit message.
Step-by-Step Example: Squash
Suppose history is:
C → Add login page D → Fix typo E → Fix button spacing
Run:
git rebase -i HEAD~3
Change the instructions to:
pick C Add login page squash D Fix typo squash E Fix button spacing
Save and close the editor.
Git combines the changes:
Before C → D → E After C'
You now have one commit representing the completed login page work.
What If a Conflict Happens?
Just like a normal rebase, interactive rebase can encounter conflicts.
Git processes commit ↓ Conflict occurs ⚠️ ↓ Git pauses ↓ Fix the conflict ↓ Stage the resolved file ↓ Continue
General commands:
git add file-name git rebase --continue
If you want to cancel the entire rebase:
git rebase --abort
Important Safety Rule ⭐
Interactive rebase rewrites commit history.
Original commits C → D → E ↓ Interactive Rebase Rewritten commits C' → D' → E'
Because commits may be recreated, changed, combined, reordered, or removed, you should be very careful when rewriting commits that have already been shared with other developers.
Beginner Safety Rule: Interactive rebase is safest when practicing on your own local branch or on commits that you know you can safely rewrite. Do not casually rewrite shared/public history.
Basic Rebase vs Interactive Rebase

Basic RebaseInteractive Rebase
git rebase maingit rebase -i HEAD~3
Replay commits onto a new baseReview and modify selected commits
Simple branch history updateHistory editing
Usually fewer choices during executionChoose actions for individual commits
Can encounter conflictsCan also encounter conflicts
Interactive Rebase Command Summary

ActionWhat it Does
pickKeep commit
rewordChange commit message
editPause to modify commit
squashCombine with previous commit
fixupCombine with previous commit and discard this commit message
dropRemove commit
Easy Memory Formula 🧠
git rebase -i HEAD~3 ↓ Open last 3 commits ↓ Choose what to do with each commit ↓ Keep? → pick Rename? → reword Combine? → squash Remove? → drop ↓ Save and close ↓ Git rewrites the history
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
-iInteractive mode
HEADCurrent commit
HEAD~3Select recent history relative to the current commit
pickKeep commit
rewordChange message
squashCombine with previous commit
fixupCombine and discard current commit message
dropRemove commit
ConflictFix → git add → git rebase --continue
Cancelgit rebase --abort

Final Definition: Interactive rebase uses git rebase -i to let you review and rewrite a selected series of commits. You can keep commits, rename their messages, combine them, edit them, reorder them, or remove them before Git recreates the rewritten commit history.
practice: In this practice, use a separate local practice repository. Interactive rebase rewrites history, so it is best to experiment on commits you can safely change.
Step 1: Check your recent commit history.
git log --oneline
Step 2: Make sure you have at least 3 recent practice commits. For example:
Commit 1 → Add login page Commit 2 → Fix login typo Commit 3 → Update login button
Practice A — Reword a Commit Message: Open the last 3 commits in interactive mode.
git rebase -i HEAD~3
You will see instructions similar to:
pick commit1 Add login page pick commit2 fix pick commit3 Update login button
Step 3: Change the commit with the poor message from pick to reword.
pick commit1 Add login page reword commit2 fix pick commit3 Update login button
Step 4: Save and close the editor. When Git asks for the new message, change it to something meaningful, such as:
Fix login validation
Step 5: Check the result.
git log --oneline
Confirm that the commit changes are still present but the message has been improved.
Practice B — Squash Commits: Create a few small commits that logically belong together. For example:
Commit 1 → Add profile page Commit 2 → Fix profile typo Commit 3 → Fix profile spacing
Step 6: Open those commits using interactive rebase.
git rebase -i HEAD~3
Step 7: Change the instructions to:
pick commit1 Add profile page squash commit2 Fix profile typo squash commit3 Fix profile spacing
Step 8: Save and close the editor. Git will combine the commits and may allow you to edit the final commit message.
Step 9: Check the history.
git log --oneline
Before Commit 1 → Commit 2 → Commit 3 ↓ squash After One combined commit
Practice C — Drop a Practice Commit: Create a harmless temporary commit, such as adding a debug line to a practice file.
Step 10: Open the required commits.
git rebase -i HEAD~3
Step 11: Change the unwanted practice commit from pick to drop.
pick commit1 Keep this change drop commit2 Temporary debug change pick commit3 Keep this change
Step 12: Save and close the editor, then check the result.
git log --oneline
Conflict Reminder: If a conflict occurs during your practice, use this general process:
Fix the conflicting file ↓ git add file-name ↓ git rebase --continue
If you want to completely cancel an unfinished interactive rebase:
git rebase --abort
Final Check: After completing the practice, explain these four commands in your own words:

Practice Goal: You should understand that git rebase -i is used to interactively rewrite selected commits. You should be able to safely practice changing a commit message, combining commits, and removing a practice commit.

qna.q: Q1. What is Interactive Rebase?
qna.a: Interactive Rebase is a Git feature that lets you review and rewrite a selected series of commits by choosing actions such as keeping, renaming, combining, editing, reordering, or removing commits.

qna.q: Q2. What does the -i option mean in git rebase -i?
qna.a: It means interactive mode.

qna.q: Q3. What does HEAD represent?
qna.a: HEAD represents the current commit.

qna.q: Q4. What does the command git rebase -i HEAD~3 do?
qna.a: It opens a selected recent series of commits for interactive editing, commonly used to work with the latest three commits.

qna.q: Q5. What does pick mean during an interactive rebase?
qna.a: pick means keep the commit.

qna.q: Q6. What does reword mean?
qna.a: reword keeps the commit changes but allows you to change the commit message.

qna.q: Q7. What does squash do?
qna.a: squash combines a commit with the commit directly before it and allows the resulting commit message to be combined or edited.

qna.q: Q8. What does fixup do?
qna.a: fixup combines the commit with the previous commit while normally discarding the fixup commit's message.

qna.q: Q9. What does drop do?
qna.a: drop removes the selected commit from the rewritten history.

qna.q: Q10. Scenario: You have a commit message called fix, but the code changes are correct. Which interactive command should you use to improve only the message?
qna.a: Use reword.

qna.q: Q11. Scenario: You have one main feature commit followed by two tiny typo fixes. Which command can combine the fixes with the previous feature commit?
qna.a: Use squash for the small commits.

qna.q: Q12. Why does commit order matter when using squash?
qna.a: Because squash combines the selected commit with the commit directly before it in the interactive rebase list.

qna.q: Q13. Can interactive rebase reorder commits?
qna.a: Yes. The commit order can be changed by reordering the lines, but you must be careful because commits may depend on earlier commits.

qna.q: Q14. What should you do if a conflict occurs during an interactive rebase?
qna.a: Fix the conflict, stage the resolved file using git add, and run git rebase --continue.

qna.q: Q15. What command cancels an unfinished interactive rebase?
qna.a: git rebase --abort

qna.q: Q16. Why should you be careful when using interactive rebase on shared history?
qna.a: Because interactive rebase rewrites commits. Other developers may already have the original commit history, which can make collaboration and synchronization more complicated.

qna.q: Q17. What is the main difference between Basic Rebase and Interactive Rebase?
qna.a: Basic rebase mainly replays commits onto a new base, while interactive rebase lets you choose actions for individual commits and rewrite the selected commit history.

qna.q: Q18. Complete the sentence: Interactive Rebase allows you to keep commits with ______, rename messages with ______, combine commits with ______, and remove commits with ______.
qna.a: pick, reword, squash, drop

items.title: When You Should Not Rebase Shared/Public History
explanation: Simple Meaning
Git rebase rewrites commit history. This is safe when the commits exist only in your own local branch, but it can cause problems when other developers are already using the same commit history.
Simple Rule: Do not rebase commits that other people may already have downloaded, based work on, or shared publicly unless everyone involved understands and agrees with the history rewrite.
Why Can Rebase Cause Problems?
Remember what happens during a rebase. Git does not simply move the old commits. It recreates them.
Before Rebase A → B → C → D ↓ Rebase A → B → C' → D'
Even if C' and D' contain similar changes to C and D, they are new commits with rewritten history.
This means a developer who already has the old commits and another developer who has the rewritten commits can have different histories.
Safe Situation: Your Own Local Branch ✅
Suppose you are working alone on a feature branch.
Only You main A → B → C \ D → E feature-login
The branch exists only on your computer. Nobody else is using commits D and E.
You can safely clean up your local commits:
git rebase -i HEAD~2
For example:
Before D → E ↓ squash After D'
This is generally safe because no other developer depends on the original commits.
Generally Safe: Rebasing commits that exist only on your own local branch.
Dangerous Situation: Shared Branch ⚠️
Now imagine two developers are working with the same branch.
Shared branch: feature-login Developer A → A → B → C → D Developer B → A → B → C → D
Both developers have the same history.
Developer A now runs an interactive rebase and changes the history:
Old history A → B → C → D ↓ Developer A rebases New history A → B → C' → D'
Developer B still has:
Developer A A → B → C' → D' Developer B A → B → C → D
Now the developers have different commit histories. This can make pushing, pulling, merging, and synchronizing more complicated.
Real-World Example
Imagine you and your teammate are working on feature-payment.
Remote branch A → B → C → D You → A → B → C → D Your teammate → A → B → C → D
You decide that commits C and D should be combined.
You run:
git rebase -i HEAD~2
You squash the commits:
Before A → B → C → D ↓ squash After A → B → CD'
Your teammate still has the original commits:
Your history A → B → CD' Teammate history A → B → C → D
The histories no longer match because the original commits were replaced by rewritten commits.
The Main Problem: Other People Depend on the Old History
The problem is not simply that the branch is on GitHub or another remote server. The important question is:
Does another person already have these commits? YES → Be very careful about rebasing ⚠️ NO → Rebasing may be safe depending on your workflow ✅
If someone has already pulled the commits, created new work based on them, or shared them with others, rewriting those commits can create synchronization problems.
Public History Example
Suppose the main branch contains this history:
A → B → C → D ↑ main
Many developers may have already pulled this history.
Developer A has A → B → C → D Developer B has A → B → C → D Developer C has A → B → C → D Developer D has A → B → C → D
If someone rewrites commits C and D, everyone else's history may no longer match the rewritten branch.
Public history before A → B → C → D ↓ Rebase Rewritten history A → B → C' → D'
This is why important shared branches such as main should generally not be casually rebased.
Common Branches You Should Usually Avoid Rebasing

Branch TypeWhy Be Careful?
mainUsually shared by the whole team
masterMay contain important shared history
developOften used by multiple developers
Shared feature branchOther developers may already have its commits
Release branchHistory may be important for deployment and team workflows
The exact branch names can differ between projects. The important concept is whether the history is shared.
Local vs Shared History
LOCAL HISTORY Only you use it ↓ Usually safe to rewrite ──────────────────── SHARED HISTORY Other people use it ↓ Do not casually rewrite it
Example: Local Feature Branch Before Push
Suppose you create a feature branch:
git switch -c feature-login
You make several messy commits:
A → B → C → D → E feature-login C → Add login form D → Fix typo E → Fix spacing
Before sharing the branch with others, you decide to clean the history:
git rebase -i HEAD~3
You combine the small fixes:
Before C → D → E ↓ squash After C'
If the original commits were only your own local commits, this is a good use of interactive rebase.
Important: Pushed Does Not Always Mean Never Rebase
A branch being pushed to a remote repository does not automatically mean rebasing is always forbidden.
For example, if you pushed a personal feature branch but nobody else has started using it, your team workflow may allow you to rebase and update it.
However, after rewriting pushed commits, updating the remote branch may require replacing the remote history. This should be done carefully because it can affect anyone using that branch.
Better Rule: Do not think only "local vs GitHub." Think "private history vs history that other people may depend on."
What Should You Use Instead?
If you need to integrate changes into shared history, a normal merge is often safer because it does not rewrite the existing commits.
Existing shared history A → B → C → D Feature work \ E → F ↓ Merge A → B → C → D ─── M \ / E → F
The existing commits remain part of the history.
Rebase vs Merge for Shared History

RebaseMerge
Can rewrite commitsPreserves existing commits
Creates a cleaner linear historyCombines histories without rewriting them
Good for cleaning personal/local commitsOften safer for shared history
Can cause problems if others use old commitsDoes not replace old commits
Simple Team Workflow
A common concept is:
Your personal feature work ↓ Make commits ↓ Clean your own commits if needed ↓ Rebase may be useful here ✅ ↓ Share with team ↓ Other developers depend on history ↓ Avoid casually rewriting it ⚠️
Before Rebasing, Ask Yourself These Questions ⭐

Question 1 Is this my own branch? Question 2 Am I the only person using these commits? Question 3 Has another developer already pulled this history? Question 4 Has someone created work based on these commits? Question 5 Is this an important shared branch such as main?
If you are unsure whether others depend on the commits, do not casually rewrite the history. Check the team's Git workflow first.
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
MY PRIVATE COMMITS ↓ Rebase can be useful ✅ ──────────────────── OTHER PEOPLE'S SHARED COMMITS ↓ Do not casually rebase ⚠️
Important Warning About Force Push
After rebasing commits that were already pushed, a normal push may be rejected because your local history no longer matches the remote history.

Git has safety mechanisms for this situation. Do not immediately use force-push commands just to make the error disappear. First understand whether rewriting the remote branch is actually safe for your team workflow.
Beginner Safety Rule: If Git rejects a push after you rebased a branch, stop and understand why before using any force-push option.
When Rebase Is Generally Safer

SituationGenerally Safe?
Your own local commitsUsually yes ✅
Private feature branch used only by youUsually yes ✅
Cleaning commits before sharing themUsually yes ✅
Shared branch used by multiple developersBe careful ⚠️
Commits already used by teammatesAvoid casual rebasing ⚠️
Main/public branchUsually avoid ⚠️
Quick Summary

Rebase rewrites history ↓ Old commits may become new commits ↓ C → D becomes C' → D' ↓ If only you use C and D → Usually safe to rebase ↓ If others use C and D → Rewriting can cause problems ↓ Do not casually rebase shared/public history

Final Definition: You should not casually rebase shared or public history because rebase rewrites commits. If other developers already have or depend on the original commits, the rewritten history can cause synchronization and collaboration problems. Rebase is generally safer for commits that only you control.
practice: No destructive commands are required for this topic. The main goal is to understand when history is safe to rewrite and when it may affect other developers.
Scenario 1 — Personal Local Branch: You create a branch that exists only on your computer.
Only you use this branch A → B → C → D feature-login
You notice that commits C and D are messy and want to combine them. Ask yourself: Is rebasing generally safe here?
Answer: Usually yes ✅ Because only you control these commits.
Scenario 2 — Shared Feature Branch: You and another developer both work on the same branch.
You → A → B → C → D Teammate → A → B → C → D
You want to use interactive rebase to combine C and D. Ask yourself: What problem could happen?
You may create: A → B → CD' But your teammate still has: A → B → C → D Different histories ⚠️
Scenario 3 — Main Branch: Imagine many developers have already pulled the same main history.
main A → B → C → D Many developers already have these commits.
Ask yourself: Should you casually run interactive rebase and rewrite these shared commits?
Answer: No ⚠️ Other developers may depend on this history.
Practice Question: For each situation below, decide whether rebasing is generally safer or requires strong caution.

1. Your own unshared local feature branch 2. A branch used by you and one teammate 3. The team's main branch 4. Three commits you created before anyone else received them 5. Commits already pulled and used by multiple developers
Expected Thinking:
Only you depend on commits → Rebase is generally safer ✅ Others depend on commits → Be careful; do not casually rewrite ⚠️
Final Practice Challenge: Explain this sentence in your own words:
"Rebase is dangerous for shared history because it can replace old commits with rewritten commits that other developers do not have."
Practice Goal: Before running rebase in a real project, you should first think: "Who else may already depend on these commits?"

qna.q: Q1. Why should you be careful when rebasing shared history?
qna.a: Because rebase rewrites commits. Other developers may still have the original commits, which can create different histories and synchronization problems.

qna.q: Q2. What happens conceptually to commits C and D after a rebase rewrites them?
qna.a: They may be recreated as new commits, conceptually shown as C' and D'.

qna.q: Q3. Is rebasing your own unshared local feature branch generally safe?
qna.a: Yes. It is generally safer because no other developer depends on the original commit history.

qna.q: Q4. Two developers have the same commits C and D. One developer rebases and creates C' and D'. What problem can occur?
qna.a: The two developers now have different histories: one has C' and D', while the other still has C and D.

qna.q: Q5. What is the most important question to ask before rebasing?
qna.a: Ask whether another person already has these commits or depends on this commit history.

qna.q: Q6. Should you casually rebase a shared main branch?
qna.a: No. Main is usually shared by multiple developers, so rewriting its history can affect many people.

qna.q: Q7. Is the rule simply 'never rebase anything pushed to GitHub'?
qna.a: No. The more important question is whether other people depend on the commits. A personal branch may be pushed but still only be used by you, depending on the team's workflow.

qna.q: Q8. Why can merge be safer than rebase for shared history?
qna.a: Merge integrates histories without replacing the existing commits, while rebase can rewrite commits.

qna.q: Q9. What should you do if you are unsure whether a branch's history is shared?
qna.a: Do not casually rewrite it. Check whether teammates depend on the commits and follow the team's Git workflow.

qna.q: Q10. Scenario: You made five commits on a local branch and nobody else has seen them. You want to combine them into two clean commits. Is interactive rebase generally a suitable option?
qna.a: Yes. Since the commits are only under your control and nobody else depends on the old history, interactive rebase is generally suitable.

qna.q: Q11. Scenario: Your teammate already pulled your feature branch and created new work based on it. Should you casually rewrite the branch history?
qna.a: No. Your teammate may depend on the existing commits, so rewriting them can create collaboration problems.

qna.q: Q12. What should you do if Git rejects your push after rebasing a previously pushed branch?
qna.a: Stop and understand why the histories differ before using any force-push option. Do not use force push just to remove the error without understanding its effect on other developers.

qna.q: Q13. Complete the rule: My private commits → ______. Shared commits used by others → ______.
qna.a: Rebase can be useful; do not casually rewrite them.

qna.q: Q14. What is the key difference between a private history and shared history?
qna.a: Private history is controlled only by you, while shared history may already be downloaded, used, or depended on by other developers.

items.title: Create a GitHub Account
explanation: Simple Meaning
To use GitHub, you first need to create a GitHub account.
Your GitHub account gives you access to GitHub's online platform, where you can create repositories, store projects remotely, collaborate with other developers, and manage your code.
Simple Definition: A GitHub account is your personal account used to access and manage repositories and other features on GitHub.
Before Creating the Account
You should have access to:

• An email address
  • A username you want to use on GitHub
  • A secure password
Your username is important because it can become part of your GitHub profile and repository URLs.
GitHub Account ↓ Username: your-username ↓ GitHub Profile ↓ Repositories ↓ Projects stored on GitHub
Step 1: Open GitHub
Open the official GitHub website in your browser.
:contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}
On the website, choose the option to create or sign up for an account.
Step 2: Enter Your Email Address
Enter an email address that you can access.
Email Address ↓ Used for account verification ↓ Used for important account-related communication
Use an email account that you regularly check and can access when verification is required.
Step 3: Create a Password
Create a strong password for your GitHub account.
Avoid using easily guessed information such as:

• Your name
  • Simple number patterns
  • Common passwords
  • Personal information that others can easily guess
Security Tip: Your GitHub account may eventually contain important projects and access credentials, so use a strong and unique password.
Step 4: Choose a Username ⭐
Choose your GitHub username carefully.
For example, if your username is:
nethaji-dev
Your GitHub profile will be associated with that username.
GitHub ↓ Username nethaji-dev ↓ Profile ↓ Repositories created under your account
Choose a professional username if you plan to use GitHub for your portfolio, projects, job applications, or open-source contributions.
Step 5: Verify Your Account
Follow the verification steps shown during account creation.
GitHub may ask you to verify your email address or complete other account verification steps.
Create Account Details ↓ Verification ↓ Account Created ↓ Sign In to GitHub
After Creating Your Account
Once your account is ready, you will have access to your GitHub profile.
Your GitHub Account ↓ Your Profile ├── Repositories ├── Projects ├── Contributions └── Account Settings
At this stage, you do not need to understand every GitHub feature. Your next topics will explain repositories, README files, remotes, pushing code, pull requests, and collaboration.
GitHub Account vs Git Installation
These are two different things:

GitGitHub Account
Software installed on your computerAccount used to access GitHub
Works locallyUsed to access GitHub online
Can track project historyCan host repositories remotely
Does not require a GitHub accountDoes not replace Git installation
Your Computer ↓ Git Tracks project history locally ──────────────────── GitHub Account ↓ GitHub Stores and manages repositories remotely
Important: Creating a GitHub Account Does Not Automatically Connect Git
Creating your GitHub account is only the first step.
Step 1 → Create GitHub account ↓ Step 2 → Create a GitHub repository ↓ Step 3 → Connect local Git repository ↓ Step 4 → Push your code
You will learn these connection steps later in the roadmap.
Your GitHub Profile
Your profile can eventually show information about your development activity and projects.
GitHub Profile ↓ Username ↓ Public repositories ↓ Projects and contributions ↓ Developer portfolio presence
For beginners, focus first on learning how repositories work. Later, you can improve your profile and add projects.
Good Beginner Setup
After creating your account, make sure you know these basic details:

DetailWhy It Is Important
GitHub usernameIdentifies your account
Email addressUsed for account verification and communication
PasswordProtects your account
ProfileRepresents you on GitHub
RepositoriesWhere your projects can be stored and managed
Security Basics ⭐
As you continue learning GitHub, remember these important rules:

• Never share your account password.
  • Use a strong and unique password.
  • Do not commit passwords or secrets into repositories.
  • Be careful when creating public repositories.
  • Understand whether a repository should be public or private before sharing sensitive project information.
You will learn more about authentication, Personal Access Tokens, SSH keys, secrets, and .gitignore later in this roadmap.
Easy Memory Flow 🧠
GitHub Website ↓ Create Account ↓ Email + Password ↓ Choose Username ↓ Verify Account ↓ GitHub Profile Ready ↓ Create Repositories ↓ Later connect Git and GitHub
Quick Summary

StepAction
1Open GitHub
2Start account creation
3Enter your email address
4Create a secure password
5Choose a username
6Complete account verification
7Access your GitHub profile

Final Definition: Creating a GitHub account gives you access to GitHub's online platform. Your account allows you to create and manage repositories, collaborate with other developers, and store projects remotely.
practice: This topic is mainly a setup task. If you already have a GitHub account, review the details below instead of creating another account.
Step 1: Create your GitHub account using an email address you can access.
Step 2: Choose a username that you would be comfortable using for your developer profile and future projects.
Example thinking: Professional username ↓ Easy to recognize ↓ Suitable for projects ↓ Suitable for a future portfolio
Step 3: Complete the account verification steps required during signup.
Step 4: After signing in, identify these areas in your GitHub account:
Your Profile ↓ Repositories ↓ Account Settings
Step 5: Write down your GitHub username. You will use it frequently when working with repositories and GitHub URLs.
My GitHub Username: ________________________
Final Understanding Check: Answer these questions yourself:
1. What is my GitHub username? 2. Is GitHub the same as Git? 3. Can Git work locally without GitHub? 4. Does creating a GitHub account automatically connect my local Git repository to GitHub?
Practice Goal: You should have a working GitHub account and understand that your GitHub account is used to access GitHub, while Git is the version-control tool installed and used on your computer.

qna.q: Q1. Why do you need a GitHub account?
qna.a: A GitHub account allows you to access GitHub and create, manage, and collaborate on repositories.

qna.q: Q2. Is a GitHub account the same thing as Git?
qna.a: No. Git is a version-control system used on your computer, while a GitHub account is used to access the GitHub online platform.

qna.q: Q3. What information do you generally need when creating a GitHub account?
qna.a: You need access to an email address, a secure password, and a username.

qna.q: Q4. Why is your GitHub username important?
qna.a: It identifies your account and is associated with your GitHub profile and repositories.

qna.q: Q5. Does creating a GitHub account automatically connect your local Git repository to GitHub?
qna.a: No. You must later create or use a remote repository and connect your local Git repository to it.

qna.q: Q6. Can Git work without a GitHub account?
qna.a: Yes. Git can track changes locally on your computer without GitHub.

qna.q: Q7. What is one reason to choose a professional GitHub username?
qna.a: Your GitHub profile and projects may later be used as part of your developer portfolio or shared with employers and other developers.

qna.q: Q8. What should you never share publicly from your GitHub account?
qna.a: You should never share your account password or commit sensitive secrets such as passwords and private API keys into repositories.

qna.q: Q9. What is the next general process after creating a GitHub account?
qna.a: You can create a repository, then later learn how to connect a local Git repository and push your code to GitHub.

qna.q: Q10. Complete the sentence: Git works mainly on my ______, while my GitHub account gives me access to the ______ platform.
qna.a: computer; GitHub

items.title: Create a Repository
explanation: Simple Meaning
A repository, often called a repo, is a place where a project and its related files are stored and managed.
On GitHub, creating a repository gives you an online location for your project.
Your Project ↓ Files + Folders + Project History ↓ Repository ↓ Stored and managed on GitHub
Simple Definition: Creating a repository means creating a project space where you can store and manage your project's files and Git history.
Example
Suppose you are creating a website called my-portfolio.
my-portfolio │ ├── index.html ├── style.css ├── script.js └── images/
You can create a GitHub repository named:
my-portfolio
The repository can become the remote location for managing this project on GitHub.
Step 1: Sign In to GitHub
First, sign in to your GitHub account.
After signing in, go to the area where you can create a new repository.
Step 2: Start Creating a New Repository
Choose the option to create a New repository.
GitHub Account ↓ Repositories ↓ New Repository ↓ Enter Repository Details
You will then configure the basic information for your repository.
Step 3: Choose the Repository Owner
The repository owner determines which account or organization owns the repository.
For your personal project, select your own GitHub account.
Repository Owner Your GitHub Account ↓ You manage the repository
Step 4: Enter the Repository Name ⭐
Give your repository a meaningful name.
Examples:
my-portfolio python-practice sql-learning weather-app
A good repository name should help you understand what the project contains.

Repository NameGood?Reason
python-practiceYesClearly describes the project
portfolio-websiteYesEasy to understand
project123Less clearDoes not explain the project
test-final-new2Less clearName can become confusing
Step 5: Add a Description (Optional)
You can add a short description explaining the purpose of the repository.
For example:
My personal portfolio website built using HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
The description helps other people quickly understand what the project is about.
Repository Name portfolio-website Description My personal portfolio website built using HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
Step 6: Choose Public or Private ⭐
When creating a repository, you must consider its visibility.

Public RepositoryPrivate Repository
Visible to other peopleAccess is restricted
Useful for open-source projects and portfoliosUseful for personal or restricted projects
Others can view the repository according to GitHub access rulesOnly authorized users can access it
Repository Visibility PUBLIC Anyone can generally view the repository OR PRIVATE Access is limited to authorized users
Important: Choose repository visibility carefully. Never place passwords, private keys, API secrets, or other sensitive information in a repository just because it is private.
Step 7: Initialize with a README
During repository creation, you may have an option to add a README file.
A README is commonly used to explain the project.
README.md Project Name ↓ What the project does ↓ How to use it ↓ Other useful information
For example:
# My Portfolio This is my personal portfolio website. Built using HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
We will learn about README files in more detail in a later topic.
Important: Empty Repository vs Repository with README
You may create a repository without adding initial files, or initialize it with files such as a README.
Option 1: Empty Repository GitHub Repository No initial project files created by GitHub ──────────────────── Option 2: Initialize Repository GitHub Repository ↓ README.md created
This difference can become important later when connecting an existing local Git repository to GitHub.
Create Repository
After entering the required details, create the repository.
Choose Owner ↓ Enter Repository Name ↓ Add Description (Optional) ↓ Choose Public or Private ↓ Choose Initial Setup Options ↓ Create Repository
After the Repository Is Created
Your GitHub repository is now ready.
GitHub Repository │ ├── Code / Files ├── Commits ├── Branches ├── README └── Repository Settings
Depending on how you created it, the repository may initially contain a README or other initialization files, or it may be empty.
Local Repository vs GitHub Repository
Remember that creating a repository on GitHub creates a remote repository. It is different from your local Git repository on your computer.
Your Computer Local Repository Project Files + Local Git History ↓ Connect later GitHub Remote Repository Online project repository
For example:
LOCAL COMPUTER my-portfolio/ ├── index.html ├── style.css └── .git/ ↓ ↓ Later connect and push ↓ GITHUB my-portfolio repository ├── index.html └── style.css
Creating the GitHub repository alone does not automatically upload your existing local files.
Important Concept ⭐
There are two common situations when creating a repository:

SituationWhat You Start With
Starting a new projectCreate repository first, then add project files
Existing local projectCreate a remote repository, then connect the existing local Git project

Situation 1 New Project ↓ Create GitHub Repository ↓ Add Project Files ──────────────────── Situation 2 Existing Local Project ↓ Create GitHub Repository ↓ Connect Local Repository ↓ Push Files to GitHub
Repository URL
After creating a repository, GitHub provides information that identifies the remote repository.
You will later use the repository's remote address when connecting Git on your computer with GitHub.
Local Git Repository ↓ Connect to Remote ↓ GitHub Repository Address ↓ Push and Pull Changes
Do not worry about the connection commands yet. The upcoming topics will explain remotes, git remote, git push, and git pull.
Simple Real-World Example
Suppose you have already created this project on your computer:
weather-app/ │ ├── index.html ├── style.css └── script.js
You want to store this project on GitHub.
Step 1 → Create GitHub account ↓ Step 2 → Create weather-app repository ↓ Step 3 → Your remote repository is ready ↓ Step 4 → Connect your local Git project ↓ Step 5 → Push your project to GitHub
Easy Memory Flow 🧠

GitHub Account ↓ Create New Repository ↓ Choose Owner ↓ Enter Repository Name ↓ Add Description (Optional) ↓ Choose Public or Private ↓ Choose README / Initial Setup ↓ Create Repository ↓ Remote Repository Ready
Quick Summary

StepAction
1Sign in to GitHub
2Create a new repository
3Select the repository owner
4Enter a meaningful repository name
5Add a description if needed
6Choose public or private visibility
7Choose README or other initialization options
8Create the repository
9Later connect and push your local project if required

Final Definition: Creating a repository means creating a project space for storing and managing files. A repository created on GitHub acts as a remote repository that can later be connected to a local Git repository on your computer.
practice: This is a hands-on topic. Create one practice repository so you understand the options available during repository creation.
Step 1: Sign in to your GitHub account and start creating a new repository.
Step 2: Use this practice repository name:
git-practice
Step 3: Add a short description:
Repository for learning and practicing Git.
Step 4: Observe the visibility options and choose the appropriate option for your practice project.
Repository Visibility Public OR Private Understand the difference before continuing.
Step 5: Notice the option for creating a README file. For this practice, initialize the repository with a README so you can see an initial file in the repository.
Create Repository ↓ Repository Ready ↓ README.md visible ↓ Explore the repository page
Step 6: After creating the repository, identify these areas:
Repository Name ↓ Files ↓ README ↓ Commits ↓ Branches ↓ Repository Settings
Step 7: Think about this scenario:
Your Computer portfolio-website/ ├── index.html └── style.css ↓ GitHub portfolio-website repository
Ask yourself: Did creating the GitHub repository automatically upload the files from your computer?
Answer: No ❌ Creating a remote repository and uploading an existing local project are separate steps.

Practice Goal: You should be able to create a GitHub repository, choose a meaningful name and visibility, understand README initialization, and know that a GitHub repository does not automatically contain your existing local project files.

qna.q: Q1. What is a repository?
qna.a: A repository is a place where a project and its related files are stored and managed.

qna.q: Q2. What does creating a repository on GitHub create?
qna.a: It creates a remote repository where the project can be stored and managed on GitHub.

qna.q: Q3. What is another common name for a repository?
qna.a: Repo.

qna.q: Q4. Why should you choose a meaningful repository name?
qna.a: A meaningful name makes it easier to understand what the project contains.

qna.q: Q5. What is the difference between a public and private repository?
qna.a: A public repository is generally visible to others, while access to a private repository is restricted to authorized users.

qna.q: Q6. What is a README file commonly used for?
qna.a: A README is commonly used to explain the project, such as what it does and how it can be used.

qna.q: Q7. Does creating a GitHub repository automatically upload your existing files from your computer?
qna.a: No. You must later connect the local Git repository and push the project files to the remote repository.

qna.q: Q8. What is the difference between a local repository and a GitHub repository?
qna.a: A local repository exists on your computer, while a GitHub repository is a remote repository hosted on GitHub.

qna.q: Q9. What are the two common situations when creating a GitHub repository?
qna.a: You may create a repository for a completely new project, or create a remote repository for an existing local project and connect them.

qna.q: Q10. Scenario: You have a project containing index.html and style.css on your computer. You create an empty GitHub repository. Are your files automatically available there?
qna.a: No. Creating the GitHub repository does not automatically upload the local files.

qna.q: Q11. What should you be careful not to store in a repository?
qna.a: You should avoid storing sensitive information such as passwords, private keys, and API secrets.

qna.q: Q12. Complete the flow: Local Repository → ______ → Remote GitHub Repository.
qna.a: Connect and push

items.title: Public vs Private Repositories
explanation: Simple Meaning
When creating a repository on GitHub, one important decision is its visibility.
The two main options are:
Repository Visibility Public 🌍 OR Private 🔒
The main difference is who can access and view the repository.
Simple Definition: A public repository is generally visible to everyone, while a private repository is accessible only to you and people you explicitly authorize.
What Is a Public Repository?
A public repository can generally be viewed by anyone on GitHub.
Public Repository 🌍 You create repository ↓ Repository is publicly visible ↓ Other people can view the code and files
For example, suppose you create:
python-learning
If the repository is public, other developers can generally visit the repository and view its contents.
GitHub │ ├── You │ ├── Developer A → Can view ├── Developer B → Can view └── Other visitors → Can view Public Repository
What Is a Private Repository?
A private repository is not generally visible to everyone.
Access is limited to you and other users who are given permission.
Private Repository 🔒 You │ ├── Authorized Developer A → Access ├── Authorized Developer B → Access │ └── Other People → No Access
This is useful when a project should not be openly visible to everyone.
Main Difference ⭐

Public RepositoryPrivate Repository
Generally visible to everyoneAccess is restricted
Useful for sharing projects publiclyUseful for restricted projects
Can help showcase your workUseful when you do not want the project publicly visible
Anyone can generally view the repositoryOnly authorized users can access it
Public Repository Example
Suppose you build a weather application and want to show it in your developer portfolio.
weather-app ├── index.html ├── style.css ├── script.js └── README.md
You may choose a public repository so other people can view your project.
You create weather-app ↓ Choose PUBLIC 🌍 ↓ Repository is visible ↓ Others can view your project
This can be useful for:

• Portfolio projects
  • Open-source projects
  • Learning projects you want to share
  • Code samples
  • Projects intended for public collaboration
Private Repository Example
Suppose you are developing a project that you do not want to share publicly yet.
new-business-project ↓ Work is still in progress ↓ Not ready to share publicly ↓ Choose PRIVATE 🔒
You can work on the repository while keeping access restricted.
This can be useful for:

• Personal projects you do not want to publish
  • Private experiments
  • Projects still under restricted development
  • Team projects that should not be publicly accessible
Important: Public Does Not Mean Anyone Can Directly Change Your Code
A beginner might think:
Public Repository ↓ Everyone can see it ↓ Therefore everyone can edit it? ❌
Being able to view a public repository does not automatically mean someone can directly modify your repository.
GitHub access permissions control who can directly make changes to a repository.
Remember: Public mainly refers to visibility. Permissions determine who is allowed to directly manage or change the repository.
Important: Private Does Not Mean Store Secrets Carelessly ⚠️
A private repository has restricted access, but you should still avoid storing sensitive information directly in your code.
Do not treat a private repository as a safe place to casually commit:

• Passwords
  • Private API keys
  • Access tokens
  • Secret credentials
  • Private keys
Private Repository 🔒 ↓ Restricted access ↓ Still follow security practices ↓ Do not casually commit secrets
You will learn later how tools such as .gitignore and secret-management practices help prevent sensitive files from being committed.
Repository Visibility Is Not the Same as Git
Git works the same basic way on your computer regardless of whether your remote GitHub repository is public or private.
Your Computer Git Repository ├── Working Directory ├── Staging Area └── Commits ↓ Connect to GitHub Public Repository 🌍 OR Private Repository 🔒
The visibility choice affects access to the remote repository, not the basic purpose of Git on your local computer.
Can You Change Repository Visibility Later?
Repository visibility can generally be changed through repository settings when appropriate permissions and account conditions allow it.
However, changing visibility should be done carefully, especially when moving a project from private to public.
Private Repository ↓ Check repository contents carefully ↓ Remove sensitive information if necessary ↓ Change visibility ↓ Public Repository
Important: Before making a repository public, review the files and commit history carefully to ensure you are not exposing information that should remain private.
How to Choose Between Public and Private?
Ask yourself one simple question:
Do I want this project to be visible to everyone? YES → Consider Public 🌍 NO → Consider Private 🔒
Decision Examples

ProjectPossible ChoiceReason
Personal portfolio websitePublicYou may want to showcase your work
Open-source projectPublicOthers can view and potentially contribute
Personal learning projectPublic or PrivateDepends on whether you want to share it
Restricted team projectPrivateAccess can be limited to authorized people
Project not ready to sharePrivateKeep it from being publicly visible
There is no single correct answer for every project. The best choice depends on who should have access to the repository.
Real-World Example
Imagine you have two projects:
Project 1: portfolio-website You want employers and developers to see it ↓ PUBLIC 🌍 ──────────────────── Project 2: company-internal-tool Only authorized team members should access it ↓ PRIVATE 🔒
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
PUBLIC 🌍 "Everyone can generally see it" PRIVATE 🔒 "Only authorized people can access it"
Public vs Private vs Permissions
These concepts are related but different:

ConceptMeaning
PublicRepository is generally visible to everyone
PrivateRepository access is restricted
PermissionsControl what authorized users can do
Visibility ↓ Who can access or see the repository? Permissions ↓ What actions can authorized users perform?
Quick Summary

Create Repository ↓ Choose Visibility ↓ PUBLIC 🌍 Generally visible to everyone Useful for portfolios and open projects OR PRIVATE 🔒 Access is restricted Useful for projects not meant for public access

Final Definition: A public repository is generally visible to everyone, while a private repository restricts access to authorized users. Choose public when you want to share a project openly and private when the project should not be publicly accessible.
practice: This topic is about understanding repository visibility. Review the following scenarios and decide which option is more appropriate.
Scenario 1 — Portfolio Project:
You built a portfolio website. You want recruiters and other developers to view your code. Choose: Public 🌍 or Private 🔒?
Expected Answer: Public is generally a suitable choice because you want to showcase the project.
Scenario 2 — Restricted Team Project:
You are working on a project. Only specific team members should access the repository. Choose: Public 🌍 or Private 🔒?
Expected Answer: Private is generally more suitable because access should be restricted.
Scenario 3 — Python Learning Project:
You are practicing Python. You may want to show your progress publicly, but you are also comfortable keeping it private. Which option is required?
Expected Thinking: Neither option is always required. Choose based on whether you want other people to access and view the project.
Scenario 4 — Repository Contains a Secret:
Your project contains: API_KEY = "secret-value" Should you make the repository private and commit it safely? ❌
Expected Answer: No. You should not casually commit secrets just because a repository is private.
Final Understanding Check:

1. Public → Who can generally view it? 2. Private → Who can access it? 3. Does Public mean everyone can directly edit it? 4. Is it safe to commit passwords because a repository is Private? 5. Which would you choose for your portfolio project?
Practice Goal: You should understand that repository visibility controls access. Public repositories are generally visible to everyone, while private repositories restrict access to authorized users.

qna.q: Q1. What is the main difference between a public and private repository?
qna.a: A public repository is generally visible to everyone, while access to a private repository is restricted to authorized users.

qna.q: Q2. Which repository type is generally suitable for a portfolio project?
qna.a: A public repository is often suitable because it allows other people to view your project and code.

qna.q: Q3. Which repository type is generally suitable when only specific team members should access the project?
qna.a: A private repository is generally more suitable because access can be restricted to authorized users.

qna.q: Q4. Does a public repository mean everyone can directly edit your code?
qna.a: No. Public mainly refers to visibility. Permissions control who is allowed to directly manage or change the repository.

qna.q: Q5. Is a private repository a reason to safely commit passwords and API keys?
qna.a: No. You should still follow security practices and avoid casually committing sensitive information.

qna.q: Q6. Does choosing Public or Private change how Git tracks commits on your local computer?
qna.a: No. Git can track your local project history regardless of whether the remote GitHub repository is public or private.

qna.q: Q7. What question can help you choose between Public and Private?
qna.a: Ask yourself whether you want the project to be visible to everyone or whether access should be restricted.

qna.q: Q8. What should you do before making a private repository public?
qna.a: Review the repository files and history carefully to make sure you are not exposing information that should remain private.

qna.q: Q9. What is the difference between repository visibility and permissions?
qna.a: Visibility controls who can generally access or see the repository, while permissions control what actions authorized users can perform.

qna.q: Q10. Scenario: You built an open-source project and want anyone to view it. Which visibility would generally be appropriate?
qna.a: Public.

qna.q: Q11. Scenario: You are working on a project that is not ready to be shared publicly. Which visibility would generally be appropriate?
qna.a: Private.

qna.q: Q12. Complete the memory rule: Public → ______. Private → ______.
qna.a: Generally visible to everyone; access restricted to authorized users.

items.title: Repository Structure
explanation: Simple Meaning
A repository contains the files and folders related to your project. On GitHub, the repository page organizes these items so you can view and manage the project.
For example, a simple website repository might look like this:
my-website/ │ ├── index.html ├── style.css ├── script.js ├── images/ │ └── logo.png └── README.md
Simple Definition: Repository structure is the organized arrangement of files, folders, branches, commits, and other project-related information inside a repository.
Basic Repository Structure
Let's understand a repository using a simple example:
my-project/ │ ├── README.md ├── index.html ├── css/ │ └── style.css ├── js/ │ └── script.js └── images/ └── logo.png
Each item has a purpose.

ItemPurpose
README.mdProvides information about the project
index.htmlMain HTML file for the website
css/Folder containing CSS files
js/Folder containing JavaScript files
images/Folder containing image files
Files
Files store the actual content of your project.
Examples include:
index.html style.css script.js app.py main.java README.md
Depending on the type of project, a repository can contain many different files.
Repository │ ├── File 1 → Project code ├── File 2 → Project styling ├── File 3 → Project configuration └── File 4 → Project documentation
Folders
Folders help organize related files.
Instead of placing every file in one location:
project/ ├── index.html ├── style.css ├── logo.png ├── banner.png ├── script.js ├── helper.js ├── photo1.png └── photo2.png
You can organize them into folders:
project/ │ ├── index.html ├── css/ │ └── style.css ├── js/ │ ├── script.js │ └── helper.js └── images/ ├── logo.png ├── banner.png ├── photo1.png └── photo2.png
This makes larger projects easier to understand and maintain.
Root Directory ⭐
The top-level location of a repository is commonly called the root directory.
my-project/ ← Root Directory │ ├── README.md ├── index.html ├── src/ │ └── app.js └── images/ └── logo.png
Items directly inside the top-level repository location are at the root level.
In this example:
README.md index.html src/ images/
are located in the root directory.
Nested Folders
A folder can contain another folder. This creates a directory structure.
project/ │ └── src/ │ ├── components/ │ ├── header.js │ └── footer.js │ └── utils/ └── helper.js
Here, components/ and utils/ are inside src/.
README.md ⭐
A common file found in many repositories is README.md.
It is usually used to explain the project.
README.md ↓ What is this project? ↓ What does it do? ↓ How can someone use it? ↓ Other useful project information
For example:
# Weather App A simple weather application. ## Technologies HTML CSS JavaScript
The .md extension means the file uses Markdown formatting.
You will learn more about README files and Markdown in upcoming topics.
Repository Files Are Versioned by Git
When you use Git, files in your project can move through Git's working areas before becoming part of commit history.
Project Files ↓ Working Directory ↓ git add Staging Area ↓ git commit Commit History
After committing changes, Git records a version of the tracked project changes in the repository history.
For example:
Commit 1 Added index.html ↓ Commit 2 Added style.css ↓ Commit 3 Added JavaScript functionality
Repository Structure on Your Computer
A local Git repository contains your project files and a hidden .git folder.
my-project/ │ ├── .git/ ← Git internal data ├── index.html ├── style.css ├── script.js └── README.md
The .git folder stores Git's internal repository information, including data used to manage commits, branches, and history.
You learned about the .git hidden folder earlier. Normally, you should not manually modify its internal files.
Important: .git Is Not Normally Shown on GitHub

The local .git folder contains Git's internal data on your computer. When viewing your project files on GitHub, you normally work with the repository's visible project files and GitHub's interface rather than browsing the local .git folder.
LOCAL COMPUTER my-project/ ├── .git/ ← Hidden Git data ├── index.html └── style.css ──────────────────── GITHUB REPOSITORY my-project ├── index.html └── style.css
Repository Structure Is Different from Repository History
This is an important distinction.

Repository StructureRepository History
Current organization of files and foldersRecord of changes over time
Shows where files are locatedShows what changed and when
Example: src/app.jsExample: Commit added src/app.js
Repository │ ├── Structure │ └── Files + Folders │ └── History └── Commits + Changes over time
Repository Structure Can Change
The structure of a repository is not fixed forever. You can add, remove, rename, or reorganize files and folders as the project develops.
Version 1 project/ └── index.html ↓ Add files Version 2 project/ ├── index.html └── style.css ↓ Organize project Version 3 project/ ├── index.html ├── css/ │ └── style.css └── js/ └── script.js
Git can track these changes when they are added and committed.
Simple Web Project Structure
A beginner web project might use this structure:
portfolio-website/ │ ├── index.html ├── about.html ├── contact.html │ ├── css/ │ └── style.css │ ├── js/ │ └── script.js │ ├── images/ │ └── profile.png │ └── README.md
This structure makes it easier to identify what each file and folder is used for.
Simple Python Project Structure
A small Python project could look like this:
python-project/ │ ├── main.py ├── README.md │ ├── src/ │ └── calculator.py │ └── tests/ └── test_calculator.py
Different programming languages and frameworks may use different project structures.
Important: There is no single folder structure that is correct for every project. The structure depends on the project's language, framework, size, and requirements.
How GitHub Displays a Repository
When you open a repository on GitHub, you can generally see the project's files and folders and navigate through the directory structure.
Repository Page ↓ Root Files and Folders ↓ Open Folder ↓ View Files Inside ↓ Open File ↓ View File Content
This allows you to browse through a project's structure without downloading every file first.
Easy Memory Flow 🧠
Repository ↓ Root Directory ↓ Files + Folders ↓ Organized Project Structure ↓ Git Tracks Changes ↓ Commits Create History
Quick Summary

PartMeaning
RepositoryContains a project and related information
Root DirectoryTop-level location of the repository
FilesContain project content and code
FoldersOrganize related files
Nested FoldersFolders inside other folders
README.mdCommon file used to explain a project
.gitHidden local folder containing Git internal data
CommitsRecord project changes over time

Final Definition: Repository structure is the organized arrangement of files and folders in a project. In a Git repository, Git also manages version history and internal repository data so changes to the project can be tracked over time.
practice: This topic is about understanding how files and folders are organized inside a repository. Use your git-practice repository or another practice repository.
Step 1: Look at the root level of your repository and identify the files and folders located directly inside it.
Repository Root │ ├── File ├── File ├── Folder └── Folder
Step 2: Create or imagine this simple project structure:
my-practice-project/ │ ├── index.html ├── README.md │ ├── css/ │ └── style.css │ ├── js/ │ └── script.js │ └── images/
Step 3: Identify which items are files and which items are folders.
Files: index.html README.md style.css script.js Folders: css/ js/ images/
Step 4: Identify the root directory and one nested file.
Root Directory: my-practice-project/ Nested File Example: css/style.css
Step 5: Think about how the structure changes when a project grows:
Small Project index.html ↓ Project grows Organized Project ├── index.html ├── css/ │ └── style.css ├── js/ │ └── script.js └── images/
Step 6: Answer this important question: Is the current file and folder structure the same thing as Git commit history?
Structure → Where files are organized now History → How the project changed over time They are related but not the same.
Final Understanding Check:

1. What is the root directory? 2. Why are folders useful? 3. What is README.md commonly used for? 4. What is stored in the local .git folder? 5. What is the difference between repository structure and repository history?

Practice Goal: You should be able to read a repository's file and folder structure, identify the root directory, understand nested folders, and distinguish the current project structure from Git commit history.

qna.q: Q1. What is repository structure?
qna.a: Repository structure is the organized arrangement of files and folders inside a project repository.

qna.q: Q2. What is the root directory?
qna.a: The root directory is the top-level location of the repository.

qna.q: Q3. Why are folders used in a repository?
qna.a: Folders organize related files and make the project easier to understand and maintain.

qna.q: Q4. What is a nested folder?
qna.a: A nested folder is a folder located inside another folder.

qna.q: Q5. What is README.md commonly used for?
qna.a: README.md is commonly used to provide information and documentation about a project.

qna.q: Q6. What does the .md extension indicate in README.md?
qna.a: It indicates that the file uses Markdown formatting.

qna.q: Q7. What is the .git folder?
qna.a: The .git folder is a hidden folder in a local Git repository that contains Git's internal repository data.

qna.q: Q8. Should you normally manually edit files inside the .git folder?
qna.a: No. You normally should not manually modify Git's internal files inside the .git folder.

qna.q: Q9. Is repository structure the same as repository history?
qna.a: No. Repository structure shows how files and folders are currently organized, while repository history records changes over time through commits.

qna.q: Q10. Scenario: A file is located at css/style.css. What does this mean?
qna.a: It means the style.css file is located inside the css folder.

qna.q: Q11. Scenario: index.html and README.md are directly inside my-project/. Where are they located?
qna.a: They are located at the root level of the my-project repository.

qna.q: Q12. Complete the flow: Repository → Root Directory → ______ + ______.
qna.a: Files; Folders

items.title: README.md
explanation: Simple Meaning
A README.md file is usually the first document used to explain a repository and its project.
It helps developers and visitors understand what the project is, what it does, and how to use it.
Repository ↓ README.md ↓ Project Information ↓ Visitors understand the project
Simple Definition: README.md is a documentation file used to explain a project and provide important information about it.
Why Is It Called README?
The name README means that it is a file people should read to understand the project.
README ↓ "Read Me" ↓ Read this file to understand the project
It is commonly placed in the root directory of a repository.
my-project/ │ ├── README.md ← Project information ├── index.html ├── style.css └── script.js
What Does the .md Extension Mean? ⭐
The .md extension stands for Markdown.
Markdown is a simple formatting language commonly used to create formatted documentation.
README.md │ ├── README → File name │ └── .md → Markdown format
Markdown allows you to write plain text while also adding simple formatting such as headings, lists, links, code blocks, and tables.
Simple README Example
Suppose your repository contains a weather application.
weather-app/ │ ├── README.md ├── index.html ├── style.css └── script.js
A basic README might contain:
# Weather App A simple application that displays weather information. ## Technologies Used - HTML - CSS - JavaScript
When Markdown is rendered, the content becomes easier to read because headings and lists are formatted.
What Information Can a README Contain?
The content depends on the project. A README does not need to contain every possible section.
Common sections include:
README.md │ ├── Project Name ├── Description ├── Features ├── Technologies Used ├── Installation ├── Usage ├── Project Structure └── Additional Information
For a small project, a short README may be enough. Larger projects may require more detailed documentation.
1. Project Name
Start by clearly identifying the project.
# My Portfolio Website
The # is Markdown syntax used to create a main heading.
2. Project Description ⭐
Briefly explain what the project does.
This is my personal portfolio website created using HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
A visitor should be able to understand the basic purpose of the project quickly.
