Project Name ↓ What is this project? ↓ What does it do?
3. Features
You can list important functionality provided by the project.
## Features - Responsive design - Contact section - Project showcase - Navigation menu
This helps readers quickly understand what the project can do.
4. Technologies Used
List the main technologies used to build the project.
## Technologies Used - HTML - CSS - JavaScript
For other projects, you might use technologies such as Python, Java, C#, SQL, or a framework.
5. Installation
If a project requires setup before it can run, the README can explain the installation steps.
Get Project ↓ Install Requirements ↓ Configure Project ↓ Run Project
For example, a more advanced project might explain which dependencies must be installed.
6. Usage
The README can explain how someone should use the project after it is installed or opened.
For example:
1. Open the application. 2. Enter the required information. 3. Click Submit. 4. View the result.
7. Project Structure
You can also explain how important files and folders are organized.
my-project/ ├── index.html ├── css/ │ └── style.css ├── js/ │ └── script.js └── README.md
This is especially useful when a project contains many folders and files.
README.md in a GitHub Repository
When a README.md file exists in a repository, GitHub commonly displays its formatted content prominently on the repository page.
GitHub Repository ↓ Repository Files ↓ README.md ↓ Formatted Project Information
This makes the README an important entry point for people visiting your project.
README for a Small Project
A beginner project does not need a huge README.
For example:
# Calculator A simple calculator application. ## Technologies Used - HTML - CSS - JavaScript
This is already enough to give visitors a basic understanding of the project.
README for a Larger Project
A larger project may require more detailed information.
README.md │ ├── Project Overview ├── Features ├── Requirements ├── Installation ├── Configuration ├── Usage ├── Project Structure ├── Contributing └── Additional Documentation
The README should contain enough information to help the intended reader understand and work with the project.
README Is Documentation, Not Application Code
This is an important distinction.

Project CodeREADME.md
Contains instructions used by the applicationContains information for people
Example: app.pyExample: README.md
Runs as part of the project when applicableExplains the project
Project │ ├── Application Code │ ├── index.html │ ├── style.css │ └── script.js │ └── Documentation └── README.md
README Can Change Over Time
A README is part of your project and can be updated as the project changes.
Version 1 README: Basic project description ↓ Project grows Version 2 README: Add features and technologies ↓ More changes Version 3 README: Add setup and usage instructions
When you modify and commit the README, Git can track those documentation changes just like other tracked project files.
Good README Writing
A good README should be clear and useful.

Good PracticeReason
Use a clear project nameHelps identify the project
Explain the project purposeHelps visitors understand it quickly
Use headingsMakes information easier to read
Keep information relevantAvoids unnecessary confusion
Update when neededKeeps documentation useful
Common Beginner Mistake ⚠️
Do not create a README only because every repository is expected to have one. The purpose is to provide useful information about the project.
Bad Approach ❌ Create README ↓ Add random information ↓ Does not explain project ──────────────────── Good Approach ✅ Create README ↓ Explain project clearly ↓ Add useful information
README and Repository Initialization
When creating a new GitHub repository, you may choose an option to initialize the repository with a README.
Create New Repository ↓ Initialize with README ↓ README.md is created ↓ Repository has an initial file
This is one reason a newly created GitHub repository may contain a README.md file even before you upload your main project files.
Simple Real-World Example
Suppose another developer opens your repository.
Developer visits repository ↓ Sees project files ↓ Reads README.md ↓ Understands what the project does ↓ Understands how to use or run it
Without documentation, someone may need to inspect many files before understanding the purpose of the project.
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
README.md "Start here to understand the project" README → Read Me .md → Markdown
Quick Summary

PartMeaning
READMEA file intended to help explain a project
.mdMarkdown file extension
LocationCommonly placed in the repository root
PurposeDocuments the project
Common ContentDescription, features, technologies, setup and usage
GitCan track README changes through commits

Final Definition: README.md is a Markdown documentation file used to explain a repository and its project. It commonly contains the project name, description, features, technologies, setup instructions, and other useful information.
practice: This is a hands-on documentation topic. Create or update a README.md file for one of your practice repositories.
Step 1: Choose a simple project, for example:
git-practice
Step 2: Create a file named exactly:
README.md
Step 3: Add a project heading:
# Git Practice
Step 4: Add a short description:
This repository is used for learning and practicing Git and GitHub.
Step 5: Add a technologies section:
## Topics - Git - GitHub - Version Control
Step 6: Your README should now have this basic structure:
README.md │ ├── # Git Practice │ ├── Project Description │ └── ## Topics ├── Git ├── GitHub └── Version Control
Step 7: View the README in your repository and check whether the heading and list are formatted correctly.
Step 8: Make one change to your README, such as adding another topic or improving the description.
README Version 1 Basic Description ↓ Modify README Version 2 Improved Description + More Information ↓ Git can track the change after commit
Final Understanding Check:
1. What does README mean? 2. What does .md mean? 3. Why is README.md useful? 4. Is README.md application code or documentation? 5. Can Git track changes made to README.md?
Practice Goal: You should be able to create a basic README.md file, use simple Markdown headings and lists, and explain the purpose of a project clearly.

qna.q: Q1. What is README.md?
qna.a: README.md is a Markdown documentation file commonly used to explain a project and repository.

qna.q: Q2. What does README mean?
qna.a: It means 'Read Me' and indicates that the file contains information intended to help people understand the project.

qna.q: Q3. What does the .md extension mean?
qna.a: The .md extension indicates that the file uses Markdown formatting.

qna.q: Q4. What is one common location for README.md?
qna.a: It is commonly placed in the root directory of a repository.

qna.q: Q5. What information can a README contain?
qna.a: It can contain the project name, description, features, technologies used, installation instructions, usage instructions, project structure, and other useful information.

qna.q: Q6. Is README.md normally application code?
qna.a: No. README.md is primarily documentation intended to explain the project to people.

qna.q: Q7. Can Git track changes made to README.md?
qna.a: Yes. README.md is a project file, so its changes can be tracked and committed like other tracked files.

qna.q: Q8. Why are headings useful in a README?
qna.a: Headings organize the information and make the README easier to read.

qna.q: Q9. What Markdown symbol is commonly used for a main heading?
qna.a: The # symbol.

qna.q: Q10. Scenario: A visitor opens your repository but does not understand what the project does. Which file should commonly help explain it?
qna.a: README.md.

qna.q: Q11. Why should you update a README when the project changes?
qna.a: Updating it helps keep the project documentation accurate and useful.

qna.q: Q12. Complete the memory rule: README → ______. .md → ______.
qna.a: Read Me; Markdown.

items.title: Markdown Basics
explanation: Simple Meaning
Markdown is a simple way to format text using plain characters.
You can use Markdown to create headings, lists, links, code blocks, tables, and other formatted content without using HTML.
Plain Text ↓ Markdown Symbols ↓ Formatted Content ↓ Easy-to-read Documentation
Simple Definition: Markdown is a lightweight markup language that uses simple text symbols to format content.
Why Learn Markdown? ⭐
Markdown is commonly used when writing README.md files and other project documentation.
GitHub Repository ↓ README.md ↓ Markdown Syntax ↓ Formatted Documentation
For example, you write this:
# My Project
Markdown displays it as a main heading.
Markdown File Extension
Markdown files commonly use the .md extension.
README.md │ ├── README → File name │ └── .md → Markdown
Other examples include:
README.md notes.md documentation.md
1. Headings ⭐
Markdown uses the # symbol to create headings.
# Heading 1 ## Heading 2 ### Heading 3 #### Heading 4
# → Main Heading ## → Second-Level Heading ### → Third-Level Heading #### → Fourth-Level Heading
Example for a README:
# Weather App ## Features ### Current Weather
2. Paragraphs
Normal text without special Markdown symbols becomes a paragraph.
This is a simple weather application. It displays weather information.
For clearer separation between paragraphs, leave an empty line.
This is the first paragraph. This is the second paragraph.
3. Bold Text ⭐
Use two asterisks before and after text to make it bold.
**Important**
This displays as bold text:
**Important** ↓ Important
Example:
This is **very important** information.
4. Italic Text
Use one asterisk before and after text to make it italic.
*Important Note*
*Important Note* ↓ Italic Text
5. Unordered Lists ⭐
Use -, *, or + to create an unordered list.
- HTML - CSS - JavaScript
This creates a bullet list.
For beginners, using - consistently is a simple approach.
## Technologies - HTML - CSS - JavaScript
6. Ordered Lists
Use numbers followed by a period to create an ordered list.
1. Install the project 2. Open the project 3. Run the application
1. First Step 2. Second Step 3. Third Step
Ordered lists are useful when the order of steps matters.
7. Nested Lists
You can create a list inside another list using indentation.
- Frontend - HTML - CSS - JavaScript - Backend - Python - SQL
• Frontend ├── HTML ├── CSS └── JavaScript • Backend ├── Python └── SQL
8. Inline Code ⭐
Use single backticks to highlight a small piece of code or a command.
`git status`
Example:
Run `git status` to check the repository status.
Inline code is useful for commands, file names, variables, and short code examples.
9. Code Blocks ⭐
Use three backticks before and after multiple lines of code.
``` git status git add . git commit -m "Initial commit" ```
Three Backticks ↓ Start Code Block ↓ Write Multiple Lines ↓ Three Backticks ↓ End Code Block
You can also specify a programming language after the opening backticks in supported Markdown renderers.
```python print("Hello") ```
Markdown can create clickable links using this format:
[Link Text](URL)
Example:
[Visit GitHub](https://github.com)
[Text](Address) ↓ ↓ Link Text Destination
The text inside square brackets is what the reader sees. The address inside parentheses is the destination.
11. Images
Markdown image syntax is similar to link syntax but starts with an exclamation mark.
![Image Description](image-address)
! + [Description] + (Image Location) ↓ Displays an Image
The description is useful for explaining what the image represents.
12. Blockquotes
Use the > symbol to create a blockquote.
> This is an important note.
Example:
> Important: Always review changes before committing.
Blockquotes are useful for highlighting notes, quotes, or important information.
13. Horizontal Lines
You can separate sections using three or more hyphens.
---
Section 1 ────────────── Section 2
14. Simple Tables
Markdown can also create tables.
| Command | Purpose | | --- | --- | | git status | Check status | | git log | View history |
This structure creates a table with columns.

CommandPurpose
git statusCheck repository status
git logView commit history
Tables are useful when comparing related information.
Common Markdown Symbols

SyntaxPurpose
# TextMain heading
## TextSecond-level heading
**Text**Bold text
*Text*Italic text
- TextBullet list
1. TextNumbered list
`code`Inline code
Three backticksCode block
[Text](URL)Link
![Text](URL)Image
> TextBlockquote
---Horizontal line
Simple README Example ⭐
Now let's combine multiple Markdown basics into one README.

# Git Practice This repository is used for **learning Git and GitHub**. ## Topics - Git Basics - GitHub Basics - Markdown ## Commands `git status` `git log` ## Learning Steps 1. Learn Git 2. Practice Git commands 3. Create projects
This uses headings, bold text, lists, inline code, and ordered lists together.
Markdown vs HTML
Markdown and HTML are different ways of formatting content.

MarkdownHTML
Simple text-based syntaxUses HTML tags
# Heading<h1>Heading</h1>
**Bold**<strong>Bold</strong>
- Item<li>Item</li>
Markdown Simple symbols ↓ # Heading **Bold** - List ──────────────────── HTML Tags ↓ <h1>Heading</h1> <strong>Bold</strong> <li>List</li>
For README files, Markdown is commonly used because it is easy to write and read.
Common Beginner Mistakes ⚠️
Pay attention to spaces and syntax.
Wrong ❌ #Heading Better ✅ # Heading ──────────────────── Wrong ❌ -HTML Better ✅ - HTML
Small syntax differences can affect how Markdown is displayed.
Markdown Is Plain Text First
One advantage of Markdown is that the original file is still readable as plain text.
Markdown File # My Project - Feature 1 - Feature 2 ↓ Even before rendering, the text is understandable.
Easy Memory Flow 🧠
Markdown ↓ Simple Symbols ↓ # → Headings ** → Bold - → Lists ` → Code []() → Links ↓ Formatted Documentation
Quick Summary

Markdown FeatureBasic Syntax
Heading# Heading
Bold**Text**
Italic*Text*
Bullet List- Item
Numbered List1. Item
Inline Code`code`
Code BlockThree backticks
Link[Text](URL)
Image![Text](URL)
Blockquote> Text
Horizontal Line---
Final Definition: Markdown is a simple text-based formatting language. It uses easy symbols such as #, **, -, and backticks to create formatted documentation such as README.md files.
practice: This is a hands-on topic. Practice the basic Markdown syntax by creating or editing a README.md file.
Step 1: Create these headings:
# My Project ## Features ### Future Improvements
Step 2: Practice bold and italic text:
This is **important** information. This is *additional* information.
Step 3: Create a bullet list:
- Git - GitHub - Markdown
Step 4: Create an ordered list:
1. Learn Markdown 2. Write a README 3. Practice formatting
Step 5: Practice inline code:
Use `git status` to check repository status.
Step 6: Practice a code block:
``` git status git add . git commit -m "Update README" ```
Step 7: Combine the basics into one small README:
README.md │ ├── # Project Name ├── Description with **bold** text ├── ## Features │ └── Bullet List ├── ## Commands │ └── `inline code` └── ## Steps └── Numbered List
Step 8: Write this Markdown yourself and observe how it is displayed:

# Markdown Practice This is my **Markdown practice** project. ## Topics - Headings - Bold Text - Lists - Code ## Git Command Use `git status` to check changes. ## Learning Steps 1. Write Markdown 2. Save the file 3. View the formatted result
Final Understanding Check:
1. What symbol creates a main heading? 2. How do you make text bold? 3. How do you create a bullet list? 4. How do you show inline code? 5. What syntax creates a link? 6. What does .md mean?
Practice Goal: You should be able to write basic Markdown for headings, bold text, italic text, lists, inline code, code blocks, and links, then use these skills to create a readable README.md file.

qna.q: Q1. What is Markdown?
qna.a: Markdown is a lightweight markup language that uses simple text symbols to format content.

qna.q: Q2. What does the .md file extension represent?
qna.a: It represents Markdown.

qna.q: Q3. Which symbol is used to create a main heading?
qna.a: The # symbol.

qna.q: Q4. How do you create a second-level heading?
qna.a: Use two # symbols followed by a space, for example: ## Heading.

qna.q: Q5. How do you make text bold in Markdown?
qna.a: Place the text between two asterisks on each side, for example: **Text**.

qna.q: Q6. How do you create italic text?
qna.a: Place the text between one asterisk on each side, for example: *Text*.

qna.q: Q7. How can you create a bullet list?
qna.a: Use a list marker such as - followed by a space and the list item.

qna.q: Q8. How do you create an ordered list?
qna.a: Use a number followed by a period, for example: 1. First item.

qna.q: Q9. What is inline code used for?
qna.a: It is used to highlight short code, commands, file names, variables, or similar text.

qna.q: Q10. What is used to create inline code?
qna.a: Single backticks around the text, for example: `git status`.

qna.q: Q11. What is the basic syntax for a Markdown link?
qna.a: The basic format is [Link Text](URL).
Heading; Bold text; Bullet list.

items.title: What is .gitignore?
explanation: Simple Meaning
A .gitignore file tells Git which files or folders should normally be ignored and not tracked.
Project Files │ ├── index.html ← Track ├── style.css ← Track ├── app.py ← Track ├── .env ← Ignore └── node_modules/ ← Ignore ↓ .gitignore ↓ Git knows what to ignore
Simple Definition: A .gitignore file contains patterns that tell Git which untracked files and folders it should ignore.
Why Do We Need .gitignore? ⭐
Not every file in a project should be added to Git.
Some files may contain temporary data, generated files, dependencies, local settings, or sensitive information.
Project │ ├── Important Source Code → Track with Git ├── Documentation → Track with Git ├── Temporary Files → Usually Ignore ├── Local Configuration → May Ignore └── Sensitive Files → Do Not Commit
The .gitignore file helps prevent unwanted untracked files from appearing in normal Git workflows.
The File Name Is Exactly .gitignore ⭐
The file name begins with a dot and has no name before the extension.
Correct ✅ .gitignore Wrong ❌ gitignore .gitignore.txt git-ignore
Make sure the file is named exactly .gitignore.
Simple Example
Suppose your project contains these files:
my-project/ │ ├── index.html ├── style.css ├── app.js ├── .env └── temp.log
You want Git to ignore .env and temp.log.
Your .gitignore can contain:
.env temp.log
.gitignore │ ├── .env → Ignore └── temp.log → Ignore
How .gitignore Works
Create File or Folder ↓ Git checks ignore patterns ↓ Matches .gitignore? ↙ ↘ Yes No ↓ ↓ Ignore Can be tracked
If an untracked file matches a pattern in .gitignore, Git normally ignores it.
Ignoring a Specific File
Write the file name on its own line.
secret.txt
This ignores a file named secret.txt when it matches the pattern.
Ignoring Multiple Files
Add each pattern on a separate line.
.env config.local temp.log
.gitignore │ ├── .env ├── config.local └── temp.log
Ignoring a Folder ⭐
To ignore a folder and its contents, you can write the folder name followed by /.
node_modules/ logs/ temp/
Project │ ├── src/ ← Track ├── README.md ← Track ├── node_modules/ ← Ignore ├── logs/ ← Ignore └── temp/ ← Ignore
Ignoring File Types
You can use the * wildcard to match patterns.
For example, to ignore all files ending with .log:
*.log
app.log → Ignore error.log → Ignore debug.log → Ignore index.html → Not matched
Ignoring a Specific File Type Example
Suppose your project creates many temporary log files.
*.log
Git can ignore files matching that pattern, such as:
server.log error.log application.log ↓ *.log pattern ↓ Ignored
Important: .gitignore Does Not Remove Files ⭐
A common beginner misunderstanding is thinking that .gitignore deletes files.
It does not delete anything from your computer.
.gitignore ↓ Does NOT delete files ❌ Does NOT move files ❌ Does NOT encrypt files ❌ Tells Git what to ignore ✅
Important: Already Tracked Files ⚠️
The most important rule is that adding a file to .gitignore does not automatically stop Git from tracking a file that is already tracked.
File created ↓ git add ↓ git commit ↓ File is already tracked ↓ Later add file to .gitignore ↓ Git may continue tracking it
This means .gitignore is mainly useful for files that are not already tracked.
Example: Ignoring an Already Tracked File
Suppose you accidentally committed .env.
Step 1 .env committed ↓ Step 2 Add .env to .gitignore ↓ Result .gitignore alone does not automatically remove it from Git tracking
To stop tracking an already tracked file, you need an additional Git command. You will learn this workflow later.
.gitignore for Sensitive Information ⭐
Some files may contain passwords, API keys, tokens, or other secrets. These should generally not be committed to a public repository.
Sensitive Information │ ├── Passwords ├── API Keys ├── Tokens └── Private Configuration ↓ Avoid committing to repository
For example, a project may use a local .env file:
API_KEY=your-secret-value
You might add the file name to .gitignore:
.env

Important: .gitignore can help prevent accidentally adding new untracked files, but it is not a replacement for properly managing secrets. If sensitive information has already been committed or exposed, simply adding it to .gitignore does not remove it from commit history.
Comments in .gitignore
You can use # to add a comment.
# Environment files .env # Log files *.log # Dependencies node_modules/
Comments help explain why patterns are included.
Simple Project Example
Consider this project:
my-app/ │ ├── index.html ├── style.css ├── script.js ├── .env ├── error.log ├── node_modules/ └── .gitignore
The .gitignore file might contain:
.env *.log node_modules/
Result:
Tracked Project Files ├── index.html ├── style.css ├── script.js └── .gitignore Ignored Patterns ├── .env ├── *.log └── node_modules/
Where Should .gitignore Be Located?
For a project-wide ignore file, .gitignore is commonly placed in the root directory of the repository.
my-project/ ← Repository Root │ ├── .gitignore ← Common location ├── README.md ├── src/ └── tests/
Placing it at the project root makes the repository's ignore rules easier to find and manage.
Git Status and Ignored Files
Suppose you have this:
Project ├── index.html ├── style.css ├── error.log └── .gitignore
And .gitignore contains:
*.log
When you check the normal repository status, error.log is generally ignored because it matches the ignore pattern.
git status ↓ Check working directory ↓ error.log matches *.log ↓ Ignored
.gitignore Is Usually Tracked
The .gitignore file itself is commonly committed to the repository.
This allows other developers working with the repository to use the same project ignore rules.
.gitignore ↓ Contains ignore rules ↓ git add .gitignore ↓ git commit ↓ Shared as part of repository
Common .gitignore Patterns

PatternPurpose
.envIgnore a file named .env
*.logIgnore files ending in .log
logs/Ignore the logs folder
node_modules/Ignore the node_modules folder
# CommentAdd a comment
.gitignore vs Git Tracking

.gitignoreGit Tracking
Contains ignore patternsRecords files that Git is tracking
Helps ignore matching untracked filesTracks changes to tracked files
Does not delete filesDoes not require files to be visible in every folder
Does not automatically untrack committed filesTracked files remain tracked until explicitly removed from tracking
Common Beginner Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ .gitignore deletes files Correct ✅ It only provides ignore rules for Git ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Adding a tracked file to .gitignore automatically untracks it Correct ✅ Already tracked files need an additional step to stop tracking ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Never commit .gitignore Common Practice ✅ Commit .gitignore so project ignore rules can be shared
Easy Memory Flow 🧠
.gitignore ↓ Contains Patterns ↓ Git checks Untracked Files ↓ Matches Pattern? ↙ ↘ Yes No ↓ ↓ Ignore Can be Tracked
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
.gitignoreFile containing Git ignore patterns
Specific File.env
File Type Pattern*.log
Foldernode_modules/
Comment# Comment
Deletes Files?No
Automatically Untracks Existing Files?No
Common LocationRepository root

Final Definition: .gitignore is a file that contains patterns telling Git which untracked files and folders should normally be ignored. It does not delete files and does not automatically stop tracking files that Git is already tracking.
practice: This is a hands-on topic. Use a practice Git repository and create a .gitignore file.
Step 1: Inside your repository, create a file named exactly:
.gitignore
Step 2: Create these practice files and folders:
git-practice/ │ ├── index.html ├── notes.txt ├── error.log ├── temp.log ├── .env └── temp/
Step 3: Add these patterns to your .gitignore file:
*.log .env temp/
Step 4: Understand what each pattern does:

PatternExpected Result
*.logIgnore error.log and temp.log
.envIgnore .env
temp/Ignore the temp folder
Step 5: Run:
git status
Observe which untracked files Git shows and which matching files are ignored.
Step 6: Add and commit only your project files and .gitignore.
git add . git status git commit -m "Add gitignore rules"
Step 7: Remember this important scenario:
File already committed ↓ Add file name to .gitignore ↓ .gitignore alone does NOT automatically stop tracking it
Final Understanding Check:

1. What is .gitignore used for? 2. Does .gitignore delete files? 3. What does *.log match? 4. How do you ignore a folder named temp? 5. Will .gitignore automatically untrack an already committed file? 6. Should .gitignore itself commonly be committed?

Practice Goal: You should be able to create a .gitignore file, ignore specific files, ignore file patterns, ignore folders, and understand the difference between ignored untracked files and files already tracked by Git.

qna.q: Q1. What is .gitignore?
qna.a: .gitignore is a file containing patterns that tell Git which untracked files and folders should normally be ignored.

qna.q: Q2. Does .gitignore delete files from your computer?
qna.a: No. .gitignore does not delete files. It only provides ignore rules for Git.

qna.q: Q3. What is the correct file name?
qna.a: .gitignore

qna.q: Q4. How can you ignore a file named .env?
qna.a: Add .env on a line in the .gitignore file.

qna.q: Q5. What does the pattern *.log do?
qna.a: It matches files ending with the .log extension, such as error.log.

qna.q: Q6. How can you ignore a folder named node_modules?
qna.a: Add node_modules/ to .gitignore.

qna.q: Q7. What symbol can be used to write a comment in .gitignore?
qna.a: The # symbol.

qna.q: Q8. Does adding a file to .gitignore automatically stop Git from tracking a file that is already tracked?
qna.a: No. Adding it to .gitignore does not automatically untrack an already tracked file.

qna.q: Q9. Where is a project-wide .gitignore commonly located?
qna.a: It is commonly located in the root directory of the repository.

qna.q: Q10. Should .gitignore itself commonly be committed?
qna.a: Yes. It is commonly committed so the project's ignore rules can be shared with other developers.

qna.q: Q11. Scenario: .gitignore contains *.log. Will error.log normally be ignored if it is not already tracked?
qna.a: Yes. It matches the *.log pattern.

qna.q: Q12. Complete the rule: .gitignore tells Git what to ______, but it does not ______ files.
qna.a: Ignore; delete.

items.title: License Basics
explanation: Simple Meaning
A license explains the rules for how other people can use, copy, modify, and distribute a project.
You create a project ↓ Add a License ↓ License defines permissions ↓ Others know how they can use the project
Simple Definition: A software license is a document that defines the permissions and conditions for using, copying, modifying, and distributing software or project content.
Why Do Repositories Need a License? ⭐
Making a repository public does not automatically explain what permissions you want to give other people.
A license helps answer important questions such as:
Can someone use my code? ↓ Can they modify it? ↓ Can they share it? ↓ Can they use it in another project? ↓ What conditions must they follow?
Without clear licensing information, other people may not know what permissions they have to use your project.
Simple Example
Suppose you create a useful calculator application and upload it to a public repository.
calculator-project/ │ ├── README.md ├── LICENSE ├── index.html ├── style.css └── script.js
The LICENSE file provides the license terms for the project.
Project Code ↓ LICENSE File ↓ Defines usage permissions and conditions
What Can a License Define?
Different licenses have different terms, but a license may define rules about:

TopicExample Question
UseCan someone use the project?
CopyCan someone copy the code?
ModifyCan someone change the code?
DistributeCan someone share the project?
ConditionsWhat rules must they follow?
Where Is the License File Located?
A license is commonly stored in a file named LICENSE in the root directory of the repository.
my-project/ ← Repository Root │ ├── README.md ├── LICENSE ← License information ├── src/ │ └── app.js └── tests/
Some projects may use names such as LICENSE.txt, but LICENSE is a common convention.
README.md vs LICENSE ⭐
These two files have different purposes.

README.mdLICENSE
Explains the projectDefines license terms
Helps people understand the projectExplains permissions and conditions
May include setup and usage instructionsMay define how the project can be used
Repository │ ├── README.md │ └── What is this project? │ └── LICENSE └── What are the usage permissions and conditions?
Common Open-Source License Types
You may see different licenses in public repositories. Each license has its own terms.
Common License Examples │ ├── MIT License ├── Apache License 2.0 ├── GNU GPL └── BSD Licenses
Do not assume these licenses give exactly the same permissions. Always read the license terms when choosing or using a license.
MIT License
The MIT License is a commonly used open-source license. It generally allows broad use, copying, modification, and distribution, subject to its license terms.
MIT License ↓ Broad permissions ↓ Use Copy Modify Distribute ↓ Follow license conditions
A common condition is preserving the required copyright and license notice.
Apache License 2.0
Apache License 2.0 is another widely used open-source license. It provides permissions subject to its specific terms and conditions.
It also includes provisions related to patents, so you should read the complete license if you need to understand its legal effect.
GNU GPL

GNU GPL licenses are commonly associated with strong copyleft conditions. Their terms can require certain distributed modified or combined works to be provided under GPL-compatible licensing conditions.

Important: License rules can be legally significant. This topic introduces the basic purpose of licenses; always read the actual license text and obtain appropriate legal advice when needed for an important project or business decision.
License Choice Depends on Your Project
There is no single best license for every project.
Choose a License ↓ What permissions do you want to give? ↓ What conditions do you want to apply? ↓ Read the license terms ↓ Choose appropriately
The correct choice depends on your project's goals and the license terms you are willing to apply.
Public Repository Does Not Mean No Rules ⭐
A public repository allows people to view its contents, but visibility and licensing are different concepts.
Public Repository ↓ People can view the project License ↓ Defines legal permissions and conditions for use
Do not assume that public code can be copied, modified, or redistributed in any way simply because the repository is publicly visible.
Can You Use Code from Another Repository?
Before reusing code from another project, check its license and follow the applicable terms.
Want to reuse code? ↓ Check repository license ↓ Read the terms ↓ Understand permissions ↓ Follow required conditions
If the project does not have clear licensing information, do not assume that you automatically have permission to reuse its code.
License File Is Part of the Repository
The LICENSE file is usually committed to the repository like other project files.
Create LICENSE ↓ git add LICENSE ↓ git commit ↓ License becomes part of repository history
This means changes to the license file can also be tracked through Git commits.
Simple Repository Example
my-project/ │ ├── README.md │ └── Explains the project │ ├── LICENSE │ └── Defines license terms │ ├── src/ │ └── Project code │ └── tests/ └── Project tests
Each file has a different purpose.
GitHub Repository Creation

When creating a repository, GitHub may provide an option to add a license template. This can help you start with a recognized license text, but you should still understand the license before selecting it.
Create Repository ↓ Choose License Option ↓ Select License Template ↓ LICENSE File Added ↓ Review and understand terms
Common Beginner Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ Public repository = anyone can use it however they want Correct ✅ Visibility and license permissions are different ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ All open-source licenses have the same rules Correct ✅ Each license has its own terms and conditions ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Copy a license without understanding it Correct ✅ Read and understand the license terms first ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ README and LICENSE do the same thing Correct ✅ README explains the project; LICENSE defines license terms
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
README.md ↓ Explains the Project LICENSE ↓ Explains Permissions and Conditions
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
LicenseDefines permissions and conditions for a project
LICENSECommon file containing license terms
README.mdExplains the project
Public RepositoryAllows public visibility but does not itself define all reuse permissions
MITCommon license with broad permissions subject to its terms
Apache 2.0Common open-source license with its own specific terms
GPLOpen-source license family with copyleft conditions
Final Definition: A software license defines the permissions and conditions for using, copying, modifying, and distributing a project. A repository commonly stores this information in a LICENSE file.
practice: This topic focuses on understanding the purpose of a license. You do not need to memorize the full legal text of different licenses.
Step 1: Look at this repository structure:
my-project/ │ ├── README.md ├── LICENSE ├── index.html └── style.css
Identify the purpose of each important file:

FilePurpose
README.mdExplain the project
LICENSEDefine license terms
index.htmlProject content/code
Step 2: Think about this scenario:
You find useful code in another public repository ↓ Before copying it ↓ Check the LICENSE ↓ Read the applicable terms ↓ Follow required conditions
Step 3: Create a practice file named LICENSE in a test repository, but do not invent legal license text. For a real project, use and review an appropriate recognized license text.
Step 4: Understand the difference:
README.md → What is this project? LICENSE → What permissions and conditions apply?
Step 5: Think about these questions before choosing a license for a future project:
Do I want others to use it? ↓ Can they modify it? ↓ Can they redistribute it? ↓ What conditions should apply? ↓ Read license terms before choosing
Final Understanding Check:

1. What is the purpose of a software license? 2. What is the difference between README.md and LICENSE? 3. Does making a repository public automatically mean there are no licensing rules? 4. Should you check the license before reusing code from another project? 5. Why should you understand a license before choosing it?
Practice Goal: You should understand why repositories use licenses, distinguish a LICENSE file from README.md, and know that different licenses can provide different permissions and conditions.

qna.q: Q1. What is a software license?
qna.a: A software license defines permissions and conditions for using, copying, modifying, and distributing a project.

qna.q: Q2. What is a common file name used to store license terms?
qna.a: LICENSE.

qna.q: Q3. Where is a LICENSE file commonly placed?
qna.a: It is commonly placed in the root directory of the repository.

qna.q: Q4. What is the difference between README.md and LICENSE?
qna.a: README.md explains the project, while LICENSE defines the project's license permissions and conditions.

qna.q: Q5. Does making a repository public automatically define all permissions for reusing its code?
qna.a: No. Public visibility and licensing permissions are different concepts.

qna.q: Q6. Name one common open-source license.
qna.a: Examples include the MIT License, Apache License 2.0, GNU GPL, and BSD licenses.

qna.q: Q7. Do all open-source licenses have exactly the same terms?
qna.a: No. Different licenses have different permissions, conditions, and requirements.

qna.q: Q8. Should you check a project's license before reusing its code?
qna.a: Yes. You should check the applicable license and follow its terms before reusing code.

qna.q: Q9. Can a LICENSE file be tracked by Git?
qna.a: Yes. Like other repository files, it can be added and committed to Git.

qna.q: Q10. Scenario: A repository is public but has no clear license. Should you assume you can freely copy and redistribute all of its code?
qna.a: No. You should not assume you automatically have permission to reuse code without clear licensing terms.

qna.q: Q11. Complete the memory rule: README.md explains the ______, while LICENSE explains ______ and ______.
qna.a: Project; permissions; conditions.

qna.q: Q12. Why should you understand a license before choosing it for your project?
qna.a: Because the license defines important permissions and conditions that can affect how the project may be used and distributed.
